--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to William, Duke of Cleves. Wier is comparing religious disagreements—which he views as manageable—to the far more dangerous social and spiritual "poison" of the belief in witchcraft.</meta>

### EPISTLE

<margin>Romans 14</margin>
*measurement <note>original: "remens," likely continuing "prout cuique uisum fuerit praemetiri" from the previous page</note> it seems to tremble, or according to the weight and quality of the talent given by God; nevertheless, these matters will often not have so much importance that they either touch the soul’s salvation in any way, or even entirely disturb or dissolve friendships.*

<margin>Opinion concerning witches</margin>
*But daily experience teaches how execrable an alienation from God, how close a bond with the demon, how much hatred among neighbors, what quarrelsome factions of neighbors, what feuds of peasants, what dissensions of cities, and how frequent the slaughters of the innocent—with the devil as the tragic author—that most fertile mother of calamities produces: namely, the opinion conceived about the prodigious power of the witches’ <term>maleficium; the supposed use of supernatural power to cause harm</term> (I do not say <term>veneficium; the actual use of poison</term>).*

*And since there are few diseases whose causes the common people, perversely instructed in the Christian religion, do not attribute to the work of witches: scarcely any other order of men is found to whom this entire business of impiety is more deeply known, and upon whom a more just occasion for taking action on this matter falls, than physicians. Their minds are so disturbed and their ears so grated by this kind of disbelief, that nothing rings so loudly among the sick as that biting and false accusation against innocent poor women for an evil supposedly inflicted in this manner.*

<margin>Reason for writing</margin>
*This Camarina <note>A reference to an ancient Sicilian marsh; a classical proverb meaning a dangerous situation that is better left undisturbed, or in this context, a foul mess being stirred up</note>, which for some time did not exhale such a virulent stench—since there was hope it would eventually perish through sound instruction from the Word of God—is now being heavily stirred up again. Thus the virus of contagion now spreads much further and wider to the destruction of many, as the spirit of storms blows horribly upon it...*

<meta>catchword: te,ex-</meta>

<summary>Wier argues that while religious differences are minor, the belief in "maleficium" (magical harm) causes social ruin and the murder of innocents. He asserts that physicians are uniquely positioned to debunk these claims, as they often hear patients falsely accuse innocent women of causing their illnesses.</summary>

<keywords>witchcraft vs. poisoning, maleficium, medical skepticism, social discord, persecution of innocent women, Camarina, religious instruction</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to William, Duke of Cleves. Weyer is describing how the "poison" of belief in witchcraft has spread because those in power—theologians, physicians, and lawyers—have failed to challenge it, leaving the public trapped in a "labyrinth" of superstition.</meta>

->### DEDICATORY<-

I feel more and more daily how much more [this poison] breathes out than ever before. That old deceiver <note>A reference to the Devil</note> observes every opportunity with such vigilance, while those whose duty it was to strike and utterly overthrow his bulwarks with the engines of Gospel doctrine <term>Gospel doctrine; the teachings of the New Testament</term> day and night have sleepily permitted his arts. 

While, therefore, almost all theologians turn a blind eye in silence to this grave impiety; while physicians tolerate the falsehood of opinions regarding the causes of diseases and their ungodly cures; while legal experts here pronounce sentences based on conviction, through a long series of years and tradition—not so much discussed by reason as seized through a certain prejudice without contradiction; while, finally, I hear no one who, pitying mortals, has either opened this whole labyrinth <note>Weyer uses the "labyrinth" as a metaphor for the confusing and illogical nature of witch trials</note> to us or at least applied a hand to healing this fatal wound: it seemed worthwhile to me if I—like a jackdaw among the Muses <note>original Greek: "koloiòs en taîs mousais," a classical proverb for an unlearned or simple person speaking among experts</note>—might at least shake the lethargy from others with my chatter. 

I hoped to provide some sort of opportunity, through a more extensive discourse and whatever small demonstration I can offer, for more deeply examining and discussing this arduous matter, which brings the greatest insult to our Christian religion. 

<margin>A wicked opinion is an indelible stain.</margin> 

Although I was not unaware that the stubbornness of a wicked opinion held without reason is an indelible stain <note>original: "tinctura," literally a dye or tint</note> that cannot be washed away, as is skillfully written by our Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity</note> in these words: *“There is no dye so hard to remove as the passion of self-directed reasoning for wretched dogmas. For it is not possible to persuade those who have been nurtured by them...”* <note>original Greek: "esti de oudemia baphē dyspoios houtōs, hōs to tou auth_ logismou pros ta mochthēra dogmata pathos. ou gar esti metapeisai tous autois syntrophon..."</note>

<sig>a 3</sig>
<meta>The catchword "τας" (tas) is the ending of the Greek word "syntrophontas" (those nurtured by), which continues on the next page.</meta>

<summary>Johann Weyer critiques theologians, doctors, and lawyers for failing to stop the spread of witchcraft superstitions and explains his decision to speak out, despite the difficulty of changing long-held prejudices.</summary>
<keywords>witchcraft, theologians, physicians, lawyers, Galen, religious duty, superstition, social critique</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle to William, Duke of Cleves. Weyer is explaining the difficulty of changing established public opinion and offering a humble justification for his work, noting that he wrote much of it during the Duke's hunting trips at Hambach.</meta>

->### EPISTLE<-

*...wickedness. For he believes that those so educated cannot be brought back to a change of heart <note>original: "resipiscentia," implying a return to one’s right mind</note> or the fruit of truth. It is not so easy to adapt a new thing to the common mind and agreement of men.*

*Yet no one will slander this undertaking of mine as if I—like some arrogant Suffenus <note>Suffenus was a proverbially bad poet mentioned by the Roman poet Catullus; he was famously unaware of his own lack of talent</note>, and far from conscious of my own insignificance—rashly presume to understand or be able to do anything more than others. I know well how meager my mental resources are <note>original: "curta supellex," literally "shortness of household goods," a Roman idiom for a lack of intellectual depth</note>, and no one knows it more surely than I; and this I know: that I know nothing. No one’s judgment is being pre-empted here. Added to this are my daily meditations and constant travels, which certainly snatch away the leisure time that ought to be diligently devoted to such late-night studies <term>lucubrations; scholarly work performed by candlelight</term>. For this reason, during the previous hunts held at Hambach <note>A hunting estate of the Duke of Cleves</note>, while I was serving your Highness and your illustrious and noble offspring by virtue of my office, I devoted myself primarily to this study.*

*Therefore, I not only gladly and honestly acknowledge, but also openly and freely profess, that many others could have, and still can, surpass this "infancy" of mine <note>Weyer refers to his own writing as "infantia," or "speechlessness," a common trope of authorial modesty</note> by many degrees—through a deeper inquiry into the truth, a clearer style, and a more vigorous and evident demonstration—both because of their sharp wit and excellence in learning, and especially because they have more leisure time. But in the meantime, I hope that those fortunate minds will be provoked by my meager writing, so that they might either instruct me more correctly by speaking—which is usually the fruit of such comparisons—or, by remaining silent, [permit] this opinion of mine, which sounds a double octave out of tune <note>original Greek: "δὶς διὰ πασῶν" (dis dia pason); a musical term meaning "completely at odds" or "totally discordant"</note> with the deep-seated religious beliefs of this age...*

<meta>catchword: com-</meta>

<summary>Weyer humbly presents his work to the Duke, admitting his own intellectual limitations while explaining that he composed the text during spare moments while serving the Duke's court at Hambach. He hopes his "meager writing" will provoke more learned men to join the debate on witchcraft.</summary>
<keywords>humility, Hambach, Duke of Cleves, scholarship, public opinion, intellectual resources, hunting</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues Weyer’s dedication to Duke William. He transitions from defending his own qualifications to explaining the multidisciplinary structure of the book and his use of case histories.</meta>

->### DEDICATORY EPISTLE 7<-

*...approve. By this reasoning, I am confident that I have brought back a sufficiently rich interest <note>original: "usuram," referring to the reward or profit from his labor</note> from my labors; nor will I regret the effort expended, if I am called back to the knowledge of truth by sounder doctrine, or at least confirmed in an opinion that is rare and heard by few. <margin>Truth is hidden in the deep.</margin> For indeed, just as Democritus most rightly taught that nature has hidden truth deep in the abyss <note>A reference to the philosopher Democritus's famous saying that truth lies at the bottom of a well</note>, so it is fitting to inquire, investigate, and search for it more vigilantly. Indeed, this is joined with greater fairness than to stubbornly defend an opinion which someone has rashly embraced.*

<margin>The argument of the work. Theological.</margin>
*The argument of this commentary of ours is partly **Theological**, by which the arts and efforts of the devil are revealed through the testimonies of the Sacred Scriptures; and it teaches how they may most safely be countered. <margin>Philosophical.</margin> It is also partly **Philosophical**, while the vain mockeries of Satan and the corrupt imagination of witches <term>sagarum; traditionally wise-women or diviners, here meaning those accused of witchcraft</term> are refuted by natural reasons. <margin>Medical.</margin> Likewise, it is partly **Medical**, where it is demonstrated that illnesses, their causes, and symptoms—which until now have been wrongly attributed to witches <term>Lamyis; refers to "Lamiae," mythical female monsters or witches</term>—arise according to the laws of nature. <margin>Legal.</margin> Finally, it partly regards the principles of **Jurisprudence**, when the punishments of infamous magicians, witches, and poisoners <term>ueneficorum; literally "poison-makers," the legal term for harmful sorcerers</term> are dealt with in a manner different from what has been practiced until now, according to the quality and magnitude of the crime.*

<margin>Why various stories are inserted.</margin>
*Moreover, I have inserted various stories throughout, primarily for this purpose: since so many diverse and multifaceted things are often reported by many regarding this business of Satan, through the comparison of our accounts, their analogy <note>original Greek: αναλογία</note>, and some sort of explanation, one might more quickly [understand the truth] of these actions and demonic delusions <term>præstigiarum; illusions or conjuring tricks used to deceive the senses</term>, and matters*

<sig>a 4</sig> <meta>catchword: many [mul...]</meta>

<summary>Weyer outlines the four pillars of his argument—Theology, Philosophy, Medicine, and Law—while justifying his use of "stories" (case studies) to expose demonic illusions. He argues that what many attribute to witchcraft is actually a result of natural illness or mental delusion.</summary>
<keywords>Democritus, theology, natural philosophy, medical causes of witchcraft, legal punishment, Lamiae, demonic illusions, case histories</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle to Duke William of Cleves. Weyer is finishing his explanation of the multidisciplinary approach (Theological, Philosophical, Medical, and Legal) and begins to address his predecessors and his critique of the infamous witch-hunting manual, the Malleus Maleficarum.</meta>

->### EPISTLE<-

*...I thought that a knowledge and judgment of many things could be reached.*

*However, lest I be judged here to have rashly overstepped the limits of my ability and profession with a stubborn opinion, trusting too much in my own brain, I proposed these paradoxes <note>original Greek: "παράδοξα"; ideas that run contrary to popular expectation or "common sense"</note> of mine to many most learned men—including those from your Highness’s own household, theologians, legal experts, and most excellent colleagues—to be read and examined with this intention: that they might stand by their judgment if they rely on reason, fall if they are proven in error, or be changed if they need addition or correction. For indeed, nothing was ever begun and finished at the same time.*

<margin>The Hammer of Witches.</margin>
*Now truly, if anyone should object that the **Hammer of Witches** <note>original: "Malleus Maleficarum," the 1486 treatise by Kramer and Sprenger that became the standard manual for witch-hunters</note> has already completed this task, once he has read the absurd idiocies—often even impious—heaped up in that book by the theologians Heinrich Institoris and Jacob Sprenger, and compared their opinion with our writing (setting aside all emotion), he will surely understand that I uphold and defend a completely different, indeed contrary, view. For I have no desire to unweave Penelope’s web <note>A classical reference to Penelope from the Odyssey, who unraveled her shroud every night; here it means Weyer does not wish to engage in redundant or futile labor</note> or to do what has already been done. To be sure, Ulrich Molitor, advisor to King Sigismund of Bohemia, said a few things on this matter in his **Dialogues on Witches and Pythonesses** <term>Lamijs & Pithonicis; "Lamiae" were mythical hags, while "Pythonesses" refers to those possessed by a divining spirit</term>; Giovanni Francesco Pico also wrote something about witches <term>strigibus; a term for night-flying witches or owls</term>; likewise Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Sponheim, proposed five questions to Emperor Maximilian; and some have also touched upon this subject in our own language...*

<meta>catchword: some</meta>

<summary>Weyer defends his work as a rigorous, peer-reviewed study and explicitly distances himself from the "absurd and impious" Malleus Maleficarum, citing other historical authors who have touched upon the subject of witchcraft.</summary>

<keywords>Heinrich Institoris, Jacob Sprenger, Malleus Maleficarum, Ulrich Molitor, Giovanni Francesco Pico, Johannes Trithemius, witchcraft, paradoxes, peer review, legal experts</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle to Duke William of Cleves. In the previous section, Weyer dismissed the "Hammer of Witches" as a collection of absurdities and mentioned that other German authors had written on the subject.</meta>

->### DEDICATION<-

...some Germans have written: but with what judgment they did so will become clear by a comparison with our work.

Furthermore, besides many serious reasons which drove me to dedicate these reflections of mine (whatever their worth) to Your Highness, this one especially influenced me: that since I have now been Your Highness's physician for thirteen years, and have often heard various opinions in Your Highness's court regarding the power and incantations of the "witches" <note>original: "Lamiarum"; Weyer uses this specific term for those he believes are mentally ill rather than truly magical</note> now reappearing in your vast territories; yet I am forced to admit, whether I like it or not, that I have heard from almost no one an opinion more certain, more in harmony with my own, or more deeply drawn from the fountains of truth than that which I have several times received from Your Highness's own mouth with these very ears. 

<margin>
The opinion of the Duke of Cleves concerning Witches.
</margin>

Namely, that witches cannot harm anyone through any malicious will, dire curse, or evil eye; but rather, their imagination being corrupted through the hidden tunnels <note>original: "cuniculos"; a metaphor for the subtle, subterranean ways the Devil infiltrates the mind</note> of the demon, and being agitated by melancholy, they convince themselves that whatever evils are actually inflicted by Satan himself, or arise from natural causes through God's hidden plan, were instead committed by them. For when the methods of their actions are brought to the scales <note>meaning to be weighed or judged carefully</note>, and their instruments are observed with more careful investigation, the vanity and falsehood of the matter soon becomes clearer than light to everyone's eyes. 

<margin>
Poisoning.
</margin>

Your Highness learnedly, prudently, and piously concedes that "poisoning" <note>original: "Veneficium"</note> is done harmfully to the destruction of humans and animals only by <term>pharmakeia</term> <note>the Greek term for both poisoning and sorcery, emphasizing the use of physical drugs or "pharmaceuticals"</note> or poisoners, using poison that is either drunk or applied. Hence it happens, that not of many mo...

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle from physician Johann Weyer to Duke William of Cleves. Weyer is praising the Duke’s wisdom and judicial restraint regarding those accused of witchcraft, contrasting his rational approach with the hysteria of others.</meta>

-># EPISTLE<-

...he <note>referring to the Duke</note> should command that punishment be immediately and severely inflicted upon these deluded little old women <note>original: "delusis aniculis"; Weyer consistently uses diminutive or pitying terms for those accused of witchcraft to highlight their vulnerability and mental state</note>. Instead, Your Highness—appointed to this station by God—wishes that after mature deliberation, an exact inquiry be made as to whether poison was actually administered; only then, if the fact is established beyond doubt, should the requirements of the law be satisfied. This quality truly and deservedly adds to your other most noble and innumerable gifts of mind and character, with which you daily adorn and illuminate the "Sparta" you have obtained <note>original: "Spartam... adornas"; a reference to the Greek proverb "Spartam nactus es, hanc exorna," meaning "You have obtained Sparta, now do your duty by her"—a call to manage one's own realm with excellence</note> (according to the aphorism <note>original: "κατὰ τὸ ἀπόφθεγμα"</note> Your Highness is accustomed to celebrate), such that you turn the eyes of both your own people and all your neighbors toward you. 

I shall say nothing here beyond my intended purpose regarding your uncommon devotion to piety; I could bring forward many memorable examples of this, most worthy of imitation, were I not afraid that I might seem to be seeking favor rather than simply reporting the truth. Let this one thing suffice: that you never see the rising sun, nor compose yourself in bed at evening, without first pouring out ardent prayers to God, and through sacred reading, faithfully committing yourself and all those entrusted to Your Highness to His protection. 

I will add nothing of your moderation in drinking, for which reason alone you stand as an admirable example not only to all your numerous subjects, 
<margin>
The character of princes is more powerful than laws.
</margin>
but you also outshine the most illustrious and powerful heroes of your own rank by right. It is no small praise—indeed, you wish it to be a fixed rule—that no one has ever seen Your Highness intoxicated. You uphold the law of King Ahasuerus <margin>Esther 1</margin> <note>A reference to Esther 1:8, where the Persian king decreed that "drinking was according to the law; no one was compelled" to drink more than they wished</note>, by which it is strictly provided that no one should urge a contest of drinking cups. <meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle from physician Johann Weyer to Duke William of Cleves. The previous page ended with Weyer describing the Duke’s personal piety and his commitment to those entrusted to his care.</meta>

->## DEDICATORY EPISTLE<-

...protection, or would even dare to swear an oath. For every person is aware of how Your Highness holds in "more than Vatinian" hatred <note>original: "odio plusquam Vatiniano"; a classical idiom for extreme, irreconcilable hatred, named after the Roman Publius Vatinius</note> all those who do not blush to profane the awesome name of God with their constant swearing. Because of this blasphemy, which makes almost every court ring out horribly, men of the Christian religion rightly grieve and mourn, seeing the open wounds that have arisen from it. 

I say nothing here of your continuous labors in reading the petitions <note>original: "libellorum supplicum"</note> and other writings that flow in daily, and in providing mature responses to them. Who would not deeply admire <note>original: "exosculetur"; literally "to kiss," implying profound respect or devotion</note> this single, incomparable example of a truly fatherly affection toward the flock of subjects committed to your protection? Among these subjects, who has ever heard the disparaging name of "Churls" <note>original: "Carlorum nomen"; likely referring to a derogatory term for commoners or peasants, similar to the English "churls"</note>—which is constantly on the lips of others—being cast at them by Your Highness? Instead, you frequently honor them with the most gentle name of "sons." 

Indeed, everyone knows that nothing is so much the object of Your Highness's zeal and care as to preserve your state <note>original: "rempublicam"</note> in perpetual and absolute tranquility. You have demonstrated this with rare, indeed divine, prudence during these most turbulent recent years, while the din of war raged everywhere around Your Highness's vast territories, yet without shaking them. 

Nor does it merit the least praise—indeed, it should be proclaimed to all posterity—that like a Maecenas <note>A famous Roman patron of the arts; the term became a synonym for a generous supporter of scholars and artists</note> to learned men, you occasionally make a singular selection of talented minds from among those whom you send to foreign regions and renowned [academies] in every discipline...

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory epistle from physician Johann Weyer to Duke William of Cleves. The previous page discussed the Duke's piety, his refusal to use derogatory terms for his subjects, and his preservation of peace in turbulent times.</meta>

-># EPISTLE<-

*You have willed that students be sent to universities at your own expense, that they be supported, and that they successfully complete their course of studies, so that they might one day be an honor and a benefit to Your Highness and the state. By this means, your illustrious retinue—being adorned with men distinguished by learning, prudence, reputation, and the knowledge and experience of affairs—ought not undeservedly be counted among the other most celebrated ornaments of your court. Yet this should seem less surprising because you, being learned yourself, have always pursued scholars with such zeal that you have never ceased, since the time you became prince, to attract and summon them into your most ample household with whatever honors and stipends. <margin>ARGUMENT of the First Book.</margin>
Furthermore, since this entire business is entangled with the <term>delusions (praestigiae): Deceptive tricks or illusions produced by demons to cheat the senses</term> and deceit of demons, so that a path might be paved toward the understanding of those things which will be said in the remaining books, in the First Book is described: what the devil is, what his origin is, what his first deceitful attempts and ruinous progress were—from Eve in the beginnings of things up to these times—and likewise what his power is, and also what he absolutely cannot do: because those limits are fixed by God, beyond which he cannot be carried.

In Roman law and early modern Latin, the word for one who kills by poison and one who kills by magic was the same, reflecting the belief that harmful magic was a form of secret assault.</term>
There follow in order those driven by various torments
*through the demon's cunning, and not without God's permission:*
Then you see by what aids of the lawful art <note>The "lawful art" here refers to medicine, which Weyer champions over exorcism.</note>
*they can be rightly healed, without the power of an incantation.*
Finally, the last section contains what punishment must be set for Magicians, or for Witches,
*or for acts of sorcery.*

---

## JOHANNES EWICH, DO-
### ctor of Medicine.

You who desire to see the demon's origin, his zeal, his powers, and his deceits,
*as if in the middle of the midday light:*
You who desire to know what the power of incantations is, and how much harm is possible,
*if love-potions <note>original: "philtra"</note> prepared in sacred ways are lacking:*
You who desire to know those men miserably driven by various torments,
*and by what art you might be able to relieve them:*
Finally, what punishment for that unspeakable, lawless sect
*should be established, so that you may spare the innocent:*
Read this book, which Johann Weyer <note>original: "Ianus Vuierus"</note> produced with skill,
*judgment, and great diligence.*
Live, excellent work, and raise a well-deserved trophy <note>original: "trophæum"</note>,
*the crowd of Circe’s profane school has been conquered:* <note>In Homer's Odyssey, the sorceress Circe turned men into beasts; Ewich uses her here as a symbol for the "school" of practitioners of magic whom Weyer has intellectually defeated.</note>
Live also, Author, happily through eternal years,
*the fame of your genius shall not be buried.*

# JOHANNES BRACHELIUS, LICENTIATE OF LAWS,
## To the Reader.

When God created the vast scrolls of the immense heaven,
And suspended the lands in the middle of the air,
And adorned the pole with stars and the atmosphere with rain-clouds:
He likewise created for Himself servants, divine
Bodies, to carry His commands through the light breezes,
And to spend their lives far from earthly cares.
From their number the most just Father thrust down one,
As he deserved, from heaven to the Stygian <note>original: "Stygias" — referring to the River Styx in the underworld; here, a classical poetic name for Hell.</note> waves.
There, bound with manacles and hard shackles,
He sits for the punishment of his crimes, and will sit eternally,
Paying for the sorrowful offenses of the sin he committed.
Yet meanwhile, if you happen to care to know
What frauds and what wicked arts he builds
Night and day for the wretched, and what nets he spreads,
Or what he is capable of:
Read this Work, the monuments of the learned WEYER;
From here you will take what you desire, from here you will teach yourself what you wish.
Moreover, [you will learn] what trust should be placed
In magical things, provided that cruel drugs <note>original: "pharmaca" — often referring specifically to poisons or harmful potions.</note> are absent;
Or by what art you will heal those oppressed by sorceries <term>sorceries (ueneficijs): From the Latin "veneficium," which originally meant poisoning. Weyer argues throughout the book that many accused of magic are actually either mentally ill or victims of physical poisoning.</term>,
And what sufficiently worthy punishment the judge
Hangs over the furious race of witches <note>original: "Sagarum" — a term for "wise women" or "fortune tellers," often used pejoratively.</note>, he narrates in a marvelous order.
But why you, memorable WEYER, have undertaken
Such great labors, I cannot yet truly discern.
"Public benefits," you say, "moved me." But who
Cares for public things now, or commonly looks up
To noble hearts and pays deserved honors to their work?
You, however, will console your too-weary mind with this:
That your fame will never die in any age.

<meta>IN</meta>

<summary>A commendatory poem by the legal scholar Johannes Brachelius praising Weyer's work. It frames the study of demons within a Christian cosmological context and highlights the book's value in distinguishing between magic, poisoning, and mental illness.</summary>

## AN ALLUSION IN PRAISE OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS **WILLIAM**, DUKE OF CLEVES, BERG, AND JÜLICH, ETC. <note>original: "CLIVORVM MONTIVM IVLIACIQVE" — These are the three duchies united under Duke William V (1516–1592), Weyer's lifelong patron and a known advocate for religious tolerance.</note>

> **Y**ou also, most august **DUKE OF CLEVES**, future fame shall sing, praised by our song. Under this **LEADER** <note>original: "DVCE" — the Latin word for leader, from which the title "Duke" is derived.</note> virtue receives its due honor; under this **LEADER** we behold a golden age reborn for the world. Under this **LEADER**, as the Muses <note>The Nine Muses of Greek mythology, patrons of the arts and sciences.</note> lead their ranks through the **SLOPES**, the Pierian Muse <note>Another name for the Muses, derived from their birthplace, Pieria.</note> is seen to travel along an **UPHILL** <note>original: "ACCLIVI" — Utenhove is engaging in an "allusio" (wordplay) on the name of the Duchy: the Latin "clivus" means a slope or hill.</note> path. Hence for you—whom virtue leads to the heavens by a **STEEP** <note>original: "CLIVOSO" — continuing the pun on the name "Cleves."</note> path—it was your destiny to be the Duke of **CLEVES**.

-> Your most devoted client, <-
-> Karl Utenhove the Younger <- <note>original: "Car. Vtenhouius F." — A prominent Flemish humanist and poet who was part of Weyer's intellectual circle.</note>

<summary>A short poem of praise for Duke William V of Cleves, using clever Latin wordplay on the Duke's title to celebrate him as a virtuous patron of the arts and sciences.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from praising the patron (Duke William V) to praising the author himself, Johannes Weyer. The poet, Karl Utenhove, continues his "Allusions"—a series of poems built around clever linguistic puns on names. Having previously played on the word "Cleves" (slopes), he now turns his attention to the name "Weyer," linking it phonetically to the Latin "via" (way) and the Greek "bios" (life) to defend Weyer against his intellectual rivals.</meta>

<page-num>26</page-num>

# TO JOHANNES WEYER,
## CHIEF PHYSICIAN <note>original: "Archiatrum" — The senior medical officer to a royal or noble court.</note> TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
### **Duke of Cleves,**
## BY KARL UTENHOVE THE YOUNGER,
### *From Book 1 of Allusions.*
### EPIGRAM.

> *That wandering vagabond, learned* **WEYER**, *seems to me*
> *to stray through the entire heavens and the entire* **WAY**. <note>original: "VIA... ERRARE" — Utenhove begins a complex pun. Weyer’s name was often Latinized as "Wierus" or "Viuarius," which Utenhove links to "Via" (Way/Path). His "straying" opponents are contrasted with Weyer's "Way."</note>
> *He who, lurking under the name of the Paracelsian sect,* <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), whose radical chemical medicine was often at odds with the traditional humanist medicine practiced by Weyer.</note>
> *believed your name was derived from* **ERRING**.
> *Unless it is because you compel those* **WANDERING** *from the right path*
> *to enter the right way (just as you do the Paracelsians).*
> *For no "straying error" gave you your surname,*
> *nor does any "straying error" drive you off course.*
> *The* **WAY** *that leads to the waters of hellish Acheron* <note>In Greek mythology, a river in the underworld; here representing a "broad path" to destruction or ignorance.</note>
> *is not* **WIDER**: *a narrow* **PATH** <note>original: "ITER" — playing on the phonetic similarity between "Weyer" and the Latin "Via" or German "Weg."</note> *gives you your name.*
> *A* **WAY** *is made by* **FORCE** <note>original: "VIA VI" — a Latin pun where "Vi" (by force/strength) sounds like the start of "VVIERVS."</note> *which leads us to the heights of the heavens,*
> *and by an uphill* **WAY** *one rises to the stars.*
> *Proceed now, blessed one, where the* **WAY OF LIFE** *leads,*
> *and by* **FORCE**, **WEYER**, *pave a* **WAY** *for yourself to heaven.*
> *Thus you shall be the Desire of the Latin* **LIFE** *and* **WAY**,
> *and in the Greek tongue,* **WEYER** *shall be the* **LOVE OF LIFE**. <note>original: "ΒΙΟΥ... ΕΡΩΣ" (Biou... Eros) — Utenhove is making a multilingual pun: "Wier-us" sounds like "Bios" (Life) and "Eros" (Love). This reflects the high-humanist fashion of finding deep meaning in the sounds of names.</note>

-> LIFE IS NOTHING WITHOUT THE MUSES AND THE GRACES. <- <note>original Greek: "ΟΥΘΕΝ, ἀτὲρ μυσέων καὶ χαρίτων, ὁ-ΒΙΟΣ." — The Muses represent the arts and sciences, while the Graces represent charm and refinement.</note>

-> *Basel, 1568.* <-

-> **KARL UTENHOVE THE YOUNGER,** <-
-> **of Ghent.** <-

<summary>A commendatory poem by humanist Karl Utenhove using sophisticated Latin and Greek wordplay to defend Johannes Weyer's reputation against Paracelsian critics, framing Weyer's name as a symbol of the "Right Path" and "Love of Life."</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Weyer, Karl Utenhove, Paracelsians, puns, humanist poetry, Basel, medicine, Muses, Duke of Cleves</keywords>

# ON THE DEVIL,
## HIS ORIGIN, EFFORT, AND POWER, Book 1.

->*On the origin of the devil, when he was created, what his essence is, and concerning his fall.*<-
->Chapter 1.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut decorative initial 'D' featuring a seated figure and floral vine motifs.</image-desc>As I am about to explain the deceptions <term>præstigias: illusions, juggling tricks, or any deceptive supernatural appearance</term> and incantations of demons, I shall begin with their primary author, the devil, and with his arts, endeavors, and power. I do this so that once he is understood, and his influence and reputation are clearly perceived, his every work may be more evidently judged. In this way, everyone may be able to look into all his actions with a clear eye of the mind, and hereafter judge them more deeply and with less hindrance.

<margin>The Peripatetics <note>Followers of the philosophy of Aristotle</note> deny the existence of demons.</margin>
<margin>Fables about demons.</margin>
However, having embraced the sacred doctrine of the Christian religion and the confession of an indubitable faith, I utterly reject the opinions of Aristotle and the Peripatetics, who contend that demons do not exist in the nature of things. Likewise, I cannot entirely approve of Plato’s fabricated distinctions, nor can I subscribe to the opinions of Porphyry, Psellus, Proclus, Plotinus, and Iamblichus <note>These were influential Neoplatonist philosophers from late antiquity who integrated magic and spirit hierarchies into their thought</note>. These men indeed wrote copiously about demons, but they recorded many things they neither saw nor knew, as if they were writing a history of a well-known matter.

<margin>Genesis 1</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 1</margin>
Therefore, [I believe that] the almighty God, the architect of the universe, before the construction of this visible world, [created] that incorporeal [host] with its admirable orders of spirits—

<sig>c</sig>
<meta>catchword: —with [completing "ordinibus"]</meta>

<summary>This page introduces a treatise on demonology, establishing the author's intent to examine the devil's power from a Christian perspective while rejecting both Aristotelian skepticism and Neoplatonic mysticism. The author asserts that demons are real entities created by God as incorporeal spirits before the physical world existed.</summary>
<keywords>demonology, Satan, Aristotle, Neoplatonism, creation of angels, spiritual hierarchy, Christian theology</keywords>

<header>On the origin and fall of demons</header>

<margin>
When the angels were created.
Exodus 33.
</margin>
...God established all things for a beautifully adorned ministry. This must be firmly believed based on the sacred history of Moses—the envoy of Divine Majesty and most faithful scribe (with whom the truth of the Sacred Scriptures declares that God spoke face to face, as if with a friend).

<margin>What angels are.</margin>
Indeed, these spirits were all good, just as all things created by the Highest Good are. They were, by nature, intelligent and incorporeal <note>original Greek: ἀσώματοι (*asōmatoi*)</note>. In their essence, they conformed to the divine nature to a certain extent, yet they remained finite. They were created so that God might be recognized and worshiped by them in the manner He Himself willed and prescribed, and so that He, in turn, might share His goodness with them for all eternity. 
<margin>
Dionysius, *On Divine Names*. <note>Dionysius the Areopagite was a Christian theologian and philosopher whose writings on the hierarchy of angels were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>
</margin>
For this reason, He endowed them with excellent intelligence, extraordinary insight, and illustrious notions of His eternal and immovable justice—like rays of light ignited from His own eternal wisdom.

<margin>
The origin of demons.
2 Peter 2.
Epistle of Jude.
Job 4.
Luke 10.
</margin>
But when certain ones among them—on account of the most excellent gifts with which they had been adorned—were carried away by their own will and grew so insolent that they eventually compared themselves to God, they did not preserve their original state but abandoned their own dwelling and sinned. An angry God stripped them of their honors, excluded them from the number of His ministers, repelled them, and drove them headlong. He has kept them in perpetual chains under darkness for the judgment of that great day.

<margin>
Isaiah 14.
Isaiah 27.
Revelation 12.
</margin>
To this event, many writers apply that prophecy of Isaiah concerning the pride and the deep fall of the most arrogant King of Babylon (whom the prophet calls Lucifer <note>The "Light-Bringer" or Morning Star</note>). This is that great dragon cast down to the earth with his angels: the ancient serpent who is called the Devil and Satan, as John says, and the "twisting serpent" of Isaiah. Not only do our theologians and those of the Hebrews teach of this fall, but even the Assyrians, Arabs, Egyptians, and Greeks confirm it in their own doctrines.

<meta>catchword: Phere-</meta>

<summary>This page describes the original state of angels as intelligent, incorporeal beings created to worship God, and details the subsequent rebellion and fall of those who became demons due to pride. The author aligns biblical accounts of the fall of Lucifer and the Dragon with the traditions of various ancient civilizations.</summary>

<header>Book the First.</header>

<margin>Ophin.</margin>
**Pherecydes** <note>A 6th-century BCE Greek thinker often credited with writing one of the first prose theological treatises.</note> describes the fall of demons: and he teaches that **Ophin**—that is, the demonic serpent—was the head and standard-bearer of the rebellious army that fell away from the will of the divine mind. **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical texts were attributed.</note> depicts this same ruin in the *Poimandres*; and **Plutarch**, in his discourse *On Interest*, indicates that the ancient **Empedocles** also knew of their fall, calling the demons "fugitives" <gloss>original Greek: δραπέτας (*drapetas*), meaning runaways or deserters</gloss> falling from heaven.

<margin>Treatise on John, 42.</margin>
Here **Augustine** speaks elegantly: "You ask where the devil came from? Surely from the same place as the other angels. But while the other angels persisted in their obedience, he fell through disobedience and pride—an angel became a devil." Likewise, in *On True Religion*, chapter 13: "Insofar as the devil is an angel, he is not evil; but he is evil insofar as he is perverse by his own will. For by loving himself more than God, he refused to be subject to Him, and he swelled with pride, falling away from the highest essence."

<margin>
Hebrews 1.
Psalms 103, 104.
Unclean and evil spirits.

Ephesians 2. 6.
1 Corinthians.
Zechariah 13.
Matthew 8, 12.
Mark 1, 3.
Luke 8, 9.
Acts 19.
Judges 9.

The human race.
</margin>
Therefore, these spirits—who were once divine, heavenly, pure, radiant, conscious of no malice, and observant of God's will alone—were sent out into ministry for those who would be heirs of salvation. They did not entirely lose their angelic essence, but they most wretchedly corrupted and blackened it, having been deprived of the light of grace. Thus, they are now called—and indeed are—spirits of the air, worldly, obscure, shadowy, and (in a single word) unclean and evil. And although they still possess the light of natural intellect, they endure a punishment for their fall that is infinitely harsher, as the light of divine wisdom has been darkened and obscured for them. They expect a heavier judgment than the human race does for its transgression—even though the human race [has also lost] the rays of supreme wisdom which [were placed] in our first parents...

<header>Concerning the pursuits of demons</header>

<margin>Genesis 1.</margin>

### *Chapter II. Why and how the devil deceived Eve, and first corrupted the world.*

<margin>The devils' incurable hatred toward God.</margin>

# On the Illusions of Demons

...only by exorcisms, where the demon must be driven from his seat by those who possess the singular gift of expelling him. Meanwhile, bells and hand-bells are purified and sanctified, with sponsors and witnesses summoned from all around for the sacrilegious plundering of even more gold. The simple folk are persuaded that these inanimate, dead objects would otherwise be carried off from their towers by the devil. Indeed, pits and ponds are pointed out—which I myself have seen, if I am worthy—where they claim with certainty that such unbaptized and unconsecrated bells were carried by a demon from the nearest towers. They say the sound of these bells is heard at the midnight hour of the Feast of the Nativity of Christ <note>Christmas</note>, or even during each of the <term>Ember Days</term> <note>original: "quatuor anni temporibus," literally "the four seasons of year." Thus it happens that the unwary take care to avoid the sound, and no one is found who has actually heard it. If anyone should happen to hear it, he would undoubtedly be mocked by the devil for his lack of faith; yet, in the meantime, people are held captive by these illusions within our own religion. Not long ago, I was led to a place near <term>Knechtsteden Abbey</term> <note>A Premonstratensian monastery located near Dormagen, Germany.</note>, where I heard this sacrilegious belief still firmly held; a pit was pointed out, and a tower was shown. 

For this reason, with great prudence and piety, the <term>Emperor Maximilian</term> <note>Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I (reigned 1493–1519).</note> included the consecration of bells among the <term>Grievances</term> <note>original: "gravamina." "Suffragan bishops have devised a scheme so that only they, and no other priest, may baptize bells for the laity. The simple folk then believe, on the word of these suffragans, that such baptized bells repel demons and storms. Consequently, a vast number of godfathers are usually employed, especially those who are powerful and wealthy. At the time of the baptism, they are asked to touch the rope by which the bell is bound, and as the suffragan leads the chant (just as is customary in the baptism of infants), they all respond together and repeat the name of the bell, even dressing it in a new garment (just as is done for Christians..."

## On the Deceptions of Demons

...[men], whom they strive to turn away from the worship and knowledge of the true Majesty, so that they might not attain the immortality which they themselves lost through their own wickedness. They therefore cast shadows and shroud the truth in darkness, so that men may not know the Lord, nor their own Father. And in order to entice them easily, they hide themselves in temples and are present at all sacrifices. Often they perform wonders, by which men are struck with awe and bestow their faith upon images of divinity and power. And later: Thus they acquire authority and fear among men who do not know them. By this cunning and these arts, they have obscured the knowledge of the true and only God among all nations. Being lost to their own vices, they rage and prowl about to destroy. For this reason, they even devised human sacrifices—they, the enemies of the human race—so that they might devour as many souls as possible.

More is found in that same work. It is no wonder, says Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> regarding the Rugians <note>A West Slavic tribe inhabiting the island of Rügen in the Baltic Sea.</note>, if they dreaded the power of those deities, from whom they remembered their own sexual debaucheries had often been punished. <margin>Why demons are able to perform such wonders.</margin>
It is not surprising that these spirits attempt various and infinite acts of this kind. Since they are of a refined substance <note>The author refers to the classical and medieval belief that demons possess "ethereal" or "airy" bodies, which are much thinner and more mobile than human flesh.</note>, they far surpass the sluggishness of earthly bodies and the slowness of our senses through their own thinness, subtlety, incredible speed, sharpness of perception, and a clearer natural light. By God's permission, they understand and can perform many things, partly in reality and partly through **illusion** <note>original: "præstigiosè"</note>.

<margin>On the Spirit and the Soul, chapter 28.</margin>
To these qualities is added—as Augustine testifies—the benefit of a much longer life, which has extended from the earliest age of time. This has granted them a remarkable experience of vastly greater things than can ever be achieved by humans in their momentary and brief lifespan. For this reason, they perform certain wonders and foretell certain things, primarily through their knowledge of Holy Scripture and the prophets, or even through probable conjecture. Sometimes they even announce in advance what they themselves are about to do, by which means they entice, bait, mislead, and defraud men. For this reason, Plato, in his *Epinomis* <note>A philosophical dialogue traditionally associated with Plato's later works, discussing the nature of the cosmos and the hierarchy of spirits.</note>, attributes to them a wonderful **prudence**, a sharp **wit**, and a tenacious **memory**.

<margin>The *Recognitions*, Book 4.</margin>
Therefore, Clement <note>Referring to the *Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions*, an early Christian work written as a spiritual travelogue.</note> relates that since these are demonic spirits, they know certain things much more quickly and perfectly; for they are not weighed down by the sluggishness of the body. He adds: "And so, those things which physicians achieve only after a long time and much labor, these spirits know without any delay or difficulty." It is therefore no wonder if they know even more than men; but it is to be feared that they bring forth the things they know not for salvation, but for the **deception of souls**, so that through these things they may teach them the worship of a false religion.

# On the Illusions of Demons

...to these [shrines or idols] the unwise flock from distant regions, the incautious venerate them, adore them, and implore their help in times of hardship, in ill health, and in whatever affliction; by which [the demon] calls them away from the worship and invocation of the true God to his own impostures for their destruction. <margin>Book 1 of the Life of St. Martin.</margin> So Sulpicius Severus <note>A Christian writer (c. 363–425 AD) known for his biography of St. Martin of Tours.</note> writes that this was the custom of the rural Gauls: in wretched madness they carried images of demons covered in white veils through their fields. Nor is it difficult for Satan to mimic the form of souls freed from the weight of the body <note>That is, appearing as ghosts or spirits of the deceased.</note>, to linger around monuments, to wander in cemeteries, and to terrify heirs or others with specters. He does this so that he may compel the unskilled and those who trust less in God to perform illicit worship, to undertake pilgrimages forbidden by religion, and to perform harmful payments of prescribed rites for the dead and parental offerings <note>original: "parentalium... persolutionem." This refers to ancient Roman customs of honoring deceased parents, which the author suggests are being misused under demonic influence.</note>.

He likewise attempts to drive those weak in faith headlong into error, while always attacking the strong in various ways, to see if by any means he might turn them aside. Similarly, he uses promises and glory to enrich the despairing, the credulous, and the mentally unwell; he lures them with the hope of happy outcomes only to destroy them, or he tortures them by instilling a fear of grim events. <margin>Michael Psellus.</margin> <note>A Byzantine monk and scholar (c. 1017–1078) who wrote extensively on demonology.</note> He also knows how to display various forms, to shape empty idols with wondrous skill, to disturb the organ of sight, and to dazzle the eyes. With singular dexterity, he proposes false things in place of true ones so they are not recognized; he veils those things which truly exist so they do not appear, and he exhibits those which in reality do not exist so they seem to be. He transforms himself into a thousand species and plays the part of Proteus <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note>; <margin>Virgil, Georgics Book 4.</margin> and as the Poet <note>Referring to the Roman poet Virgil.</note> sings:

> Then various shapes and the faces of wild beasts mock him.
> For suddenly he will become a bristly boar, and a black tigress,
> A scaly dragon, and a lioness with a tawny neck,
> Or he will give forth the sharp sound of flames:
> Transforming himself into all the wonders of nature,
> Into fire, and a horrible beast, and a flowing river.

He is also accustomed to corrupting the minds of men with various mockeries of phantasms <note>original: "phantasmatum ludibrijs." These are mental hallucinations or "tricks of the mind" rather than physical objects.</note>, to disturb those who are awake, to terrify those who are sleeping with nightmares, and to lead travelers from the right path...

# On the Tricks of Demons

In this manner, he can convulse the nerves and muscles inordinately and cruelly against the person's will. He often stirs up <term>tetanus</term> <note>original: τέτανον; a state of rigid muscle contraction</note> so that the neck remains immobile along with the body, and is bent toward neither side, but is stretched equally in both directions. c 4

First, it seems expedient that a fast of three days be undertaken, along with the celebration of some Masses and devout prayers—specifically, the seven penitential psalms <note>A collection of seven psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143) traditionally used in the Church to express sorrow for sins.</note> frequently repeated. When these are finished, four or five devout priests are to be summoned and called. I believe this is more fittingly done by devout members of religious orders <note>Monks or friars, as opposed to "secular" priests who worked in parishes.</note> who are free from worldly affairs and have their minds lifted toward God, so as to drive away horror and terror. These men should approach the place in which the spirit is accustomed to show itself, with humility of heart and a right intention, ceasing all superstitious inquiry. Nevertheless, they should not go without certain ceremonies, since the Church uses ceremonies in the conferring of all sacraments and in the Mass. Therefore, let a candle be taken that was blessed on the day of the Purification <note>Also known as Candlemas, a feast day where candles are blessed for use throughout the year.</note> and lit; let there be holy water, the sign of the cross, and, if it pleases, a thurible <note>A metal censer used for burning incense during religious rites.</note> with incense. While approaching, they should pray the seven Psalms and the Gospel of Saint John. Having entered, they should sprinkle the place with water and incense it. I do not say, however, that all these things are required by necessity, but I judge them to be expedient; for I do not have a foundation of necessity for these things from Scripture, but I have read some examples of the saints regarding them. The holy stole <note>A long silk band worn around the neck by a priest, signifying his sacramental authority.</note> also does not seem to be useless. It should be noted, according to the same doctor <note>likely referring to a specific theologian or "Doctor of the Church" cited previously</note>: It is perhaps not expedient for all people indifferently to be present at the aforementioned revelations and apparitions, except for those of a very strong "complexion" <note>original: "complexionatis" — referring to a person's physical and mental temperament or constitution</note>, who are not easily terrified: because I think I know through experience that some, upon seeing these things or the places of punishment, have fallen into incurable illness. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On another occasion, the most learned **Melanchthon** <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560) was a German reformer and a primary collaborator of Martin Luther. He was known for his interest in such supernatural reports.</note> recounted that he had an aunt. While she was sitting quite sorrowfully by the hearth after her husband's death, behold, two figures entered the house. One of these appeared in the likeness of her husband and claimed to be the woman's deceased spouse; the other, quite tall, had taken the form of a **Franciscan monk** <note>A member of a Catholic religious order; in Protestant literature of this time, demons often appear in the guise of monks to criticize Catholic practices.</note>. This "husband," approaching the hearth, greeted his grieving wife and commanded her to be without fear. He asserted that he had come to give her certain instructions. He then desired the tall monk to withdraw into the **stove-room** <note>original: "hypocaustum"; a heated parlor or living room common in northern European homes.</note> for a while.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Thereupon, starting his speech, he most greatly prayed, entreated, and earnestly implored that **priests** <note>original: "sacrificulos"; a somewhat derogatory term used by reformers for those who performed the sacrifice of the Mass.</note> be hired to recite masses for him. As he was about to depart, he desired her to give him her right hand. Although she was terrified and trembling, she gave him her hand after he promised he would do her no harm. Even though she was not physically injured, the hand seemed to be so badly burned that it remained **black** forever after. Afterward, he called out the Franciscan, and having gone out together, they vanished without delay.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Furthermore, by the report of the same man, it was heard that a monk once approached **Luther's** <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the central figure of the Protestant Reformation.</note> house, knocking violently at the doors. When a servant opened them and asked what he wanted, the monk asked whether Luther was at home. Having recognized the situation, Luther ordered him to enter, because he had not seen a monk for a long time. Having entered, the monk said he held certain **Papistical errors** <note>Referring to Roman Catholic doctrines that Luther had rejected.</note> and wished to consult with Luther about them. He proposed **syllogisms** <note>Formal logical arguments used in academic and theological debate.</note>, and after these were solved by Luther without difficulty, he brought forward others that were less easy to explain.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Luther, somewhat annoyed by this, burst out with these words: "You are causing me much trouble, for I had other work to do." Rising at the same time, he showed the monk the explanation of the passage he had proposed. During this discussion, noticing that the monk’s hands were not unlike the **claws of birds** <note>original: "avium unguibus"; a traditional sign in folklore that a person is actually a demon in disguise.</note>, Luther said: "Is it you? Listen, this sentence has been pronounced against you," and he immediately pointed to a place in **Genesis** <note>Genesis 3:15, a key verse in Christian theology regarding the defeat of the devil.</note>: *The seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent.*

## *Natural and Artificial Things are Sometimes Judged to be Demonic. Chapter XVII.* ##

<margin>Natural things in the great world.</margin>
Many things frequently appear before our eyes which are thought to be the mockeries and actions of demons beyond the laws of nature, although Mother Nature herself—the parent of all things—produced them for certain causes and for reasons that are not obscure. Of this kind is that **will-o'-the-wisp** <margin>Will-o'-the-wisp.</margin> <note>original: "ignis fatuus," literally "foolish fire."</note>, which they also call a "burning candle." This is an exhalation raised to the lowest region of the air and ignited there by **antiperistasis** <note>A term from Aristotelian physics referring to the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat concentrating when surrounded by cold.</note>. For while it rises, it is repelled by the cold of the middle region and appears as if leaping, seeking lower places; hence it even seems to lead one who follows it toward water at night. Indeed, it sometimes appears, not without horror, to precede or follow those walking, riding, or sailing, lasting for a long time in the air. **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist whose "Natural History" was a standard reference for early modern scholars.</note> calls such a **meteor** <note>In this period, "meteor" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, or light.</note> "Castor and Pollux" <note>This refers to St. Elmo's Fire, a weather phenomenon where luminous plasma is created by a coronal discharge from a sharp or pointed object in a strong electric field.</note>.

Such a fire also exists that licks the hair and fur of animals, and likewise the clothes of men: namely, by such an exhalation dispersed through the air, struck together and inflamed, adhering to the said parts. And fires of this sort, non-burning and harmless, are more frequently seen in damp, viscous, rotten, marshy, and smoky places, such as in kitchens, valleys, cemeteries, beneath gallows, and wherever many **corpses** <note>original: "cadauera."</note> have rotted. From these places rise fatty, thick, and viscous vapors, yet they are less hot than those carried to the highest region of the air. These, emerging continuously, are ignited by collision, as I said, just as fire is drawn out from two flints struck together.

In addition to these, some call a certain plant "Star of the Earth," <note>original: "Stellam... herbam." Likely referring to *Nostoc*, a type of cyanobacteria that appears as a jelly-like mass on the ground after rain, historically called "star-slough" or "star-jelly" and believed to be the remains of fallen meteors.</note>

which is commonly called **Moonwort** <note>original: "Lunaria"; likely *Lunaria annua*, also known as Honesty.</note>, and it encloses its seeds in a round pod. When this is open at night, it admits the rays of the moon to such an extent that it appears to shine like a star. The inhabitants of the place, seeing this, flee as if from a wicked specter. Some prepare poisons from this; with this, they provoke demons; and with this, the **alchemists** <note>original: "Chymici."</note> render their Mercury fixed and stable. The most learned **Gessner** <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a famous Swiss naturalist.</note> calls this the "Greek Moonwort."

*Sosigenes*, the teacher of *Alexander* <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note>, attempted to provide a reason in the third volume of his work **On Vision** <note>original: "de Visu."</note> as to why certain things appear to glow in the darkness. These **flame-like things** <note>original: "Flammulenta"; referring to bioluminescent objects.</note>, he says, participate to some degree in the nature of the ether and the **fifth element** <term>quintessence: in ancient physics, the celestial material that makes up the stars, distinct from earth, water, air, and fire</term>. By this kinship, it happens that they illuminate the air or any other transparent body brought near them. He argues the reason they do this most especially at night is that the greater light [of the sun] is then absent. Otherwise, it happens during the day that their meager light is, as it were, faded and overwhelmed by the greater light. Therefore, when they shine at night, they lightly illuminate the nearest surrounding air—not so much that other things can be seen by it, but so that they alone might claim themselves from the darkness. And this is caused by the smallness of the portion from which the light proceeds and flows; for even fire itself, although it sends its splendor further and more widely (so much so that it reveals other things even if they are further away), yet if the fire is too small, the eyes grow dim to everything else, and the fire is scarcely sufficient even to be seen itself.

<margin>
Monstrous natural things.
</margin>

Thus, many things are often regarded as miracles and are thought to happen contrary to the nature of things among men, which are nonetheless both natural and frequently occur. For instance, during the consulship of **Servius Flaccus** and **Quintus Calphurnius** in Rome, an infant was born with the **lower part of its nature solid** <note>original: "posteriore naturæ parte solidus"; likely referring to an imperforate anus, a birth defect where the opening is missing.</note>; and another in the consulship of **Servius Galba** and **Marcus Scaurus** at Nursia which, although it let out a cry, immediately expired; and another at Fiesole from a handmaid during the consulship of **Gaius Perpenna** and **Marcus Perpenna**. For in our own **medical observations** <note>The author, Johann Weyer, was a physician and often used clinical cases to debunk "magical" claims.</note>, we have taught that it is neither new nor rare for a child to be born without a natural opening to pass waste, fluid, or anything else, and that this lacks neither a natural explanation nor a remedy. Nor is it a miracle when a **woman is changed into a male** <note>Early modern writers often recorded cases of what we now understand as intersex conditions or delayed male puberty.</note>, which I shall explain more fully in Book 4, Chapter 24; although many might happen to think such a thing is demonic. Chapter 16 of Book 4 also pertains to this.

Moreover, we see and wonder at the many miracles daily performed by actors and **jesters** <term>ioculatoribus: entertainers, from which we get the word "juggler," who performed tricks and sleight of hand</term> through the swift agility and diligence of their hands. <margin>Book on Incantations</margin> **Pomponatius** <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), an influential Italian philosopher who sought natural explanations for "miracles."</note> recounts that he saw a certain man of this kind named Reatius at Mantua and Padua, who performed unbelievable feats. A certain **Turk** <note>During this period, travelers from the Ottoman Empire often performed exotic "feats of strength" in European cities.</note>, wandering here and there through the cities of Italy, among other wonders which he exhibited to the people, appeared to break an iron pestle by a great blow of his fist, and likewise by the mere twisting of his hands, through pre-arranged dexterity. Someone not unlearned in the art of the **traveling performer** <term>circulatorie artis: the trade of the 'circulator,' a wandering medicine-showman or street magician</term> once confessed to me that a deception is fostered by these jesters in the exhibition of such miracles because they first prepared suitable instruments for such a spectacle. These instruments they vary in many ways with the speed of their hands, while they call the eyes of the spectators to themselves with various speech, keeping them fixed and deluding them. 

**Julius Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a famous scholar and physician.</note>, as well as **Matthiolus** <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a renowned herbalist and physician.</note>, describes a remarkable and mocking imposture of this class of men. Into wine they mix the powder of a certain root, by the taste of which the throat is seized with spasms; and to the one they wish to deceive, they command that he suck a finger dipped in this wine, as if for the sake of pre-tasting it. Then immediately, having put the finger moist with wine into his mouth, the victim unwillingly presses it with his teeth, not without pain and a cry. Meanwhile, as if consoling the grieving man with flatteries, the performer smears the arteries of the temples and the wrist with some other medicine <note>likely a topical hallucinogen such as henbane or belladonna</note>; then he encourages him to pick up a coin thrown on the ground. There, leaning forward, at first he is unable to lift himself up; soon, driven mad by the power of the ointment, he collapses. And immediately, in the manner of one who fears he is drowning in water, he "swims" on the ground and simultaneously cries out that he is being overwhelmed by the waves. Therefore he is raised up by the performer, then, as if about to avenge himself, he first begins to reproach the evildoing with a slanted and grim face, and soon to attack the man

Furthermore, the balanced steps of rope-walkers or **tightrope-walkers** <term>schœnobaton: from the Greek for "rope-walker"</term>, leveled to a scale or balanced by weights on both sides, are accustomed to increase the wonders of nature. At the same time, as if they had been softened by fire, he could carry a long beam of twenty feet or more and a foot thick upon his shoulders, held upright for some time without the help of his hands, and move it from one shoulder blade to the other. My son **Theodorus**, a legal scholar, saw these things and reported them to me, being an eyewitness of all the aforementioned things along with many others.

# Book One. That certain artificial things in animals sometimes appear demonic. Chapter XVIII.

<margin>Miracles in brute animals.</margin>
<margin>Johannes Leo in the *Description of Africa*, Book 3. <note>Leo Africanus (c. 1494–1554) was a famous traveler and geographer whose descriptions of Africa were highly influential in Renaissance Europe.</note></margin>

In a suburb of Memphis among the Egyptians called *Beb Elloch* <note>Bab al-Luq, a district in Cairo.</note>, while many such things are commonly performed daily, there is often a certain actor who, when he has danced a little, turns to his donkey and says in a loud voice that the Sultan is planning a great building project; therefore, he will have need of all the donkeys of *Alcairus* <note>original: "Alcairi"; Cairo.</note> (for so Memphis is now called) to carry lime, stones, and other things of that sort. Then the donkey suddenly collapses to the ground, lifts its feet into the air, swells its belly, and closes its eyes just as if it were dead. Meanwhile, the actor complains to the bystanders 
<margin>The wonderful docility of the donkey.</margin>
about the fall of the donkey, earnestly asking that they grant him assistance to buy another. Having collected what money he can from the men individually, he says: "Do not think the donkey is dead. Then, turning to the donkey, he warns it to rise up immediately. But while the animal does not move from the spot, it is beaten with frequent blows of a staff. When it is still not roused, the actor repeats the story and says again to the common people: "Know that the Sultan has issued an edict that tomorrow all the people shall go out of the city for the sake of seeing a triumph, and all the beautiful and noble women shall ride upon the finest donkeys, and shall in turn provide them with oats and excellent water from the Nile." Scarcely has the actor finished these words than the donkey, standing up on its feet, leaps forward braying, and jumping about as if full of joy. Then, continuing the story, the actor says: "The Governor of our village has asked to borrow this elegant donkey of mine for his deformed and old wife." The donkey, as if in pain, folds back its ears; then, limping on one foot, it pretends to be injured. Then the performer asks: "Do the young women smile upon you?" The donkey, bowing its head, seems to nod in agreement. "Come then, there are many young women here; point out the one who pleases you above the others." The donkey, surveying the circle of spectators, selects a more respectable woman, walks toward her, and touches her with its head. The spectators break out in great laughter and shouting: "Hey!" you say, <margin>African History, Book 9.</margin> "the donkey's woman!" In this same way, he teaches camels to dance to certain rhythms. <margin>The dancing of camels.</margin> They place a young camel for half an hour in a place prepared like a heated room <term>hypocaustum: an ancient Roman underfloor heating system</term>, where the floor has been heated by fire. Then, while someone beats a drum outside, the camel—not because of the sound, but because of the fire beneath which hurts its feet—lifts now one leg, now the other, just like a dancer. Having been accustomed to this exercise for a year or ten months, when it is led out in public and hears the drum, it immediately dances, remembering the time when it felt the heat under its feet. Believing itself to be standing on that same floor, it appears to dance by pulling back its feet alternately; and thus, shaping its nature through habit, it observes this behavior forever.

<margin>The Dove of Muhammad.</margin>
Muhammad, following the instruction of his teacher Sergius the monk, had accustomed a dove to feed from his ear. The deceiver pretended this dove was the Holy Spirit and boasted that it announced the secret counsels of God to him whenever it flew to his ear for food. The impious common people did not notice this, being deluded by the demon whose interest it was to build an unspeakable sect upon these foundations. However, when a dove flew past the ears of Saint Athanasius as he walked through the city, the heretics and Arian schismatics <note>followers of Arius, who denied the full divinity of Christ</note> immediately interpreted it as if the most holy Athanasius were a sorcerer—certainly at the instigation of that same Master of Deceit <note>the Devil</note>, in order to make his doctrine suspect.

<margin>The Muhammadan Bull.</margin>
Furthermore, so that the crafty man Muhammad might further deceive his people, who were devoted to their bellies and to sleep, he raised a certain bull that was accustomed to take food only from Muhammad's hands. Between its horns, he tied a most impious book written by himself, titled the *Al-Quran*. While the simple people were gathered, he called out to the bull with a loud voice from a certain hidden place where it was lurking. When he had finished declaiming many things concerning the laws, the bull suddenly burst forth, [receiving] many [praises] from him—

**Cyprian** <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage, a 3rd-century bishop and martyr</note> in his second sermon *On Jealousy and Envy*: "He <note>the Devil</note> goes around each one of us, and like an enemy besieging enclosed walls, he explores and tests whether there is any part of our members less stable and less faithful, through whose entrance he may penetrate to the interior. He presents enticing forms and easy pleasures to the eyes, so that he may destroy chastity through sight. He tempts the ears with melodious music, so that the sound, through a sweeter hearing, may loosen and soften Christian vigor. He provokes the tongue to abuse; he instigates the hands, through provoking injuries, to the petulance of murder. To make a man a cheater, he presents unjust gains; to capture the soul with money, he brings in ruinous profits. He promises earthly honors so that he may take away heavenly ones; he displays false things so that he may steal away the true. And when he cannot deceive secretly, he threatens openly and plainly, stretching forth the terror of turbulent persecution, always restless and always hostile to defeating the servants of God; crafty in peace, violent in persecution."

The same author in his eighth letter, book 1: "Avoid the poisoned tongue of the devil, who from the beginning of the world has always been deceitful and a liar; he lies to deceive, he flatters to harm; he promises good things to bestow evil; he promises life to destroy. Even now his words shine, and his poisons are manifest: he promises peace, lest one be able to arrive at peace; he promises salvation, lest salvation come to the one to whom he promises it; he holds out the Church <note>original: "Ecclesiam spondeat"</note> while he acts so that he who believes him..."

These demons are not accustomed to harm the miners, but they wander about in the shafts and tunnels; and although they do nothing, they nevertheless seem to exercise themselves in every kind of labor, as if now they were digging veins, now pouring what has been dug into vessels, now turning the hauling machine. Although they occasionally pelt the workers with gravel, they very rarely hurt them. Nor do they ever cause harm unless they themselves have first been provoked by mocking laughter or curses. Therefore, they are not very different from those demons who rarely appear to men, yet daily perform a portion of the household labor and care for the beasts of burden. # On the Deceptions of Demons

<margin>The diversity of demons and their philosopher.</margin> The philosophers who believed in the existence of demons divided them into three categories. Some believe they are all immortal and all evil, as well as weak; such was the view of Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, an 11th-century Byzantine scholar known for his work on demonology</note>, who, being a Christian, subscribed to the opinion of the Christians. Others believe they are mortal, and that some are good while others are evil—powerful, yet looking out for themselves through the fear of death. The third distinction belongs to the Platonists, who affirm that they are immortal, powerful, and familiar to us, being partly good and partly evil. Furthermore, there is a consensus among all these philosophers that demons are natural beings, whom Plato places in charge of sorceries, incantations, magic, *sorcery* <note>original Greek: γoητείας (goēteias), referring to low magic or witchcraft</note>, the arts of priests, and oracles.

<margin>The distinction between good and evil demons.</margin> Furthermore, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote 'On the Mysteries'</note> distinguishes good from evil demons more clearly and openly than Proclus in his work *On the Mysteries*: "Gods," he says, "angels, and good demons do not appear in a phantasmal <note>meaning illusory or imaginary</note> manner, but in a way that is entirely their own and true. But evil spirits appear in a phantasmal and deceitful way; they simulate the presence of gods and good demons. Therefore, they command their worshiper to be just, so that they themselves might seem good, just like the gods. But because they are evil by nature, when they are asked to inflict evil, they do so willingly and lead us toward unjust acts. These are entirely the ones who lie and deceive in the oracles, and who advise and carry out shameful things." Gods and good demons, however, never deceive, nor do they contribute to iniquity. Moreover, the nature of evil demons is inconsistent with itself, unstable, and self-conflicting, persuading one thing at one time and another at another. But the nature of the higher beings is constantly consistent with itself and always maintains the same tenor in action. Plato, Porphyry, and many other Platonists sometimes judged evil demons to be good; for Plato had drawn his philosophy from the Egyptians and other barbarians <note>In this context, 'barbarians' refers to non-Greek civilizations</note>, according to the judgment of Plutarch.

<margin>Clement, Book 4 of the *Recognitions*.</margin> However, the "rule of thumb" by which spirits are distinguished is proposed by Peter in the writings of Clement, Book 3 of the *Recognitions* <note>An early Christian philosophical romance attributed to Clement of Rome</note>: "The signs performed by one who is from the evil one benefit no one; but those...

It cites authorities like Psellus, Iamblichus, and the pseudo-Clementine Recognitions to provide a framework for identifying demonic deception.</summary>
