For the things a good person does are beneficial to men. For tell me, I ask you, what utility is there in showing walking statues? Or in making dogs of bronze or stone bark, making mountains leap, flying through the air, and other such things which you say Simon <note>Simon Magus, a sorcerer mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, often cited as a practitioner of "useless" magic.</note> has done? But those things which are from the Good are directed toward the salvation of men: such as those things which our Lord performed, who made the blind see, made the deaf hear, raised up the weak and the lame, put to flight sicknesses and demons, made the dead rise again, and other such things which you see being done even through me. Therefore, the Evil One is unable to perform these signs which are profitable for the salvation of men and confer some good upon humanity.

By Saint Anthony <note>Saint Anthony the Great (c. 251–356), the "Father of All Monks."</note>, as Saint Athanasius is written to have reported, they are distinguished by this reasoning: The appearances of the Holy Spirit are with a praiseworthy and calm countenance. Wherefore our mind, not at all troubled, but gentle and placid, is illuminated by the rays of the light of angels; then, burning with a desire for heavenly gifts, it longs to be unburdened from this lodging of the body and mortal dwelling, and hastens with those whom it sees toward that eternal tabernacle. Although, because of the lot of human frailty, one might be somewhat terrified by the brightness of the first sight, nevertheless their grace is so great that they suddenly take away all fear. Thus Gabriel, when he spoke to Zacharias in the temple, and the angels when they announced the divine birth of the Virgin to the shepherds, as well as those who kept watch around the Lord’s body, showed themselves to the secure minds of those seeing them and commanded them not to fear. ### Chapter XXIII.

<margin>Limits of action are established for the devil.</margin>

# Book One.

He has instilled in every created thing its essence, form, property, strength, and function, so that whatever has been established must either act or not act according to the innate movement of its nature. Beyond this power granted from the beginning, a thing can do nothing of itself; nor is anything granted to it by God other than what it is capable of by that same reason. Otherwise, God would be in opposition to Himself, which is entirely foreign to His nature. To make this understood more clearly, I wish to demonstrate it with an example. If it were permitted to me by the Divine Majesty to fly through the air with the birds, or to crawl through the bowels of the earth with the earthworms, or to live in the waters with the fish, I certainly would be unable to do so. This is because it would contravene the order of God established from the origin, and the natural power instilled in me by God, since He created me a man <note>Latin: *hominem*</note>, who ought to live on the land with other men. Thus, from the beginning, it was commanded to the birds that they fly in the air; the hospitality of the waters was committed to the fish; the surface of the earth was assigned to the trees and plants; and the power to burrow deeper into it was given to the earthworms and maggots:

> But truly, swift stags do not graze in the ether,
> Nor do the seas leave the fish naked on the shore,
> Nor, with the boundaries of both wandered through in exile,
> Does the Parthian drink from the Saône, or Germany from the Tigris.
> <note>The author is quoting Virgil’s *Eclogues* (1.59-62) to illustrate that the laws of nature prevent things from existing outside their proper environments.</note>

No less have the laws and limits of their own power been prescribed for spirits, beyond which they cannot move even a hair's breadth, even if God were to wink and permit everything. However, He permits nothing that cannot happen within its own order. This does not detract from the omnipotence of God, but rather demonstrates the impotence of the demon. The demon cannot create even a single fly (for this is the gift of God alone, who is the sole source and origin of every true essence), nor can any creature—be it angel or man—attribute that duty to itself. Likewise, a demon cannot engage in sexual intercourse <note>Latin: *concubitum*</note> and thereby procreate; for it lacks the organs and the matter which are granted only to living animals...

Whatever he is able to work out of this power, God permitting, must be granted to him; yet in the execution of it, he is quite often restrained by a bridle, so that he does not accomplish even what he is capable of. He is indeed a minister for the vengeance of God, an executor of His justice and a tormentor <note>The author uses "tortor" to describe the demon's role as a punisher under divine law, not an independent agent.</note>, but only in that category where he prevails by natural virtue, and no further.

By the same reasoning, you may easily demolish the common objection regarding the powers of Witches <term>Lamiarum: a term for "witches" or "sorceresses" often associated with child-snatching spirits in antiquity</term>, namely that they perform miracles of things surpassing human strength with the assistance of the devil. On the contrary, these women are capable of nothing beyond the innate virtue of human nature, even if a demon should cooperate a thousand times over. Rather, on account of their sex and age—due to a constitution of the body that is unfit, being cold, moist, thick, and sluggish—they actually hinder the work of the thin demonic substance. Thus, if the demon should require their cooperation, he would be disturbed and inhibited in the execution of his work. For many things are possible or natural to him as a spirit by the guidance of nature which, on account of the thickness and slowness of the human essence, far and wide exceed the boundaries of our nature.

Therefore, it must be asserted that the most just God does not concede just anything, but only those things which the naturally constituted divine order demands. If you are unable to reach the reasoning of this order from the organized principles and logic of things, turn the eyes of your mind toward the books of truth, and contemplate with a clear ray of light what has been granted to the devil thus far; for in these, as if upon...

->If you observe the judgments of the interpreters more attentively in all these places, wherever any mention is made of these portents: such as in Exodus chapters 7, 9, and 22; Leviticus 19 and 20; Deuteronomy 18; Jeremiah 27; Daniel 2; 4 Kings 21; and 2 Chronicles 33.<-

Because of such diversity and disagreement among interpreters in the aforementioned passages, I consulted a man most learned in every respect and highly skilled in languages, Master Andreas Masius <note>Andreas Masius (1514–1573) was a famous Flemish humanist and expert in Near Eastern languages.</note>, who explained the Hebrew words regarding magical matters used here—seven in number—with these words.

<margin>Chafaph.</margin> The first, namely <term>כשף</term> *Chafaph* <note>original: "Chasaph"</note>, I see constantly rendered in the common Latin Bibles as if it signifies a "maleficent person" <note>Latin: *maleficum*</note>. By this, they mean men driven to madness by a demon, who through evil arts harm livestock, crops, and even men themselves—or at least believe they are harming them. Because of these crimes, they are called "evildoers" <note>Latin: *malefici*</note>, whom the Law of Moses willed to be removed from life.

<margin>Mechassepha.</margin> In Exodus 22, this decree is found: <term>מכשפה לא תחיה</term> *Mechassepha lo techayyeh* <note>original: "Mechassepha lo techajje"</note>: that is, **"You shall not suffer a sorceress to live."** For the noun <term>מכשפה</term> *Mechassepha*, which the law uses here, is derived from *Chafaph*. It is placed in the feminine gender, as the interpreters say, not because the law wishes men to go unpunished, but because that sex, due to its natural simplicity, is more frequently open to the snares of the demon.

Therefore, the Greek translation, which we attribute to the Seventy Elders <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, rendered that decree more freely: <term>φαρμακις ὴ πρδιβιωσον</term> <note>original: "pharmakis ou peribioson"</note>: that is, **"You shall not keep poisoners alive"** (using the masculine sense to include the feminine). I notice, moreover, that the aforementioned word <term>כשף</term> *Chafaph*, and those derived from it, are hardly ever explained in the Greek translation in any other way than to signify "poisoning" <note>Latin: *veneficium*</note>. That is, they use these Greek words:

<margin>Pharmakis.</margin> <term>φαρμακις</term> (*pharmakis* - a sorceress/poisoner),
<margin>Pharmakis.</margin> <term>φαρμακα</term> (*pharmaka* - drugs/potions), <term>φαρμακων</term> (*pharmakon* - of spells/medicines), and others of this inflection. For it is also commonly believed that those whom we call "evildoers" practice and achieve their wicked arts not without certain medicated substances—to say nothing of the Greek and Latin authors. ## Book Two.

Ezra, a writer of great renown among the Hebrews, says that the word <term>Chafaph <note>original: כחף. A Hebrew root often associated with sorcery or whispering spells.</note></term> properly refers to prestidigitation: that is, those delusions by which things are presented to our eyes differently than they actually are. Even if we were to grant him this—though it certainly does not seem to me that this can be easily proven from Holy Scripture—nevertheless, in the second chapter of Daniel, where we read that Nebuchadnezzar summoned, among other interpreters of his dream, the <term>Mechaffepim <note>original: מכשפים. Usually translated as sorcerers or magicians.</note></term>: if you translate this as "illusionists," I do not see what they could have brought to the explanation of the dream by their art, which is entirely false and deceptive. Therefore, the interpreter of that passage, Levi son of Gerson <note>Referring to Gersonides (Ralbag), a prominent 14th-century Jewish philosopher and commentator.</note>, a supreme philosopher among that nation, says that the *Mechaffepim* are those who profess the astral art of drawing down spirits from heaven, and of enticing them into certain characters <note>talismanic symbols or figures</note> fashioned and prepared at specific hours and during the courses of the stars; and once enticed, of inciting them to either the benefit or the harm of whichever men they wish, or even compelling them to any other duties, such as the foretelling and signifying of hidden things. But I, if you also require my judgment, would think that this word has a broad application and refers to any magical art whatsoever; and I see that the common opinion of the Hebrews is also in this view.

The second word was <term>Kasam <note>original: קצם. Usually transliterated as Qasam; refers to divination.</note></term>. Aben Ezra <note>original: "Aben Eldra"; referring to the 12th-century biblical commentator Abraham ibn Ezra</note> interprets them as those who know the secrets of the qualities of things and of nature. However, the reality of the matter shows they were not such, since those effects which are read of in Exodus 7 and 8 could not have been produced by natural power. <margin>The deceptive Magus, the Witch, and the Poisoner are called by the same name by the Germans.</margin>
Furthermore, among our Germans, the Magus—a professional deceiver and frequently a learned man—is called by one and the same name, *Zauberer* <note>German: sorcerer or magician</note>, as is the female hag or *Lamia* <note>A mythical female demon; here used to mean a witch</note> who is deluded by the devil due to the weakness of her mind and a corrupted imagination, and the poisoner who studiously employs venom. From this it happens that whenever mention is made of witches or poisoners, people immediately bring up Pharaoh’s illusionists—who are far removed from the actions of witches and poisoners—being deceived by the German ambiguity. Therefore, I am not at all ashamed to testify openly that all the German writers, as many as I have happened to read in that language so far, have stumbled heavily in this kind of argument, even if they have prefixed beautiful titles to their books and seem to have produced testimonies of Holy Scripture. This is especially true because they attribute too much to these *Lamiae* in disturbing the air and bringing about diseases; they seem to imprudently supply the drawn sword and the burning scythes to the most cruel executioners without judgment, discretion, or any mark of compassion. In this variety of opinions, lest the confusion of names pour forth darkness, it has pleased me for various reasons in this undertaking of ours to separate the infamous Magus from the *Lamia* and the poisoner. This is so that in this most ulcerated century of ours—which is still so unlearned in this business—matters may become known (which is the use words ought to serve) and those of whom I speak may be distinguished; and so it may be clearly seen where I depart from the poorly-rooted opinions of others...

## What a Notorious Magician is. Sorcery and Theurgy.
### Chapter II.

<margin>Notorious Magician.</margin>
<margin>The magic of the Egyptians is divided into two types in the ill-omened account of Calasiris in Heliodorus's *Ethiopian History*, where he is described as an Egyptian <term>Prophetes</term> <note>original: "προφήτης"; a high-ranking priest or interpreter of oracles</note>, that is, a master of magic.</margin>
Therefore, the name of "notorious magician" shall be used more generally, and not restricted by such narrow boundaries; whereas the designation of "witches" <note>original: "Lamiarum"; referring to the mythical child-devouring demons, often used for witches</note> and "poisoners" shall be circumscribed by stricter limits. For I now define a **Magician** as one who—having been voluntarily taught by a demon, by others, or from books—recites, whispers, or applies a prescribed formula of words (whether they be foreign and unknown, or known), or uses any characters, exorcisms, and dire curses.

To these, add Apuleius and Artephius: the latter, in his *Compendium of Theological Study*, claims that he traveled through all the regions of the East for the sake of seeking out wisdom, and that he reached Tantalus, who was sitting upon a golden throne and teaching about heavenly matters, nature, and morals—though Tantalus was nonetheless taught by Artephius himself. This magic was illustrated and almost perfected by Democritus of Abdera, who unearthed the books written on Magic by Dardanus (the most skilled of the Egyptian magicians) which had been hidden in his tomb. Democritus explained them in proper volumes of commentaries based on the discipline of Apollonice, Captidenis, and Dardanus the Phoenician. Following that same example of Dardanus, Numa Pompilius—the Roman King and High Priest—wished for twelve books he had composed on this kind of trickery to be buried with him in his grave. There also exist books by Hermes on this craft. Furthermore, according to Pliny, <margin>Book 30, chapter 1.</margin> Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato sailed abroad to learn this art, engaging in what were more like exiles than mere travels.

# On Infamous Magicians

The history found in Matthew, chapter 2 <note>original: "Matth.2."</note>, is significant; for the Magi recognized the moment and the place of the birth of the Son of God from the prophecies which had been scattered in that Babylonian kingdom during the time of the Israelite captivity, being warned by a star. They understood that this star did not shine by chance, nor was it ignited from physical matter by the guidance of nature, but was truly kindled by divine power to signify the birth of Christ and to lead them to the place where He was.

The infamy of the former [wicked magicians], however, will shine forth even more clearly from what Cicero writes in his *On Divination* <note>original: "in Diuinationib. Cicero"</note>: that among the Persians, the magi practice augury and divination, gathering in a temple for the sake of study and conversing among themselves. And what is much more serious, Proclus, in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, while demonstrating most extensively this natural sympathy and kinship—and if you will, compassion—of things, records that the magi were also accustomed to use the invocation of deities through this kind of consensus of things. Laertius also testifies that they gave occasion for much idolatry, having rashly fabricated many types of superstitions and false beliefs. From this, the ignominy of the art is clear: that under the pretext of a divine name, it leans toward the cunning of demons; ensnared itself in the most entangled errors, it seizes the less cautious and hurries them headlong into destruction.

But would that there had remained in the later Magicians that religious scruple which belonged to the Persian Magi, the Egyptian priests, and the Gallic Druids: who judged it a wicked thing to commit those sacred mysteries of magic to written records, lest they become known to the common people. Thus, finally, it might have been hoped that that monstrous craftsmanship of the devil, so destructive to the human race, would utterly perish. In the same way, it is now necessary for Theologians and Physicians to strive with every kind of effort to ensure that this most pernicious of arts, full of frauds, be exiled as far as possible from the sacred rites of our religion, and be entirely exterminated and driven far from the camps of divine Medicine; since it [infects] both with its counterfeit exorcisms and prayers of barbarian words... <note>The sentence continues on the following page.</note>

<margin>Book 2 of the Sentences, Distinction 4, Chapter 7.</margin>Therefore, *Peter Lombard* <note>A 12th-century theologian whose "Sentences" became the standard textbook for medieval theology</note> rightly and piously says: The magic arts are practiced through the knowledge and power of demons. Yet, both power and knowledge are granted to them by God, either to deceive the deceitful—as was the case with the *Egyptians*—or power is even granted over the mages themselves, so that through the operation of these same spirits they might appear marvelous to those by whom they were to be damned. Alternatively, it is granted to warn the faithful not to desire such things as if they were great achievements, or to exercise and prove the patience of the righteous. Nor should it be thought that the matter of visible things serves the whim of demons; rather, it serves God, by whom this power is granted.

### Concerning Certain Magical Books.
### Chapter V.

Furthermore, these mages do not only boast that eminent men, holy patriarchs, and the angels of God are the authors of such wicked and execrable doctrines; they also do not blush to display books supposedly delivered by the angels *Raziel* and *Raphael* to *Adam* and *Tobias*. They do this so that they might beautifully adorn their Empusa <note>original: "Empusam"; a shapeshifting female demon from Greek mythology, here used metaphorically for a monstrous or deceptive thing</note> with this pretense. <margin>Magical books.</margin> However, to anyone looking more deeply into the canon of their precepts, the manner of their rituals, the usage of their words, the type of characters, the barbaric order of their construction, their unlearned phrasing, the force of their opinions, and their absurd subject matter, these books—like those mentioned before—manifestly betray themselves. It is certain that their inscriptions are adulterated and forged, containing nothing but pure impostures. It is clear that they have all gushed forth in our own age from a single cesspool of conspiracy, and they do not in the least savor of the language or antiquity of the *Chaldeans* and *Hebrews*. Nor do they recognize the dual character of the *Egyptians*—one for sacred matters and the other for profane. Meanwhile, they are filled with the most ruinous abominations...

## Book Two.

<margin>The Magical Elements of Peter of Abano.</margin>
The practitioner, while resting, is immediately snatched into an ecstasy <note>original: "extasin"; a trance-like state</note>, in which that being reveals itself who shall announce all things. In this way, oracles are also delivered through dreams, if—after other matters have been administered according to the prescription—the actor enters his bed with his thoughts fixed upon that thing which he desires to know, and falls asleep in that manner. Into these dreams the devil undoubtedly insinuates himself, when things so strongly impressed upon the imagination and thought still cling to the organs serving the imagination. Those things which are required in the invocation of an evil spirit are pursued with the same [mock] sanctity. Here, consecrated objects are also employed, necessary both for the defense of the invoker and his companions, as well as for the binding and constriction of spirits: such as sacred papers, metal plates <note>original: "laminae"</note>, pictures, pentacles, swords, scepters, and garments of suitable material and color. Seats are even set out for the spirits, who, once invoked, are invited to drink and eat. Following this is subjoined that most pestilential little book, entitled the *Heptameron*, or the *Magical Elements of Peter of Abano* <note>A famous 13th-century grimoire of planetary magic</note>.

<margin>The use of the Mass and baptismal water.</margin>
This book, like all others of that kind among the rejected readings, is most fittingly consecrated to Vulcan <note>i.e., committed to the flames/burned</note>. In it, the circle and its composition are described, likewise the names of the hours and the angels presiding over them—names far too barbaric—just as are the nomenclatures of the angels of the four seasons of the year. It includes also the consecrations and blessings of the circle and of the fumigations <note>incense offerings</note>, the exorcism of the fire upon which the fumigations are placed, and the garment and the pentacle made on the day and hour of Mercury, while the moon is waxing, upon paper—specifically the parchment of a kid-goat—whereon the Mass of the Holy Spirit has first been said and baptismal water sprinkled. There follows the mode of operation: an impious exorcism of aerial spirits and a blasphemous prayer to God, to be recited within the circle toward the four parts of the world; then visions and apparitions stirred up by the power of the exorcism, with the horrific invocation of the exorcist; likewise the absurd names of the angels of the Lord’s Day <note>Sunday</note> and its conjuration, as well as those for each individual day of the entire week.

# Book Two

He preserves [the art]: first, he arranges the names of the spirits themselves, then he organizes their conjurations <note>original: "adiurationes," referring to formal commands or oaths used to summon spirits</note>, and subscribes the characters <note>symbolic seals or sigils</note> of each one. Finally, he distinguishes the figures from which, according to the individual conjurations, the appropriate names of the spirits may be drawn and elicited whenever necessity arises. In these types of figures, he divides the spirits themselves into **four [ranks]: Emperors, Dukes, Counts, and Servants**.

He claims there are only twelve Emperors of the whole world, just as many as the winds are said to be by the philosophers. From these, he designates four as the principals: those of the **East, South, West, and North**, whom he calls the Great Emperors. Under each Emperor, he places **Dukes**, I believe thirty or forty of them. Under each Duke, in turn, are **Counts** in greater number, and under the Counts, innumerable **Servants**. In this manner, therefore, he turns to the execution of his art.

When he wishes to reveal his plans to a distant friend (for these he calls "secrets"), he writes, in place of a letter, a certain prayer affected with a pretense of wonderful holiness and devotion. He imprints it with the character of one of the twelve Emperors and sends it to the friend who (as he says) knows the art. Having received the paper, the friend opens it; at the foot of the letter, he first observes to which Emperor the character belongs. If it is the Prince of the East, he turns toward the East, spreads the letter open toward that region of the sky, and immediately searches his books for the conjurations by which that Prince may be compelled to send one of his subjects to him.

**He draws out two conjurations**; the first he utters over the still-open letter while looking toward the dawn. Once it is spoken, that Emperor immediately sends one of his subordinates—either a Duke, Count, or Servant—who, flying forth at once, becomes visible to the man from a distance, like a cloud or a mist hanging in the air. Then, when he has completed the words of the second conjuration, that spirit approaches nearer, coming close to his ears [to deliver] the desired [secrets] of the friend...

# Book Two

(Pliny writes that the battle line trembles and turns its back) <margin>Hippocrates, Book 14, Chapter 17</margin> <note>The author cites Pliny the Elder and Hippocrates to illustrate the terrifying power attributed to certain plants.</note> with *phanade*, *adamantide*, and similar terrifying monsters among plants used by the magi. By the singular goodness of God, these have now been erased from human memory for our benefit and utterly abolished; God wishes them to be entirely removed. Indeed, the number of these deceptive actions and things is immense, and it is better that they remain hidden. At the very least, it is useful to warn those who are too cautious or credulous, lest they be deceived and led astray by impiously dragging in divine names or wickedly twisting the words of Holy Scripture, as we have observed happening until now. They purge and excuse themselves for this most grave offense by claiming they invoke sacrosanct names and mix the Word of God into this diabolical craftsmanship <term>opificio diabolico: the "work" or "manufacture" of magic</term>, where by a horrible crime the most holy name of God is profaned, and by abominable abuse, the divine Scripture is defiled.

And although these idle men boast quite gloriously that they can summon demons or command them through these unjust and impious methods—and the demons seem to obey their illicit murmurs and nods as if bound and compelled—nevertheless, the demons hold these "masters" and "commanders" more closely bound and enslaved to themselves. These men are forced to place their faith in whatever demonic specters, ghosts, or deceptive images and mocking forms are presented to them. From this, however, they can never hope for much benefit, except that they please themselves more in this way and draw others into admiration of them, as if they were experts in uncommon or curious matters. Meanwhile, the demons pretend they are being compelled; although, as Porphyry <note>Porphyry of Tyros (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonic philosopher who wrote extensively on the nature of demons.</note> testifies, they actually desire to come so that they may thereafter ensnare others with their illusions. Jean Fernel <margin>Book 1, On the Hidden Causes of Things</margin> <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a prominent French physician who explored the intersection of medicine and the supernatural.</note> writes that he saw a certain man draw various specters into a mirror by the power of words; these specters would then express whatever he commanded, either in writing or in true images (as he says), so clearly that everything was promptly and easily discerned by those sitting nearby. ### *The Illusory Actions of Pharaoh’s Magicians. Chapter VIII.*

Furthermore, so that this story and the power—or rather the mockeries—of magicians may be more clearly exposed to everyone's sight and more deeply understood, come, let us contemplate with undeluded eyes and investigate with skillful inquiry the attempts, works, and power of Pharaoh’s magicians or sorcerers. Thus, satisfaction will be given to those who, whenever mention is made of certain deceived and mentally harmed "little women" <note>original: "muliercularum"; a dismissive term often used by period authors to describe those accused of witchcraft as victims of melancholy or delusion</note>, immediately take refuge in the example of Pharaoh’s voluntary magicians, as if the profession of both were the same; I perceive them to differ far and wide.

<margin>Exodus 7. The truth of the transformation in the work of Moses.</margin>
<margin>The illusion of Pharaoh’s magicians.</margin>

By this proof, he testifies that he was sent by the God of heaven and earth, the sole founder of all things within them (for to Him alone belongs the power to create and truly transmute things). However, when the Scripture says that the same thing was done by Pharaoh’s magicians through incantations, one who looks deeper into the matter will understand that it was not the same metamorphosis that was truly shown by Moses. Rather, at most, an illusory form of a serpent appeared, cast over the royal sight. For this reason, the lying face of the serpent of magical vanity was devoured by the true serpent of Moses, as a revelation of the trickery: so that the lie might be swallowed up by the truth.

*The Pythian woman in Endor did not raise Samuel, but a specter of the devil in his likeness.*

# Second Book

<page-num>175</page-num>

Once the words by which the demon was summoned had been uttered, the question was proposed. Then, at first, a thin sound without a voice was heard, which was the sign of the entering demon; afterwards, as the water surged, faint voices emerged from it, by which the question was answered. However, these voices were intentionally made very faint, so that the demon could not be caught in a lie regarding things it did not know.

<margin><term>Catoptromancy</term> <note>original Greek: Κατοπτρομαντεία; divination by mirrors or reflections</note></margin> This differed from the former method in that it delivered answers not by voice, but by pictures. Round glass vessels were set out, filled with the clearest waters, and lit candles were placed around them. When the summoning of the demon with a secret murmur was finished and the question put forward, a pure boy or a pregnant woman was employed to gaze intently and accurately into the glass and look around, and to ask, command, and demand answers. These the devil finally showed by images impressed upon the water and shining back through the transparent glass.

<margin><term>Catoptromancy</term></margin> One divines from bright and polished mirrors, in which the images of the proposed things, fashioned or returned by the devil, shine forth. The Emperor Didius Julianus <note>A Roman Emperor who reigned briefly in 193 AD; historical sources claim he used mirrors to foresee his fate</note> used this method; and it is written that he foresaw many things that happened by the warning of Satan.

<margin><term>Crystallomancy</term> <note>original Greek: Κρυσταλλομαντεία; divination by crystals</note></margin> From crystals crafted and polished—the devil playing his games within them (for in most of them he lurks hidden in a very minute form or sometimes stored in another material)—he announces to his Magi <note>practitioners of magic</note> the depicted marks and figures of events and sought-after things, as if prophesying.

<margin><term>Dactyliomancy</term> <note>original Greek: Δακτυλιομαντεία; divination by rings</note></margin> It is so called when sorcerers divine from rings crafted according to certain positions of the heavens, or consecrated by a demonic rite. Yet very many who use these forbidden modes of demonic divination live with far too much impunity among people of the Christian name. From a similar workshop, someone recently offered a ring consecrated with the same superstition to a nobleman for twenty crowns...

<margin>Hydromancy <note>original: "ὑδρομαντεία"</note></margin>
<gloss>Hydromancy</gloss> is practiced in various ways. A small cup was filled with water, and a ring suspended by a thread from a finger was balanced over the water; and so, with certain words conceived, a declaration or confirmation of the matter sought was demanded. If what was proposed was true, the ring, by its own nodding motion and not by being pushed, would strike the cup a set number of times. They say that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, often associated with religious and magical rites</note> practiced this, and consulted the gods summoned into the water. Other methods of this kind also exist.

<margin>Onychomancy <note>original: "ὀνυχομαντεία"</note></margin>
<gloss>Onychomancy</gloss> was performed by smearing oil and soot onto the fingernail of an unpolluted boy, with his fingers turned toward the light. For there was a belief that images of the desired things were formed from the mixture of oil, soot, and sunbeams; however, the devil, that craftsman of a thousand deceits, shaped these so that they seemed to be reflected and shine forth from this mixture on the nail.

<margin>Coscinomancy <note>original: "κοσκινομαντεία"</note></margin>
<gloss>Coscinomancy and Axinomancy</gloss> are used by Magicians to bind and uncover the hidden authors of crimes, and to manifest other obscure matters. 
<margin>Axinomancy <note>original: "ἀξινομαντεία"</note></margin>
They perform the latter with an ax fixed upon a round stake and adjusted to a level, and with a preface, they list the names of the suspects in order. At the mention of the person for whom the ax—even by a slight impulse—whirls around or nods, they declare that person guilty of the fault. Thus in Homer, the suitors of Penelope are said to have betrayed themselves by using a Jet stone <note>original: "Gagate"; a type of lignite coal believed to have magical properties</note> placed upon burning coals. They administer the former <note>Coscinomancy</note> with a sieve placed upon shears, the shears being grasped and lifted by only two fingers; and likewise, an adjuration is made through six words, understood neither by themselves nor by others: *dies, nues, ieschet, benedoeset, donuina, enite—*

However, in men, these impure spirits are unable to produce the sounds and voices of their prophecies with such foulness; instead, they are forced to speak through a more honorable part of the body, namely the mouth, as was said above regarding Eurycles, who was made famous by Aristophanes <note>A reference to the Greek comic playwright; Eurycles was a famous Athenian prophet believed to have a spirit dwelling in his belly.</note>. When Hadrianus Turnebus <margin>How these men prophesy.</margin> (then the Royal Professor of Greek literature, and later of Philosophy and Eloquence) was interpreting Aristophanes' *The Wasps* in Paris in the year of Christ 1560—while my sons, Theodore, now a lawyer, and Henry, a physician, were listening—it was openly discussed that he had once seen in Paris <note>original: "Lutetia," the Roman name for Paris.</note> a man very similar to that Eurycles of Aristophanes, a cunning fellow named Peter of Brabant. Whenever he wished, he would speak from the lowest part of his body; his mouth was indeed open, but his lips remained unmoved. By this means—whether by art, practice, or the deception of a demon—illegally imposed himself upon many people everywhere.

For instance, when he was desperately in love with a certain beautiful maiden in Paris who was fatherless, and he could not persuade the surviving mother to betroth her to him, they eventually spoke back and forth on the matter. He emitted a voice from his body which seemed to be the woman's deceased husband complaining about the severity of the punishments <margin>A fabricated complaint of a dead man concerning Purgatory.</margin> he was enduring in Purgatory because of his wife's lack of trust, specifically because she denied their daughter to Brabantio, an excellent man who had sought her so often. Terrified by these complaints and taking pity on her husband, she assented to the scoundrel's petition. However, it became quite apparent that he had sought not so much the daughter as the dowry settled on her by her father in his will. For six months later, when he had squandered the girl's goods, he abandoned both the wife and the mother-in-law and fled to Lyon.

# Book Two

<margin>Another son of his.</margin>
There, he had learned that a certain merchant and money-changer <note>original: "trapezitam," a banker or money-changer</note> of immense wealth had died. Since this man was considered most unjust, because he had scraped everything together during his life by hook or by crook <note>original: "per fas ac nefas," through right or wrong</note>, Brabantius approached his son Cornutus, his sole heir, who was walking in the portico behind the cemetery. He signaled that he had been sent to teach him what needed to be done. However, while he was telling him that he ought to think of his father's soul and reputation rather than his death, a voice was unexpectedly heard in the middle of the conversation, resembling the father. Although Brabantius produced this from his belly, he nevertheless feigned being wonderfully terrified. 

The son was moved by this voice, hearing into what state his father had fallen because of his injustice, and by what great tortures of purgatory <note>The Catholic concept of a place of purification after death</note> he was being tormented, both for his own sake and for the son's, because he had left him as the heir to ill-gotten goods. He claimed he could be freed in no way unless a just expiation was made by his son, and the required alms were bestowed upon those who were in the greatest need at that time. These, the voice said, were Christians captured by the Turks; therefore, he should believe the man who was speaking with him. Cornutus was told that this man had been dispatched by pious people to Constantinople to ransom them, and for that reason had been divinely sent to him. 

Cornutus, a man not at all wicked, did not perceive the trickery in these things he heard. However, because that word concerning "money" seemed harsh, he replied that he would deliberate on it, and ordered Brabantius to return to that place the following day. Meanwhile, being anxious, he began to doubt the place in which he had heard the voice, because it was shady and dark, and suited for human ambushes and echoes. Therefore, on the next day, he led him to another open, flat place, unhindered by any briars or shadows. 

Where, nonetheless, the same song was repeated during their talk, with this even added: that he should immediately count out six thousand Francs to Brabantius and ransom three Masses <note>Religious services offered for the souls of the dead</note> for each day for the salvation of his father; otherwise, there would be no redemption in the underworld <note>original: "inferos," the lower regions or hell</note>. Whereupon the son, bound by conscience and religion, although reluctantly, committed that very sum to the faith of Brabantius, with every legitimate receipt...

<margin>The Muhazzimin.</margin>
There is found in Fez, in Africa, a type of itinerant sorcerer and magician whom they call the *Muhazzimin* <note>a term for exorcists or those who use incantations</note>. These are said to cast out demons most readily of all; and because the outcome sometimes follows their prophecy, it is impossible to say how much that fact increases their reputation. If they are unable to cast one out, they assert it is an "aerial spirit" <note>a spirit of the higher air, thought to be more difficult to command than lower demons</note>. The method of adjuring the demon is generally this: first, they draw characters and several circles in a brazier or any other place; then they describe certain signs on the hands and forehead of the possessed person and fumigate him in strange ways. Afterward, they compose a song and inquire of the demon how and in what manner he entered here, who he is, and what his name is; finally, they command him to depart.

# _Book Two_

<margin>The magical divination of the Turks.</margin> Even today in the cemeteries or public marketplaces of Constantinople, Turkish men and women—especially those from Egypt, who were idolaters from the beginning—profess the art of fortune-telling, seeking their livelihood from it. These people prophesy by marking figures in the sand, or by casting tied dice and collecting the sum of the marks, while muttering and reading some unknown thing in a book. Or, mixing wax with oil, they wait until it has cooled and then divine from the characters that appear. Sometimes they predict the future using water, mirrors, glass, and similar instruments. They are undoubtedly so instructed by the master of impiety and <gloss>unbelief <note>original Greek: ἀπιστίας</note></gloss> that I would not hesitate to say they have sucked such poisonous milk, as if from their mothers' breasts, over a long series of years. 

Apuleius reports something similar regarding a certain soothsayer named Diophanes: <margin>Book 2 of _The Golden Ass_.</margin> "A certain Chaldean <note>A term often used in antiquity for astrologers or magicians from the Near East.</note> stranger at Corinth is now unsettling the whole city with his wonderful responses; for a fee, he proclaims the secrets of the fates to the common people: which day confirms the marriage bond, which makes the foundations of walls permanent, which is profitable for the merchant, which is favorable for the traveler, or opportune for ships. Finally, when I inquired about the outcome of this journey of mine, he gave many responses, both quite wonderful and varied enough." 

But the Erythraean Sibyl <note>A priestess presiding over the Apollonian oracle at Erythrae, famous for her prophetic verses.</note> testifies that all these things are false: <margin>Lactantius, Book 2 on the _Origin of Error_, chapter 17.</margin> <gloss>all these things are seen as deceptions, as foolish men do not have eyes to see <note>original Greek: ἰπὰ πλάων πάντὰ τάδ’ ὀρῶνται, ὡς ἄφρονες ἄνθρωποι ὀφθαλμοῖς οὐκ ἔχοντες</note></gloss>.

<note>original: "De magis infamibus"</note>

...and that he <note>referring to a demon or fallen spirit</note> should ever be thought to submit to the will of a human—a being inferior by nature and nearly equal in malice—is absurd. For he is a spirit noble by nature, yet most wicked in malice due to his rebellion. Would he, who refused to submit his nature to God the Creator, ever choose to surrender himself to a man against the laws of nature? How can one who violates the covenant of nature ever keep a pact for our benefit? Add to this that he is a liar and the father of lies <note>A reference to John 8:44</note>, twisting whatever is true toward falsehood and whatever is good toward malice. Who, unless they are of a disordered mind, would trust him to inquire about future truths? Such things he either does not know at all—because they are not known to his nature or have not been revealed from above—or if he does know them, he wraps them in lies with malicious craft. Even if he occasionally speaks the truth plainly, he does so either by compulsion or, if acting freely and willingly, it is with an evil intent and the worst possible end in mind. He does this so that he may strike more ruinously in the future; by offering some minor truth of little practical value, he later inflicts a more atrocious wound through another matter (which, unless fully understood, will bring grave trouble or destruction). That **Fisherman of Tartarus** <note>The devil, described here as a hellish fisherman using truth as bait</note> cautiously hides his lie like a poisoned bait or a deadly hook. Foolish, therefore, is the man who goes to consult him; but far more foolish is he who returns from it, unless he repents.

Meanwhile, I do not deny that since he understands the natures of things, he knows many things from natural causes before they are perceived by the human intellect. He knows them more exactly because his genius is more sublime. He announces these things to the ignorant like a thief, especially those things whose beginnings he has seen in action, so that he might be believed to prophesy and to have foreknowledge of the secrets of things. **Giovanni Francesco Pico** <note>Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola (1467–1533), a philosopher who wrote extensively against divination</note>, a distinguished philosopher, disputes this matter copiously, learnedly, and piously against magical foreknowledge in nine books *On Foreknowledge*, especially in Book 7. **Chrysostom** <note>St. John Chrysostom, an early Church Father</note>, in his *Homily 18 on the Gospel of John*, says: "The prediction of the future is the work of the immortal God alone." If demons have ever predicted anything, it is the foolish and incautious common people...

# Book Two.

<margin>Book 4, Chapter 14.</margin>
Wherefore Favorinus <note>A Roman philosopher and orator known for his skepticism</note>, as recorded in Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, author of 'Attic Nights'</note>, wishing to deter and drive away young men from those <term>casters of nativities</term> <note>original: "genethliacis"; those who predict a person's fate based on their birth stars</note> and others of that kind, who promise that they will tell all future things through prodigious arts, concluded with arguments of this sort that they should by no means be approached or consulted: "Either," he says, "they say adverse things will happen, or prosperous ones. If they say prosperous things and they deceive you, you will become miserable by waiting in vain; if they say adverse things and they lie, you will become miserable by fearing in vain. If they return true answers and those are not prosperous, you will become miserable in your soul from that moment, before you become so by fate. If they promise happy things and those are to come to pass, then clearly there will be two inconveniences: both the anticipation will weary you while suspended in hope, and that hope will have already withered the fruit of your future joy." Therefore, one must in no way employ men of this kind who presage future events.

Accordingly, I leave a more exquisite enumeration of these diabolical arts to those who have learned them, and who—by the counsel, leadership, and work of their master and teacher <note>referring to the Devil</note>—dare to practice them perpetually to their own destruction and that of others, whom they most ruinously lead into a fellowship of their nefarious crimes. It is a matter of grief, however, that this plague creeps so monstrously through the whole Christian world and rages too much: especially where the voice of the Gospel sounds more obscurely, and where the truth of divine worship seems to be defiled by I know not what pagan rites and superstitious rituals, undoubtedly devised by demonic cunning for the deception of men.

# On Infamous Sorcerers

They soon affirm it to be so: covering their own failure in the works of the sacred art with this veil, and slipping away no differently than that unlearned crowd of surgeons. They immediately attribute to the saints—such as Quirinus, Anthony, or any other—the gangrene, or necrosis, or spreading ulcers <note>original: "gangrænam uel sphacelum uel phagedænam"; these terms refer to various stages of tissue death and eating sores</note>, or other malignant ulcers that are stubborn to cure. These were not, however, so wicked from the beginning, but gradually degenerated into such malice through the ignorance of those treating them, based only on certain formulas for ointments and an uncertain, dangerous *medical neglect* <note>original Greek: ἰατροφία (iatrophia)</note>. Yet these truly evil-doers study how to cautiously decline the slander—or rather, the legal action that should justly be brought against them—under the pretext of this name of "sorcery."

Of this kind also are those "new men" who have recently become insolent from the smoke of the chemical fire, having crawled forth from the school of a certain 
<margin>Theophrastus Paracelsus.</margin>
Theophrastus Paracelsus—a man truly most foul-mouthed. They are the slaves of a peculiar arrogance, *self-love* <note>original Greek: φιλαυτία (philautia)</note>, and empty glory. From his book titled *Paragrammon*, they first committed to memory the most filthy words of an insane man, with which they stain, slander, reject, and busily trample underfoot the ancient and sacrosanct medical art. They have fabricated new principles with new words which they themselves do not even understand, nor can they defend with reason, content with the heap and pile of useless words with which Paracelsus filled his writings. He boasts that he is the monarch of medicine and the inventor of the true art; his followers likewise hold, worship, and venerate him as such. Thus, until now, that most useful of arts—and one especially necessary, if anything is, for preserving the human race—has been masked. # Book Two

<margin>Genesis 50</margin>
Joseph desired that the body of his father be embalmed with spices by physicians <note>original: "a medicis"; Joseph, son of Jacob, appears here as an early patron of medical practitioners</note>; likewise, Moses promulgated laws on behalf of physicians by the command of God. Similarly, the eulogy of 
<margin>Exodus 21</margin>
Jesus, Son of Sirach <note>Also known as the Book of Ecclesiasticus</note>, is not in vain, for he wished physicians to be treated with due honor because the Most High created them for necessity. Furthermore, it would be foolish to suggest that 
<margin>Matthew 9</margin>
Christ took a simile from something that did not exist in the nature of things when he taught that the healthy have no need of a physician, but rather the sick. The Book of Truth also testifies that Saint 
<margin>Colossians 4</margin>
Paul called and greeted Luke as a physician, and indeed a "beloved" one. These figures certainly cultivated the ancient medicine which is based on reason and confirmed by both experience and logic—the same medicine that we still practice today. 

I say nothing here of that "Monarch" and inventor of medicine supposedly arriving in these final days, Theophrastus Paracelsus <note>Paracelsus claimed to be the "monarch of medicine," a title the author clearly mocks</note>. Nor do I here dismiss chemistry <note>original: "chymia"; referring to alchemy as applied to medicine</note>, which is no small part of medicine and which I value highly, as do all the ancients with me. I congratulate our art that it is now so wonderfully adorned by it. However, I cannot yet bring myself to believe that its power can extract oils, or that powders and salts can be fashioned from sulfur, vitriol, antimony, and other such minerals and metals to cure any disease whatsoever. Nor can I believe that those various herbs—known to us through sight, smell, taste, and touch, which we have used with such happy success against diseases based on the testimony of experience—were not endowed with such excellent qualities from the very beginning.

But to proceed with my purpose: a certain leader of this school and a wandering pretender to nobility—whose name is unworthy of being publicized—was summoned within three months to a nobleman in the land of Jülich <note>original: "terra Iuliacensi"; a historical duchy in what is now western Germany</note>. This man promised a restoration of good health within a month. He heavily attacked the previous physician who had earlier applied a cautery <note>term: cautery; a medical instrument used to burn or sear tissue to treat a wound or infection</note> near the joints. They also understand that their medicines are not actually made from **purest gold** and **precious stones** dissolved by the force of fire—which they nevertheless boast about shamelessly enough so that they might more freely empty the coffers of the sick by demanding thousands of coins. Meanwhile, there is nothing less present in their medicines than gold or gems; and rightly so, since such things often contribute nothing to our medical purpose. Instead, they give the sick **poisons**, or things that are for the most part poisonous...

### On Notorious Sorcerers

<meta>The catchword "eſt ac" from the bottom of the previous page would lead into a sentence like "It is and...", though the text here begins with a fresh point.</meta>

I will not inappropriately introduce here, in passing, an opinion from the booklet of the elder ***Hippocrates*** <note>The famous Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>, or another memorable man (as ***Galen*** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries.</note> prefers), regarding the ***Sacred Disease*** or ***Comitial Disease*** <note>original: "Morbo sacro aut Comitiali"; both terms for epilepsy. It was called "comitial" because Roman political assemblies (comitia) were abandoned if someone had a seizure, seen as a bad omen.</note>, which the Greeks call ***Epilepsy***. In this work, after he had first demonstrated that there is nothing more divine in this evil than in other diseases, he spoke as follows:

<margin>*The excellent opinion of Hippocrates against cunning physicians and sacrilegious sorcerers.*</margin>

> Those who first proclaimed this disease to be "sacred" seem to me to have been the same kind of men as are now **mages** <note>original: "magi"</note>, **purifiers**, and **charlatans** <note>original: "circulatores"; literally "circulators" or street-performing quacks who gathered a crowd.</note>, and certain arrogant men who pretend to be exceedingly pious and to know something more. Thus, veiling and pretexting their lack of counsel and intellect with divinity, since they had nothing to offer that would be of benefit, and lest their ignorance become manifest, they proclaimed this affection to be sacred. Having gathered suitable reasons, they established a safe course of treatment for themselves: offering **purifications** <note>original: "expiamenta"</note> and **incantations**, and commanding the patient to abstain from baths and from many foods unsuitable for sick men to eat, and so forth. Then they prescribed that a black cloak must not be worn, for the color black is mortal; nor should one foot be crossed over the other, nor one hand over the other, for they claimed all these things were impediments to the cure. They attribute all these things to divinity, as if they know something more, offering other pretexts so that if the patient recovers, the glory and skill may be attributed to them; but if he dies, their excuses are placed in safety. They have a pretext that they themselves were not the cause, but the gods were. For they offered no medicine to be eaten or drunk that could make them seem responsible. And a little later: Thus, saying and devising such things, they pretend to know something more and deceive men, proposing **lustrations** <note>Ceremonial washings or purifications.</note> and purifications to them, since their words for the most part extend to God and the demonic. But to me, truly, they seem to speak not of piety, as they themselves think, but rather of **impiety**; and that their gods are not, and their piety and divinity are impious...

<summary>The author quotes Hippocrates' famous treatise on epilepsy to argue that healers who claim a disease is "divine" or "sacred" are usually charlatans hiding their own ignorance. Hippocrates exposes how these "mages" use rituals and dietary restrictions to ensure they receive credit for cures while avoiding blame for deaths.</summary>

# Book Two

...is and wicked, as I will demonstrate. For if they claim to be able to abolish the moon, obscure the sun, and create storms and fair weather, 

<margin>
Those who boast of having power over the air are impious.
</margin>

as well as rain and droughts, and to make the sea or the earth sterile, and all other things of this kind—whether they boast of this power from sacred mysteries, or from some other profession or meditation—whoever occupies themselves with such pursuits seems to me to be truly impious. They seem to believe that gods do not exist, or if they do exist, that they have no power, and cannot prevent even the most extreme evils. By doing this, how can they not be offensive to the gods themselves? For if a human being, using incantations and sacrifices, can abolish the moon, obscure the sun, and create storms or fair weather, I would certainly not consider any of these things to be divine, but rather human; for the power of divinity would then be surpassed by human will and reduced to slavery. 

Perhaps, however, these matters are not quite so: but rather, men who are in need of a livelihood <note>original: "uictūs indigi"; implying these "healers" are motivated by poverty and the need for money.</note> contrive and devise many diverse things, turning to all sorts of explanations for this disease, assigning the cause to God in each specific form of the affliction. For they mention these things not once, but repeatedly. 

<margin>
Later people, being excessively religious, replaced the names of idols with the saints of our own religion, to whom they dedicated those various types of epilepsy.
</margin>

Indeed, if the patients imitate goats, or if they let out a bleating sound and gnash their teeth, and if they are convulsed on their right sides, they say the **Mother of the Gods** <note>Cybele, an ancient Phrygian goddess whose cult involved frenzied music and dancing.</note> is the cause. But if they emit a sharper and more agitated sound, they liken it to a horse and say that **Neptune** <note>The god of the sea, also associated with horses.</note> is the author. If they even pass some excrement—which often happens to some patients under the strain of the disease—the name of **Hecate Enodia** <note>Hecate "of the Wayside," a goddess associated with magic, the night, and the underworld.</note> is invoked. If they produce a thinner and more frequent voice, like small birds, it is **Apollo Nomius** <note>original: "Apollo Nomius, id est pastor"; Apollo the Shepherd.</note>. If they discharge foam from the mouth and kick with their feet, **Mars** <note>The god of war.</note> bears the blame. Furthermore, whatever terrors attack by night, including fears, deliriums, leaping out of bed, horrors, and fleeing outdoors, they say these are the snares of **Hecate** and the assaults of **heroes** <note>Refers to the spirits of the "mighty dead" or ancestral spirits believed to cause madness.</note>; and for these they use expiations and incantations...

...mind, and they make the deity into something most wicked and impious (in my own judgment). For they perform purifications with blood for those seized by the disease <note>epilepsy, which the ancients often called the "Sacred Disease."</note>, and likewise for those defiled by other crimes, or the unjust, or those poisoned by men, or those who have committed some wicked deed. These are the very people who ought to be doing the opposite: namely, offering sacrifices and praying, and having gone to the temples, pleading with the gods. But now, they do none of these things; instead, they perform "purifications," and some of these cleansing offerings they hide in the earth, others they cast into the sea, and others they carry away to the mountains where no one may touch or tread upon them. However, these things ought to be brought to the temples and offered to God, if indeed God is the author. Yet I do not believe that a human body is defiled by God—that is, the most filthy <note>the mortal body</note> by the most pure <note>the divine</note>. But even if it should happen to be defiled by someone, or suffer some trial, the body would surely desire to be purged and purified by God rather than be further defiled.

<margin>Hippocrates' Christian-like sentiment. <note>original: "Christiana Hippocratis sententia." The author is highlighting how the ancient Greek physician's view of divine purity aligns with Christian theology.</note></margin>
Therefore, it is God who purges and purifies the greatest and most wicked sins, and who stands as our liberation. We ourselves designate the boundaries of temples and shrines for the gods, so that no one who is not pure may cross them; and as we enter, we are sprinkled with water—not as if we are being defiled, but so that if we have some prior crime, we may be purified. And regarding <term>expiations</term> <note>religious rituals intended to provide atonement or cleansing from sin</note>, this is how the matter seems to me. Truly, this disease appears no more divine to me than the rest; rather, it has a nature like other diseases, and a cause from which each arises. Its nature and cause come from the same God from whom all other things come. Thus far Hippocrates: whose arguments I have seen fit to recount at length, as they are not useless to our purpose.

# Book the Second

<margin>Nero discovered that the magical arts are empty.</margin>
Nero discovered that the magical arts were empty and utterly false. Indeed, it is said that his passion for the lyre and tragic songs was no greater than his craving for magic, as his supreme fortune in human affairs spurred on the deep-seated vices of his soul. First of all, he desired to command the gods, and there was nothing he wished for more nobly. No man ever favored any of the arts more strongly. To this end, he lacked neither wealth, nor strength, nor the talent for learning, and other resources that the world could hardly endure. He remains a vast and certain example of the falsity of that art which he eventually abandoned. The <term>Magus</term> <note>a member of a priestly caste from Persia skilled in astrology and ritual</note> Tiridates had come to him, bringing other magicians with him, and had even initiated him into magical banquets:
<margin>† elsewhere: "had invited."</margin>
yet, even when Nero gave him a kingdom <note>Nero crowned Tiridates I as King of Armenia in 66 AD</note>, he was unable to receive this art from him. Consequently, he was persuaded that it was unstable, ineffective, and empty, possessing only certain shadows of truth. However, in those shadows, it was the <term>poisonous arts</term> <note>original: "veneficas pollere artes." The author distinguishes between "magic" and "venificium," which involves harmful sorcery or poisoning</note> that prevailed, not the magical ones. Nero, having been perhaps too curious in investigating the magical arts, abolished them because he had perceived no sign or proof of certain truth in them. For their vanity had crept so far that they were an object of hatred and even execrable to the wise pagans. The practitioners of these arts are also forbidden and condemned by the most severe mandate of God in Leviticus, and also in 
<margin>Leviticus 19, 20.

<margin>Why the moon is said to be drawn down from heaven.</margin>
As Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman historian and philosopher (c. 46–120 AD).</note> relates, Aglaonice <note>original: *Aganice*; a Greek astronomer of the 2nd or 1st century BC, often called the first female astronomer.</note>, the daughter of Hegetor of Thessaly, was skilled in the eclipses of the stars during full moons. When this woman predicted these events to credulous, simple women, it was believed that she was drawing the moon down from the sky by her chanting. The emptiness of the pact is also shown by this: once entered into, they are forced to observe certain ceremonies against the statutes of the Church. <margin>Matthew 17.</margin>
<margin>1 Peter 4. 5.</margin>

<margin>Book 1 of *On Christian Doctrine* and it is read in 26, question 2, that which is.</margin>

<margin>Euchites and Gnostics.</margin>
To the aforementioned trifles, I would like to add from Psellus <note>Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine scholar whose works on demonology were influential in the Renaissance.</note> concerning the Euchites <note>A sect also known as Messalians, often accused of heretical rituals.</note> and Gnostics, who are said to perpetrate unspeakable sacrifices so that they might conceive demons with their whole heart. ## On the depraved imagination of melancholics. Chapter VII.

<margin>The corrupted imagination of melancholics.</margin>
Furthermore, lest it should seem too absurd that the instruments of the imaginative faculty <note>The "imaginative faculty" was considered a physical part of the brain in medieval and Renaissance psychology that processed sensory data.</note> in these poor women are corrupted in this way, and the keenness of their eyes distorted (as I have shown before), consider the thoughts, voices, visions, and actions of melancholics <note>In the humoral theory of medicine, "melancholy" was an excess of black bile, believed to cause depression, delusions, and even madness.</note>. You will understand how all the senses are often depraved in these people because of the melancholic humor occupying the brain and altering the mind. Some believe themselves to be brute animals, imitating their voices and gestures. Some think they have been turned into earthenware vessels; for this reason, they yield the way to those they meet so they won't be broken in a collision. Others fear death, yet sometimes inflict it upon themselves. Many imagine themselves guilty of crimes, so that, being fearful, they shudder at whoever they see entering their presence, fearing they will be seized, led away as captives, and dragged to the tribunals to be punished. A certain noble old man, sometimes leaping suddenly from his seat, believed he was being attacked by enemies; these he would seize and, in his own opinion, shove them all together into an oven behind him. Another feared that Atlas, who sustains the whole world on his shoulders, would grow weary and, exhausted, cast off his burden, so that everyone would be crushed by the intolerable ruin. I knew an Italian melancholic who believed he was the monarch and emperor of the whole world, and that this title belonged to him alone; otherwise, he was well-composed, eloquent, and afflicted by no other disease. I saw one who stubbornly refused food and drink, imagining he had been condemned. There are those whom a conscience full of scruples torments so miserably that, "seeking knots in a reed" <note>A Latin idiom (*nodos in scirpo quaerere*) meaning to look for difficulties where there are none.</note>, they imagine guilt where there is none; and...

...distrusting divine mercy, believing themselves destined for the underworld <note>original: "orco"; in this context, the author refers to Hell.</note>, they constantly deplore their fate with diligent lamentations night and day. However, the mind of this priest <note>original: "sacrifico"; literally one who performs sacrifices, here used for a Christian priest.</note> was damaged, just like that man who promised he would compel the Archangels Gabriel or Michael to come to him, and that they would give answers to great questions when interrogated. I also know of a case where someone suffering from the vice of melancholy <term>melancholia: a condition believed to be caused by an excess of "black bile," leading to depression or delusions</term> would shout that someone smelled of sulfur and pitch, and would judge any food offered to him to taste of pepper. It was recognized that these perceptions were as far as possible from the truth of the matter. Likewise, he asserted that his private parts were so corrupted by inflammation and stench that he feared gangrene was beginning to develop, while in the meantime those areas remained free from any defect. Countless other examples could be heaped up here, where you may see all the senses corrupted in various ways by that single humor, or by the smoky vapor of black bile <note>original: "atrae bilis"</note> infecting the seat of the mind, from which it is certain those fantastical monsters are produced. Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> also teaches in his work *On the Differences of Symptoms* that the imaginative faculty is sometimes entirely corrupted and dissolved by other humors, as in catalepsy <term>catalepsis: a physical state of rigidity and loss of consciousness</term>; but most often it is corrupted as in delirium. There are also times when it fails and is weakened, which happens in lethargy <term>lethargus: a state of prolonged sleepiness or lack of energy, then considered a medical disorder</term>. Therefore, why should the devil, as a spirit, not be permitted—with God's connivance—to insinuate himself into the organs of the senses and stir up humors or vapors convenient for himself...

## On the Phantasy, and How It Is Corrupted.
### Chapter VIII.

<margin>The Phantasy.</margin>
Regarding the phantasy <note>The mental faculty we now call the imagination</note>, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher from the 3rd–4th century AD</note> writes thus: "The phantasy is innate to all powers of the soul; it shapes and fashions all likenesses of mental forms and appearances. It transmits visions or impressions from some powers into others: those which flash from the senses, it stirs into opinion; those which come from the intellect, it offers to opinion in the second place, but within itself, it receives images from everything." This faculty certainly fashions and expresses all actions of the soul and adapts external things to internal ones. Here, Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous Renaissance philosopher (1433–1499) who revived Platonic thought</note>, the Platonist, in his explanation of Priscian the Lydian—the philosopher who interpreted Theophrastus’s book *On Phantasy and Intellect*—says in Chapter 2: "The imagination fashions the actions of reason under the condition of sensible things, and it can produce phantasms <note>mental images</note> more widely than the acts of the senses. It surpasses the sense; for because it produces images even when nothing is moving it, the imagination is like a Proteus <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will</note> or a chameleon." The same author says in Book 13, Chapter 1 of *Platonic Theology*: "Four effects follow the phantasy: appetite, pleasure, fear, and pain. All of these, when they are intense..."

...each thing [is perceived]. For this reason, only those who understand [this] tremble and fear. Add to this that when the objects of the senses are absent, their mental images <term>phantasmata: mental representations of sensory perceptions that remain in the mind after the object is gone</term> remain, and imaginations persist, as **Aristotle** testifies in the second book of *On the Soul*. From there, through the local motion of the sensory forms remaining in the **faculty of imagination** <note>original: "uirtute phantaſtica"</note>, along with the humors in which they are contained as if in a vessel, things appear that do not exist. Thus, in the book *On Sleep and Wakefulness*, the same author says: when a great deal of blood descends to the sensory center, the forms conceived in the imagination descend at the same time. *For the imagination is a certain storehouse of forms received through the senses.* For this reason, demons can move the humors and the spirits <term>spiritus: the subtle vapors that early modern medicine believed traveled through the nerves to communicate between the mind and body</term> of the internal and external senses. By doing so, they can introduce certain appearances into the organs, just as if the things themselves were truly occurring to us from the outside, whether we are sleeping or awake.

Furthermore, **Aristotle** teaches in his book *On Dreams* that the images appearing in dreams are carried to the head and the sensory organs, just as the images of clouds are raised up, and different faces of animals are represented in the watery or earthy vapor which is carried from the earth by the sun’s heat into the middle of the air. In this way, the images of dreams take on different shapes following the vapors that are raised up. Thus, a hot and dry **choleric** vapor <term>choler: yellow bile, associated with fire and a hot, dry temperament</term> seems to stir up flames. But when a **phlegmatic** vapor <term>phlegm: a cold and moist humor</term> rises, it is recognized by its sweetness when it flows to the organ of taste, and it produces dreams involving water. But from the black **melancholic** vapor <term>melancholy: literally "black bile," the humor associated with heaviness, fear, and sadness</term>, something horrible appears, appearing as an image of demons. Therefore, the devil willingly inserts himself into this humor, as if it were the most suitable material for his deceptions <note>original: "ludibrijis"; refers to the devil's "play" or "mockery" of human perception</note>. Furthermore, that which rises from **burnt choler** <note>original: "cholera aduſta"; an overheated or "scorched" state of bile believed to cause the most severe forms of melancholy and madness</note>, which is accidental melancholy, is felt as stinging, wounding, sharp, and imbued with the bitterness of gall. Similarly, that which evaporates from **pure blood** appears beautiful and delightful, such as the sight of roses or flowers, dances, music, and whatever pleasures are joined with vanity. And in this manner [illusion] occurs...

<header>### Book Three.</header>

<margin>The Inn</margin>
**Peter Damian** <note>An influential 11th-century monk and cardinal known for his writings on church reform and miracles</note> tells of two old women on the public road that leads to **Rome**, whom **Augustine** calls "innkeepers" <note>original: "stabularias"</note>—that is, those who take in travelers for a fee (for a "stable" <note>original: "stabulum"</note> is strictly called a public and commercial lodging). These two, dwelling in a single hut and both steeped in the same wicked craft, would sometimes transform a traveler arriving alone into a horse, a pig, or a donkey, and sell them to merchants for a set price. One
<margin>The fiction of a youth changed into a donkey.</margin>
day, they received as a guest a youth who earned his living through **theatrical gestures** <note>likely an acrobat or mime</note> and turned him into a donkey. They made a great profit from him, for he entertained passers-by with the miracle of his movements; he moved in whatever way the old women commanded or gestured. His intellect had not perished, only his speech. The old women made a huge gain from this. When a neighbor found out, he bought the donkey at a high price. However, this warning was given by the women: that he must be guarded so that he did not go down into the water. Having been kept from water for a long time, he finally found himself under less careful guard and threw himself into a nearby lake. By rolling about there for a while, he was **restored to his own form**. When his keeper met him and asked if he had seen the donkey, the youth replied that he was the donkey. The servant reported this to his master, and the master reported it to **Pope Leo** <note>Pope Leo IX (1049–1054)</note>, a most holy man of that age. The convicted old women confessed to the deed. When the Pope doubted, **Peter Damian**, a most learned man, confirmed it by citing the example of **Simon Magus** <note>A biblical figure often depicted in folklore as a powerful sorcerer who could change his appearance</note>, who had impressed his own image upon Faustinianus. A wondrous story about King Duff, harmed by witchcraft, if it were true.

I shall present a remarkable story on this subject from the historian Hector Boethius <note>Hector Boece (c. 1465–1536), a Scottish philosopher and historian known for his often legendary history of Scotland.</note>, which was nevertheless refuted by Girolamo Cardano <note>An influential Italian polymath and physician (1501–1576).</note>, so that from this case, other narrations of this kind may be judged in the same way. The story goes as follows: King Duff fell into a disease that was not so much severe as it was difficult for even the most learned physicians to recognize (taking into account the lifestyle and physical constitution of the Scots at that time, whom foreign diseases had not yet invaded). Indeed, without any sign of bile, phlegm, or an excess of any other faulty **<term>humor</term>** <note>In ancient medicine, the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern health.</note>, or a lapse from the natural human temperament, the illness gradually afflicted Duff. For by night, lying down under a perpetual sleeplessness, he was dissolved into an immense sweat; by day, scarcely relieved from the pain he had suffered at night, he would give himself over to rest. His body was consumed by a slow wasting, very much like one who is exhausted.

His skin clung rigid, showing to onlookers the veins, nerves, and the very form and position in which the human bones were set. The motion of the spirits from the heart was smooth and uniform; the touch of the heart-vein and artery demonstrated that the **<term>vital moisture</term>** <note>original: "vitale humidum"; a concept in humoral medicine referring to the fluid necessary for life and internal heat.</note> had not exceeded its proper balance. He possessed a lively color, and the vigor of his ears and eyes was intact and temperate; he had a rather frequent appetite for food and drink.

Since the physicians wondered at these signs of health in a man languishing and afflicted with much pain, and though they had performed what was their duty, they found nothing by which the superfluous and harmful sweat might be restrained, or which might provoke sleep; instead, the king was tormented more and more every hour by sweat and continuous sleeplessness. Turning to the consolation of the patient (for in their opinion, this was the only thing left to do), they prayed that he might hope for the best regarding his health and not lose heart, for it would be that external [remedies...]
