For this reason, **Titus Livy** <note>The famous Roman historian who wrote the history of Rome.</note> rightly abstained from such things, **Herodotus** <note>The "Father of History," often criticized in the Renaissance for including tall tales.</note> is justly condemned for them, and **Saxo Grammaticus** <note>A 12th-century Danish historian known for recording the legends of the North.</note> is praised. 

Furthermore, it is most relevant that Boece found these things already written down, and the event itself lies outside the bounds of traditional history. However, in the recounting of history itself—such as the customs of the nation, the wars, the battles, the number of the slain, or the names of those who took part in battles or conducted themselves vigorously, the origins of families, the causes of wars, the reckoning of time, and the deeds and succession of princes, which serve as the very limbs of history—he was most diligent. 

Indeed, in those matters pertaining to history, there was nothing so small—such as the location of the region and cities, their size, the towns, islands, groves, mountains, new types of plants, four-legged animals, birds, serpents, fish, the fertility of the soil, the changes of the winds, the mildness of the sky, the pools, marshes, distances, and all other rare things useful for understanding history—that he neglected, omitted, or described differently than it truly was. In such matters, he believed the history should be adorned, either because he believed them to be true, or perhaps because he had not been initiated into the sacred mysteries of philosophy.

I warned the man not to proclaim such things further, lest he be considered a fool and run the risk of his life. Therefore, he threw himself into difficult business affairs; and with his way of life changed, while enjoying the company of others, he returned to his senses. The retention of seed and menstrual blood is also a cause for many of this disease, or its origin or its increase.

In general, this deception consists of three main things: the images produced by **black bile**, the persistence of those who are seized by this blight, and the fraud of the judges. For formerly it was permitted that the same people who accused should also condemn, and to them the goods of the condemned would return. ### *The foolish fantasy of witches, and the falsehood of stories on that subject, as demonstrated from the Danish history of Saxo Grammaticus. Another charming example of a delusional woman is added. Chapter XV.*

So that this fantastical folly may be most clearly evident to everyone's eyes, I will faithfully set down a story from Saxo Grammaticus <note>original: "Ioanne Grammatico"; referring to the 12th-century Danish historian Saxo Grammaticus, author of *Gesta Danorum*.</note>, woven by him among other things as if it were true. However, anyone who brings it back to the scales of reason will easily judge it to be purely false, or remarkably adorned with lies (which I say with the leave of a man who is otherwise learned)—specifically, whether one can obtain the supreme gift of reason and eloquence, and the gift of successfully dealing with things by hand, through the tasting of a pleasing, or rather virulent, feast. Thus he writes in Book 5 of the *Danish History*: 

Eric and Roller were the sons of Regner the fighter, born of the same father but of different mothers. They called the mother of Roller, who was also the stepmother of Eric, Craca <margin>The saga of Craca:</margin> <note>original: "Craca saga"; "Saga" here refers to a wise woman or witch in Nordic contexts.</note>. Furthermore, he saw three snakes hanging from above by a thin rope, from whose mouths a flowing poison dripped liquid into the meal drop by drop. Two of them were pitch-black in color, while the third appeared whitish with scales and hung slightly higher than the others. This one was held by a knot in its tail, whereas the others were held by a cord passed through their bellies. Thinking this matter was consistent with sorcery <term>maleficio</term> <note>harmful magic or witchcraft</note>, he kept what he had seen in silence, lest he be thought to be accusing his mother of witchcraft <term>veneficij</term> <note>the crime of poisoning or sorcery</note>. This part was composed of the more potent dark substance. By pushing the white part, which had first been placed near him, toward Roller, he managed his dinner more fortunately. To ensure his clever maneuver was not noticed, he said, “In this way, when the sea is surging, the stern is often turned into the prow.” This was no small display of the man's ingenuity, masking his calculated deed with metaphors borrowed from common nautical practice.

And so, Eric, now refreshed by this auspicious feast, attained the highest peak of human wisdom through its internal workings. Indeed, the power of that meal, beyond what one might believe, implanted in him such an abundance of all knowledge <note>original: "scientiarum copia"</note> that he was even skilled in interpreting the voices of wild beasts and cattle. For he was not only most expert in human affairs, but he could even translate the sensory sounds of animals into an understanding of specific emotions. Furthermore, he possessed such courteous and ornate eloquence that whatever he wished to discuss, he would immediately polish it with the charm of proverbs.

But when Craca came in and saw that the bowl had been moved and that the better part of the porridge had been eaten by Eric, she grieved that the fortune prepared for her son had instead passed to her stepson. She soon began to plead with him through her groans, asking that he might never fail to help his brother with his own power—a brother whom his own mother had intended to shower with so many riches of newfound happiness. For by the savory taste of that meal, Eric had gained the height of reason and eloquence, as well as the grace for conducting conflicts successfully...

### That the air can in no way be disturbed by witches: and how they are led by the devil into this belief in their own power. Likewise, that crops are not spirited away by charms. Chapter XVI.

<margin>How witches are deluded by the demon in the stirring up of the air.</margin>
These little old women are furthermore mocked by the devil in a singular way concerning the stirring up of the air. As soon as the devil foresees—more quickly and easily than men—a change in the weather or storms arising from the movement of the elements and the course of nature; or if he understands that a plague is to be inflicted by the hidden will of God (the execution of which pertains to him), he then agitates the minds of these poor women. He imbues them with various images and multiple suggestions, making them believe that they themselves are about to disturb the air, stir up storms, and provoke hailstorms, whether out of envy toward a neighbor or for revenge against an enemy. 

And so he instructs them to sometimes throw ferns <note>original: "filices"</note> behind their backs toward the west; at other times, to throw the sand of a rushing stream into the air; often to dip a broom into water and sprinkle it toward the sky; or to make a small pit and, having poured in urine <note>original: "lotio"</note> or water, to move a finger within it. Frequently, they boil pigs' hair in a pot; sometimes they place beams or wood crosswise on a riverbank and perform other such delusions <note>original: "deliramenta"</note>. To entangle them more tightly, Satan fixes a day and an hour already known to him by the natural signs mentioned before. When these women see the success—that is, the arrival of the desired disturbances in the air—they are even more confirmed in their belief, as if the event followed their own actions, when in truth they could not draw out even a single drop of water. Nor does it befit a person of sound mind to think that the elements obey the futile actions of insane women,

<meta>catchword: menta, (the conclusion of the word "elementa" or elements)</meta>

<summary>Weyer argues that witches have no actual power over the weather; instead, the devil observes natural signs of coming storms and tricks the women into performing useless rituals so they believe they caused the weather themselves.</summary>

This would undoubtedly happen if storms, rains, hailstorms, and lightning were at their disposal, following them whenever and however they commanded. In this way, divine power would be overcome by human will, as if reduced to slavery, as Hippocrates beautifully teaches. Therefore, this sentiment from Seneca is correct:

<margin>In the booklet on Epilepsy <note>Though the margin cites a work on epilepsy, this quote is famously from Seneca's *Natural Questions*, Book 4.</note></margin>
> The ancient, unrefined times believed that rains could be drawn down or repelled by chants; it is so obvious that none of these things can happen that one does not need to enter the school of any philosopher to understand this matter.

If, however, they have convinced themselves that they can perform something extraordinary through a wicked curse or a certain mumbling of words, I would say with Socrates,

<margin>Words of incantation can do nothing.</margin>
that incantations are words that deceive human souls, either through interpretation, or through the instilling of fear, or through despair. I feel these things are not worth a hair, since in truth they can produce no natural effect. For that reason, they cannot even change health into sickness, even though little old women falsely believe they can. Yet, such diseases are often summoned and inflicted by the devil, with God's connivance <note>or "permission"</note>, because of the lack of faith of these people and their poorly conceived opinion regarding the power of witches. I wish the same to be said of crops, which can in no way be harmed by the words of incantations or curses, but rather by a demon (with God's permission) or by actual poisonings <term>veneficiis</term> <note>The Latin *veneficium* can mean both sorcery and the literal administration of poison.</note>. Much less can crops be transferred elsewhere, even though the ancients drank in a different opinion from the breasts of the poets, which has also been passed down to us. Hence that law of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BCE.</note> is famous:

-> AWAY ANOTHER'S STANDING CORN BY CHARMING <-
-> IT: THEY SHALL NOT INCANT, NOR SHALL THEY <-

<margin>Pliny, Book 18, Chapter 6.</margin> C. Furius Cresinus teaches us what the real "chants" and "sorceries" are by which crops are lured away and transferred into another's field. Having been freed from slavery, Cresinus was earning much more abundant harvests from a very small plot of land than his neighbors were from their vast estates. Consequently, he was held in great envy, as if he were luring away others' produce through evil spells <term>maleficijs; harmful magic or sorcery</term>. For this reason, he was summoned by Spurius Albinus on a day of the curule chair <note>A formal legal summons before a Roman magistrate.</note>. Fearing conviction, and when the tribes were about to vote, he brought all his rustic equipment into the forum. He led forth a sturdy daughter who was (as Piso says) well-cared for and well-clothed, along with excellently crafted iron tools, heavy mattocks, weighty plowshares, and well-fed oxen. Then he said: "These, Citizens, are my sorceries. I cannot show you, or bring here into the forum, my late-night labors, my vigils, and my sweat." And so, he was acquitted by the unanimous vote of all.

Therefore, I am rightly compelled to wonder greatly, and to grieve deeply from my soul, that in recent years—even in those parts of the Empire and neighboring places where the voice of the Gospel is believed to ring out most clearly—magistrates have not turned the eyes of their minds toward the hand of God (either testing or punishing) when a vineyard has been ruined by a storm or a harvest cut down while still in the blade. Instead, neglecting God, they have looked toward numerous little women of delirious and slippery minds. They have dragged them into squalid dungeons—dwellings of demons—and into grim torture chambers. There, having been driven to confess to the storms being stirred and the losses being brought about, these women were solemnly consecrated to Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcano solenniter consecratæ"; a classical euphemism for being burned at the stake, Vulcan being the god of fire.</note>. However, there is no doubt that they were deluded in their minds by the devil, who corrupted their imagination with mockeries and illusions, so that they confessed to having done things they could not do. This is just as often the case with the possessed, the melancholic, those pressed by the nightmare <term>incubo; a sensation of being crushed during sleep, often attributed to a demon</term>, werewolves <term>Lycaones; people suffering from the delusion of being wolves</term>, dog-men <term>cynanthropi; a similar delusion of being a dog</term>, the demented, the foolish, and children. For the air and the elements do not obey the will and power of a malicious woman or any other wicked person, so that...

To speak frankly, it is an absurd error if anyone believes that the devil is subjected to the command of a delirious, old, and malicious woman. She is indeed subject to him in such a way that she often yields to his will in thought, speech, and deed; however, he is certainly not able to obey her beck and call at his own whim, even if both desire the same thing. This is because he is always compelled to obey the command of God alone, and occasionally the command of His faithful ministers. In the destruction of things by the force of the turbulent air, or in any other manner, the "spirit of storms" awaits the nod and consent of the one God whenever God intends to either test or chastise His own people. His true ministers, in the name of Christ, are able to cast out demons from time to time. 

Therefore, it was fitting for both the magistrate and the common people—who believe their eyes are fixed upon the light and rays of truth—to be led toward a different opinion. If these mad old women were actually able to perform what they confess to, scarcely enough grain would remain to sustain the human race. Indeed, nothing in the natural world would remain uncorrupted, nor would man himself survive. Furthermore, there would be no need for such great preparation in wars, where every kind of weapon and the most pestilential materials are forged at the greatest expense...

### Book Three.

...[of the de]vil's <note>Completing the word "diaboli" from the previous page</note> instruments in wars, why should it be denied to our witches <term>Lamiae: a term for witches, originally referring to a child-devouring demon in Greek mythology</term>? Who, in no ordinary way—at least according to the opinion of these people—are able to destroy everything, throw heaven and earth into confusion <note>original: "caelum terrae miscere," a Latin idiom for causing total chaos</note>, and bring the enemy into line, even without the shedding of blood, if you so wish: or with his most severe torments, at their own will and whim, without any hesitation, and without expense? I frequently mourn from my heart that this persuasion regarding the power of witches, derived from lying poets, has struck such tenacious roots even in the minds of many pious people. But it is certain that our sins deserve that harsh scourge <note>The author suggests that God allows people to be deluded by these beliefs as a punishment for their sins</note>.

Although it will be objected that humans perpetrate said crimes by the impulse of a demon, and conversely, that the devil operates here also from the suggestion and will of wicked people, I respond that these things do not necessarily follow. It is necessary to distinguish between the substances of things from which actions are produced. For the property of a demon—a ministering spirit of God <note>The author views demons as fallen spirits who are still ultimately part of God's created order and subject to His limits</note>—is one thing; that of a terrestrial human is another. He [the demon], indeed, as a spirit, can insinuate himself into a person and agitate them, whence the person is called "demoniac" or "possessed by a demon" <note>original: "daemoniacus, uel a daemone obsessus"</note>. However, a terrestrial human cannot in turn force themselves into a demonic spirit so that they might similarly borrow the name and operate through it.

While a cruel war was raging between the kings of Denmark and Sweden in the year 1563, it was written from the Danish camp that the King of Sweden was leading four old witches <term>Lamiae</term> around among his troops, who by their chant <note>original: "carmine," meaning a spell, incantation, or ritual song</note> might hinder every victory for the Dane, so that he could do no damage to the enemy. Furthermore, those who were besieged by the King of Sweden would be rendered powerless and prone to surrender. And although no faith had previously been given to this rumor, it was later written that one of these witches was captured by a soldier of the noble Count Gunther of Schwarzburg <note>Gunther XLI, Count of Schwarzburg-Arnstadt (1529–1583), a prominent German military commander</note>, the leader of the army, who confessed these things.

## Book Three

...embrace the blessing and grace of the heart in the abundance of the grain supply <note>original: "annonae," referring to the yearly harvest or grain market</note>.

Nor should I omit here that, around the time when that disastrous storm afflicted the provinces of Upper Germany, I also, by the chance of my affairs, suffered a not-insignificant loss from a storm of hail—or rather of ice—in the territory of Ravenstein <note>A historical lordship in the present-day Netherlands</note>, not far from Grave <note>A fortified city in the Netherlands</note>. This storm so scattered and shook out the crops, which had been successfully harvested and arranged in the field in bundles of four to dry (as is the custom among us), that you would have said they were completely threshed and the field sown anew. Consequently, the farm manager <note>original: "uillicus," a steward or bailiff of an estate</note> did not wish to replant the field for the coming year, but only to turn the earth with the plow, as it was saturated with more than enough grain and made fit for returning a profit. I also saw branches from the trees, cut as if by an ax, scattered here and there through the fields by the violence of that ice. However, this wind blew in a straight path, rather than being scattered, so that the neighboring fields on either side felt almost nothing or very little of the misfortune. Yet to the pagan Virgil <note>The Roman poet (70–19 BC)</note>, such a disturbance of the air near harvest time did not seem so miraculous, as he wrote in the first book of the *Georgics*:

> Often I, when the farmer led the reaper into the golden fields, and was already stripping the barley from its brittle stalk, have seen all the battles of the winds clash together, which far and wide would tear up the heavy crop from its deepest roots and hurl it on high; just so with a black whirlwind would winter carry away both the light stalk and the flying stubble. Often also an immense column of waters comes from the sky, and clouds gathered from the deep mass together a foul storm with black rains; the high heaven falls, and with a great deluge it washes away the joyous crops and the labors of the oxen; the ditches are filled, and the hollow rivers swell with a roar, and the sea seethes with breathing inlets. The Father himself <note>A reference to Jupiter in Virgil's original, though Weyer's readers would interpret this as God</note>, in the midst of a night of clouds, flashes...

Those who consider this candid admonition to pertain to themselves will surely remember these things, presented with sincerity and singular zeal of mind. If, however, it should please many men of a peevish disposition to kick back, or to grow insolent toward me either petulantly or in earnest, they may do so for all I care—provided they do not labor against the testimony of conscience and truth, and provided the glory of God and the peace and utility of the Christian commonwealth are sought.

Indeed, the peasants have offered a very easy handle for this disbelief, as they are less confirmed in a living trust in God. In many ways even at this time, according to their disbelief, they are harassed by Satan, so that at one time they think milk has been taken away, at another time a fetus, at another the crops, and at another even the herd has been killed by <term>Lamiis|Witches or female night-monsters from folklore</term>. They refer the entire logic of agriculture not to the blessing of God in true faith, but to the mere whims of <note>original: "anicularum," referring to "little old women," often used disparagingly for those accused of witchcraft</note> old women.

<margin>Book 16, *On Subtlety*, exercise 349.</margin>
I shall add the words of the most learned man **JULIUS SCALIGER** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a celebrated Italian scholar and physician</note> to Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous polymath whom Scaliger frequently criticized</note>: You say that the constancy of the evildoer <term>maleficium|the act of performing harmful magic</term> contributes to the efficacy of the harm. Did you think that the emotion of any person acts upon anyone other than the one whose emotion it is? Nor is it true that a human can be harmed by another human through words. For who taught him those words? Not another man. For who taught that one? Not a heavenly intelligence. For who would dare to make such an intelligence the author of a charm <term>fascinum|the "evil eye" or a binding spell</term>? Therefore, it is the evil demon: not to make the man more powerful, but to deceive him with his own credulity, and to have him as a companion both in impiety and in eternal destruction. Thus, the demon himself acts; that foolish and senseless man thinks he acts by his own voices.

Furthermore, on the contrary, someone might perhaps object that rain can be stirred up by spells for harm by evildoers, since it is established from written law that some evoke rain for the sake of health. For there is Law 4 in the *Codex* under "On astrologers and sorcerers" <note>original: "C. de mathemat. & mal." referring to the *Codex Justinianus* 9.18.4</note> by Constantine, which admits those who are able to obtain rain through prayers, spells, or medicines, or anything that pertains to the health of men, etc. <term>Bartolus|Bartolus de Saxoferrato (1313–1357), one of the most influential continental jurists of the Middle Ages</term> says there: "The sum and intent of the law is, in my opinion, that if anyone uses these arts for the utility of men, they are permitted—as <term>Josephus|Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</term> writes concerning Solomon in Book 8, chapter 2—which are otherwise forbidden in themselves, and especially if they are turned to someone's destruction." To this I respond briefly, with all due respect: I believe the Christian Emperor [Constantine] believed there was some power in these things, no differently than many others, and indeed most <term>laypeople|original Greek: ἰδιῶται (idiotai), meaning common or unlearned persons</term> and poets. From this it follows that he did a great injury to God in this matter—thinking that God could be compelled to grant us this or that not by pious vows and prayers for the forgiveness of sins, but by impious protestations and incantations. Indeed, he opened a wide window to the devil when, having abandoned the true God, he considered what he might achieve through the ministers or ministries of Satan.

## *On natural sleep-inducing medicines, by which Witches are sometimes deceived; likewise on their ointments, and certain sleep-bringing plants that intensely disturb the mind.*
### Chapter XVI.

<margin>Witches are sometimes deluded by Satan through the use of natural medicines.</margin>

<margin>Chapter 26.</margin>
of Naples, writes in Book 2 of *Natural Magic*, or *On the Miracles of Natural Things*: "So dreadful a desire," he says, "has invaded the minds of men, that they abuse those things which nature has bestowed for the convenience of mortals; by heaping many of these together, they compose the ointments of witches. Although they themselves mix in a great deal of superstition, it is evident to anyone looking closely that the effects occur through natural power. I shall report what I have learned from them.
<margin>The ointments of witches.</margin>
They obtain the fat of boys by boiling it in a bronze vessel with water, thickening that which settles at the very end of the boiling process. Then they store it and put it to constant use. With this they mix <term>wild celery|eleoselinum</term>, <term>aconite|aconitum; also known as wolfsbane</term>, poplar leaves, and soot. Or it is made another way: <term>water parsnip|Sium</term>, common <term>sweet flag|acorum uulgare</term>, <term>cinquefoil|penthaphyllon</term>, bat's blood, sleep-inducing <term>nightshade|solanum somniferū</term>, and oil. (And if they mix different ingredients, they will differ little from these). They prepare these together and rub them onto all parts of the body, having rubbed the skin beforehand so that it grows red and heat is recalled, making thin and porous what had been thickened and tightened by the cold. In order that the flesh might be relaxed and the pores opened, they add fat—or oil serving in its place—so that the power of the juices might descend deep within and become more potent and vigorous; I have no doubt that this is the cause of the effect. Thus, on a moonless night, they seem to be carried through the air to banquets, music, dances, and sexual unions with handsome youths, which they especially desire. So great is the force of the imagination and the habit of these impressions, that almost that part of the brain called the 'memory' becomes full of such things. And since they are themselves very prone by nature to belief <note>The author suggests women are naturally more impressionable or "gullible" in the view of 16th-century medicine</note>, they seize upon these impressions in such a way that their <term>spirits|the "animal spirits" thought to circulate in the nerves and brain</term> are transformed, thinking of nothing else day or night. They are aided in this by the fact that they eat nothing but beets, roots, chestnuts, and legumes <note>beans and lentils</note>."

This monk had previously driven a nail through the layman's other hand, and had persuaded the layman of everything under the appearance of the Holy Virgin. They did this to abuse his simplicity and madness, along with three other religious brothers who were aware of the fiction, for the sake of confirming their own order's standing. For this reason, the drugged man was even placed upon the altar in the chapel of the Blessed Virgin, where, as if seized by catalepsy, he remained motionless to the point of astonishment in the sight of the gathered crowd, with his knees bent...

### *Concerning the illusion of the demonic incubus, and the natural disease of the incubus. Chapter XVIII.*

<margin>
The imaginary intercourse of a demon with a woman.
</margin>
From here, let us now approach the phantoms <note>original: *laruas*</note> of incubi and succubi <note>In folklore, an incubus is a male demon that lies upon sleepers; a succubus is the female counterpart</note>, investigating diligently and at greater length what truth is nurtured in these matters: so that this phantom of false belief may be shaken once and for all from the minds not only of the common folk, but also of the prudent. Therefore, since old women—deluded and driven mad by the witchcraft and trickery of this heresy—think they are being pressed down by a demon and suffering incubi, it will be demonstrated by the most evident reasons that this sexual union (like almost everything else) is purely imaginary, arising from a damaged mind, or that at most a tickling sensation is stirred by some friction or other, with the imagination of the act added: and that no true intercourse occurs.

For while I was a virgin living in Galilee, an angel of God entered into the house where I was staying. Not while I was sleeping, but while I was awake, he announced to me that I would bear a son through the Holy Spirit <note>original: "è Spiritu sancto"</note>, and he commanded me to give him the name JESUS. Thus, while I was a virgin, I conceived through that vision; and I gave birth to JESUS, remaining a virgin to this very day."

Neither can it happen by nature, nor does philosophy agree, that spirits stripped of bodies could be seized by the love of women, or be able to procreate from them. For desires have their own source and lower origins: if the cause is missing, the effect is missing. <margin>A spirit does not have flesh and bones. Luke 24 <note>original: "Spiritus carnem & ossa non habet."</note></margin> Where there are no reproductive organs, there is no desire for intercourse. Where there is no food and drink, there is no seed. Where succession and propagation were not required, nature did not provide the desire for procreating. Just as naked spirits <note>This refers to incorporeal beings like angels or demons who lack a physical "coat" of flesh.</note> cannot thirst or hunger, so they cannot be inflamed by the lust of Venus <note>A classical way of referring to sexual desire or "libido."</note>. It is also absurd to claim that there are two kinds of demons: both the angels themselves who fell into lust, and the souls of the Giants. For the Giants were men, and demons should not be made out of men; nor was it their "fall" that they burned with love. Therefore, the demons of these stories are mythical—both those supposedly seized by lust and those born from them. They would be just like Hector, Achilles, Aeneas, and Hercules in the works of the Poets: born from humans and gods. These are the words of Agostino Steuco <note>An influential 16th-century Italian scholar and Vatican librarian.</note>: from whose opinion, proven by reason and truth—although Lactantius <gloss>in his specific hypothesis</gloss> <note>original: "ἐν ὑποθέσει"</note> may differ—he does not depart <margin>Book 1 of *On Religious Instructions*, chapter 8. Eusebius relates a no less notable instance of adultery involving Saturn. A priest of Saturn, named Tyrannus, acting as if giving a divine response from the deity, used to speak to all the noble and leading men who were worshipping in the temple—those whose wives had pleased him for his own lust. He would say that Saturn had commanded that the man's wife spend the night in the temple. Then, once silence fell, he would creep through secret passages and subterranean entrances into the hollow cavities within the statue of Saturn itself. For that statue was hollowed out from behind and carefully attached to the wall. With the lights burning inside the shrine, he would suddenly bring forth a voice through the hollow bronze statue to the woman—who was intent and praying—so that the unhappy woman would tremble with both fear and joy, because she thought herself worthy of a conversation with such a great deity.

### *That all stories confirming the fiction of diabolical intercourse are merely fables. Chapter XXX.*

<margin>

### Of Witches
<margin>Chapter 26.</margin>
<margin>In the treatise *On Witches and the Spirit of Divination*.</margin>

That same Vincent <note>Vincent of Beauvais, a 13th-century Dominican scholar</note> writes of a miracle of the same credibility from Geoffrey of Auxerre <note>A Cistercian abbot and disciple of St. Bernard of Clairvaux</note> in Book 3; reporting that a certain dean of priests had lived for some time in that kingdom with the sister of the Duke of Burgundy (who was betrothed to King Roger of Sicily). Speaking to her, he could not extract even a word; therefore, having covered her with a cloak, he led her home and finally took her as his wife in a solemn ceremony.

Having been rebuked at one point by a companion for having embraced a phantom <note>original: *phantasma*; here meaning a spirit or apparition</note>, he grew terrified and, drawing his sword, threatened his spouse that he would kill the son he had fathered by her unless she spoke and confessed her origin. She said, "Woe to you, wretched man, you are losing a useful wife while you force me to speak. I would have remained with you, and it would have been to your benefit if you had allowed me the silence imposed upon me. But now, you shall not see me hereafter." And she vanished instantly. The boy, however, grew up and began to frequent the sea-baths. Finally, one day, in the presence of many, that phantom woman snatched the boy as he met her in those same waves.

Ulrich Molitor, Doctor of Laws <note>A 15th-century legal scholar known for his influential dialogue on witchcraft, *De Lamiis et Pythonicis Mulieribus*</note>, judges that this boy was a demon appearing in the form of a child, and the mother was a <term>succubus</term> <note>a demon in female form believed to have sexual relations with men</note>, which is to say, a demon. Likewise, he considers the knight [who fathered Merlin] to be an <term>incubus</term> <note>a demon in male form believed to father children with humans</note>, and Merlin to be a changeling <note>original: *suppositicium*; a fraudulent substitute</note> born from a mother deceived by the demon's trickery. But to me, these are merely fables upon which far too many people in that blind age wasted good hours and committed them to paper for posterity.

However, because of the pain, the woman in labor fell into a **faint** <note>original: "deliquium"; a loss of consciousness or swoon</note>. When she came to herself, she felt she had been delivered of her burden. But the boy was nowhere to be seen, which made everyone wonder beyond measure. 

It happened, however, the next day, that while the mother was waking from sleep, she found the infant next to her in the bed, wrapped in swaddling clothes; she even offered him her breasts once or twice. Yet not long after, while she was sleeping again, the infant was snatched from her side and was never found again. They said that I know not what papers with **magical signs** <note>original: "magicis notis"; symbols or characters used in folk magic or sorcery</note> were found in the lock of the door. My brother-in-law related these things to me—a man truly as famous for his nobility, learning, and piety as he is most worthy of trust—who, being joined by marriage to Antoine, heard these things from the woman’s husband, from his brother and his brother's wife, and from others who had often been present.

Furthermore, lest I seem to act the part of **a silent character** <term>original: κωφὸν πρόσωπον (kōphon prosōpon); a "mute" or "dummy" role in Greek theater</term>, standing stunned in this so skillfully arranged drama, I wished to briefly add what I feel about this. Since this matron, **possessed by a demon** <note>original: "daemonio obsessa"</note>, believed she was suffering witchcraft at the hands of an innocent mistress, her torment first increased by the hidden permission of God’s will, and the devil devised these more serious **mockeries of pregnancy** <note>original: "impregnationis ludibria"; the author suggests the entire pregnancy or birth was a demonic illusion designed to deceive</note>, her womb...

### On Witches <note>original: "De Lamyis"</note>

Then these women of unsound mind believe that the evil which appears was constructed by a demon, or otherwise born from the hidden will of God, or a defect of nature: especially since they think, through a false persuasion, that they are imbued with a new power from some silly or blasphemous muttering or malicious curse. Thus recently at Hamm <note>Hammonæ: likely the city of Hamm in Westphalia</note>, a certain Hessian judge recounted that he had asked a certain celebrated and notorious witch <term>saga: a female sorceress or wise-woman; Weyer uses this to denote someone accused of witchcraft</term>—whom he was then holding in chains, and who was later "consecrated to Vulcan" <note>original: "Vulcano consecratam"; a classical euphemism for being burned at the stake</note>—by what means a person might avoid the evil spells <term>maleficia: harmful magic or "black" witchcraft</term> of witches? And she answered in all seriousness: that one should keep old shoes, worn out and consumed by age and much use; as if, truly, by their work, evil spells could be inflicted. Whose mind is so stunned that he does not perceive these to be trifles?

<margin>Vile things or drugs buried in remote places cannot cause harm.</margin>
It does not seem probable to me that even distinguished and learned men should think that vile things or harmful drugs hidden somewhere could induce harm when stepped over or passed by from a distance, or that they could be violently carried from even the most remote space toward those they target, as if shot from a bowstring. For if such virulence is inflicted by the innate power of a poison, it must necessarily strike anyone who either steps over it or passes by, since poisonous matter is incapable of choosing its victim. Experience and the reality of the matter teach otherwise. But if only those toward whom those old women bear ill will are harmed, the harm does not happen by the breath of poison, but by the logic of sorcery. 

I have already shown that such a thing has no power to that extent; since, however, harm seems to follow from this, it remains that the harm is stirred up by Satan himself, with God's permission, either because of the lack of faith of the person being harmed, or so that he may be tested here as Job was <note>Refers to the biblical Book of Job, where God allows Satan to test a righteous man’s faith through suffering</note>. It is he who blinds and maims. Meanwhile, the demon firmly suggests and persuades the mind of this old woman—who buried the poisonous material or whatever else—that what was perpetrated by him, or what happened otherwise, was done by her, so that she believes and asserts it was her own doing.

# *Who are properly called poisoners, and memorable examples of poisonings.*
## Chapter XXXVI.

But now let us proceed to the **Poisoners** <note>original: *Veneficos*</note>, or, if the word were allowed, "Venom-makers" <note>original: *Venenificos*</note>. The Greeks call them *pharmakeas* <note>original: $\phi\alpha\rho\mu\alpha\kappa\acute{\epsilon}\alpha\varsigma$; those who deal in drugs or charms</note>, as well as *pharmakeutas* <note>original: $\phi\alpha\rho\mu\alpha\kappa\epsilon\upsilon\tau\acute{\alpha}\varsigma$</note>, and *pharmakeutrias* <note>original: $\phi\alpha\rho\mu\alpha\kappa\epsilon\upsilon\tau\rho\acute{\iota}\alpha\varsigma$</note> for the women—those initiated into a most destructive art which one may call <term>Poisonous Magic (Magia venefica)</term>, if you wish. It is well established that these people stir up dangerous diseases with the most cruel symptoms by administering drugs or poisons made from any substance—whether from the category of metals, plants, animals, or excrement, or from mixed bodies—whether given as a drink, smeared on, or hidden somewhere so that they strike by their vapor <note>Weyer is referring to the historical belief that "venomous" substances hidden in a room could infect the air and kill through inhalation.</note>. Some they lead into a wasting away of the body and a weakening of the strength; for others, they dissolve the structure of the joints and torture them with various agonies; some they torment with long-lasting sickness; and for many, they cut short their life headlong, as if the thread of life were suddenly snapped, sometimes with intolerable pains.

<margin>Sabellicus, Enneads, Book 4, Chapter 4.</margin>
<margin>Horrendous poisonings.</margin>
Horrendous are the things that Antonius Sabellicus <note>Marcantonio Sabellico (1436–1506) was a renowned Venetian historian. Here he recounts an event from ancient Rome, originally recorded by the historian Livy.</note> writes in these words: "An infamous year followed, during the consulship of Marcus Claudius Marcellus and Titus Valerius Flaccus (or Potitus, as others have written) <note>This refers to the year 331 BCE.</note>, when many of the leading fathers of the Senate died of a similar illness and outcome. A certain slave girl came to Quintus Fabius Maximus, the <term>Curule Aedile (a high-ranking Roman magistrate responsible for public order)</term>, and declared that she would reveal the cause of that slaughter if she were given a promise that this disclosure would not bring her harm from her masters. After Fabius reported the matter to the Consuls, and the Consuls to the Senate, and after immunity was granted by the consensus of the order, it was revealed that this slaughter happened through the fraud of women: that there were many women who were cooking poisons for the destruction of their husbands, and if they would go with her, it would result in many being caught in the act of poisoning. Men were sent to follow the slave girl; they found certain women [cooking] medicines..."

Around the year of our Lord 1536, nearly forty men and women entered into a conspiracy, among whom was the executioner himself. Since a plague had previously raged and was just beginning to subside, they prepared an ointment. By smearing this on the bars of the city gates, they infected those who handled the bars. They also prepared a powder which they secretly sprinkled on clothing to spread the disease. For some time the trick remained hidden, and many were carried off—even those joined by blood or marriage. It was even said that money was paid to these poisoners for the sake of securing inheritances. 

But when they had *murdered the brother and only son* of a man named Necius, and it was noticed that hardly anyone was dying except the masters of the houses or their sons, suspicions arose. At the same time, they observed that a woman named Androgina was sneaking into houses, and that those whose homes she entered were the most likely to die. Once the conspiracy was uncovered, they were all put to death with the most exquisite tortures. They also confessed that they had planned to slaughter the entire citizenry by smearing the benches during a crowded procession for a certain Saint; more than twenty jars had been prepared for this purpose. The same thing was later attempted in Geneva...

It is also established that others in Milan greased the door-bars <note>original: "uectes inunxiſſe"; this refers to the "untori" or "anointers," individuals accused of spreading the plague by smearing infectious ointments on door handles and bolts.</note>; but when subjected to interrogations, since they confessed nothing and no one had died, they were released. **Bassianus Landus** <note>A 16th-century Italian physician and philosopher from Piacenza.</note> writes that in Padua, a certain monk repeatedly conspired with many others who, during a time of plague, secretly threw infected linens into houses so that the contagion would spread to many; they also suffered punishment.

In the noble **Petrini** family of **Bologna**, there were two brothers, one of whom, a married man with a numerous offspring, lived in the same house with his widowed mother; the other, however, the younger one, in the hope of obtaining the entire inheritance, decided to do away with the whole family by throwing arsenic into a wine vat. When they were tortured by severe symptoms from its use, the most famous physicians were called together: **Matteo Corti**, **Giovanni Maria Betti**, and **Hispanius Philippaldus**. They soon came to suspect poison because they realized that neighbors, who had by chance entered the house and drunk that wine, were also tormented by the same agonies. Therefore, on their advice, the vessel was broken, and once the wine was poured out, arsenic was found. From this point, the physicians began treatment and restored everyone, except for the mother, a weak old woman, and an infirm boy. The poisoner took flight, and thus the perpetrator of the poisoning became known. This crime happened in August of the year 1538.

<margin>Helidaeus Paduanus of Forlì, physician.</margin>
Furthermore, in **Bologna**, a certain murderous son-in-law offered his mother-in-law Spanish flies <note>original: "cantharides"; these are blister beetles containing cantharidin, a toxic substance that causes severe irritation and bleeding in the urinary tract.</note> mixed with an extract of cassia. When she was so cruelly afflicted with torments of the bladder that she even passed a large amount of blood from the bladder, **Master Helidaeus Paduanus of Forlì**—a most famous physician very experienced in the practical works of the art—cured her with great success; just as **Master JOHANNES ECHT**, a most distinguished physician of Cologne and formerly his pupil, recounted...

The girl, having confessed to the poisoning, was sentenced to death; however, through the intercession of others on account of her youthful age—for she had scarcely reached her fifteenth year—she was again granted the benefit of life and committed to life in prison. From there, after a few months, soldiers freed her by breaking the iron bars. I have chosen to recount this crime as briefly as possible so that anyone, taught by this example, might look after their own affairs more providently.

I also saw an old woman who, out of jealousy, had given arsenic with some vegetables to her innocent husband, from which he died with the most bitter tortures; she, however, was submerged in water as a public punishment.

When the governor <note>original: *satrapa*</note> saw her, looking beardless, and thinking her to be the official from Arnhem, he asked whether at such a youthful age he dared to strike off three heads at once? She replied that this task should be entrusted to her, and that this was not the first time she would appear on that "theater" <note>An old term for the public scaffold where executions were viewed like a play.</note>, as she had frequently "tested that same risk" before. She then seized the ropes with which she was to bind the prisoners.

The Prefect, along with his entire retinue, was struck with utter amazement. Having soon learned the truth from the executioner's servant—whom he forced to confess the truth under oath—he ordered the defendants to be returned to custody. ### On love potions, hippomanes, and other amorous trifles. Chapter XXXVIII.

<margin>Love potions</margin>
To this subject also belongs the love-cup or *drug* <note>original: *pharmacum*</note>, called a *philtron* <note>original: φίλτρον</note> by the Greeks. This substance corrupts the senses, stirring up various hallucinations and furious passions in those who take it. Juvenal mentions it:

<margin>Satire 6.</margin>
> One man brings magic incantations; another sells Thessalian
> **Love potions**, with which they have the power to vex a husband's mind.
> <note>original: *Philtra, quibus ualeant mentem uexare mariti.* Thessaly was famous in antiquity as the land of witches.</note>

To this we may also refer the verses of Laelius in the first *Apologia* <note>A defense speech against charges of magic</note> cited by Apuleius:

> They root out all kinds of **love potions** from every side:
> The *Antiphates* <note>A black stone or coral believed to have protective properties</note> is sought,
> Little wheels, fingernails, ribbons,
> Small roots, herbs, twigs,
> Golden oaks, two-stringed charms,
> And the "sweetnesses of whinnying horses."

<margin>Hippomanes</margin>
In this category of poisoning or sorcery <note>original: *veneficij*</note>, a place is held by the <term>hippomanes</term> <note>literally "horse-madness"; a legendary substance used in philters</note>. This is a notorious little piece of flesh, about the size of a dried fig, round in shape, somewhat flat and black in color. It appears on the forehead of a newborn foal. The mother, immediately after giving birth, devours it by licking and wiping the foal. If it is snatched away beforehand, she feels a total aversion to her offspring and will not allow it to nurse. Because of this, they say it possesses the greatest power to incite love when it is turned into powder and drunk in cups mixed with the blood of the beloved. Hence Pliny says that a "poison of love" is born in horses. Mention of this has been made by Aristotle, Solinus, Columella, and others—likewise Virgil:

<margin>
Aristotle, *On the History of Animals*, Book 6, Ch. 18 & 33. Book 8, Ch. 42. Columella, Book 6, Ch. 27.
</margin>

The name given to this poison is <term>ἱππομανές</term> <note>Transliteration: *hippomanes*. Formed from the Greek *hippos* (horse) and *mania* (madness).</note>, because it ignites the torches of love in men, much like the unbridled lust of a mare. Into this, he had included hippomanes—not with such accurate craftsmanship that the horses should have been driven to such a frenzy by its mere appearance—and yet it attracted them so much, and drove them with such madness, that they would break their reins and rush <unclear>violently</unclear> toward it.

Among these love poisons are also numbered: the hair from the tip of a wolf's tail and its "rod" <note>Referring to the animal's penis, often used in medieval and ancient talismans.</note>, the *remora* <note>The "suckerfish," believed in antiquity to have the power to stop ships in their tracks.</note> fish, the brain of a cat, and lizards—specifically the gecko known as the *stincus*. Likewise, a bone from a green frog that has been eaten away in an anthill: for they say that by the touch of the bone from the left side, love is excited, while the right side causes discord. Or, as others report, the bones of a frog eaten by ants are cast into water; some of these float on the water, and some sink. Those that float, when bound in white linen and hung upon the person, win love, while those that sink produce hatred in the person touched by them. Another similar experiment involves swallow chicks: those of a single brood or nest are taken, placed in a jar, and buried in the earth so that they perish, suffocated by hunger. Later, when they are dug up, those found dead with their beaks gaping open are used for love; those with closed beaks serve to provoke hatred. It is also claimed that if a man binds the womb of a hyena to his left arm and looks upon a woman, it is effective for his purpose. These potions are also sometimes composed of excrement, or animals born from rot, or from materials innate to our own bodies—which, however, being illicit, deservedly disturb and change the mind rather than compel it to love. Thus the drinking of the menses of women, especially those who are bilious and quarrelsome <note>In the "humoral" theory of medicine, "bilious" or choleric people were thought to be hot-tempered and prone to anger.</note>, so fascinates and infects those who drink it that it renders them moon-struck and insane. There are also other "philtres" <note>A philtre is a drink or charm intended to arouse love or desire.</note> taken from the clothes of the dead, from candles, needles, and generally from those things prepared for the sake of funerals; these are gathered all the more willingly because they contain more nonsense than truth...

## That love potions, hippomanes, and all other things of that kind, induce madness more quickly than they procure love.

### Chapter XXXIX.

Furthermore, it is the opinion of many notable men that philtres, <term>hippomanes</term> <note>A substance associated with mares in heat or a growth on a foal's forehead, famously used in ancient sorcery.</note>, and whatever else of that kind, have little or no power in truly procuring love, but rather stir up madness more quickly. > Nor try the harmful virus of a mare in heat. <note>original: "nocens uirus amantis equæ"</note>
> Snakes are not split in half by Marsian <note>The Marsi were an Italian people renowned in antiquity as snake-charmers and wizards.</note> chants,

# On Poisoners

<margin>Love incantations are utterly vain.</margin>
Among the first Christians, it seems to have been believed that love could be won through the magic art, as seen in the law issued by Justinian <note>Flavius Justinianus (r. 527–565 AD), the Byzantine Emperor who codified Roman law.</note> in the *Code*, under the section "On Sorcerers" <note>original: "C. de malefi." referring to the Codex Justinianus, Book 9, Title 18: *De maleficis et mathematicis*.</note>, in those words: "Or if they are discovered to have turned the minds of modest friends to lust by magic arts." However, Saint Epiphanius of Palestine <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his "Panarion" (Against Heresies).</note>, in Book 1, Volume 2, Section 30 of his work *Against Heresies*, teaches that love incantations of this kind—by which the chastity of women is attacked—are utterly vain when the name of Christ and the sign of the cross are set against them. A noteworthy history confirms this. Furthermore, that Sicilian constitution which begins with the words "Love Cups" <note>original: "Pocula amatoria"</note> considers it frivolous and mythical that such cups could extort love. Read also the story written by Saint Jerome in the *Life of Saint Hilarion* (Book 5, Chapter 12) regarding a virgin dedicated to God who was solicited for love by a young man using the magic art; there you will see my own opinion added in a few words.

# On Sorcerers
<meta>catchword: -rations</meta>

"Enough with these slanders," said Olympias. "For you do not carry potions in your luggage." <note>original Greek: "αἱ διαβολαί. οὐ γὰρ ἐν σκευῇ φάρμακα ἔχεις". Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great, said this to a woman accused of using witchcraft to enchant the king; she realized the woman's "magic" was simply her own beauty and character.</note> "Farewell," she said, "to these false accusations: for you possess the power of <term>sorcery</term> <note>veneficium: here meaning the "poisoning" or "enchanting" power of a love potion</note> within yourself." And she was no longer angry with the girl, nor with her husband. To this point belongs that saying of Menander <note>A famous Greek comic playwright (c. 342–291 BC).</note> found in Stobaeus's *Anthology*, chapter 65: <margin>True love-charms.</margin> "A kind character is a true love-charm; by this, a woman is accustomed to conquer her husband." <note>original Greek: "ἐστ' ἀληθὲς φίλτρον εὐγνώμων τρόπος, τούτῳ κατακρατῶν ἀνδρὸς εἴωθεν γυνή."</note> Within lies the true <term>philter</term> <note>a love potion or charm</note>—kindly manners—by which a woman is wont to win over her husband.

And indeed, these are the true "sorceries" of love. For if any wives use other <term>philters</term> and amorous drinks, we should loathe and despise them. Just as Plutarch asserts in that book he wrote *On Preserving Health*: it follows by a similar reasoning that wives should detest husbands who employ such things. And as the same Plutarch writes in his *Advice on Marriage*, just as fishing by means of drugs <note>referring to the practice of poisoning water to stun fish</note> catches the fish quickly and easily, but spoils them and makes them quite unfit for the table; so those who attempt to subdue their spouses with amorous arts and incantations for the sake of pleasure end up living their lives with people who are stunned, senseless, and ruined.

For Circe <note>The enchantress from Homer’s *Odyssey*.</note> (as he adds) was not helped at all by those she had drugged, nor did she make any use of them once they had taken the form of asses and swine. But Ulysses, who possessed his wits and behaved prudently with her, she pursued with incredible love. So says Plutarch. Therefore, having exploded the myths of <term>philters</term> and magical vanities, let us strive to obtain the love of our wives through mutual love toward them, and with other women through chastity and whatever other honorable and pious pursuits. In this way, the fourteenth law of marriage <margin>On the Laws of Marriage.</margin> of the most learned and celebrated legal scholar André Tiraqueau <note>A famous 16th-century French jurist known for his works on marriage law.</note> shall remain inviolate:

-> Husband and wife shall utterly abstain from incantations, potions, and other magical <term>philters</term> of that kind, by which love is believed to be procured: <-

But rather, let them rely on mutual affection between themselves and other honorable means <meta>continuation of the sentence ending in the catchword "rationibus" (means/reasons)</meta>

### How sorcerers harm animals,
### Chapter XL.

<margin>Sorcery destroys animals.</margin>
Furthermore, sorcerers harm and destroy animals by throwing drugged fodder in their path, or by scattering it elsewhere so that it might be tasted or inhaled. I by no means deny that the same can be achieved through rubbing or external application; however, it is important to remember that some people intentionally hide wolf dung in stalls. When the livestock notice this by smell and fear their voracious enemy, they are driven into a wondrous frenzy due to a certain <term>antipathy</term> <note>a natural, instinctive repulsion between certain animals, like sheep and wolves</note>. As a result, the ignorant firmly believe the animals are being tormented by witchcraft, and they seek advice from the very "experts" of this sorcerous art. For the same reason, they say that a wolf’s tail hung in a stall for oxen or horses scares them away from eating. For, struck by fear because of the scent, they forget their food even though they are hungry; just as we experience happening to humans in times of great fear.

In the Duchy of Württemberg, not far from Tübingen, an executioner who was well-versed in <term>sorcery</term> <note>original: "veneficij" - this term encompasses both poisoning and witchcraft</note> displayed a specimen of his skill upon livestock in the year 1564. Indeed, since by legal agreement the hides of dead animals and other useful parts fell to him <note>as the "knacker" or person responsible for disposing of carcasses, the executioner profited from the remains of dead livestock</note>, he secretly killed oxen, sheep, and pigs in the pastures with poison. As a result, by selling an excessive number of hides, as well as an almost infinite weight of tallow and fat in Augsburg <note>original: "Augustæ Vindelicorū"</note> and Strasbourg <note>original: "Argētinæ"</note>, he became wealthy in a short time. Therefore, when suspicion arose, he was accused of sorcery and, subjected to the interrogations familiar to him, he confessed to the whole matter. He paid the penalty, being torn apart with glowing-hot tongs...

# Book Four.

...by the artifice [of a foolish woman] <note>The word fragment "-tulæ" likely completes a word like "stultæ" (foolish) or "aniculæ" (little old woman) from the previous page.</note> were they thus agitated in varied ways beyond nature, miserably driven mad, physically contracted, torn, and pulled apart? But by whose art does Scripture <note>original: "Scriptura"</note> testify that they are oppressed by this dire calamity? By the Demon’s. By whose cooperation or command? By no one else’s, but only by the malice of the demons' own will and by God's permission through His secret counsel, so that they might be tested, punished, or corrected. Nor will you find anywhere in the vast volume of the Old and New Testaments an example where Satan used or even required the work of some <term>witch</term> <note>original: "Lamiæ" — Weyer uses this term to refer to those accused of witchcraft.</note> in afflicting bodies. ### Chapter II. Concerning monstrous things cast out from the mouth, which many arguments show were never inside the body.

<margin>Materials cast out from the mouth were not all [originally] inside the body.</margin>
To this belongs the rejection of monstrous things through the mouth, by which that <term>deceiver</term> <note>original: "præstigiator" — literally a juggler or illusionist; Weyer uses this to describe the Devil as a master of sleight-of-hand.</note> so dazzles the senses of certain people that they do not doubt these things were drawn from the very center of the body. These are mostly scraps of coarse woolen cloth, likewise iron nails—sometimes of considerable size—and fragments of them; iron and brass buckles, needles, pins, and many of them, sometimes tied together or inserted into cloth, or bundles of thread. These things have been seen by me. Sometimes bones are also vomited, or even **undergarments** <note>original: "subligacula" — breeches or loincloths.</note>, and other far more absurd monstrosities of that kind. Often, their size even exceeds the natural dilation of the **esophagus**, even when stretched and pulled apart as much as possible in a living human; nor is there any other passage wider than the mouth leading inward. By this single irrefutable argument, I will easily prove that these things were thrust into the mouth by the imperceptible subtlety and speed of the demon—our eyes being overcome by his swiftness, or deluded by a <term>glamour</term> <note>original: "faſcino" — a spell affecting the sight.</note>, or by an intervening body of air—or otherwise moved there, whether from within, from without, or from both sides...

What I myself saw, observed, and did in a case of this kind not long ago, I will add in a few words for the sake of those who judge that I have provided something worthwhile. A certain honorable woman named Helwich, while she was caring for an infant in Düsseldorf in March of the year 1564, swallowed two pins <note>original: "aciculas"</note> she was holding in her mouth—one large, the other smaller—perhaps because she feared the child might fall. Being finally called to her, I ordered that no food or drink be offered until I had tried to see if they could be pulled back out with a slender curved forceps <note>original: "incuruo forcipe subtili"</note>, which I ordered to be brought without delay. I had scarcely departed when a small draft of liquid was given to her, by which the pins were pushed down into the lower parts of the throat, a little above the opening of the stomach. 

When a new torment arose there with stinging pain, I was called back. I ordered beer with butter and rye bread—common among our people—cut rather thick, to be given quite copiously, and that she should sleep in an upright position, for it was night. I judged that the pins could be driven down into the cavity of the stomach in this way, and that because they were stuck, they could not be safely returned through the throat by vomiting, which contracts these parts and might drive objects deeper by that effort. In this way, at three o'clock in the morning, they were pushed down to the stomach by the weight of that bread. 

Then, on the second day, I treated her with fatty broths to loosen the bowels <note>original: "alui iusculis pinguibus"</note> and buttered beer. She was then commanded to lie on her right side with her belly free, with pillows placed under her thigh and arm, so that the needles might descend from the stomach through the pylorus <note>original: "pilorum" — likely a spelling variation or error for "pylorum," the opening from the stomach to the intestines</note> to the intestines with less hindrance. ### *Because of the connection to the previous story, the healing of this girl and the others that followed after the formula of blessing was recited by the women arrested on that account is briefly joined here.* Chapter IIII.

<margin>The formula of blessing commonly used in the cure of witchcraft <term>maleficium</term>.</margin>
Furthermore, when the women I mentioned a little earlier were imprisoned and brought before the council, and the Imperial Senate ordered them to bless the men who were suffering in various ways—on the suspicion that they were victims of witchcraft—using the prescribed formula, namely: *I bless you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, in your goods, blood, and livestock* <note>original Latin: "Benedico tibi in nomine Patris & Filij & Spiritus sancti, in tuis bonis, sanguine & armento"</note>; and when they did as they were ordered, the sick were immediately healed. Each person was blessed by the woman whom he suspected was the "mother" of his torment, or whom he believed to be so based on the suggestion of the "Pythian" accuser <note>The "Pythian" refers to a divining spirit or demon, here suggesting that the accusations came from possessed individuals or professional diviners</note>, the demon, or his minister, who was also held in custody. Lest the interrupted sequence of the story delay or disturb the reader, I will follow up briefly here with those matters which otherwise belong to the argument of the following book.

<margin>It is not necessary for the one who bound the spell to be the one to loosen it.</margin>
Here, that rule <term>canon</term> worn out on everyone's lips was ratified: *She who has bound, the same must also loosen* <note>original Latin: "Quæ ligauit, eandem quoque soluere necesse est"</note>. You will gather the absurdity of this opinion in this way: If she is a witch <term>lamia</term>, she is thought (according to common opinion) to have a pact and communion with an evil demon <term>cacodæmon</term>, and by his help to bind others with various cruel tortures; it is also believed that she can, by her own will, loosen them from her own and Satan’s work—that is, the torments—using the same demonic help with which she had previously bound them. But she is the slave and property of him to whom she is believed to have bound herself by pact and agreement. Therefore, you may trust more certainly that she can personally effect nothing through divine words. If any power is to be granted to these words when recited, they will more quickly obtain their effect through the command of God when pronounced by faithful ministers of the Church and men of pious character, rather than through those women who are judged to have professedly renounced God's society and declared war as enemies.

Indeed, whatever the devil binds, Christ, his Apostles, and his ministers have loosed; rather, they drove him away from his very work. This was the unique ministry of Christ, in whose name he appeared. Nor could the disciples—on account of some degree of unbelief—inhibit Satan’s harassment and drive him away, for which they were severely rebuked by Christ. Our Church Canons, reason, and experience all teach that "medicine consists of contraries" <note>A principle in ancient medicine (*contraria contrariis curantur*) suggesting that a disease is cured by its opposite; here, Weyer argues that evil cannot be cured by an evil agent like a witch</note>.

<margin>Matthew 12. Mark 3. Luke 11. Nothing good is done in the name of a demon.</margin>
When Christ had healed the blind and mute man harassed by a demon, and was accused by the scribes and Pharisees of casting out demons by the protection of Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he confuted them, saying: "How can Satan cast out Satan? And if a kingdom is divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand; and if a house is divided against itself, that house cannot stand; and if Satan has risen up against himself and is divided, he cannot stand, but has an end. He who is not with me is against me; and he who does not gather with me, scatters."

<margin>God does not wish his glory to be proclaimed by the wicked. Psalm 49.</margin>
Nor does God wish his glory—which shines forth in the healing of men in his name—to be proclaimed by the wicked, as the divine prophet teaches in these words: "But to the wicked God says: Why do you recount my justices and take my covenant into your mouth? Since you hate discipline and cast my words behind you. You have given your mouth over to evil, and your tongue fashions deceit" <note>Psalm 49 in the Vulgate, corresponding to Psalm 50 in modern Bibles</note>. From this it is clear that by such a "cure" <note>referring to the forced blessings mentioned on the previous page</note>, these women cannot be proven guilty of incantation or harmful magic <term>maleficium</term>, and the legal rule is rendered weak. Origen elegantly said: "The sorcerers do not know how to bless, because demons do not know how to do good." But as for the fact that they are healed, it happens for no other reason than when the devil, by God's permission and because of unbelief, has tormented these bodies, so that he might [lead] the afflicted, the bystanders, and those to whom this unusual evil became known, then finally as a mistress...

[They appear] in some part naturally; but in the truth of the matter, they are not <term>natural species<note>original: *species naturales*. As I have frequently seen, and handled with my own hands, things which at the start (as I said) appeared true and natural, and retained in themselves some kind of hardness; yet in a short time, as has been said, they were resolved and perished.

### Chapter VI.

<margin>
From *On the Hidden Causes of Diseases*, chapter 8.
A woman harmed by witchcraft vomits nails and needles.

Antonio Benivieni <note>Antonio Benivieni (1443–1502) was a Florentine physician often considered a pioneer of pathological anatomy.</note> relates that a new and remarkable type of disease occurred in his time. A girl in her sixteenth year, suffering from a pain that began in the lower part of her belly, was tormented by convulsions in her hands. When she broke out into a horrible screaming, her whole belly immediately swelled up, so much so that you would have believed she was eight months pregnant. Her voice having failed, she suddenly threw herself here and there across the entire bed; sometimes, bringing the soles of her feet up to her neck, she would spring back onto her feet, falling down and leaping up again, doing this same thing repeatedly until, gradually returning to herself, she was restored in some manner.

When asked what she had done, she was completely ignorant of it. Indeed, we, searching for the causes of this kind of disease, judged that this evil arose from <term>suffocation of the womb<note>original: *matricis suffocatiõe*. A common medical diagnosis of the era, also known as "the mother" or "hysterical passion," where the uterus was believed to move or release "vapors" that caused physical and mental distress.</note></term> and from foul vapors rising upward, and thereafter striking the heart and brain. But when no progress was made with medicines, she became more ferocious; looking around with grim eyes, she finally broke out into vomiting, by which she threw up long and curved nails, and brass needles, together with wax and matted hair. And most recently, from her breakfast, a piece of such great size that no person's throat could have swallowed it whole.

Since she had done this very thing quite often even while I was watching, I judged her to be held by an evil spirit, who, while doing these things, dazzled the eyes of the onlookers. Therefore, having been commended to <term>ecclesiastical physicians<note>original: *ecclesiasticis medicis*. In this context, it refers to exorcists or clergy who specialized in the "medicine of the soul."</note></term>, she afterwards proved the matter with more manifest signs and arguments. For we both heard her prophesying and, moreover, saw her doing things which surpassed all the power of disease and also exceeded human understanding. Thus far Benivieni.

All these things were certainly not in the body, but were the work of the devil—who was <term>bewitching<note>original: *effascinátis*. Refers to the demonic power of "fascination" or the "Evil Eye," which Weyer argues tricks the human senses into seeing things that aren't there.</note></term> the eyes of the spectators—so that the thrusting of this material into her mouth might not be noticed, through his illusions and speed...

### Histories of the same theme.
### Chapter VII.

The son of a Treasurer at Morlaix <note>A town in Brittany, France.</note>, having suffered somewhat from ill health, believed it had been brought upon him by a certain poor woman to whom he had brought a basket full of herbs for pig fodder; in giving thanks, she had pressed his shoulder. He was fatigued by these mockeries for about half a year; then, they vanished gradually, just as they had begun. There is no doubt that these things were permitted because of the lack of faith of the parents and the youth; for when he was seen to be somewhat burdened by illness according to the natural order, they did not attribute it to a natural defect or to the will of God, but to the "impression" or influence of the poor woman. God therefore permitted this delusion of the devil, in the ways that have been explained, until perhaps they came to their senses.

### On possessed boys. Chapter VIII.

In Amsterdam, which is the maritime trading hub of Holland, the following account was written to the most distinguished man, Master Hadrianus Nicolai, Chancellor in Guelders: On the eighteenth of March in the year 1566, after eight or ten weeks had passed, about thirty boys in this city began to be tortured in a horrific manner. They were seized as if by a sudden madness or frenzy and thrown prostrate upon the ground; however, there were interruptions, and this torment would last for a whole or half hour. Upon rising, they remembered absolutely nothing of the torture or the things that had occurred; rather, they thought they had only been sleeping. Physicians were consulted there because the illness was believed to be natural, but they achieved nothing. 

Afterward, because of a suspicion of sorcery <note>original: *maleficium*, a term used for harmful magic or witchcraft</note>, they turned to the boys' guardians, who made just as little progress with their prayers and various other methods of driving the affliction away. Finally, because it was believed they were being besieged by a demon, counsel was sought from a good many exorcists, for the boys—though ignorant—uttered many things that surpassed their natural capacity and age. The exorcists first, according to their custom, read rites, performed exorcisms <note>original: *conjurarunt*, literally "swore against" or "adjured"</note>, and employed the rest of their spiritual armor against the assault of the demons, but with no success. 

While these readings were being performed, the boys vomited up numerous needles, as well as pins, thimbles <note>original: *digitalia*</note>, scraps of cloth, pieces of pots, glass, hair, and other things of that kind; however, no complete cure followed from this. We grant, of course, that creatures of God, formed in His very image, do not have the power—outside of His authority—to change the nature of things. Nor can they insert hard or sharp materials into a body—exceeding the size of the passages through which they would need to pass—in a way that is entirely painless and leaves no wound. For a demon, by whatever craft he possesses, cannot pull open or stretch the esophagus, the throat, or any other part wider than they were made to be from the moment of their first creation, as I have shown more extensively elsewhere. If you still insist that an iron nail lay hidden in the affected area before the incision was made, how could it have been pressed in so imperceptibly, without any injury to the skin or flesh? Furthermore, why did the pain in the other flank <note>original: *hypochondrio*; the region of the abdomen under the ribs</note> not cease once the nail (which was thought to be causing the agony) was cut out? It is a most celebrated rule among natural philosophers <note>original: *physicis*; refers to those who study the laws of nature and medicine</note> that when the cause is removed, the effect is removed. Therefore, the objects found in the stomach during the post-mortem dissection were, without a doubt, placed there by the demon during the act of cutting. In this way, the devil sows the seeds of discord, leading us to immediately accuse others of the crime of sorcery—believing they orchestrated these things with the demon's help—even though they are actually innocent.

### *Diabolical harassment in the Kentorp monastery, attributed to witches. Chapter 11.*

To this subject belong the monstrous and manifold convulsions of the noblewomen and other virgins shut away in the Kentorp convent near the Old March <note>the *Altmark* region</note>, in the County of Mark near Hamm. These were stirred up by demons and described in Book One, Chapter Eleven. Truly, these women breathed out a most foul breath from their mouths during the fit itself and shortly after; the seizure would otherwise invade once a day, sometimes more often, and was occasionally prolonged for many hours. During the onset of the evil, some who were convulsing remained conscious; they could hear, and many later affirmed that they could even recognize those standing nearby. For during the seizure, due to the convulsions of the respiratory parts <note>original: *spiritualium partium*; the organs of breath and voice</note> and the tongue, they were less able to speak. They were not all tortured with equal ferocity, nor in the same way, but some more mildly than others. But this was common to nearly all of them: when one of them was agitated, the others in separate rooms would also be seized, merely upon hearing the noise of the disturbance, and would be harassed in the same wretched manner.

Furthermore, so that the origin and growth of this calamity might be known—along with the tragic final act of this drama, which that old murderer <note>a traditional epithet for the Devil, referencing John 8:44</note> aimed for in this harsh spectacle—and so that we may more cautiously counter the devil's malicious attempts in those rare and horrific harassments, I will narrate in good faith and in a few words what I learned through diligent inquiry from the mouth of an elder and prudent virgin, consecrated to this community, who was the very first to be so harshly afflicted. This woman, named *Anna Loingou*, when she first suffered pain in her left <term>hypochondrium</term> <note>original: *hypochondrio*; the area of the upper abdomen, then believed to be the source of "melancholic vapors" that caused fits</note> and was thought to be seized by <term>epilepsy</term>, was sent primarily for religious reasons to the *Nonhertic* monastery, where she drank from the skull of *St. Cornelius* <note>St. Cornelius was the patron saint invoked against epilepsy, often called "St. Cornelius's sickness"</note>:
