In milk there are three substances: butter, cheese, and whey. If the milk begins to turn slightly sour with age—which usually happens faster in summer and slower in winter—and is then cooked, the dissolved cheese soon unites with the butter and hardens, so that it can be drawn out and extended into very long, tenacious threads, like ductile flax. And if it is wound around stretched pieces of wood, it reaches such a state of dryness that it becomes brittle and can easily be reduced to powder. <note>The author provides a natural explanation for a physical phenomenon that might otherwise be mistaken for a demonic miracle.</note>

Let a girl also be added to this account, one known to me, who was a servant to a noble maiden in a convent. ### On the affliction of sorcery.

On the second day of July—specifically the day sacred to the Visitation of the Blessed Virgin Mary—while she was about to clean her sister’s shoes, she pulled out her sister's knife. (There were actually two knives joined in the same sheath, identical in shape and decorated with engraved bronze hilts.) She sat down on a lower seat because her strength had been consumed by a long-lasting fever, leaving her quite weak. Unexpectedly, an old woman entered the house, asking if the fever was still troubling the girl and how she was faring after her illness. After the girl gave her an answer, the old woman left the house again without saying another word. 

Once the shoes were cleaned, the girl placed the knife in her lap <note>original: *sinu*; this refers to the fold of her garment or her lap</note>. When she later searched for it diligently and could not find it, she was struck with fear. While she was searching every corner carefully and anxiously, she noticed a black dog of horrific appearance lying on its belly under the table. She hoped that by driving the dog away, the lost knife would be revealed and returned to its owner. However, the dog became indignant; it bared its teeth with a growl and simultaneously fled through the door with a great leap. 

Soon after, it seemed to the girl that something like a cold fluid was flowing down from her head toward her back. This was followed by a fainting spell, and she remained as if dead and without sensation until the third day. <margin>3</margin> At that time, she finally began to breathe a little and was refreshed by food and drink. When she was asked with great concern what kind of evil had seized her, she replied that she knew for certain that the knife she had pulled from her sister's sheath was stuck fast, pierced into the left side of her body; she claimed she could feel the pain in that very spot. 

Although her parents and others contradicted her—believing she was suffering from <term>melancholy</term> <note>In the 16th century, melancholy was considered a physical illness caused by an excess of "black bile," often resulting in delusions or deep depression</note> or was somewhat delirious due to the long illness, fasting, or some other accidental hardship—she nevertheless persisted so much in her complaints, constant tears, and sleeplessness that she lost her mind. She would often refuse food for two days at a time, even when she was gently invited or sternly urged with threats. Nevertheless, she usually had her—

### Book Four.

There were frequent intervals and pauses, so that she might even lie down quietly; however, she could not do so for long because of the continuous pain by which she was so tormented that she had to lean on a staff, completely bent over. This also increased her mental anguish and diminished her comfort: while she most certainly believed that a knife was fixed within her body, others persistently disagreed with her. Then she said: “Until now you have denied me your belief that a small knife is stuck in my body; but when the feast of the Visitation of Mary <note>Celebrated on July 2nd</note> appears again, you will most clearly understand and see that it is fixed in my body.” Thus, on the thirtieth of June, such a great quantity of pus erupted from the ulcer that the swelling subsided somewhat, and from there the tip of what looked like a knife appeared. <margin>The possessed girl.</margin>
Arriving here on the fourth of July, the surgeon asked the parish priest to first speak with the girl, to comfort her, and to instruct her in the Word of God, while carefully observing her response; this was because it seemed to almost everyone that she was occasionally tormented by a demon. Along with her response, she added that she would gladly submit to this method of cure, even if she knew she must die.

It matched the other knife <note>referring to the second knife from the pair mentioned on the previous page</note> exactly, though it was somewhat worn away around the middle of the sharp iron blade. Through the surgeon's work, the ulcer healed. This is the account published in German concerning this prodigious event.

### Chapter XIV.

While everyone cries out with one voice that this wonderful spectacle was truly produced without any demonic trickery <term>original: *praestigias*; refers to illusions or "sleights of hand" performed by a demon</term>, and admits no alternative interpretations or explanations, I will not hesitate to interpose my opinion here by way of a simple interpretation. I shall strive—with the benefit of God, for His glory, and in contempt of the demon and his deluded crowd of followers—to show as briefly as possible that the knife was not in the body, but rather that demonic illusions and mockeries were cast before the eyes of all, and that the girl was possessed by a demon. This I will do although I am well aware that many will cry out against me with a Stentorian voice <note>A voice as loud as fifty men, named after Stentor, the Greek herald in the *Iliad*</note>.

<margin>The demon’s aids in this deceitful act.</margin> First, it ought to have been observed that the simple girl had been troubled by a long fever, which, from its duration, I gather was a quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where the fever returns every fourth day, historically associated with "black bile"</note>. This arose from an abundance of the gravest and blackest melancholic humor <note>The "four humors" (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) were thought to govern health; an excess of black bile caused "melancholy" and was believed to attract demons</note> which had putrefied in the body. This humor very often also obstructs the spleen, and produces in it a tumor, hardness, and an abscess; on such an occasion, it is not rare for a quartan fever to leave such an "offspring" behind it. <margin>Gender.</margin> <margin>Age.</margin> <margin>Long illness.</margin> With this foundation laid—namely, the female gender, youthful age, and the weariness of a long illness—the demon builds and fabricates the rest of his work with vigilant and untiring zeal. For in such individuals, it is much easier to gain credit for his delusions than in men of mature age and good health. <margin>The melancholic humor is most suitable for the devil.</margin> To aid his handiwork, he took up the humor most suitable for his actions, namely the melancholic humor. The girl’s brain and body were so far from being purged of this substance that they were still highly burdened by it. Indeed, with how much affection he is accustomed to immerse himself in this juice—as if it were something analogous <note>original Greek: *ἀναλογικῶς* (analogikos)</note> to himself and his actions—and by its aid to induce marvelous phantoms and rare imaginations, I have already shown in the previous book <margin>Chapter 24</margin> with such demonstration that I judge a repetition to be not at all necessary.

If you think you are not yet satisfied by this interpretation and still contend that the knife was truly drawn out from inside the body, tell me: how and through what passages was it injected? For that which is extracted from somewhere must first have been put in. It could not have been sent from the head toward the back and to the side by a demon without any visible injury—as we might observe a fluid dripping through the pores—that is simply impossible. Through the mouth, matter can only be carried to the gullet, the stomach, the intestines, and the anus; certainly not a knife. Even if I were to concede that it was taken in through the mouth, it could not have reached that part of the side unless the stomach and the peritoneum <note>The lining of the abdominal cavity</note> were first sliced open from the side, which would result in a fatal wrecking of the girl's life. From the anus, in turn, no other passage lies open than to the intestinal coils, the stomach, the gullet, the throat, and the mouth.

### The ridiculous manner of introducing hard objects into the body. Chapter 15.

Furthermore, a certain doctor describes an absurd and futile method by which hard materials of this kind are introduced into the body by witches <term>Lamijs<gloss>In this context, Weyer refers to women accused of sorcery or 'hexing' others</gloss></term> with the help of the devil. This is found in a small German book circulating under the name of Jacob, the Free Lord of Lichtenberg. I am surprised that Ludwig Milichius <note>A 16th-century theologian and author of 'Zauberteufel' (The Magic Demon), a popular work on the dangers of sorcery.</note>, a man otherwise pious and learned, approved of this in his German book titled *The Magic Demon*. By these authors, it is asserted that the pores of the body are stretched by the devil, and through them are inserted straw, pig bristles, wood splinters, leather, clippings, threads, fish bones, thorns from shrubs, and any sort of sharp materials. Then, they claim, the pores are closed up so that whenever the "architect" <note>A metaphorical term for the devil as the designer of these deceptions.</note> wishes, the hidden things can be pulled out again. The doctor adds these comparisons: 

Just as when someone hides a stone under water, even if the hand is withdrawn and the stone is not left there, one knows how the stone got there; so also, by a natural reason, a lightning bolt penetrates the pores of a scabbard without injury and melts the iron within. It is in a similar way, they say, that these delusions occur, which inflict even more harmful marks <note>original: *stigmata*</note> and wounds. These are his words.

Anyone even slightly acquainted with the study of nature will understand without difficulty that these arguments are quite meager. Since those pores were made extremely tight by nature from the first creation, I affirm that it is utterly impossible <note>original Greek: *ἀδύνατον* (adynaton)</note> and can in no way happen that they could be harmlessly pulled apart by a demon so far as to transmit straws, pieces of leather, or knives, and then collapse back, only to release the substance—which had been preserved for so many days or months—at Satan's will and whim. For the pores of the body were constricted so narrowly by the Creator from the beginning that they transmit nothing thicker or more solid than the thinnest fluid, such as sweat or vapor. We observe this same principle even in hard and thick stones, especially bricks, and in wood; their pores indeed transmit liquid...

## Certain things are found naturally in bodies that are sometimes attributed to witchcraft.

### Chapter XVI.

<margin>Various contents of abscesses, in Galen book 2 to Glauco & book 14 of the Method, & Celsus book 5, chapter 4.</margin>
Meanwhile, we know from the teachings of Galen <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> and Cornelius Celsus <note>A 1st-century Roman encyclopedist known for his medical work *De Medicina*.</note> that substances resembling stones, tufa <note>A porous rock formed from calcium carbonate.</note>, sand, shards of pots, wood, coals, hair, and oil-dregs can be born through natural reason even within the cavities of <term>steatomata<gloss>cysts filled with fatty, suet-like matter</gloss></term>, <term>atheromata<gloss>cysts filled with a porridge-like or "gruel" substance</gloss></term>, and other <term>apostemata<gloss>abscesses or inflammatory swellings</gloss></term>. On another occasion, Dr. Solenander <note>Reiner Solenander (1524–1601), a respected physician and friend of Weyer.</note> treated an elderly matron in the Town of the Lucchese <note>Likely Borgo a Mozzano near Lucca, Italy.</note>, the wife of Hieronymus Luchesini, a Lucchese nobleman. ## Concerning those afflicted by sorcery

...his wife, a sickly woman, suffered from time to time from colicky pains, and then was most severely tortured by them. After the second or third day of treatment, with many remedies skillfully applied, she finally, beyond everyone's expectation, passed a ball—or rather a tufa-stone <note>original: "tophum"; a porous, stone-like concretion found in the body.</note>—not very heavy, slightly larger in size than a pigeon's egg. After its rejection, the pain gradually ceased, and her former health returned. *Fallopius* <note>Gabriele Falloppio (1523–1562), a famous Italian anatomist and physician.</note> affirmed these things to the wonder of others, stating that the same thing had happened at another time to the most noble physician *Frisimelica* <note>likely Francesco Frigimelica, a professor of medicine at Padua</note> when he was vexed by colicky pains, and to a certain third person.

<margin>Otters and lizards found in bodies.</margin>
In the year 1549, it is recorded that in *Hungary*, near the *Tisza* <note>original: "Thaysę"</note> river, men were found in whose bodies complete otters and lizards were discovered. Whether this seems probable, let it be the judgment of others. Although I am not unaware that prodigious worms are sometimes born from a natural cause within the human body. Concerning a certain girl, a false suspicion was spread that a serpent was clinging to her stomach, causing torments, and from time to time climbing up to her throat; she was under my care, and is now doing well.

<margin>A worm eight feet in length.</margin>
It also happened five years ago, as trustworthy people have reported, on an island near *Maaseik* <note>original: "Masecum", a town in present-day Belgium.</note>, that a certain peasant, after continuous belly pain and having taken theriac <note>A famous ancient medical concoction used as an ointment or potion, believed to be an antidote to poison and various ailments.</note> against that evil, passed a worm eight feet in length and one finger thick, with a sort of horned mouth, not very unlike a duck's beak. Quite often, various forms of intestinal worms are seen to be ejected from the mouth.

Large black balls, the size of a large fist, uniformly spherical, without a seam, very tightly stuffed with small soft hairs, taken from the stomach and intestines of healthy young cattle destined for slaughter—I kept these in my possession for several years. # Book Four.

<margin>The origin of hairballs in an ox’s stomach</margin>
...pleases a natural explanation. Calves still living on their mother's milk, if they are ever deprived of nourishment, or otherwise becoming unruly in their frisky age <note>original: "petulca aetate"</note>, run to their mother or another cow. They suck so greedily upon her legs or whatever hairy part they can reach—especially the back of the hips—that they even make the area hairless. By this strong and frequent sucking, the hairs are drawn into the stomach, and through frequent movement and playful jumping, they are gradually gathered into a mass. Usually, they are enveloped in milk or chyme <term>chyle/chyme: the semi-fluid mass of partly digested food</term>, or a sticky, phlegmatic juice. With the passage of time, this becomes more tenacious and takes on the appearance of a membrane. Indeed, this thin skin of the hairballs was seen to be covered at first with a whitish, slimy substance immediately after the dissection; then, having dried out little by little, it resembled dyed leather, even turning blackish. When this was cut away in one part with a knife, uniform soft hairs of this kind (the sort we see found on those aforementioned parts of the cattle) appeared quite compacted together. Those who are accustomed to veterinary matters and have more closely observed the rearing of beasts of burden will more quickly agree with this opinion and give it credit. Thus, I wish to detract nothing at all from reason, even if at times a thing appears to be among the miracles of nature, whether manifested openly or cherished in secret. 

But as for those things which are fashioned outside the order of nature and the limit of known reason by Satan, the craftsman of a thousand tricks—by deceit and illusions, so that he may entice those who do not believe into his snare—and which are thought to be incantations (in whose name the innocent are frequently accused and punished), even though no one truly cooperates, albeit they may do so in their imagination: these I set forth so that the truth may be known, separated from falsehood. I do this so that the mockeries of the demon, being more deeply understood, may be disregarded, and that innocent blood may hereafter be spared. By a more just judgment, let the accusers—the peculiar slaves of the devil (others call them "diviners" <note>original: "divinos"</note>, but to me they shall be sorcerers <note>original: "malefici"</note>)—be hissed away by a changed form of the badly-rooted custom of the court.

Another person also keeps by him a smooth hairball of this kind...

They contend that the needle was first absorbed by the mesenteric veins.

I will add here in passing that the example of that needle returned through the urine moved many who are ignorant of dissection <note>dissection: the study of anatomy through the opening of bodies</note>; they falsely believe it penetrated from the stomach to the liver through the mesenteric veins, then through the larger vein to the narrow passages of the kidneys, and from there to the bladder. They think the mouths of the fibers in the living are more open to receive a needle. In fact, the needle, by its own sharp point, gradually and over a long period of time penetrated through the intestines (since whatever is propelled by nature makes a path for itself); from there it was able to be excreted through the fleshy part of the bladder and then through the urinary tract. In the same way, one should judge the case of an iron arrowhead, which, led by nature, moved through suitable parts for two years. I will easily prove this with other marvelous examples.

# *The Most Learned Physicians are Often Deceived by the Possessed.*
### *Chapter XVII.*

<margin>
A girl possessed by a demon.
</margin>
Furthermore, we find that even the most skilled physicians, and those most practiced in the works of their art, are frequently circumvented by the actions of a demon. A memorable example of this occurred not long ago: a most distinguished physician judged a twenty-year-old girl to be suffering from <term>melancholia: a medical condition then believed to be caused by an excess of "black bile," often associated with deep depression or delusions</term>. After she had passed about eleven sleepless nights, he offered her, according to his art, pills made of <term>hound’s-tongue: (original: *cynoglossa*) a plant used in early modern medicine to soothe the senses and induce sleep</term> to bring on rest. 
<margin>
The physician is mocked by the possessed girl.
</margin>
As soon as one pill was swallowed, the sick girl, closing her other eye with her finger, said: “See how well I sleep now.” Soon, being subdued by the demon in that possession, she asserted—and not wrongly—that the doctor was being mocked; she perceived she was being ridiculed by him. Because the physician had not revealed to anyone that he was administering those pills to produce sleep, he began to think that the demon could perceive the secret thoughts of men (an idea suggested by that ironic objection regarding the sleep generated by the tiny swallowed pill). 

<margin>
The demon does not know the thoughts of men.
</margin>
To this I say: the demon knew that a physician had been called to cure the possessed girl. Therefore, by vigilantly observing every part of his treatment plan and the preparation of the medicines—as a spirit is capable of doing—the demon quickly understood through natural reason that those pills were intended for provoking sleep. Using this as an opportunity, it was not difficult for the demon to mock and laugh at the doctor. That the demon does not know the thoughts of men is a doctrine also passed down by <term>Augustine: St. Augustine of Hippo, a central figure in Western Christianity whose writings on demons were highly influential</term>.

The next day, he was led into court, and after hearing the magistrate’s accusation and the planned proceedings, he requested that a patron be allowed to him in that extreme necessity; this was granted. This most cunning Doctor of Law argued many points and defended him shrewdly, showing that the soldier had been falsely accused and condemned. He demonstrated that the host had actually committed violence against the soldier after the man had been robbed of his money, revealing the entire sequence of events exactly as they happened, and even where the money was being kept hidden. However, the host denied this most boldly, even devoting himself to the devil and cursing several times that he might be snatched away by him if he actually had the money. At last, the Doctor of Law, decorated with his little blue hat, ceased his defense of the case, seized the host, and carried him through the marketplace up into the air; where he ended up, no one ever knew.

<margin>A woman is carried away by a demon because of her wicked oaths.</margin>

The rest of the people, terrified, followed to see where the woman was being led; they saw her hanging in the air for some time outside the village, and then they found her dead, having been cast headlong into a field.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that some are thought to be "bound" by incantations <note>spells or ritual words</note>, so that they are rendered entirely impotent in intercourse, as if they had been castrated: this can happen from natural causes for various reasons, when the organs of joining are damaged or hindered either by nature or by accident, which can also be weakened by a consumed drug. The same is believed regarding a wolf's penis <note>original: "lupi uirga," a common item in folk magic</note> tied or untied in someone’s name. Likewise, if some malevolent person merely knocks at the door of the chamber in which a groom lies with his bride, and shouts while driving a knife into the door: if the groom responds, then the one preparing the sorcery breaks off the tip of the knife, leaves it in the wood, and departs in silence; it is said the groom can do nothing in sexual matters that night. ### Concerning Various Bindings. Chapter XXI.

<margin>Various bindings.</margin>
<margin>See book 4, chapter 17.</margin>
Here, let the delusions of manifold <term>binding</term> <note>original: "ligatio"; the magical practice of "tying" or "binding" to prevent a person or object from functioning</note> be briefly reduced into a catalog: such as binding for love or for hatred; for illnesses and for health, and similar things. Part of these are fabrications; part, if such outcomes are observed, should not be attributed to these wicked bindings, but to [natural] causes...

While **Reiner Solenander** <note>A famous 16th-century German physician and traveler</note> was once staying with a friend in **Gallicano** <note>A town in the province of Lucca, Italy</note> in the region of Lucca under the **Apennines**, the shouts of a peasant were heard from the road, who was chasing a fox with his voice. Then Solenander’s companion said, "What if I take the prey away from it?" and presently, having turned over a stone of modest size that happened to be in the way, he "bound" <note>original: "firmat," literally "makes firm" or "fixes in place," referring to the magical practice of binding</note> the fox, which stopped and set down its burden. The man ran up, and as the fox fled, he took the prey. Later, he told how he had accomplished this solely by the turning of the stone, which he claimed must always be heavier once the prey has been taken; however, it seemed that he muttered several words during the actual overturning of the stone. When they returned to Gallicano, the peasant from whom the hen had been snatched demanded it back. The other refused to return it. He was then called into court and accused of taking the hen; he did not deny the act, but defended himself by saying he had obtained it by the best possible right, since it had been snatched from the jaws of a fox. At last, after the case had been discussed for some time, the judge pronounced the sentence: that they should cook the hen together, and enjoy it with one mind along with several good friends.

# On those affected by sorcery.

> Only the mind remains unshaken,
> Even as it groans over the monsters it endures.

> And the herbs lack the power
> To change the heart,
> Though they may change the limbs.

<margin>In the dialogue regarding the Ass.</margin> To these fictions, and the tale of Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124–170 AD), author of *The Golden Ass*, the only ancient Roman novel in Latin to survive in its entirety.</note> transformed into a donkey, let the metamorphosis described by Lucian <note>Lucian of Samosata (c. 125–180 AD), a satirist who wrote a similar tale titled *Lucius, or The Ass*.</note> be added. He set out for Thessaly <note>A region in Greece traditionally famous for witchcraft and sorcery in antiquity.</note> specifically to learn the magical arts. By chance, he stayed at a lodging where he saw a woman smear herself with an ointment and transform into a crow. Lucian, wishing to anoint himself with the same liniment, fell into an error and used a different one, by which he was turned into a donkey. Later, after being led into a theater strewn with various herbs, he was restored to human form by eating roses, following the instructions of a maidservant.

We should not attribute powers to herbs and poisons that are not related to their observable qualities or their entire substance. Indeed, it is well known that men are not transformed into beasts by these physical means alone; it follows, therefore, that such efficacy is impressed upon them by *carmina* <note>original: "carminibus." This refers to incantations, chants, or ritual songs used in magic.</note>. <margin>From *The City of God*, Book 18, Chapter 18.</margin> Let the opinion of Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Church Fathers. For when we were in Italy, we heard such reports from a certain region in those parts, where they said that women innkeepers, trained in these evil arts, were accustomed to give travelers medicated cheese. This should be understood in this way: since demons do not create natures <note>The author argues that only God can create or change the actual essence of a living thing; demons can only manipulate existing matter or perception</note>, they can instead do something such that things appear to be what they are not.

Instead, the *phantasticum* <term>phantasticum: the imaginative or "image-making" faculty of the mind that produces dreams and visions</term> of a man—which varies through types of innumerable things while thinking or even dreaming, and although it is not a body, it takes on forms similar to bodies with marvelous speed while the man’s bodily senses are dormant or suppressed—can be brought to the senses of others in some ineffable way in a bodily figure."

He continues: "...so that the bodies of the men themselves lie elsewhere, living indeed, but much more heavily and vehemently than in sleep, with their senses locked. That *phantasticum*, as if embodied, appears in the likeness of some animal to the senses of others, and the man seems to himself to be such as he might seem to be in dreams, even carrying burdens. If these burdens are real physical objects, they are carried by demons to mock men, while those looking on see partly the real bodies of the burdens and partly the false bodies of the beasts of burden."

<margin>The father of Praestantius, in a long and deep sleep, thought he had been turned into a horse.</margin>
For a certain man named Praestantius used to recount what happened to his father: that he took a certain poison in a piece of cheese in his own home and lay in his bed as if sleeping, yet he could in no way be awakened. After several days, however, he said the man woke up as if from sleep and narrated what he had experienced as if it were a dream: namely, that he had become a pack-horse <note>original: "caballum"</note> and, among other beasts of burden, had carried the soldiers' grain supply <note>original: "annonam"</note> which is called Rhaetic <note>original: "Retica"; referring to Rhaetia, a Roman province in the central Alps</note> because it was being transported to Rhaetia. It was discovered that everything had happened exactly as he narrated it, though to him it seemed only to be his own dreams.

Another man also reported that at his home during the night, before he went to rest, he saw a certain philosopher very well known to him coming toward him. This philosopher explained several Platonic points to him which he had previously refused to explain when asked. And when this philosopher was later asked why he had done in another man’s house what he had refused to do in his own, he replied: "I did not do it, but I dreamed that I did." Thus, what one man saw in his dreams was exhibited to the other through a phantastic image <note>The "phantastic image" refers to a demonic projection that makes someone appear to be present when they are actually elsewhere</note> while he was awake. 

These stories have come to us not from just anyone, whom we might think unworthy of belief, but from those reporting them whom we would not imagine to be lying. Therefore, regarding the stories recorded in literature—that the Arcadians <note>Ancient people of the Peloponnese often associated with myths of lycanthropy, such as the legend of King Lycaon</note> were usually turned into wolves by the gods (or rather by demons), and that Circe changed the companions of Ulysses <note>original: "Vlysis"; the Greek hero Odysseus</note> with her incantations—it seems to me it could have happened in the way I have described, if indeed it happened at all. 

As for the "Birds of Diomedes" <note>original: "Diomedeas uolucres"; in myth, the companions of the hero Diomedes were turned into birds after his death</note>, since their species is said to endure through a continuous lineage, I believe they were not actually transformed men. For such illusions <note>original: "præstigiæ"</note> are not difficult for demons when they are permitted by the judgment of God. But because that maiden was later found alive, it was easily understood that a doe had been substituted for her. However, because the companions of Diomedes suddenly disappeared and never appeared again anywhere else...

The Latins, as some would have it, call this insect the *tipula* <note>original: *tipulam*; likely referring to a water-strider or a similar aquatic insect known for erratic movement</note>, which is common in marshy places. The Greeks call this "lycanthropy" <note>original: *lykanthrōpian*</note>, which is the conversion of a man into a wolf; some also call it "wolf-like melancholy" following Marcellus <note>referring to Marcellus Sidetes, a physician of the 2nd century AD</note>, or "wolf-like insanity." Those seized by this evil, due to the vaporous fumes of black bile <term>black bile: or "atra bilis," one of the four humors in ancient medicine, believed to cause madness or depression when in excess</term>, believe themselves to have been changed into wolves or even dogs. Consequently, they leave their homes, mostly at night, imitating wolves or dogs in everything. These people are pale, and their eyes are hollow and dry; they see unclearly and weakly, their tongues are extremely dry, they are very thirsty, and their mouths lack saliva. Their lower legs are so ulcerated that they cannot be healed, due to frequent stumbles and the bites of dogs. 

These patients are treated by bloodletting <note>original: *sanguinis missione*</note> until they faint, a diet of "good juices" <note>nutritious, easy-to-digest food</note>, sweet baths, whey, and "hiera" made from bitter apple <term>hiera ex colocynthide: a traditional, potent herbal purgative</term> according to the recipes of Rufus, Archigenes, or Justus, as well as theriac <term>theriaca: a complex ancient medical concoction used as an antidote and general cure-all</term>, and other remedies useful for melancholy. Before an episode, their heads are bathed with sleep-inducing liquids, and their nostrils are anointed with opium. Sometimes it is even necessary to administer a sedative drug. It is likely that this natural defect and the alienation of the human mind provided the occasion for the story in Ovid <margin>Book 1 of the Metamorphoses</margin> regarding Lycaon, the King of Arcadia, whom Ovid imagined was changed into a wolf by Jupiter because of his crimes. ## *That many are thought to be demoniacs who are agitated by melancholy, and vice versa.*
### *Chapter XXV.*

Regarding the depraved imagination of melancholics and their subsequent actions—sometimes delusional and ridiculous, and sometimes even heavy, serious, and horrific deeds—I have said enough in Book 2, chapter 23, so that there is little need for repetition. Hence, such people are often judged to be either fools or possessed by demons, just as, in turn, those possessed by spirits <term>energumeni <gloss>from the Greek "energoumenos," meaning those "worked upon" or "driven" by an internal force, specifically a demon</gloss></term> are sometimes called melancholics. Therefore, an exquisite judgment is required here to discern between the two conditions, which are also very often intertwined. For the devil most willingly insinuates himself into the melancholic humor <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, "humors" were bodily fluids believed to control health and temperament; "black bile" caused melancholy</note> as a material suitable for his mockeries, as I recalled before. ### *Two memorable histories of faked demonic possession:*

### *incantations. Chapter XXVI.*

<margin>Fabrications of demonic possession.</margin>
<margin>The beggar Justus, a faked demoniac.</margin>
In this historical series of those who are harassed by the malice of demons, it would not be outside my purpose to recount a natural—yet rare—fabrication of demonic possession, which I once saw in Nijmegen <note>original: "Neomagij"</note> in Gelderland, in a certain beggar named Justus. This man, so that he might beg for a more generous sum of money on a suitable occasion, lay down before the doors of the church, feigning that a demon had dominion over him. For he would leap up with perpetual restlessness, and his belly would throb while he lay there; sometimes he also feigned a threatening flight, a violent assault, and a grim distortion of his face. Guards flanked him on both sides—his wife and a harlot—who, pretending to struggle against him as he lunged forward, lied about having to restrain him with iron tools. Meanwhile, being highly skilled in the rhetorical speech of beggars, they worked strenuously to elicit more abundant alms from the people coming to this place on Sunday morning. At length, the magistrate came to suspect a deceitful plot. Officers <term>lictores <gloss>attendants or bailiffs who carried out the orders of magistrates</gloss></term> were employed to lay hands on him as he left the cemetery around lunchtime, a time when this place is safe from crowds of people. For to arrest a man of this kind in such a place was considered a matter of religious scruple, and was held to be a sacrilege on account of the profanation of a sacred place. Finally, however, once the robbery <note>original: "latrocinio," here referring to his fraudulent theft of alms</note> was discovered...

### Chapter 30: Livestock are sometimes killed by poisons, but most often by plague.

<margin>Poisoning of livestock.</margin>
<margin>Plagues of living creatures.</margin>
Furthermore, no one denies that draft animals are sometimes ruinously afflicted by a poison that has been administered, or so placed that it harms them through its vapors. However, it is recorded by the best writers on agriculture and the veterinary art <note>original: "mulomedicinę"; specifically the medicine of mules and horses</note>—both ancient and modern—that these animals are more often struck down in great numbers, even to the point of total destruction, by a severe plague peculiar to them, which does not infect humans. Likewise, they are suddenly taken off by other headlong diseases specific to their own kind, some of which are also familiar to humans, while others are unique to the cattle. Yet these diseases are frequently believed to be <term>witchcraft</term> <note>original: "maleficia"</note> by men of common wit, to name no others.

We often observe this, and remember it happening in years past, that a certain plague killed only oxen. At other times it creeps in to kill swine, or sheep, and another sort to destroy chickens. Virgil describes beautifully the plague that carries off cattle and wild beasts:

<margin>Virgil, *Georgics*, Book 3 <note>The original margin note says "1. Georg.", but the quote is from Book 3</note></margin>

> *and it glowed with all the heat of autumn,*

In the year one thousand five hundred and fifty-two, while my colleague was practicing medicine at the baths of Lucca, Franciscus de Pergula—the local representative <note>original: "uicarius"</note> for the Luccans in that place—related that there, around the village of Menabia above the baths, at the end of May, a certain disease grew so strong among the cattle and was so pestilential that as soon as they were seized by it, they would swell up and fall down dead. The peasants, when they noticed this, immediately slaughtered those that were suddenly afflicted. Among these it was observed that if the blood of these infected animals touched the bare body of a human, it would produce <term>anthraces</term> <note>original: "anthraces"; referring to carbuncles or malignant boils, likely the disease now known as anthrax</note>. These (which seemed a wonder) were harmless if they were not opened; however, if they were opened and not immediately marked with a cautery <note>a hot iron used to burn and seal the wound</note>, they spread very widely and were the cause of death for some. The meat of the recently injured and slaughtered cattle, when cooked and eaten, brought no discomfort; but the broth from the meat was found to be lethal to anyone who drank it.

The ancients recorded that when <term>Therionarca</term> <note>a legendary herb said to numb or paralyze wild animals</note> grows in Cappadocia and Mysia, all wild beasts become numb wherever it is brought near them, and they are only revived by the sprinkling of hyena urine.

THE method of treatment here will be partly <term>prophylactic: preventative medicine intended to ward off disease or harm before it occurs</term> <note>original: "προφυλακτική"</note>, which is the most desirable part of healing, so that one may be preserved from bewitchment and the mockeries of incantations. # Book Five.

Whether these afflictions are sudden or long-lasting, known or unknown, arising from natural causes or from something beyond nature, these men soon entice the sick toward the seeking of illicit help. Indeed, these same individuals are often not ashamed to show off such help by promising certain health, prostituting it for sale. These are men who are clearly inept, crude, and unlearned, wickedly faking a knowledge of sacred medicine—a subject they have not even "greeted from the doorstep" <note>original: "à limine quidem ſalutarunt." A Latin idiom meaning they have no even basic or introductory knowledge of the subject.</note> (at least, I speak here of such men, not of those who are good and respected for their piety). They do this so that they might cover their fraudulent actions behind this "hanging ivy" <note>In antiquity, a bunch of ivy hung outside was a sign of a tavern or a shop; here it refers to a false advertisement or a deceptive front.</note> as if with a beautiful cloak. This is especially true when they are by profession churchmen—priests or monks—of whom, as examples and teachers of the flock, it is considered a sin to even harbor a dark suspicion.

But perhaps these magicians claim this prerogative as their hereditary right, as if the art were handed down from hand to hand. This is because the Egyptian priests (from whom Pythagoras, Empedocles, Democritus, and Plato learned magic) <margin>Galen, Book 4 on the *Composition of Medicines according to Kind*, and Book 6 of the *Epidemics*. Herodotus, Book 1.</margin> used to record the remedy by which any person was restored to health and deposit it at Memphis in the Hephaesteum—the sanctuary of Vulcan <note>The Roman name for the Greek god of fire and smithery, Hephaestus.</note> and Isis. In the same way, the Greek priests, who were the overseers of magic, kept their observations in the inner sanctuaries of the temples of Apollo and Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine.</note>, including those stored at Pergamon. The priests, as if taught by the oracle of Aesculapius, would share these observations with the sick, by whom they are usually accepted with the greatest confidence. 

There exists a holy opinion regarding the impudence of these men, written by the excellent Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note>. Although he was a pagan by religion, he refutes them here not only with wit but with piety, accusing them of ungodliness: 

<margin>On the Sacred Disease <note>Hippocrates’ famous treatise on epilepsy, which he argued was a natural illness rather than a divine punishment.</note>.</margin> "Those," he says, "who boast that they can drive away the symptoms of diseases with purifications and magical incantations are men lacking a livelihood. They attribute their words to a demon so that they might appear to the common people to know something more, and thus they deceive men. For they 'purify' those seized by disease—men defiled by blood and crimes, the unjust, and the poisoned..."

Indeed, from Sylvester II to Gregory VII, that distinguished magician (who, as Benno reports, would shake out his sleeves whenever he wished so that fire leaped out in the manner of sparks, mocking the eyes of the simple with these miracles as if they were a sign of holiness), it is written in their *Lives* that all the Popes were sorcerers. There one may read of execrable examples of that sort, by which they would entice women into love, being devoted to sacrifices to demons in forests and mountains. I have preferred to bury these things in silence, lest the commemoration of the crimes and poisonings <note>original: "ueneficia." In Latin, this term can mean both poisoning and sorcery/witchcraft.</note> of men placed at such a height of dignity be seized upon as a reproach. Although perhaps a few such men existed, it comes into doubt for no one that the greater number were free from these evil arts. Therefore, there is no reason why our modern-day practitioners of evil should cover themselves with this "cloak" <note>The author uses "pallio" (cloak) metaphorically to mean a pretext or a covering for their sins.</note> or use it as an excuse. Yet it is to be deplored that nowhere will you find any class of men so unjust and unpunished as most of these.

According to their custom, they claim these objects are imbued with a greater power from on high against the power of Satan than they were granted in God's first creation. Martin de Arles, a professor of Theology, writes to this effect: "Many are of the opinion that when bells are rung on the very day of Saint John <note>The Nativity of St. John the Baptist (June 24th), a day often associated with Midsummer folk customs.</note>, or on the eve of Saint Agatha, they believe they not only drive away the <term>Lemures</term> <note>original Latin: "lemures." In Roman mythology, these were restless or malevolent spirits of the dead; here used generally for ghosts or demons.</note>, but also <term>Lamiae</term> <note>original Latin: "lamiae." Witch-like monsters or nocturnal demons from classical folklore.</note>, so that they can neither be carried about from place to place nor even cause harm."

<margin>Treatise on Superstitions, numbers 8, 9, and 14.</margin>
The same author says in the same treatise: "These men are magicians, <term>pythones</term> <note>original Latin: "pythones." In a biblical and legal context, this refers to those possessed by a spirit of divination or mediums.</note>, and necromancers, to whom the foolish and unwise people run every day to learn the future or so that lost items may be restored. Through them, as it is commonly reported, appearances of demons occur in glasses or rings, where they come when summoned to predict what has been asked or to reveal what has been stolen. And as it is said, these <term>arioli</term> <note>original Latin: "arioli." Soothsayers or diviners who interpret omens.</note> always strive to mix sacred things among their superstitions, as the simple people who flock to them testify. For these wretched men themselves, on the same day they do not fear to perpetrate such wicked acts, even have the wretched audacity to celebrate the sacrifice of the Eucharist." Master Johannes Nider <note>Johannes Nider (c. 1380–1438) was a Dominican theologian whose writings were among the first to detail the perceived rise of a new sect of witches in Europe.</note> shows this in his *Preceptorium* [Book of Precepts], saying: "Witches wish the instruments of their malice to be touched by the sacraments of the Church or by other divine things; for example, by drawing a thread through holy <term>chrism</term> <note>original Latin: "chrisma." But as the same doctor [Nider] recounts, these things happen by the instinct of the demon for a three-fold reason. First, so that men may not only become faithless through such occasions, but also sacrilegious, [violating] divine things as much as lies in...

### On the healing of those harmed by witchcraft

...[con]taminating, so that they offend their Creator more, and more deeply contaminate their own souls, and cause more people to fall into sin. Second, so that God, being gravely offended by men, according to the opinion of the blessed Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), whose writings on the "city of God" and the nature of demons were foundational for medieval and early modern views on magic.</note>, grants the demon greater power over evil men; to whom God in His anger concedes what He would deny in His mercy. Third, so that under the appearance of an apparent good, they might more easily deceive the simple-minded, who think they have obtained some divine power through contact with holy things and prayers, when in fact only more serious sins have been committed. Thus far that author. In other superstitions practiced by these rural folk, even if demons are not expressly invoked, they nevertheless insert themselves into the acts and superstitions so that the minds of men may be deceived. Thus far that theologian. 

And in Case 2, Question 8 <note>A reference to the *Decretum Gratiani*, the standard collection of Catholic Canon Law at the time.</note>: Bishops are held captive by the devil who, having abandoned the Creator, seek help from the devil. And later: Take note that when witchcraft <term>maleficium</term> <note>original: "maleficium." In this context, it refers specifically to harm or illness caused by hostile magic or a curse.</note> is permitted by the hidden judgment of God, one must not resort to magicians, necromancers, and soothsayers for a solution and remedy—as in our own time these common people do not fear to flock everywhere to certain wicked priests—but rather to God, through humble confession and devout prayer, as held in Case 33, Question 1, the last chapter. Nor should evil be done so that good may result. More on this in the same place. 

The same author later adds: As for why no one should resort to the aforementioned necromancers, sacrilegious persons, and diviners, beyond the fact that they sin mortally and become partakers of their guilt and damnation, the reason is this: because they, even if by God's permission they sometimes speak the truth, their testimony is not to be used, because they more often deceive and lie. It is clear, since in the spirit of truth there is no falsehood; but in the spirit of lies, there are also many truths, so that a single hidden falsehood may deceive, as Gerson <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a famous French theologian and Chancellor of the University of Paris, known for his work on "discerning spirits."</note> says in *On the Testing of Spirits*: "For this reason," he says, "Christ forbade the demoniacs, and Paul the <term>pythoness</term> <note>original: "pythonissam." A woman possessed by a spirit of divination, as described in the Bible.</note>, <margin>Acts 16.</margin> from testifying to the truth which they were acknowledging."

### The execrable abuse of Holy Scripture and the names of God in magical cures for diseases. Chapter IV.

At this point—so that [the magic], disguised in its own <unclear>hateful</unclear> colors, might win over the minds of many and, with its borrowed allure <term>lenocinio</term> <note>A term suggesting a "pimping" or seductive enticement, implying that magic dresses itself up in holy words to seduce the innocent.</note>, cautiously entice others—the pure words of Holy Scripture, or words mixed into the practice, as well as the names of God, are twisted <note>original: "contorquéntur"</note> whether they like it or not. Truly, let those who more deeply understand the mystical word of God, His essence, and His living power, judge how appropriately this is done. But we must admit that this abuse of the word of God is utterly detestable, and this profanation of the most holy name of God must deservedly be called a horrible crime. Indeed, no lie is heard more impudently, or is more insulting toward God, than when a sentence of Scripture is brought forth or the name of God is pronounced [with...]

A reference to the Paschal Lamb in Exodus, applied to Jesus on the cross in the Gospel of John.</note> <margin>Against toothache.</margin> They believe that if anyone, while uttering these words, touches the teeth while the Mass is being performed, the toothache is calmed. <margin>Against fever.</margin> Another person, before the onset of the fever, washes their hands along with the sick person, reciting that Psalm <margin>Psalm 144.</margin> <note>In the modern numbering, this is Psalm 145.</note> in secret for the healing of the fever: *I will extol thee, my God, O king.* There is one who, having taken the hand of the sufferer, says: "May this fever be as easy for you as the birth of Christ was for the Virgin Mary."

Against the same [fever]: Take three Mass-breads <term>panes Missales</term> <note>original: "panes Missales." These are unconsecrated communion wafers (hosts).</note>; on one write: "As is the Father, so is the life"; on the second: "As is the Son, so is the holy"; on the third: "As is the Spirit, so is the remedy." <note>These phrases are a corruption of the Athanasian Creed, which begins "As is the Father, so is the Son..."</note> These three inscribed hosts are to be given to the feverish person, so that he may swallow them on each evening of three consecutive days; but on the condition that, once they are swallowed, he consumes no food or drink on that same day. He is also ordered to recite the Lord's Prayer <term>orationem Dominicam</term> fifteen times each evening, and the Angelic Salutation <term>salutationem Angelicam</term> <note>The "Hail Mary" prayer.</note> just as many times, to the glory and praise of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Another against the same: Lead the sick person on the sixth day <note>Friday.</note> toward the East before sunrise; he shall stand with hands outstretched toward the sun, then say these words: "Today is that day on which the Lord God went to the cross: but just as the cross shall never come to him again, so may neither heat nor cold <note>A reference to the alternating chills and burning heat of a fever.</note> come to you ever again: In the name of the Fa † ther, and of the Son †, and of the Holy † Spirit." Then recite nine times three Lord's Prayers and three Angelic Salutations. For these to be effective, they must be performed not on one day, but on three consecutive days.

I saw not long ago, in the possession of a nobleman of great authority, an execrable book that was written down—one most worthy of the flames. It was full of exorcisms, frequent signing of the cross, and formulas from Holy Scripture ending "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." These were used not only against any diseases, but against whatever obstacles might occur: so that if even an iron shoe fell off a horse on a journey, it was believed that by immediately reciting a prayer of this kind, the horse would proceed with an unhurt hoof to the stable, even if it were very far away.

### Magical methods for investigating a thief, harming a witch, and averting a spell, involving the blasphemous abuse of the divine name and Holy Scripture.

#### Chapter V.

<margin>
A demonic method for investigating a thief.

I will insert here a method for investigating a thief—not foreign to this subject—which certain people prescribe to be tested as follows. Turning toward the East, make a cross on a crystal with olive oil; and let "Saint Helen" be written beneath the cross. Then let a chaste boy, born of a legitimate marriage <note>original: *ex legitimo toro natus* (born from a lawful bed). Traditional magic often required "purity" or legitimacy from the medium.</note>, about ten years of age or thereabouts, take the crystal in his right hand. Prostrated on your knees behind him, you shall recite this prayer three times with the highest reverence: "I beseech you, holy Lady Helen, mother of King Constantine <note>Saint Helena (c. 246–330 AD) was the mother of Constantine the Great and is credited in tradition with finding the "True Cross" in Jerusalem.</note>, who found the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by that most holy devotion and finding of the cross, and by that most holy cross, by that joy which you had when you found that most holy cross, and by that love which you had toward your son, King Constantine, and by those highest goods which you enjoy eternally, that you might show in this crystal whatever I ask and desire to know, Amen." And when the boy sees an angel in the crystal, you shall ask whatever you wish, and the angel will answer. This you shall do at sunrise, when the sun has already emerged and the air is clear and bright.

Girolamo Cardano, *On the Variety of Things*, Book 16, chapter 93.

Afterward, let them be taken out before sunrise. Then let a bowl with water be placed upon a circle marked with a cross, both transverse and oblique <note>Likely referring to a combination of a standard cross (+) and a saltire (X).</note>, upon which is inscribed: **"Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands"** <note>original Latin: "Christus uincit, Christus regnat, Christus imperat," a traditional liturgical acclamation known as the Laudes Regiae.</note>. Each pebble is to be cast into the water in the name of each suspect: and when the pebble belonging to the guilty party is reached, then the stone stirs up a heat like a glowing iron. It is not difficult for the devil to fake such a boiling <term>ebullitio</term> <note>original: "ebullitionem," a bubbling or boiling effect.</note> in order to burden and deceive an innocent person.

"For this reason," he says, "I pray you that these words do not escape your mind."

For one must argue against and curse impious dogmas and those things which proceed from heretics, but one must spare the men themselves and pray for their salvation.

## On the sacrilegious, as well as the genuine, use of the Word of God, and the impious method of healing witchcraft.
### Chapter VII.

<margin>The genuine use of the Word of God.</margin>
Furthermore, what sacrilege would you consider more grave than—having stubbornly shaken off all memory of one's own salvation—to so wickedly abuse the venerable name of God? Is it not a grave sin to do violence to his most holy word, and to seize and twist it toward demonic illusions <note>Original: *praestigias*. This refers to the deceptive tricks or "glamours" attributed to demons.</note> to cover up insults against God? This is the very Word which Jesus Christ, the Son of God—overcome by love for the human race—brought forth from the secret bosom of the eternal Father and proclaimed for the sake of wretched and lost men. He did this so that, although they were separated from God by the fall of their first parents and had fallen away from all grace, they might learn from this Word that they have been restored to favor. He intended for them to have certain and expressed testimonies of the divine will toward them, by which they might lift themselves up and be instructed during true terrors of the soul and the wavering floods of distracted senses—as Peucer <note>Caspar Peucer (1525–1602), a German scholar and physician who wrote a famous treatise on divinations and sorcery.</note> teaches more at length in his commentary *On Divinations*.

...that the efficacy of this cure is propagated, and that it cannot be transferred to others, is a claim rashly persuaded to the credulous. They use similar portents of demonic voices against toothache: **Galbes galbat galdes galdat.** <note>original: "Galbes galbat galdes galdat." These are nonsensical, rhythmic incantations intended to sound mysterious or magical.</note> This ridiculous text is also hung [as an amulet]: **Scrapers and toothed sickles, resonate the pain of the teeth.** <note>original: "Strigiles falceſq; dentatæ, dentium dolorem perſonate."</note>

Certain people, for every kind of intermittent fever, join two parallel twigs in their middle sections through the power of words; by this very contact, they bind them into the shape of a cross, which they hang around the neck. This indeed relieves many, but they are almost always the ones who suffer a more severe relapse. Against fevers, the **Turks** apply a round piece of wood to the chest and then strike it with another similar piece of wood, murmuring I know not what. Certain superstitious monks used to hang a small slip of paper around the neck against these same fevers, ordering the patient to pour out certain prayers at each onset of the illness and to hope for recovery after the third onset. 

Who does not recognize the trickery here? In the first place, confidence has a very great power, and at the beginning of an illness, advice is rarely sought. Secondly, in acute diseases where the illness is already fully developed, it is almost impossible for the condition not to change after so many paroxysms <note>A paroxysm is a sudden attack or increase in the intensity of symptoms, like a fever spike.</note>. If health resulted from the power of God or a demon because of something written, why does it not follow immediately? They take these written words, **"Gibel God gave,"** <note>original: "Gibel got gabet," likely a corrupted Germanic phrase used as a charm.</note> and place them on the beak of a chicken. Then, with a very sharp stylus, they pierce the head straight through the middle. The chicken jumps up and lives, especially in summer. However, the reason for this is hidden: the head and brain of a chicken are divided by bone on both sides. Between these, in the middle, there is a distinct gap which the stylus can easily penetrate; and so, the brain being uninjured, nothing of its life is lost. 

Furthermore, the common people, who are unskilled in such matters, believe that this power resides in the words. Yet if that power emanated from them, why does the same thing not happen if the head of a goat, a human, or a dog is pierced? To these, add that charm of Constantine for catching fish: **"Lord of Hosts."** <note>original: "Iao Sabaoth," a Greek/Hebrew invocation of the Divine Name common in magical papyri.</note> Rightly, therefore, <margin>Simple Medicines, book 6.</margin> **Galen**, although a pagan, mocked **Chariachirus** and **Bamachius** <note>Obscure writers or figures associated with superstitious medicine.</note> and preferred **Dioscorides** <note>Pedanius Dioscorides (c. 40–90 AD), a Greek physician and author of 'De Materia Medica,' a foundational text on herbal medicine.</note> to them...

### Book Five. 475

...who has handed down medicine without incantations and superstitious words, unlike those others. The same author in Book 10 of *On Simple Medicines* <note>original: "Sim." Likely referring to Galen's *De Simplicium Medicamentorum*, a standard medical textbook of the era.</note> says: "It is the substance which is hung [as an amulet] that works, not barbaric voices, as some tricksters are accustomed to use."

<margin>No voices correspond with the images of the heavens.</margin>
Furthermore, it surpasses all folly that many claim certain voices correspond with certain images of the heavens <note>This refers to astrological talismans or signs of the Zodiac.</note>; and that certain words, spoken with solemnity, change the senses of men and beasts. They claim that by these means, images are seen in a consecrated mirror, women are moved to love, the elements are changed, the earth is variously affected, fire ceases to burn, and diseases are cured.

<margin>Giovanni Francesco Pico discusses these matters at length against Al-Kindi in Book 7, Chapter 6 of *On Superstitious Presaging against Magic*.</margin>
O incomparable madness! What is this power, I ask, where is it derived from, and where is it received? For if the entire power of words depends on "celestial harmony," as Al-Kindi <note>Al-Kindi (c. 801–873 AD) was an Arab philosopher who theorized that everything in the universe emits "rays" and that spoken words could focus these cosmic powers.</note> contends, why can that harmony not work by itself, since it is the superior cause? He will perhaps say that the heavens act through a mediating and proximate cause—that is, through words. But let him show whether this power of acting is received in the sound, or in the voice, or in the external words themselves.

For in nature, sound precedes voice, and voice precedes words; for words are made of voice, and voice is made of sound. This is because words include voice and sound, and the definition of voice contains sound. There can be sound without voice, because it is naturally prior; for the same reason, there can be voice without words. But without voice and sound, there are no words. 

Therefore, if the power is received in the sound, and it is by sound that it moves the elements, then that power could be communicated to every sound of even inanimate bodies <note>The author argues that if "sound" itself were magical, a falling rock or a crashing wave would have the same power as a magician's spell.</note>; thus, neither voice nor words would be necessary. But if the power is in the voice—since voice belongs to most living creatures besides man—the same thing could also be done by brute animals. 

But if you say the power is received only in human words, I ask where that power is taken from: is it in the first syllable, the middle ones, or the last? If it is in a single syllable, then it is no longer "in the words"; and furthermore, that syllable perishes the moment it is spoken. The same reasoning applies to the others. Therefore, it is concluded that in no way can this virtue,
->operating from the heavens,<-
exist within words.

# On magical healing through ligatures, amulets, characters, images, rings, or seals. Chapter IX.

<margin>The vanity of ligatures and amulets.</margin>
**H**ere, magical ligatures <note>original: "ligaturae"; these were knots or cords tied around a person or object to "bind" a spirit or a disease.</note> and amulets <note>original: "periapta"; charms worn around the neck for protection.</note> have their place, along with other items, especially those stealthily drawn from the Holy Scriptures. By these means, people are driven to folly <note>The author implies that the use of holy words for magic is a form of spiritual madness or delusion.</note> against the efforts of demons, incantations, and witchcraft. An example of this is when the first chapter of the Gospel of John is written in tiny letters on a slip of paper, consecrated by the recitation of a Mass, and tied around the neck; it is believed to be a marvelous amulet against incantations and the machinations of the devil. But if this little scrap of paper is held to have any efficacy, then surely those who 
<margin>The Word of God is not a dead letter, but spirit and life, John 6.</margin>
openly and constantly carry the Holy Scripture in their hands or sleeves will obtain a singular advantage against the maneuvers of Satan. Yet, unless it is rooted in our souls—where it might be stirred into action as if by a vital spark—the letter remains dead, even if it be hung, tied, carried, rubbed, muttered over, inscribed, stamped on seals or rings, drunk, eaten, or even swallowed a thousand times. John Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD) was an important Early Church Father known for his preaching.</note> confirms this:

<margin>Homily 43 on Matthew, Chapter 23.</margin>
> "Some," he says, "namely priests, carry a certain part of the Gospel written around their neck. But tell me, foolish priest, is not the Gospel read and heard by everyone in the Church every day? Therefore, if the Gospels placed in the ears do no good, how can they save when hung around the neck? Furthermore, where is the power of the Gospel? In the shapes of the letters, or in the understanding of their meaning? If it is in the shapes, you do well to hang it around the neck; if in the understanding, then they are more profitable when placed in the heart than when hung around the neck."

If you maintain the fear of God and endure suffering bravely rather than following after those evils, this brings you very close to being a martyr.

<margin>The trifles of characters, images, rings, and seals.</margin>
Furthermore, little importance should be given to characters drawn by hand, or to images, rings, and seals traced or engraved with this or that figure—even if they are marked with symbols at specific moments when the heavens are in certain positions and in a particular place. Just as no influence from the stars is imprinted upon works made by human hands, so too, even if they are endlessly adorned with divine signs, names, or words from the Holy Scripture, nothing of true power is added to or taken away from their substances by whatever shapes they take. God bestowed upon each individual thing its own wondrous and peculiar powers to produce specific effects from the beginning of creation. Indeed, no new mixture of qualities <term>qualitatum mixtura: in medieval science, the specific blending of the four primary qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry) that gives a substance its properties</term> is established there. No new and essential form is infused into a material that was already clothed in a suitable temperament of qualities from its first creation. Instead, for a body already shaped by its own matter and form—by which it exists—and adorned with its own natural balance, only a new appearance is added through human art. To this appearance, the stars contribute nothing, nor do the qualities existing in the air at that time. In fact, to state the reality of the matter once and for all, I am not ashamed to freely profess that this entire heap of invented appearances is empty and ineffective—even if people try to dazzle me with the philosopher *Thābit* <note>original: "Thebit"; referring to Thābit ibn Qurra, a 9th-century scholar whose "De Imaginibus" was a foundational—and controversial—text on astronomical talismans.</note> and the master of magic—

They even suggest that a groom should urinate through a wedding ring so that he might be released from sexual impotence and bewitchment—on the authority of the physicians Nicolaus and Guilelmus Varignana, and the surgeon Pietro d’Argelata. If someone wishes to be released from love, they suggest placing the lover’s dung in the beloved’s shoe; the perceived odor will shatter the love. Truly, the cause of that "virtue" is all too manifest; there is no reason to twist it into some hidden occult property.

<margin>Pliny, Book 24, chapter 4.</margin>
It is also handed down that all closed things can be opened by the touch of the herb *Ethiopis* <note>A legendary plant described by Pliny the Elder said to have the power to dry up ponds and open any lock.</note>, provided that certain songs <note>original: *cantilenis*; rhythmic incantations or charms.</note> are murmured at the same time. To this same topic we must refer the story of a certain man in Venice condemned to the noose, for whom all doors were opened and iron bars cast down when only a single herb was brought near, over which certain signs <note>original: *signaculis*; magical seals or symbols.</note> had been chanted.

But if such power is inherent in the herbs, why are songs murmured or signs applied? Or if the songs and signs possess this virtue, why are the herbs summoned? If you say that the combination of the two achieves this efficacy, I object that it is pure superstition. While I wish to detract nothing from the miracles of otherwise natural things, I frankly affirm that nothing at all should be attributed to such little songs and signs. Since those herbs do not work unless the chants and signs are applied, it follows that no such power resides in them either. If you reply that an effect indeed follows: it certainly happens through the work of a demon playing along here by reason of the song or sign, so that he may bind the unwary more tightly and more securely with such mockeries.

Tell me, why did you dare to enter a girl of God?" The demon replied: "To preserve her as a virgin." [Hilarion asked]: "You would preserve her, you betrayer of chastity? Why did you not rather enter into him who sent you?" He answered: "To what end should I enter into him, who already possessed my colleague, the demon of love?" However, the saint did not wish to order the signs <note>the magical charms or sigils</note> to be sought out before he had purged the girl or the young man. He did this lest the demon should seem to have departed because of the usual incantations, or lest the saint himself should seem to have placed any faith in the demon's words. He asserted that demons are deceivers and clever at pretending. Once her health was restored, he rebuked the girl: Why had she done such things through which a demon could enter? Thus far the account of Jerome. But it is my opinion that the lying demon obsessed the girl’s love <note>meaning her emotional state or the "spirit" of her infatuation</note> rather than the girl herself. Nor did this occur by the power of the words or the figures carved into the plate; rather, it was because she had provided an opening to the devil. Just as Hilarion reproaches her, the power was granted to the devil to exercise his deeds because of her own actions.

# On the cure of injuries from sorcery.

<margin>Thomas Aquinas in his *Against the Gentiles*, *On the Secret Works of Nature*, and especially in the second part of the *Summa Theologica*.</margin>
Martin de Arles <note>A 16th-century Spanish theologian known for his work on superstitions</note>, a theologian, writes that it is an error to believe that objects—whether baptized, conjured, or consecrated (or rather, cursed) through the arts of mages and on specific days—obtain the wonderful powers described in the books of such arts. St. Thomas proves, by the testimony of Augustine in the tenth book of *The City of God*, that the opinion of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD) who explored how statues might be animated by divine or daemonic forces</note> regarding the construction of such images was false. It is indeed true that natural things receive their forms and virtues from the celestial bodies; however, artificial images <note>man-made objects like statues or talismans</note> can absorb no power from the artist’s craft, nor can they attain any force other than that which they possess by reason of their material. A shape or figure is not a principle of change or action; therefore, gold in the shape of a specific image has no cause for power greater than gold in any other shape. But if some other effect appears to result, it is brought about by the operation of demons mocking mankind, according to Augustine.

Thus, such "astronomical images" <note>original: "imagines astronomicæ"; here referring to astrological talismans intended to capture planetary influences</note> acquire their power through a demon. The proof of this is that these images must be inscribed with certain characters <note>sigils or occult symbols</note>, even though such signs contribute nothing to natural power. Nevertheless, astrological signs differ from magical idols in this way: in the composition of magical items, there are express invocations of demons, and thus such effigies belong to "express pacts" <note>formal, conscious agreements</note> entered into with demons. But in the making of astronomical images, there exists a "silent pact" <note>original: "tacitum... fœdus"; an implied agreement where the user may not realize they are inviting demonic aid</note> with demons through certain characters and figures discovered by the demons themselves; the demons assist those who impress these characters. Thus far the author.

<margin>Book 18 of *On Subtlety*.</margin>
Thus it is skillfully written by Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a renowned Italian physician and polymath</note>, a philosopher and physician: although people attribute no small power to seals—such as those of the Sun for honors from magistrates and favor with princes, of Jupiter for riches and friends, of Venus for pleasures, of Mars for boldness, of Mercury for cleverness, of Saturn for patience in labor, and of the Moon for the favor of the common people...

<margin>Cardano, *On Variety*, Book 16, chapter 90.</margin>
<margin>Similar points in Agrippa’s *On Occult Philosophy*, Book 1, chapter 33, and Book 3, chapters 29, 30, and 31.</margin>
I am not unaware that stones may be useful, but their shape contributes nothing. In the same place, where he recounted the decrees of Artephius <note>A legendary figure to whom several alchemical and magical texts were attributed; he was said to have lived for a thousand years</note>—the greatest practitioner of that magical folly—it may be judged that mages were not only deceptive, but truly out of their minds. He describes the strange characters of the planets, as well as rings marked with terrifying planetary signs and seals fortified with monstrous forms. But he immediately adds: "These are characters devised by a deceitful mind, and it is certain that they possess no power. For what do these characters have in common with the planets themselves, which are spherical?" And do not think these names are significant just because they are Arabic, Chaldean, Hebrew, or Greek; for even if they were Latin, what more power would be in them? Therefore, they must be mere fictions <note>original: "figmenta mera"</note> and of no virtue; if you contend that they do obtain power, it can only happen through a pact with demons. For who was able to find such things, except through the persuasions of demons? Yet it is well established that demons now teach nothing of substance. 

They will say, however, that these forms are fixed in the Ninth Sphere <note>In medieval cosmology, the Ninth Sphere or *Primum Mobile* was the outermost moving sphere that dictated the motion of the lower stars and planets</note>, which are seen in India. So indeed did that wicked man of Abano <note>Peter of Abano (c. 1250–1316), a famous physician and philosopher often posthumously accused of heresy and magic</note> imagine. But let it be conceded: who, then, later taught that *this* character belongs to the Sun, and *that* one to Saturn? From this it is clearly evident that these were the pure inventions of men mocking their fellows. Many more such delusions of the mages from the works of Artephius are recited there in order.

If mages contend that they use natural things—characters, shapes, herbs, and words—while otherwise claiming to detest public dealings with demons, they are refuted here. For it is most thoroughly proven by Aristotle and all natural philosophers that active virtues cannot reside in shapes, nor in letters or any characters whatsoever, since these are nothing other than a composition and order devised by an artisan, whether painting or sculpting. Furthermore, it is well-witnessed that material images cannot work beyond their own species and form, much less produce miraculous effects above the laws of nature.
