## On the healing of injuries caused by witchcraft

Demons do not heal, but capture men by deceit. And rightly did that most admirable **Justin** <note>Justin Martyr, a 2nd-century Christian philosopher and apologist</note> teach that demons are like robbers. For just as robbers are accustomed to seize certain men and then return them to their kinsmen once a ransom has been agreed upon, so too those whom you consider to be gods <note>The author is addressing pagans or those tempted by superstition</note> work their way into the limbs of certain men. Then, manufacturing their own glory within those men through dreams, they command them to go out in public; and in the sight of everyone—after they have satisfied themselves with the worldly things they desired—they fly away from the sick. By erasing the disease produced by their own trickery, they restore the men to their former health. **Saint Jerome** also testifies that although certain miracles can be performed by magical power—such as those that pertain only to curiosity and vanity (just as **Simon the Sorcerer** <note>Also known as Simon Magus, a figure mentioned in the Book of Acts who attempted to buy spiritual power</note> pretended that statues could walk, talk, laugh, and the like)—nevertheless, those things which are beneficial, such as the healing of the weak, the giving of sight to the blind, and similar acts, cannot be achieved by magical arts or by demons.

From this, **Augustine**—and it is read in the *Decrees*, Causa 26, the final question—gives this warning: 
> "Let faithful priests warn their peoples so that they may know that magical arts and incantations can provide no remedy for any human infirmities, nor can they heal anything in weak, limping, or even dying animals; rather, these things are the snare and the ambush of the ancient enemy <note>A traditional term for the Devil</note>, by which that faithless one strives to deceive the human race. And if any cleric shall have practiced these things, let him be stripped of his rank; if a layman, let him be excommunicated." 

Almost the same is read in the book *The City of God*, and in Causa 26, question 2, at the end, where it is taught that such a "cure" should be called death rather than life.

This fact did not escape **Galen** <note>A prominent Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire whose views dominated Western medicine for centuries</note>, who affirmed that the one in whom many people place their trust heals the most. From the histories of our ancestors and the recent memory of our fathers, many recall examples and assert that not a few people—through some sort of credulity and religious feeling toward vows made to saints, or from the touch or sight of bones (I will not say the caskets themselves) which were reported to have been collected and preserved from the corpses of certain people—have recovered their lost integrity of strength. In these cases, the restoration of health overcomes their weakness <term>αδυναμίαν <gloss>adynamia; physical weakness or lack of strength</gloss></term>, with the devil acting as the sole author of this entire impious cult. Indeed, they say that from this source, an opinion was born and pervaded the minds of men, and as it grew and was strengthened by age, it became deep-rooted: they believe that vows alone offered to statues are more effective and much more powerful at uprooting and extirpating illnesses that have arisen in the body than any remedies combined. They add that this custom has grown so common that if any adversity should happen, divine help is not sought, but instead those saints are called upon for assistance who are believed to preside over and rule such evils...

# Book Five.

<margin>The power of steadfast credulity.</margin>
However, how much steadfast **credulity** <note>original: "credulitas," here meaning a naive or stubborn readiness to believe</note> is worth has become well known among the common people. Superstition requires credulity, just as true religion requires faith. Indeed, fixed credulity is so powerful that it is believed to work even miracles in the midst of false opinions and actions. For anyone in their own religion—even a false one—so long as they most firmly believe it to be true, lifts up their spirit by that very reason of credulity until they are assimilated to those spirits who are the leaders and princes of that religion. Thus, they seem to perform those things which nature and reason cannot discern. 

But hesitation and distrust weaken the intended work, not only in superstition but even in true religion; they enervate the sought-after effect, even if it has been confirmed by much use. Moreover, how superstition imitates religion is shown by examples, says **Agrippa** <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous scholar of the "occult sciences" whose work is being cited here to show how magic mimics holy rites</note>: 
<margin>On Occult Philosophy, Book 1, chapter 4.</margin>
namely, when worms and locusts are excommunicated so they do not harm the crops; when bells and images are baptized, and many more such things. 

But because those ancient magi, and those who stood out as authors of that art among the ancients, were **Chaldeans**, **Egyptians**, **Assyrians**, **Persians**, and **Arabs**—whose entire religion was perverse and defiled by the worship of idols—we must take the greatest care. We must not permit their errors to dominate over the pure truth of our Christian religion. For this would be blasphemous and an **abomination** <note>original Greek: "βδέλυγμα" (bdelygma), a term often used in the Bible for something spiritually detestable or foul</note>.

### It is shown through quite charming stories how much reckless credulity prevails in magical healings.

Moreover, I shall show through ridiculous examples what that reckless **credulity** <note>original: "credulitas," a naive or stubborn readiness to believe</note> can achieve. First, I received a quite charming story from a man of the Church, a theologian of no small reputation. He related that a certain scoundrel <note>original: "nebulonem," a rascal or worthless person</note> happened to visit a poor woman who had been suffering for some time from a chronic inflammation of the eyes <note>original: "lippitudine," a condition involving redness, discharge, and irritation</note>. Having promised a most certain cure for her eyes, he hung a small scroll around her neck. He strictly warned her not to remove, open, or read it, asserting that no help whatsoever could be expected from it if she failed in any way in this regard. The woman, bolstered by great hope and confidence, even restrained herself from weeping—which previously had worsened the malady of her eyes—and in this way, she gradually recovered. At last, having attained health, the scroll was treated carelessly and fell off. Upon noticing the loss of that in which she had uniquely placed her faith, her tears returned and the ailment broke out again. Meanwhile, the scroll was found by someone else, opened, and read; it was said that these words were inscribed in the German tongue:

<margin>A ridiculous note hung from the neck.</margin>
> May the devil scratch your eyes out and shit in the holes. <note>original German: "Der teüffel kratze dir die augen auß, vnd ſcheiſſe dir in die læcher."</note>

If it were translated word for word, it sounds like: *May the Devil tear out your eyes, and fill their sockets with his own filth.* If there had been any power in these words, her eyes would have been torn out and destroyed, and the cavities stuffed full of the demon’s excrement. Not entirely unlike this is a case reported by Pliny regarding Marcus Servilius Nonianus, a leading man of the city. Out of fear of eye inflammation, before he would even name the ailment or let anyone else mention it to him, he would tie a paper inscribed with the two Greek letters **P** and **A** <note>The Greek letters Rho and Alpha; such alphabetic amulets were common in folk medicine</note>, bound with linen thread, around his neck.

Concerning the treatment of injuries caused by witchcraft.
<meta>catchword: conce-</meta>

<margin>Homeric healing.</margin>
...attempting it (in his treatise on Homeric healing) <note>original: *Homerica medicatione*. This refers to the ancient practice of using poetic incantations for healing, named after Homer, who recorded such practices in the *Odyssey*</note>, though he had previously denied its efficacy. The reason for this name was that Homer recorded how blood was stanched with words and diseases were cured through mysteries. Nor was Aetius <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine physician</note> ashamed to use a superstitious charm to chant out thorns and small bones stuck in the throat or tonsils. I mentioned above, from Benivieni <note>Antonio Benivieni (1443–1502), a Florentine physician regarded as a pioneer of pathological anatomy</note>, how a weapon was pulled from a chest using a charm. Marcellus <note>Marcellus Empiricus, a Roman medical writer known for blending folk remedies with medicine</note> also repeatedly urges the use of charms; Octavianus used them as well in his *Euporista* <note>meaning "Easily Procured Remedies"</note>. Likewise Quintus Serenus, who teaches that the word **Abracadabra** <note>original: "Abracadabra"</note>, inscribed on paper in a specific shape he describes and hung from the neck, frees one from fevers, and especially from the semi-tertian fever <note>a severe form of malaria</note>.

Gordonius <note>Bernard de Gordon (c. 1260–1318), an influential professor of medicine at Montpellier</note> likewise, and many other more recent physicians who were more inclined toward superstitions, even though they were leaders in their field, held charms in high regard. They found no few remedies for hemorrhages, epileptic seizures <note>original: *comitales accessiones*, literally "the assembly disease," so named because a Roman public assembly would be dissolved if anyone had a seizure</note>, difficult childbirth, intermittent and wandering fevers, worms, wounds, fistulas, dislocations, hernias, and I know not what else.

<margin>Book 1 of the Method, chapter 11, on Homeric healing.</margin>
When you see the experience of these things (says Augerius Ferrerius <note>Auger Ferrier (1513–1588), a French physician and astrologer</note>, whose learned opinion I will quite appropriately quote at length here) placed before your eyes and confirmed by the authority of so many illustrious men, what will you do? For to go against things which are exposed to the senses is not the mark of a sane man; yet to invalidate the experiments of learned men is reckless. You will say, "But what do you, who urge these things, really think?" I will speak freely. For I am not a superstitious man, nor a lover of fables, but a student of the truth. When I applied myself to this study with all my mind and effort, I wished also to touch upon these prodigious cures, lest I should be found lacking in any part of the works of the medical art. I have thus discovered that the outcome of this treatment does not flow from magical characters or from the charm; rather, such is the **power of our mind** <note>original: *vis animi nostri*</note> that if it persuades itself of something honorable, and persists firmly in that persuasion, it [achieves] that very thing...

For the **enchanter** <note>original: *praecantator*</note> so moves the mind of the non-resisting patient that the pain is gradually extinguished while he murmurs or works with **magical signs** <note>original: *characteribus* - specific symbols or letters used in occult practices</note>. This is not without miracle. But if by chance the patient distrusts <note>the original OCR *difficat* is likely a transcription of *diffidat* (distrusts)</note>, or thinks the remedy is completely ridiculous, or has bystanders who undermine his faith and mock the remedy in his presence, the enchanter will have no power, because he has the mind of the other person resisting his persuasion.

I will insert here that I remember a certain noble girl's toothache was eased by a noble man with a **charm** <note>original: *carmine* - literally a song or poem, used here as a healing incantation</note>. But after she was rebuked for allowing an impious method of healing, she repented of the deed: because of this, the pain returned, though it later vanished of its own accord. But he who approaches chanting without faith and persuasion will waste his effort—unless by chance he finds a mind so dull that it does not realize it is being deceived by the pretense. It is not, therefore, the charms, nor the magical signs that can do such things, but the **power of a confident mind** in harmony with the patient, as was most learnedly said by the Poet <note>Marcus Manilius, a 1st-century Roman poet and astrologer, from his work *Astronomica*</note>:

> A spirit lives in us, not in the depths of hell nor the stars of heaven;
> The spirit that thrives within us performs those wonders.

But that confidence and firm persuasion is gained by unlearned minds through the opinion they have formed about **magical signs** and sacred words. For the learned and those who have an understanding of things, there is no need for external things; instead, having recognized the power of the mind, they can perform miracles through it, such as those Philostratus <note>Gaius Flavius Philostratus, the biographer of Apollonius</note> reports about **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a 1st-century philosopher and reputed miracle-worker</note>, when from

### On physical bindings, charms, and amulets; likewise, that demons are neither attracted nor put to flight by any plants or earthly matter. Chapter XVIII.

<margin>Physical bindings.</margin>
However, I do not wish to suggest here that all faith in <term>physical bindings</term> <note>original: *ligaturis*—objects tied to the body for healing</note>, <term>charms</term> <note>original: *periaptis*—items worn as protective ornaments</note>, and physical amulets is misplaced. For many substances, by reason of their specific or individual (if I may call it so) constitution during their creation, are imbued from heaven with some power which, through an innate and hidden antipathy, may inhibit and bind the actions of certain other things; hence the origin and name of "physical bindings." Thus the presence of a diamond and other things prevents the operations of a magnet so that it does not attract iron; similarly, oil takes away the power from amber and "binds" it, so that it cannot attract chaff.

The *Oenothera* <note>A plant likely related to the evening primrose, though historically its identification varied</note> (according to <term>Crateuas</term> <note>A famous Greek physician and herbalist from the 1st century BCE</note>), if tied around the neck or hung from a yoke after being sprinkled with wine, tames the wildness of all animals.

<margin>On physical charms and amulets, see the physician Theodorus Priscianus [writing] to Eusebius in his final book. Galen, books 6 and 10 of *On Simple Medicines*.</margin>
Furthermore, certain physicians contend that truly physical charms and amulets are supported by natural reason, and that certain <term>vapors</term> <note>original: *ἀτμούς* (atmoi)—exhalations or microscopic particles</note> flow down from their substance. These, being secretly drawn in through breathing, are able by their power to alter the cause of a disease and restore the body. For this reason, we hang the fresh root of a male <term>Peony</term> and the red-flowered pimpernel <note>original: *anagallidem*</note> to ward off the threats of epilepsy. Likewise, we bind the dung of a wolf and its intestine to one afflicted by the torments of colic pain—not (as the physician Pamphilus thinks) because of the power of an incantation, but for a hidden natural cause (as I have said), or perhaps due to "harmonic spirits," as the followers of **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who revolutionized medicine with chemical treatments</note> believe. Wherefore <margin>Book 10, *On Simple Medicines*.</margin> **Galen**, taught by their experience, warns that one should trust in charms in such a way that it is their physical substance, and not the words of the magicians' incantations, that provides the help. Theophrastus held the same opinion, saying that those absurd things [should] rather <margin>Book 9, *History of Plants*.</margin> be thought...

### Chapter XIX.

<margin>
Sulfur.
Asphalt.
Sea water.
Things that expiate demons.

In this kind of religious practice, **sulfur** was believed to have its own place for cleansing <note>original: *expiandum*; to purify or drive out evil through ritual</note> evil demons through fumigation. Proclus writes that priests were accustomed to use it in purifications, as they did **asphalt** or washing with **sea water**; this is because sulfur purifies by the sharpness of its odor, while sea water purifies due to its "fiery" portion. Hence, Ovid says of the witch Medea:

> Three times she purifies the old man with flame, three times with water, three times with sulfur. <note>original: *Terq; ſenem flamma, ter aqua, ter ſulphure luſtrat.* From Ovid's *Metamorphoses*, describing the rejuvenation of Aeson.</note>

The herb **cinquefoil** <note>original: *pentaphyllon*; literally "five-leaf"</note> was also thought to cleanse, and therefore ancient priests employed it for this purpose; just as they did **olive branches**, which are said to be of such great purity that they claim an olive tree planted by a harlot will either remain perpetually fruitless or wither away entirely.

<margin>Book 1, chapter 5 of *Memorable Things*. Against storms.</margin>
Furthermore, it was believed that the assault of demons of the air is dissolved and calmed by a louder noise and the smoke of foul-smelling herbs. For this reason (**Gaudentius Merula** <note>An Italian scholar and humanist of the 16th century</note> says), as if they flowed from the workshop of the **Academics** <note>A reference to the followers of Plato's Academy, suggesting these ideas have a philosophical pedigree</note>, even now Italian women burn foul-smelling fodder in the open air when storms are imminent. Priests, however, in the manner of the **Thracians** <note>An ancient people from Southeast Europe, often depicted in classical texts as warlike and ritualistic</note> (who, when a storm approached, would roar at the clouds with a horrible clamor, armed with drawn swords and rattles), fly to the noisy cymbals, which are called **bells**; they trust more in those bellowings—which are empty before God—than in prayers and fasts.

<margin>Book 3, chapter 8, *On the Northern Peoples*.</margin>
**Olaus Gothus** <note>Olaus Magnus, a Swedish bishop and writer</note> writes something very similar about his own countrymen, who, when a crash was stirred up in the clouds, would shoot arrows from their bows into the air. They did this to show they wished to bring aid to their gods, whom they thought were then being attacked by others. Not content with that reckless superstition, they also kept hammers of unusual weight, which they called **Jovial Hammers** <note>original: *Mallei Iouiales*; hammers dedicated to Jove/Thor, used to mimic thunder</note> <margin>Jovial Hammers.</margin>, encased in massive bronze and worshipped with great religious devotion. They used them so that through them—just as if by **Claudian thunders** <note>A reference to the *Tonitru Claudianum*, a theatrical machine used in Rome to simulate the sound of thunder</note> and through a common resemblance of things—they might express the crashes of heaven, which they believed were provoked by hammers. By imitating the power of such a sound with the appearance of blacksmiths' tools, they considered it a truly religious act to be present in the wars of their gods. This use of Jovial Hammers lasted until the year 1130 after the birth of Christ.

Among our ancestors as well, a persuasion grew through a long series of years, fueled by the unsound teaching of parish priests: that **mugwort** <note>original: *artemisia*; a plant long associated with protection and the summer solstice</note> hung before houses on the feast days sacred to **St. John the Baptist**, and likewise other shrubs and plants, and

<margin>From the Pontifical service book. Exorcised water.</margin>
To this subject belongs water, created by the almighty Creator for countless uses, which takes on new powers through these words: *I exorcise you, creature of water, in the name of God the Father Almighty, and in the name of Jesus Christ His Son our Lord, and in the power of the Holy Spirit, that you may become exorcised water to put to flight every power of the enemy, and that you may be able to uproot and cast out the enemy himself along with his apostate angels.* <note>original: "Exorciso te creatura aquæ in nomine Dei patris omnipotentis..."</note> Alexander I, the Roman Pontiff <note>Traditionally the fifth Pope, serving in the early 2nd century</note>, was the authority who decreed that such lustral water <note>Water used for ritual purification</note> should be consecrated to drive away demons, and that it should be kept in the church and at home. ## That no demon is extracted by a root; against Josephus and concerning the root called Baaras.

### Chapter 20.

<margin>Josephus, *Antiquities of the Jews*, Book 8, Chapter 2. Crinitus, Book 9, Chapter 1.</margin>
Moreover, as for the boast of Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian</note> that, in the presence of the Emperor Vespasian, he saw a certain Eleazar of the Hebrew nation apply a ring to the nostrils of a person possessed by a demon—under the seal of which a root discovered by Solomon had been placed—and that he drew the demon out through the nostrils of the person smelling it:
<margin>A story mocked for its use of a ring and a root to extract a demon.</margin>
and when the man had suddenly fallen to the ground, Eleazar banished the demon using a song of conjuration attributed to Solomon. Here it must certainly be confessed that Josephus the Jew, as well as Vespasian the pagan and Eleazar the Hebrew, were all deceived by the tricks of the devil. The demon only pretended to be drawn out by the power of a root ascribed to Solomon; he yielded not by force, but of his own accord, by God’s permission. (For the devil feigns being coerced so that he may more effectively drive others out of their minds.) He did this so that more faith might be placed in a ring or in the fiction of a root—materials wholly unfit for casting out a demon—rather than seeking refuge in the legitimate order through the one God, who alone repels Satan. And so that the conclusion of this story might be completed with a fiction matching its beginnings—to cover this act, impious in itself, with a respectable cloak—and so that it would not be called into question as a fraud, but rather gain weight, the art was ascribed to Solomon...

After this, there is no fear for those who take it. It is worth the effort to capture it despite such dangers because of a single power. For those which are called 'demons'—the spirits of the most wicked men, which enter into the living and kill those who are not helped..."

# Book Five.

...[if the demon] were not [present], this [root] quickly drives them away, even if it is only brought near the sick. Thus far Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (37–c. 100 AD), a Romano-Jewish historian.</note>. But less faith will be given to the root if the manner of its collection is examined with a clearer eye of the mind.

Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus (c. 175–c. 235 AD), a Roman author and teacher of rhetoric.</note> writes nearly the same things in Book 14, Chapter 27, concerning the magical herb <term>Cynospastos</term> <note>original: "Cynofpafto"; from the Greek for "dog-pulled," referring to the method of its harvest.</note>, which is called by another name, <term>Aglaophotis</term> <note>original: "Aglaophotis"; literally "bright-light," referring to its supposed nighttime glow.</note>, and is thought to be the same as the *baaras*. This herb stays hidden during the day among other plants (from which it does not differ in the least) and is in no way recognized; but at night, shining like a star and flickering with a fiery brilliance, it easily comes into view. Therefore, people leave a mark fixed at its roots; without this, they would recognize neither its color nor its appearance during the day. Once the night has passed, they return and identify the herb by the mark, yet they take care not to pull it up or even dig around it. For they say that the first person who, being ignorant of its nature, touches it, will perish. Therefore, they bring a young dog that has been kept hungry for the space of a day, and they tie a strong cord very tightly to the lower stalk of the plant, fastening the other end to the dog. They then throw many pieces of roasted meat to the dog, while they themselves retreat as far as possible. The dog, moved by the scent, rushes toward the meat and tears the herb out by the roots. If the sun sees these roots, the dog soon expires and is buried with certain secret ceremonies, as if it had died for their benefit. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD), a Roman author and natural philosopher whose *Natural History* was a primary source for medieval and Renaissance science.</note>, in Book 4, Chapter 17, mentions the *Aglaophotis* among the magical herbs recorded by Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 460–370 BC), often associated in later lore with alchemy and magic.</note>. He notes it received its name from the admiration of men for its extraordinary color. It grows among the marbles of Arabia on the Persian side, and for this reason, it is also called *marmaritis*. The magicians certainly use it when they wish to summon gods.

<margin>A little man fashioned from a mandrake root.</margin> Almost the same fiction is told about that artificial <term>homunculus</term> <note>Latin for "little man." In this context, it refers to a root carved to look like a human, often sold as a magical charm.</note> fashioned from the roots of the mandrake, reeds, bryony, and other plants. # On the cure of injuries from witchcraft.

...millet grains, in those places where they want hair to grow. Then, having made a small pit, they cover them with thin sand for as long as it takes for those grains to sprout roots: which they say happens within twenty days at most. Finally, they dig them up and split the roots that have grown from the grains with a very sharp knife, and they arrange them so that they resemble head hair, a beard, and other body hairs. Commonly, however, the ignorant and simple are persuaded that these roots, representing a human likeness <note>This refers to the "Alraun" or mandrake root, which was often carved or manipulated to look like a tiny human figure.</note>, can by no means be dug up except with great danger to life: with a dog tied to the roots to dig it up, and its ears stopped with pitch, lest those digging hear the root's cry <note>A famous legend held that the mandrake screamed when uprooted, killing anyone who heard it.</note>: because when the voice is heard, the diggers are endangered and perish. It is amazing how much power is attributed to this artificial <term>homunculus</term> <note>original: "homuncioni"; a "little man" or artificial humanoid creature.</note>—supposedly born under the gallows from the urine of a hanged thief <note>A common folklore belief that mandrakes grew where the fluids of a hanged man hit the ground.</note>—according to the popular belief, against storms and I know not what other calamities. But these are mere trifles.

<margin>Chapter 26, question 5, "Bishops."</margin>
It is memorable what is read in the second part of the *Decretum* <note>The *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon Law compiled in the 12th century.</note>: The devil, always hiding under veils, betrays himself while he fakes things that belong to the persons through whom he strives to deceive. But if anyone objects and says, "How do those things happen which those diviners predict for the future? Or how can they provide healing to the sick, or inflict sickness on the healthy, if they have no inherent power or authority of their own?" Let them receive this response from us: That no one ought to believe them for the reason that what they predict sometimes happens, or they seem to heal the weak or harm the healthy: because this happens by the permission of God, so that those who hear or see these things may be tested, and it may appear with what 
<margin>Deuteronomy 13.</margin>
faith or devotion they regard God. Just as it is read in Deuteronomy that Moses, by the divine word of God, commanded the people: that a prophet or a dreamer of dreams must not be believed, even if the sign and wonder he spoke of comes to pass, if he leads one away from the true worship of God.

### The most serious abuse of common sacrificial exorcists <note>original: "sacrificulorum"; a disparaging term for priests who perform rituals or sacrifices without true spiritual authority.</note>. Chapter XXI.

Furthermore, for the cure of those believed to be affected by witchcraft <term>maleficium</term> <note>Damage or harm believed to be caused by harmful magic.</note>, or oppressed by a siege of Satan, inept, rash, and audaciously bold men rush in. These men are churchmen by profession, but in the filth of their lives they are far too worldly (just as the actor of a play requires such a role and stage). Following their prescribed exorcisms and a set formula of certain ceremonies, they attempt to dissolve the disease and drive out the demon. Sometimes, <margin>Collusion.</margin> the demon—willing and in collusion—yields to their curses and oaths, so that it may strengthen their impiety. Indeed, these exorcists should, by the best right, be counted among enchanters <term>incantatores</term> <note>Specifically those who use chants, spells, or rhythmic formulas to produce effects.</note>.

Here, so that I may briefly relate some of their observations—from which you may measure the rest, just as one knows a lion by its claw—a diligent search is made after the confession of the one to be purified by conjurations. <margin>Superstitious mock-cure.</margin> They look in every corner of the house, in the bedding and pillows, or under the threshold of the door, to see if any "material of witchcraft" <note>Physical objects like feathers, hair, or charms thought to hold a spell's power.</note> can be found, which is then to be burned.

<margin>Abuse of exorcisms.</margin> Truly, this practice by no means originated from the Apostles or the primitive Church. For if someone is entirely cured from the devil's harmful act by exorcisms, why would those trifles hidden in corners or buried in the earth—which in no way touch the body or strike it with their breath—be harmful?

Next, the person injured by witchcraft holds a blessed candle in their hand while kneeling; they are also sprinkled with lustral water <note>Holy water used for ritual purification.</note>, and their neck is encircled with a priest’s stole. Besides prayers, the common Litanies are recited, adding to the invocation of the saints: "Pray for him," or "Pray [all of you]," and "Be merciful," "Deliver him, O Lord." In place of simple prayers, exorcisms are employed, which are continued at least three times a week, so that by multiplying these intercessions, the grace of health may be obtained. The theological authors of the *Hammer of Witches* <term>Malleus Maleficarum</term> <note>original: "Mallei maleficarum"; the infamous 15th-century handbook on the prosecution of witches.</note> prescribe this form, <margin>Part 2, question 2, chapter 6.</margin> though it stands against the evident doctrine of Christ:

This is so much the case that I knew at one time that the priest of that "Cloaked One" <note>original: "Palleati"; Saint Augustine refers here to a priest of a pagan deity—likely Serapis or Attis—who wore a philosopher's cloak (*pallium*) and claimed his god was also a Christian to lure the faithful into idolatry.</note> was accustomed to say: "The Cloaked One himself is also a Christian." Why is this, brothers, except because Christians cannot be seduced otherwise? Therefore, do not seek Christ anywhere else than where Christ wished himself to be preached. And in the way he wished to be preached, so hold onto him, so write him in your hearts. He is a wall against all attacks, and against all the snares of the enemy. Do not fear: the enemy does not tempt unless he has been permitted, or sent. He is sent as an evil agent, by the ruling power of God. He is permitted when he asks for something: and this, brothers, does not happen except so that the righteous may be tested and the unrighteous punished. Why then do you fear? Walk in the Lord your God: be certain that if he does not wish you to suffer, you will not suffer; what he has permitted you to suffer is the whip of a father correcting you, not the punishment of a judge condemning you. We are being trained for the heavenly inheritance, and do we disdain to be whipped? These are the words of Augustine.

<margin>
Words consistent with the purpose are needed in driving out Satan.
</margin>
How then will that recitation of the Gospels be powerful for driving out a demon, or for overturning his works, when the words used are not consistent in their meaning with this specific purpose? For where Christ, and his disciples, and later holy men cast out demons, they spoke with words specifically suited and designated for this business, and they answered (as it is said) according to the proper form. For if the desired power consisted simply in the pronunciation of unsuitable words, then certain of the wandering Jewish exorcists would have achieved no less—indeed, even more—for they attempted to invoke the name of the Lord JESUS over those who had evil spirits, saying: "We adjure <note>To command solemnly under oath or under the threat of a curse.</note>

A certain man serving as a pastor in the village of Dürwiß, near Eschweiler, promised with great arrogance <note>original: "elato supercilio"; literally "with a raised eyebrow," indicating pride or haughtiness.</note> that he wished to free a girl named Helena—who was oppressed by demonic possession in the village of Lohn, located near Aldenhoven in the Duchy of Jülich—through his own exorcisms. One of them, specifically Johann Windelius, the pastor in Beeck, who was present at the proceeding, recounted the whole matter to me in order and, at my request, wrote it down. 

To this exorcist, who for some time had been sweating in vain with his oaths to drive out the demon, the spirit finally said that he would remain there because many of his colleagues were milling about around the glass <note>original: "vitrum"; likely referring to a window or a glass vessel used in folk magic, which the demon used as a distraction.</note> placed there to light the room, as is customary, and that they were encouraging him. That wretched pastor, having trusted the author of lies, immediately turned toward the glass to drive them out, since the demon had pointed them out there. When he saw that he was wasting his effort, he finally broke out in indignation with these Latin words—which he perhaps hoped the demon would not understand:

> If you have any power of migrating into Christian blood, migrate from her into me. <note>original: "Si ullā habes poteſtatē trāſmigrandi in Chriſtianū ſanguinē, transmigra ex illa in me."</note>

<margin>* A memorable story concerning the spirit of Orléans.</margin>

In the year 1534, the wife of the Provost <note>original: *Prætor*; a high-ranking local magistrate or provost.</note> of Orléans <note>original: *Aurelia*; the Latin name for the city of Orléans, France.</note> had stipulated in her will that she should be buried without any pomp or noise. For when someone departs this life in France, funeral heralds hired for this purpose travel through the more crowded parts of the city, summoning the multitude by the sound of bells. They then announce the name and titles of the deceased, and having exhorted the people to pray to God for the dead, they declare when and where the burial is to take place. Furthermore, when the funeral procession is conducted, mendicant monks <note>Monks who lived by begging, such as the Franciscans or Dominicans, often hired to add solemnity to funerals.</note> are usually employed, and many lights are carried before the body. These things are done competitively and with a certain rivalry; the more magnificent the display, the greater the gathering and admiration of the people. But that woman, as I mentioned, wished for none of these things to be done for her. 

Her husband, who cherished the memory of his spouse, complied with her wishes. To the Franciscans, in whose church she was buried next to her father and grandfather, he gave only six gold coins as a gift, though they had hoped for a much larger prize. Later, when he was cutting and selling wood from his forest, he refused to give them timber for free when they requested it. They took this very poorly; and since they already thought little of him, they devised this plan for revenge: they would claim that his wife was eternally damned. 

The architects of this tragedy were Colimannus and Stephen of Arras <note>original: *Atrebatensis*</note>, both doctors of theology. Colimannus was an exorcist and had ready at hand all his equipment usually employed in such matters. They managed the business in this way: they placed a certain young novice above the vault <note>original: *testudo*; the arched ceiling or roof space of the church.</note> of the church. In the dead of night, when they came to mutter their prayers in the customary manner, he raised a great noise. Adjurations and exorcisms were employed, but he said nothing in reply. Ordered to give a sign by which he might declare whether he was a mute spirit, he again, at the same time

[The hidden accomplice] makes a commotion and a din: this served as a signal. Once this foundation was laid, the monks approached several citizens—men of high standing and known to be supporters of their order. They told them that something distressing had happened at their monastery, though they did not yet explain the nature of the matter; they simply asked that the citizens might be willing to attend their nightly prayers. When these men had arrived and the prayers had begun, the accomplice stirred up a noise from the upper floor. When asked what he wanted and who he was, he indicated that he was not permitted to speak: he was therefore ordered to respond to questions through signals. 

A hole had been made in the ceiling, through which, by pressing his ear to it, he could catch the voice of the exorcist <note>In this context, the monk performing a ritual to communicate with or expel a spirit.</note> and understand him. He also had a board <note>original: *tabulam*; likely a wooden plank or tablet used to create loud knocking sounds.</note> at hand, which he struck when questioned so that it could be heard by those below. 

First, he was asked if he was one of those buried there. After many names of those whose bodies were entombed there were recited in order, they finally came to the wife of the Provost. When her name was mentioned, the signal was given, and he demonstrated that he was her spirit. He was then asked whether she was damned, and by what merit or fault of her own? Was it because of greed, or lust, or pride, or for failing to practice charity? Or was it indeed because of the recently born heresy and Lutheranism? <note>original: *Lutheranismum*; the monks were exploiting the contemporary religious tension of the Reformation to frame the woman as a heretic.</note> 

Next, he was asked what he intended by that noise and restlessness? Was it so that her body, buried in a sacred place, should be dug up and moved elsewhere? To all these questions, just as he had been instructed, he responded through signals, by which he affirmed or denied a point depending on whether he struck the board twice or thrice. 

When he had signaled that the cause of her damnation was the Lutheran heresy and that her body ought to be exhumed, the monks asked the citizens they had invited to provide testimony of what they had seen with their own eyes. They were asked to sign the formal records <note>original: *actis*; the legal or official transcripts of the event.</note> which had already been prepared in the preceding days. 

These citizens, after deliberating on the matter, refused to do so, fearing they might offend the Provost or bring trouble upon themselves. Nevertheless, the monks removed the unleavened bread—which they call the host <note>original: *hostia*; the consecrated bread used in the Catholic Mass.</note> and the body of the Lord—along with all the relics of the saints, and moved them to another place, performing their Masses there...

Because the monks were refusing to submit to judgment, relying on their own privileges and immunities, the King selected certain men from the Paris Parliament <note>original: *senatu Parisino*</note> to investigate the case, granting them full authority. The Chancellor Antoine Duprat <note>original: *Antonius Pratensis*</note>, who was both a Cardinal and the Pope's legate throughout France, did the same. 

Therefore, since they had no grounds for legal exception, the monks were brought to Paris <note>original: *Lutetiam*</note> and compelled to answer; however, no confession could be forced from them. They were placed under separate guards, and the novice <note>The young monk who had been hiding in the ceiling to play the part of the spirit.</note> was held in the house of Senator Fumé. Although he was frequently urged to speak, he refused to confess anything, fearing that he would later be murdered by the other monks for bringing a stain upon the order and causing such disgrace. But when the judges promised him both immunity from punishment and that he would never be returned to the monks' power, he recounted the whole plot in order. When brought before the others, he maintained the same testimony. The monks, even though they were convicted and caught almost in the very act of their wrongdoing, still rejected the judges and boasted of their privileges. Yet this was in vain; by common counsel, a sentence was passed, and they were condemned to be taken back to Orléans <note>original: *Aureliam*</note> and cast into prison—

### The most certain method for curing witchcraft.
### Chapter 24.

It seems to us that a far different method must be undertaken here than what we have received through long-established custom in driving out Satan and healing his spells—one more in conformity with the doctrine of Christ and the Apostles. First of all, whenever some evil seems to manifest itself in someone beyond the order of nature, one must flee, according to God’s ordinance, to the one who <margin>Ecclesiasticus 38</margin> is famous for his profession, doctrine, and use of art, to distinguish more deeply the diseases, their differences, signs, and causes: namely, to a physician of good conscience. 

For indeed, such rare and serious symptoms often arise in diseases which, although they spring from a natural impulse, are nonetheless immediately attributed to witchcraft by those unskilled in such matters and of little faith: as frequently appears in various types of convulsions, melancholy, epilepsy, suffocation of the womb <note>original: *uteri suffocatione*; a historical medical term often associated with "hysteria," then believed to be caused by the displacement or "suffocation" of the uterus.</note>, putrefying seed, and the manifold effects of poisons.

# Book Five.

[He should be a man] of [good] doctrine, holding the mystery of the faith with a pure conscience <note>original: "mysterium fidei cum pura conscientia"; a reference to 1 Timothy 3:9 regarding the requirements for church leaders.</note>, known for the innocence of his life, not dishonorably greedy for gain, and not a drunkard, so that a good testimony might be offered to him by the pious. To such a man, one should transfer the burden of care. Meanwhile, it is worth remembering that many things do not arise from witchcraft <note>original: "maleficio"</note>, but from hidden natural causes, which sometimes escape the notice of physicians; for just as there is a secret property in things for helping, so there is for harming, which a physician does not always recognize.

Nevertheless, such great effort will be applied by the physician here if, perhaps, the patient seems by nature—whether from illness or some other source—to be burdened by a melancholic humor <term>melancholic humor: In the ancient system of "humors," this was "black bile," a physical fluid thought to cause depression, erratic behavior, or madness.</term> (into which, as a material suited to its operations, a demon is not unwillingly accustomed to creep) or by some other malignant fluid, so that the patient may first be gently purged by medicine. For Pomponatius <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525), a Renaissance philosopher who explored natural explanations for seemingly supernatural events.</note> records that the ancient exorcists, whom he calls "petitioners," purged the bodies of the possessed of black bile <note>original: "atra bile"</note> before any conjuration. Indeed, these people are for the most part infested by twin diseases: namely, of the body, born from the melancholic fluid; and of the mind, such as madness, grief, fear, hatred of life, and despair. With these, the sworn enemy of the human race <note>A common epithet for the Devil.</note> torments such men night and day, and pricks them with mournful temptations in such a way that he seems to gnaw at their liver like the eagle did to Tityus in the underworld <note>In Greek mythology, the giant Tityus was punished in Hades by having his liver eternally eaten by vultures or an eagle.</note>. The "Conciliator" <note>Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1316), a famous physician known for "reconciling" medical and philosophical disputes.</note> says in his exposition of that problem that he has seen from experience that once that humor is expelled, those who were "possessed" no longer perform wonders. Also, the physician Galgarandus, most famous in Mantua, perfectly cured the wife of a certain cobbler who was agitated by a demon and sounding out various languages, using this same medical method.

A certain melancholic girl in the Borgo confessed that she was possessed by the spirit of the poet Virgil, having been subjected to exorcisms for a long time. ### Chapter XXVI.

<margin>Any kind of affliction must be borne patiently.</margin>
Therefore, we must bear with an even and patient mind whatever afflictions happen to the flesh, whether they occur by the laws of nature or beyond nature <note>The author distinguishes between "natural" illnesses and "supernatural" harm caused by witchcraft or demons.</note>. The same must be done if immense pain, anguish, grief, sadness, or temptation should invade the soul. Let the example of the most holy **Job** be always brought before our eyes like a mirror. Though he was tried in so many ways and pressed by such a mass of calamities and miseries, he exalted God with praises (even though at times, weighed down by the heavy burden of evils, he seemed to break out into the words of a mind lacking patience). Although he was conscious of no evil deed on his part, he did not accuse the demon, nor did he complain that such great distresses were inflicted on him by the devil or by any man; rather, he acknowledged that these things happened to him by the will of a most just God. So much so that when his wife reproached him, saying, *"Where now is your God, in whom you trusted?"*
<margin>Job 2</margin>
he did not lose heart, but replied: *"You speak like a foolish woman. If we have received good things from God, why shall we not patiently endure the bad?"* Thus it is fitting for us too, in our affliction, to direct our eyes and mind toward God, and to calmly submit ourselves and our affairs to His most just will—

With God’s permission, Satan afflicted him [Job]; but after his patience remained unbroken, God restored everything to him most abundantly with a great increase. God's hand is not shortened even now; He is able to do that same thing, and things infinitely greater. Why then should the violence or malice of any man, or even of the demon himself, terrify us? ### The Virtue of Almsgiving. Cap. XXIX.

<margin>Almsgiving.</margin>
To these things should be added, in proportion to one's means, the sharing of resources, their distribution to the poor, and the making of offerings. Paul, in his letter to the <margin>Philippians 4</margin> Philippians, calls this a scent of sweet fragrance, an acceptable and pleasing sacrifice to God. He also <margin>Romans 12.</margin> earnestly exhorts the Romans to patience in affliction, to persist in prayer, and to share in the <margin>Acts 10.</margin> needs of the saints. Likewise, Cornelius the centurion of the Italian cohort—a religious man who feared God, performing many acts of almsgiving for the people and always praying to God—heard this voice from an angel: "Cornelius, your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended as a memorial <margin>Tobit 12.</margin> before God." And the angel Raphael said to Tobit: "Almsgiving is good, more so than hiding away treasures of gold; for almsgiving delivers from death, and it is that which purges sins, and causes one to find mercy and <margin>Tobit 4.</margin> eternal life." Likewise, Tobit the father said to his son before his death: "Give alms from your substance, and do not turn your face away from any poor person: for in this way it shall happen that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you. In whatever way you are able, be merciful. If you have much, give abundantly; if you have little, strive to share even that little willingly. For you store up a good reward for yourself on the day of necessity."

# On the treatment of those harmed by witchcraft

...can be more conveniently and faithfully restored and healed, choosing the method of restoration according to each person's necessity. One should not try to fit everyone with "one shoe-mold" <note>original: "uno calopodio"; a proverbial expression meaning a "one-size-fits-all" approach</note> (as is the custom of certain foolish liars, impostors, and leaders of superstition and impiety). Nor should one persist in trying to drive out the demon with loose formulas of prescribed words that are poorly suited to the case, or with certain invented rituals and substances that contribute nothing to the matter. In such instances, the demon only laughs and mocks, or excellently feigns flight as if he were forced out—though he actually leaves of his own accord—so that he may involve us deeper in the labyrinth of unbelief if we believe he was driven away by these forbidden means. For this reason, he often leaves bodies, and indeed willingly, so that he may possess and dominate their souls with less hindrance.

As for those young women <note>The author is likely referring to nuns in a convent</note> who are kept strictly shut away and not permitted to go out—which I personally cannot approve of in such a case—or those who have resolved in their hearts to bravely endure the merciful hand of God and the Father’s rod with true self-denial, just as Job did: let them offer mutual help to one another during the intervals between their torments, comforting each other and observing the prescribed manner as much as possible.

<margin>Younger women should not be admitted to such a spectacle.</margin>

And let not the younger ones be admitted to a spectacle of this kind, lest they be terrified by the rarity and violence of the torments and contract some harm, since the devil lies in wait for them with great greed.

When they received this from His hand and submitted themselves with all their heart under His powerful arm, completely denying themselves and embracing humility to such an extent that they resisted all their passions and overcame them—and in short, conformed their lives with their whole soul to the standard of the divine word—then gradually all those dread afflictions vanished. I wanted to include this pious part of that virgin's letter for just reasons, because that advice corresponds exactly to my purpose; and lest anyone should rashly believe that such virgins are far removed from the number of the pious, even if I do not deny that many things are still lacking in them, which are omitted due to ignorant and unsound information.

He was to tell the returning spirit that he was not his own master <note>original: "sui iuris"; a legal term meaning one has the power to act for oneself</note>, but lived under the command of others, and therefore he could not obey the spirit's wishes due to a lack of resources. 

After this was done, the spirit responded: "Tell the Sub-prior," for he had conceived a hope of achieving his purpose through him. Therefore, when the Abbot noticed that the demon persisted and that the monk did not resist his illusions with enough confidence, he instructed him once more and more correctly, earnestly urging him to come to his senses and not to offer such willing ears to the tricks of Satan. He most severely threatened that if Philip continued to listen to the spirits <note>original: "manes"; a classical term for the souls of the dead, here used to describe the ghostly apparition</note> as he had done until now, he would beat him with whips, and indeed do so formally in the presence of the chapter. 

Consequently, the spirit, seeing his efforts were in vain because of the abbot’s constancy and Philip’s spirit being more uplifted by trust in God against the fraudulent and deadly designs of the demon, never returned and departed elsewhere. ### Chapter 31.

A certain humble woman named **Bartholomæa**, in the village of **Well**, began to act in an unusual way during the Mass. Whenever the hymn that begins **"Glory to God in the highest"** <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis Deo"</note> was sung in the **German language**, she would suddenly be seized as if by a demon and appeared to be cast into a trance <note>original: "extasin"; a state of being "outside oneself," often interpreted then as a sign of possession</note>, causing great distress among the people. She remained in that state of torment until the singing was finished. 

For some time, this behavior was overlooked, but because the woman did not stop, the lady of the village, **Anna of Virmont**, finally summoned her to the castle. She asked her humanely and kindly why she allowed herself to be overcome during that particular song, since the German words were exactly the same as the Latin ones, without any change in meaning. She read the German hymn to her and explained the words, showing that there was nothing absurd, nothing impious, or anything that should cause any offense within them. Therefore, she commanded the woman to be of good courage, warning her that she was now going to sing that same German hymn right there in the chamber. She threatened that if the woman allowed herself to be cast down again, she would apply a remedy that she had learned was especially useful for driving out such a "demon." 

Soon, at the start of the song, the woman threw herself to the ground in the same spot she had previously chosen to prostrate herself. Without delay, the noblewoman—a wise and sensible matron—along with her daughter **Katarina of Biland** <note>original: "Katarina Bilandia"</note>, a woman of excellent character, lifted the woman's clothing and applied sharp rods <note>original: "uirgas"; flexible switches used for discipline</note> with appropriate zeal. Meanwhile, the woman tried to pull her garment back down with her hands to ward off the stinging <note>original: "titillationem"; here referring to the sharp physical sensation</note>.

### The method of casting out demons in the ancient Church.
### Chapter 34.

Furthermore, lest anyone slander this counsel of ours as being foreign to the customary practice of our churchmen, or decide it should be rejected, I will here faithfully append the words of the blessed Clement <note>Clement of Rome, traditionally the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, though modern scholars date the work to the late 4th century.</note>. In these words, he beautifully describes the familiar form of driving out Satan in the ancient and purer Church—a form that conforms to our own instructions—found in Book 8, Chapter 32 of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. James, the son of Alphaeus <note>One of the Twelve Apostles.</note>, says: An exorcist is not ordained, for this contest <note>original: "certamen," referring to the spiritual struggle or "wrestling" against demons.</note> is a matter of spontaneous goodwill and of the grace of God through Christ, by the intervention of the Holy Spirit. For he who receives the gift of healing is revealed by God through revelation, since the grace that is in him is evident to all. And in the same book, Chapter 7: After the <term>catechumens</term> <note>Prospective converts receiving instruction before baptism.</note> have departed, the deacon shall say:
<margin>The possessed.</margin>
Pray, you <term>energumens</term> <note>original: "energumeni," from the Greek for "those worked upon" by external spirits; the possessed.</note>, that is, those troubled by unclean spirits: pray all of you intently for them, that the merciful God, through Christ, may rebuke the unclean and wicked spirits, and rescue His servants from the power of the enemy. May He who rebuked the legion of demons and the prince of evil, the devil, now rebuke those who rebel against piety, and free His own creations from the devil's harassment, and cleanse those things which He founded with great wisdom. **A**lthough there are sometimes physical causes for madness, whether <term>paraphrosyne</term> <note>original Greek: παραφροσύνης; a medical or psychological state of derangement or being "beside oneself."</note> or <term>mania</term> <note>original Greek: μανίας; a state of frenzy or madness.</note>, it is nevertheless most certain that devils enter into the hearts of some men and produce madness and torments in them, either alongside physical causes or without them. If indeed draft animals are thought to suffer from something beyond the course of nature (which is, however, very difficult to know for certain, since they often either graze on poisonous plants in the pastures or are drawn in by the inhalation of a pestilent vapor), first of all, an antidote <term>pharmacum — a medicinal drug or remedy</term> against poisons or similar afflictions can be offered to them. Furthermore, we should administer whatever else we judge useful based on natural conjecture and the medical art—which Vegetius teaches learnedly and copiously in his four books on the veterinary art <note>original: *mulomedicina* — literally "mule-medicine," a term for veterinary care of draft animals</note>, as do Columella, Caesar Constantinus, and many other ancient and more recent authors—while waiting for a successful outcome with moderate patience. Cato used certain ceremonies, solemn sacrifices, and words and vows dedicated to Tellus <note>The Roman goddess of the Earth</note> so that she might nourish strange trees; he even pleaded with the trees themselves to migrate and grow in foreign soil. He also offered entreaties to turnips while they were being sown, that they might provide generously for himself, his household, and his neighbors; and he poured out prayers to Mars so that the fields and the cattle might be preserved.

He would then secretly remove the hidden material of the spell—namely, the wolf excrement—and the evil was quickly driven away. For **when the cause is removed, the effect is taken away.** In this way, he made quite a profit from this profession; however, he was eventually warned by good men to put an end to such falsehood in a timely manner, lest the punishment deserved by a forger should catch up to him.

If the cause of a disease can be removed through being known, the effect will fall away at the same time. The school of physicians knows the poisons, the signs of those that have been swallowed or otherwise infected, and simultaneously their proper antidotes; it is not my purpose to explain them here. But if it happens that those so affected wander off to rash men of another school <note>likely referring to "cunning folk," unlicensed healers, or superstitious diviners</note>, the unfortunate souls truly experience the risk of death quite often—even if the pestilential power of the poison is slow, with the virulence increasing step by step and finally striking at the heart’s vital tinder <note>original: *vitalem fomitem* — a metaphor for the innate heat or fuel that sustains life in the heart</note>.

### On the Infamous Punishments of Magicians

Thus, if someone is afflicted by a stubborn disease unknown to the unlearned commoners and not of a common sort, and that person seeks advice by trusting in their counterfeit knowledge, these "religious" men persuade them that the disease (which actually arises from a natural cause and is not obscure to more learned physicians) is the result of magic or an incantation. They even add "signs" by which an often innocent woman is pointed out as if with a finger. These men both invent the disease and impose an invincible slander upon the innocent. ### Chapter II

<margin>Diviners and soothsayers are to be held as disturbers of the Commonwealth and as falsifiers.</margin>
Many magicians, moreover, puffed up by the spirit of Python <note>original: *Pythonis spiritu* — a biblical and classical term for a spirit of divination, referencing the serpent of Delphi</note>, profess the art of divining: they boast that they can reveal who has stolen lost property, where such things are hidden, and other secret or even uncertain matters. However, these men—whether led on by the smoke of self-love <note>original: *φιλαυτίας* (philautias) — excessive vanity or conceit</note> so that they might be held in at least some regard, claiming for themselves an occult art and a science they do not know; or driven by their own malice to deceive; or enticed by the pursuit of greed to make a fraudulent profit—even if they occasionally know little or nothing through the cooperation of Satan, they nevertheless glory in their knowledge of divination. Once branded by this undeserved cautery <note>metaphorically, a branding iron or a permanent stain on one's name</note>, these victims suffer great slander in the years to come. In this way, numerous families and famous neighborhoods, which were previously continually peaceful, are torn apart and disturbed by heavy rivalry and hatred. 

I truly believe that the authors of such fatal discord and execrable slanders should be held in no other regard than as seditious disturbers of the Commonwealth and as falsifiers. It is fitting that, at the very least, silence should first be imposed upon them by the magistrate; then, a discretionary fine should be levied according to the nature of the offense; and unless they cease from their wrongdoing, they should be punished with exile. I remember this was once prudently done in the case of a certain soothsayer named Joachim by the most distinguished order of the Royal Senate in Guelders <note>original: *Geldros* — the Duchy of Guelders, a historical region in the Low Countries</note>. # On the Punishments of Infamous Magicians

<margin>Others who summon the spirits of the dead.</margin>
In the law *multi* under the section of the Code <term>On Sorcerers and Astrologers</term> <note>original: *C. de maleficis & mathematicis*—the "mathematicians" in Roman law were specifically those who cast horoscopes or used numbers for divination</note>, it states: "Many, using magical arts, do not hesitate to disturb the elements, to ruin the lives of the innocent, and, by summoning the spirits of the dead <note>original: *manibus accitis*</note>, they dare to stir up trouble so that each may destroy his enemies with evil arts. Since these people are foreign to the laws of nature, let a deadly plague <note>original: *feralis pestis*—here used as a legal metaphor for the death penalty</note> consume them." This was decreed on the Nones of December during the consulship of Constantine Augustus for the ninth time and Julian for the second time; the former was called Constantine the Second, and the latter was made Caesar not long after, eventually being surnamed "the Apostate."

However, it has been demonstrated more than enough that our "witches" <note>original: *Lamias*—a term for mythological man-eating demons, here used to refer to women accused of witchcraft</note>, being uneducated, old, and senile, practice no such arts. They are unable to move or corrupt the elements by any rational means, nor can they harm any man, nor can they compel demons to hurt others. Therefore, this decree does not concern them in the least. If there are any who plot against the lives of men and use violence against them, this must be done by poison; thus, such women are called, and truly are, <term>poisoners</term> <note>original: *ueneficæ*—in Latin, the word for witch and poisoner is often the same</note>. Let them be punished according to this edict.

<margin>Imperial laws enacted against diviners, magicians, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners.</margin>
Likewise, in Book 9 of the Code, the Emperor Constantine Augustus wrote to Maximianus: "No soothsayer <note>original: *aruspex*—a priest who interpreted the future from the entrails of animals</note>, no priest (that is, a teacher of forbidden magic), nor any of those accustomed to administering such rites, shall cross the threshold of another person’s home, even for any other reason. Let the friendship of such men, however old it may be, be rejected. That soothsayer who enters another's house shall be burned alive; and the person who summoned him with persuasions or rewards shall be deported to an island after the confiscation of his goods."

The same Emperor to the people: "Let no one consult a soothsayer, or an astrologer <note>original: *mathematicum*</note>, or an oracle-teller. Let the perverse profession of augurs and prophets fall silent. 

<margin>Chaldeans, magicians, and sorcerers.</margin>
The Chaldeans <note>original: *Chaldæi*—a term often used for professional astrologers and fortune-tellers</note>, the magicians, and the rest whom the common people call 'sorcerers' <note>original: *maleficos*</note> because of the magnitude of their crimes, shall not attempt anything in this regard. Let the curiosity for divining be silenced for everyone forever." The same Emperor Constantine Augustus, etc., to Thaurus, the Praetorian Prefect: "Even though the bodies of those endowed with honors are usually exempt from torture, except for those..."

<header>Book Six</header>

...crimes which are demonstrated by the laws. Even if magicians <note>original: *magi*</note>, in whatever part of the earth they may be, must be believed to be enemies of the human race: nevertheless, because those who are in our own retinue <note>original: *comitatu*—referring to the imperial court or household</note> strike at majesty itself, if any magician, or one accustomed to magical contests—who is called a "sorcerer" <note>original: *maleficus*</note> in the common usage of the people—or any diviner using entrails <note>original: *aruspex*</note>, or a soothsayer <note>original: *ariolus*</note>, or certainly an augur <note>one who reads the flight of birds</note>, or an astrologer <note>original: *mathematicus*—in Roman law, this term specifically referred to those who cast horoscopes</note>, or someone hiding some art of divination by interpreting dreams, or certainly anyone practicing anything similar to these, is discovered in my retinue or that of the Caesar: let him be stripped of the protection of his rank and not escape torture and torments. If indeed he is convicted, and resists those revealing his own crime by denying it, let him be handed over to the rack <note>original: *eculeo*—a horse-shaped torture device</note>, and let him endure punishments worthy of his own crime with metal claws furrowing his sides.

No one ought to consult a diviner, and everyone must cease from divining: and he who acts to the contrary is punished. This is stated according to *Salicet* <note>Bartholomaeus Salicetus (1330–1412), an influential Italian jurist and professor of law</note>.

No one ought to consult an enchanter about things that are to come, nor astrologers <note>original: *Chaldæos*—literally "Chaldeans," a common term for practitioners of celestial divination</note>, nor sorcerers: and he who does so shall be subject to the capital punishment of the avenging sword. *Vivianus* <note>Vivianus Tuscus, a 13th-century legal commentator known for his "Glossary" on the Roman Code</note>.

Those who invoke demons, or enchant wax images, are punished. So says *Salicet*.

Those performing enchantments for an evil end are to be punished: but according to Canon Law, they are punished even if they do so for a good end. [See 26. question 2. chapter *illos*; and the chapter *ex tuarum* under the section *On Sorcerers*; and the final chapter of said title, where the Gloss appears]. *Bartolus* <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato, one of the most famous continental jurists of the Middle Ages</note>, *Salicet*.

*Ulpian* <note>Domitius Ulpianus, a Roman jurist from the 3rd century AD whose writings make up a large part of the Digest</note>, in the law "Likewise in Labeo," section "if anyone," in the Digest *On Injuries*, says that those who promise any illicit divination are bound by the constitutions of the emperors, according to the law "No one has" in the Code *On Mathematicians*.

Divination and the consultation of divine matters are condemned in the Synod of Toledo and in the Decretal letters <note>letters of the Pope formulated as laws</note>.

Gregory, as found in Question 26, Case 5, "If anyone": If anyone observes soothsayers, diviners, or enchanters, or has used phylacteries, let him be anathema <note>Excommunicated or cursed by the church</note>. <gloss>The Glossary states: Phylacteries are called here the papers in which incantations are contained.</gloss> The same author, in Question 26, Case 5, "Against": We exhort your brotherhood with pastoral vehemence to keep a watchful guard against idol-worshipers, diviners, and fortune-tellers; if you find they are unwilling to amend their ways from such things, if they are slaves, we wish them to be chastised with lashes; but if they are free men, they are to be directed toward a strict punishment worthy of confinement.

Augustine, as read in Question 26, the last case, "Let them admonish": Let the faithful priests admonish their people so that they may know that magic arts and incantations can provide no remedy for any human infirmities, etc. And if any cleric performs these things, let him be degraded <note>Stripped of his clerical rank</note>; if a layman, let him be anathematized.

The same from the council of Pope Martin: If anyone, following the custom of the pagans, introduces diviners or fortune-tellers into his home, as if to cast out evil or to find sorceries, or to perform the purifications of the pagans, let them perform penance for five years.

# Book Six

<margin>On criminal proceedings and tortures</margin> At this point, I shall add my own brief explanation regarding criminal actions and tortures.

**Article 17.** No person shall be handed over to prison or subjected to interrogations <note>original: "quaestionibus"; here referring specifically to judicial torture</note> based solely on the evidence provided by an infamous sorcerer or anyone else practicing the art of divination. Furthermore, that sorcerer and the accuser shall be punished for it. If a judge proceeds with a case based on such an accusation from a sorcerer, he shall be held liable to pay for and compensate the expenses, the tortures, the injury, and the losses of the punished person.

**Article 35.** If anyone has wished to teach someone the magic art, or has threatened another with the same and harm follows; or if the same person has been on familiar terms with male or female enchanters, or has used suspicious things, methods, or words pertaining to incantations; and if that same person has maintained the reputation of a sorcerer—these signs are seen as sufficiently consistent with reason to justify that they be subjected to interrogation.

However, the path by which proceedings are now conducted is much different. Now, solely from a malicious accusation, or the false and ignorant suspicion of the foolish and unrefined common people, old women—deluded and possessed by the devil, or rather, harmed by a demonic curse <note>original: "maleficio"</note>—are cast by officials into terrible dens of thieves and caves of evil spirits <note>original: "cacodaemonum"</note>. Soon after, they are handed over to be tortured by cruel executioners, with various methods of unspeakable torments devised through intolerable tyranny. For whether they wish it or not, even if they are most innocent, this bloody butchery <note>original: "carnificina"</note> does not cease until they confess to the crime. Thus it happens that, once placed among such bloodthirsty men, they would rather offer their innocent souls to God amidst the flames in a moment of time than endure the cruelty of these fierce and tragic tyrants, the Phalarides <note>A reference to Phalaris, a Sicilian tyrant famous for his extreme cruelty and the "brazen bull" torture device.</note>...

But when He finally appears, from whom nothing is hidden—the searcher of hearts and minds, the knower and judge of even the most hidden truth—your actions will be made public, O you stubborn tyrants, O most cruel followers of Phalaris, O bloodthirsty judges, O executioners, torturers, and savage robbers! # On the Punishments for Infamous Magic

...any inconvenience that may have followed from it.

In the first place, it is commanded here that a prudent investigation first be conducted to inquire by what material, by what means, and at what place and time the <term>maleficium</term> <note>A Latin term for a "wrongdoing" or "evil deed," specifically referring to harmful magic or sorcery</note> was committed: whether it be a case of poisoning, or a diabolical art and mockery, or whether it actually exists in the nature of things and can be accomplished; also, whether it was done with such instruments or means, and whether these were even suited to the purpose intended. For this reason, counsel must be sought from those who more deeply understand substances and their powers <note>Likely referring to physicians, natural philosophers, or apothecaries</note>: and furthermore, what harm they were able to bring or inflict by means of these things, since for the most part these items are found to be worthless and ineffective—mere trifles, in fact—as will be taught more extensively later in Chapter Seven.

> **Article 98.** If anyone has caused harm to another through incantations, let him be punished here by the penalty of death, and indeed by the flames. <note>This refers to Article 98 of the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the criminal code issued by Emperor Charles V in 1532.</note>

But he who has used incantations without loss to anyone shall pay the penalty according to the magnitude of the offense; and in that matter, the judge shall seek counsel, just as was written above regarding the seeking of such advice.

Here, it ought not to come into doubt at all whether someone has actually suffered a loss by the power of incantations: if that has happened, it must necessarily have been <term>veneficium</term> <note>Latin for poisoning or sorcery involving drugs/potions</note>, otherwise not. For by a mere look, by words, by a curse, or by any foolish material hidden under a doorway or elsewhere, no injury can be induced, as is demonstrated in many ways throughout these books.

# Book Six

### The history of Pope Sylvester II is presented to those who are recovering their senses, to which is attached a fiction concerning the miserable end of a certain wicked woman. Chapter V.

<margin>81. The history of the magician Sylvester II and his repentance.</margin>
For those who are returning to their right minds <note>Latin: *resipiscentibus*; referring to those turning away from the practice of magic</note>, I wished to present the famous example of the Roman Pontiff Sylvester II, drawn from Platina, Nauclerus, Peter of Prémontré, Cardinal Benno, the Chronicle of Brother Martin of the Dominican Order, and others. This man, previously called Gerbert, a Frenchman by birth, attained the Papacy (as they say) through evil arts. For as a youth, he was installed as a monk in the monastery of Fleury in the diocese of Orléans; having left the monastery, he followed the devil, to whom he had entirely enslaved himself, and set out for the city of Seville in Spain for the sake of the "liberal arts," where he ingratiated himself with a Saracen philosopher skilled in magic. At the house of this magician host, he had seen a book of necromancy <note>The practice of communicating with the dead or using hidden demonic knowledge</note>, which he desired to steal secretly. Since, however, it was guarded quite religiously and cautiously, Gerbert finally obtained it in secret to read through the magician's daughter, with whom he had established a domestic familiarity. Having received it in good faith <note>Used ironically here, as he intended to steal it</note>, Gerbert meditated on his departure, yet feared the danger to himself arising from the theft. Therefore, driven by ambition and a diabolical desire for power, Gerbert first obtained the Archbishopric of Reims by bribery, then that of Ravenna; finally, in the year 1000 (as Peter of Prémontré records; though others say the year 997), he attained the Papacy with greater effort, with the devil assisting him. This was done, however, on the condition that after death he would belong entirely to the one by whose frauds he had climbed to that height of dignity. Although he meanwhile concealed his magic arts during his Papacy, he nevertheless kept a brass head in a hidden place, from which he received answers whenever he [sought] anything from the evil spirit...

### Chapter VI.

Since indeed the "Witches" <note>original: "Lamiae," a term for female witches or night-monsters</note>, as they are called, are for the most part little women of the female sex, usually old, melancholic by nature <note>In the 16th century, "melancholy" was a medical diagnosis involving an excess of black bile, thought to cause hallucinations</note>, lacking control of their minds, rashly despairing in spirit, and having little faith in God: the devil joins himself more freely to them as if to suitable instruments. Truly, if you examine the whole matter with a sharper mental gaze according to the standard of what can and is done by a demon, and what is believed to be accomplished by humans as his proposed tools, you will find that whatever has been done was designated by the devil.
