# On the punishments of infamous sorcerers

<margin>Code, Book 9, on the custody of the accused, law 1.</margin> In the school of the ancients, it was held that the custody of those who are later to be punished should by no means be a punishment in itself. Yet, we have seen that a dire punishment is often inflicted even upon the innocent by a horrific prison—those who, beyond their merit, have at times been thrust into it. But just as the principles of equity and compassion are undermined and neglected, so too has the very name and proper use of "custody" almost vanished among most people. Thus it happens that these poor creatures of God—shuddering from long solitude, the filth of the prisons, the foul darkness, and various apparitions of demons—are already somewhat unhinged in their minds by the devil's constant suggestion, fascination, and delusion. When they are then further tormented by various tortures and subjected to atrocious interrogations, they prefer to exchange such a bitter life for a single moment of death. They will freely confess to any shameful acts proposed to them rather than be thrust back more fiercely into those same caves of stinking prisons and headlong onto the racks <note>The "equuleus" was a wooden rack used for stretching the body during interrogation.</note>.

In this manner, it happened not so long ago that they drove a little old woman with torments to the point where, already destined to be sacrificed to Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcano litanda" — meaning to be burned at the stake; Vulcan was the Roman god of fire.</note>, she confessed that she had produced the incredible harshness, extreme cold, and most enduring ice of the recent winter of the year 1565. Nor were there lacking serious men who believed these things to be truer than truth itself, even though nothing in the entire nature of things is more absurd. This was written to me by Master Antonius Houæus, a man most distinguished in learning, piety, and reputation, the Abbot of Echternach, who for many reasons is uniquely and always to be honored by me.

# Book Six

<meta>catchword: shepherds</meta>

With a great cord bound crosswise to the right foot, it is observed by magistrates and executioners in many jurisdictions that <term>Lamiae</term> <note>Witches or sorceresses; in classical mythology, a Lamia was a child-eating demon, but here used for those accused of witchcraft</note> charged with sorcery, when cast into the water, are never submerged but float on the surface. They treat this as a certain experiment and an infallible sign. Truly, it is beyond ridiculous and a wonder that any person endowed with even a slight sense of reason would grant the smallest amount of faith to such a tasteless persuasion.

<margin>The cause of floating.</margin>
Indeed, I dare to assert that the natural causes of floating—such as lightness, porosity, the containment of sustaining breath, the agility of a living body, and other natural factors of that kind—are no more present in these bodies than in others, or in the springs themselves, as I must admit. If anything of this sort appears to happen outside the order of nature, it is done by the Devil supporting the women (concerning whom there is often false suspicion) so they do not sink. This happens while God shuts his eyes to the matter because of the unbelief of the magistrate who admits this deceptive experiment. Thus, that impostor, a murderer from the beginning <note>A reference to John 8:44, describing the Devil</note>, eventually leads the judge into an unjust sentence through this fraud. Hippocrates also teaches that a woman is endowed with thinner flesh and is more tender than a man.

# On the punishments of infamous magicians

By the shepherds, a small portion <note>original: "portiuncula"</note> of the host, sanctified by the sacrifice of the Mass, is placed beneath the threshold of the temple to be stepped upon; it is believed that if a witch <note>original: "sagam"</note> is inside the temple, she will then be unable to leave. Likewise, take splinters of oak wood from which someone has been hung or has strangled themselves; let them be sprinkled with holy water <note>original: "aqua lustrali"</note> and placed at the entrance of the temple. She will not be able to exit unless you remove the splinters.

In a small book of Conjurations printed at Rome and Avignon, one reads the following: To correct and identify a female sorceress <note>original: "maleficam"</note>, take a new milk pail, a new cheese mold, and a new pewter vessel. Milk from all the cows you own just enough milk so that you can form or make one cheese in the name of that sorceress. Form the cheese using the aforementioned vessels, and when the cheese is made, pierce the entire cheese with a sharp iron ring <note>original: "armilla acuta"</note>. By this means, the sorceress herself will be exposed in her face, etc. Consider also the sorceress by her forehead, because the devil scrapes it with his claw after her consent to destroy the sacred unction of baptism, so that she bears a mark <term>stigma: a physical brand or sign of shame</term> on her forehead; this, however, she always strives to veil with a head-covering <note>original: "peplo"</note> as much as she can. Whether this truly happens in such a way, see Book 2, Chapter 20.

Furthermore, it is believed that a "king of the bees" <note>the queen bee, though thought to be male in early modern biology</note> devoured by witches <note>original: "Lamijs"</note> strengthens them so that they do not confess their crimes under torture. But the reasoning here is the same as in other cases: namely, a superstitious credulity. On the contrary, Democritus mentions that the *Achemenis* plant <note>original: "Achemenidon"</note>, which grows in the *Tardistylis* of India, is the color of amber and grows without leaves. If its root is divided into lozenges and drunk during the day with wine, the guilty will confess everything during the night through various tortures of the imagination caused by divine spirits. See also Chapter 11 of this, our Fifth Book.

# Book Six.

### What must be done in the investigation of a committed crime, and that one must not rely on confession alone. Chapter VIII.

It was proper to observe this rule—which is by no means deceptive—regarding interrogations: that concerning each of those shameful acts already confessed, an accurate inquiry should be made with sound judgment. One must ask whether the hardships and calamities which the accused say others have suffered, and which they admit to having inflicted, are actually so, or if they even exist in the nature of things. And if it is found that certain people have indeed been harmed, or have suffered diseases or loss, such that these evils are thought to have been designated by those who have already confessed; then, one must investigate more deeply by what means, materials, or instruments they were perpetrated. Furthermore, one must ask whether those means, materials, or instruments are fit and suitable for producing effects of that kind. In this matter, the judgments of famous physicians, who possess knowledge of natural things and their properties, should be called into counsel, just as the laws <note>The author refers to the *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina*, the Holy Roman Empire's criminal code of 1532, which required medical testimony in certain cases.</note> require to be done in other relevant cases.

<margin>*The confession of one who is mentally impaired must not be relied upon.*</margin>
For just as one must not rely on the confession of a person who is melancholic <note>In the 16th century, "melancholy" was a medical diagnosis for a form of depression or psychosis believed to cause delusions.</note> or mentally impaired, so too punishment must not be rashly inflicted based on the confessions of these women. This is unless, through certain circumstances and evident demonstrations, a case of sorcery <term>veneficium: literally "poisoning" or "sorcery" through drugs</term> or poisoning is established beyond doubt—namely, by a drug having been administered or smeared on, or deposited in a place from which it is manifest that it could infect by its vapor.

<margin>*In a criminal action, the proofs ought to be clearer than the midday light.*</margin>
Indeed, proofs ought to be clearer than the midday light, especially in what is called a criminal action; this is the praiseworthy opinion of the Legal Consultants. For in this business of "evil-doing" <term>maleficium: a harmful act of magic</term>, many things are said turbulently, either from a sinister opinion or suspicion, or maliciously from a wicked disposition. Many things are also spread confusedly about others because of the difficulty of diseases or the loss of property, or out of a lack of faith, because people do not sufficiently surrender and subject themselves entirely and from the heart to the just will of God—

# On the punishments of infamous magicians

<note>The header refers to "De magorum infamium poenis," a common legal and theological topic regarding the penalties for those accused of witchcraft.</note>

These stories are spread abroad and are further confirmed by the confessions of old women who have been deluded by a demon. Here, the devil pours cold water <note>original: "frigidam suffundente," a metaphor for dampening reason or causing confusion</note> and faithfully drives the nail of his machination. If anyone lends a ready ear, believing the accusation and confession to be valid, they will eventually find themselves so deluded and entangled—as if in an inexplicable labyrinth—that they will never find a way out, especially if they decide to carry out everything they have heard according to the standard of the laws and the rigor of justice. Such is the art of Satan: to involve and confound matters with such subtle tricks that they cannot be untangled by any sagacity of Theseus <note>The mythical hero who escaped the Labyrinth</note>, nor explained by the wisdom of Oedipus <note>The hero who solved the riddle of the Sphinx</note>. Thus, I have learned through experience and the observation of practice that it is better either to have stopped entirely at the beginning and kept oneself within bounds, or to have retreated early. This prevents a window from being opened to the devil—who was a murderer from the beginning—through open lies or truth corrupted by deceit and falsehood, by which he might insinuate himself into our judicial actions. There will never be a shorter path to cutting off every opportunity for Satan to advance further; otherwise, there will seem to be no limit or end to the lies, false calumnies, and accusations, with the weight of truth occasionally mixed in only so that the deceit may remain hidden.

# Book Six.

# On the punishments for infamous sorcery

<margin>Refutation of the confession.</margin> I ask you, however, let the confession be examined in a few words. As for her confessing that she defected from God and adhered to a demon, that shall not be a criminal matter in a civil court. For how many of us are there who do not do that very thing? Since <margin>John 8, 1 John 3. He who commits sin is of the devil.</margin> everyone who commits sin is a slave to sin (as Christ teaches). He who commits sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning. In this, the children of God and the children of the devil are manifest. Everyone who does not practice justice is not of God, nor is he who does not love his brother. <margin>Matthew 12, Luke 11.</margin> He who is not with me, says Christ, is against me; and he who does not gather with me, scatters. But having been admonished, we are able to recover our senses, and there is a place for repentance. What, therefore, forbids that she too, having been refuted and better instructed, might have been able to be brought back to the knowledge of herself? Let this find a place among the patrons of the *Book of Conformities* <note>original: "libri Conformitatum"; a 14th-century work comparing the life of St. Francis to Christ, often criticized by skeptics for its supernatural claims</note>, where it is read that a certain monk desired a wife, and prayed to the devil to bring her to him, promising he would be his, having handed over a contract signed by his own hand and sealed with blood. Who else, I ask, gave the name "Bernard" to this suitor than he himself? # On the punishments for infamous sorcery

<margin>
A third ridiculous confession.
</margin>
The harm was immediately attributed to sorcery <note>original: "maleficio"</note>. For this reason, hands were laid upon a woman, who unhesitatingly confessed that it had happened through her evil arts. She claimed that she had flown through a hole in a glass window (which she pointed out, and it was of such a size that it could hardly admit a finger) while they were lying in wait for fish. She further claimed she had committed herself to the sea in a mussel shell <note>original: "mytuli testa," called a "mosselscolp" by our countrymen</note> and had crossed over to the herring station. There, by her incantations, she had chased away the herring and put stones in their place. Chiefly on the basis of this sentence, she was handed over to be devoured by the flames.

<margin>
Its refutation.
</margin>
In this confession, one ought to have weighed whether it is in the nature of things—even with the devil working however he wishes according to his strength—for a full-grown human being to be transported through the narrowest crack in glass, not even capable of holding a finger. A human is not made of blowable spirit alone, nor composed of a ductile or meltable substance, but is compacted of solid bones, tough cartilage, dry tendons, ligaments, nerves, and membranes, in addition to muscular flesh. Even if the body could have been resolved into vapors, the glass ought to have been shattered by the force of them breaking through all at once. Likewise, it should have been brought to the standard of reason how a woman of advanced age, in a tiny mussel shell with such a heap of stones, could have plowed through a changing and turbulent sea. Nor was there any need for this crossing in a shell for one who had just flown so swiftly through the narrowest hole in the glass. Indeed, this entire confession is so tasteless, futile, dissonant, absurd, and lying, that anyone not entirely devoid of mind would be able to judge that this poor woman was either raving, or driven by melancholy <note>a historical medical term for deep depression or mental imbalance</note>, or otherwise led by a depraved imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, or possessed by a demon who either ruled her tongue or produced the voice from her. Let such judges devise whatever glosses <note>interpretive explanations</note> they wish; a sentence so bloodthirsty cannot be rightly pronounced in a matter that is either unknown or situated outside of reason and the nature of things.

## Book Six.

That these women suffer from the disease of black bile <note>original: "atrae bilis"; referring to the medical theory of the four humors, where an excess of black bile caused "melancholy" or madness</note> is revealed by their way of life, the quality of the air, the very form and appearance of their face and body, and their very words—full of foolishness and (if I may say so) impossibility—as well as their grim expression while speaking. This is further shown by an event that occurred during the time of Filippo Visconti, Prince of Milan <note>Filippo Maria Visconti, reigned 1412–1447</note>. The matter happened exactly as my father related it. A certain farm manager named Bernard had been condemned for this profane art <note>sorcery or witchcraft</note>; otherwise, he was a simple and honest man, and for that reason very dear to his master. But because he could be moved neither by threats nor persuasions to repent, he was demanded by the judges for the punishment of fire. His master, who felt pity for him and was favored by the Prince, obtained permission—though the judges were reluctant—to keep the man with him for twenty days upon giving a guarantee. He began, therefore, to nourish him, not as a physician would, but as a noble friend would a countryman. Four fresh eggs in the morning, just as many in the evening, along with sweet and pleasant wine, as well as meat and rich broths. Afterward, when he saw the man recovering from his long lethargy, he urged him to abandon those false, absurd, and dangerous persuasions and adhere to the Church. But few words were needed; he came to his senses. Having become an excellent Christian, he persevered until death without complaint from others—a man whom the cruelty of the judges would have undeservedly afflicted with a cruel execution.

He added that the Lord of Chasney <note>original: "dominum de Chuſnee"</note> arrived on the scene, and though they wished to harm him and leaped at him several times, they did so in vain.

<margin>7</margin>

Michael’s palate found the flesh pleasing, though he ate little of it; however, it did not sit as well in the stomach of Peter, who devoured his portion repeatedly. They also confessed to having slit the throat of a certain girl, sucking her blood and devouring her neck. Similarly, they destroyed a third girl and ate the opening of her stomach because of Peter’s ravenous jaws. On another occasion, they killed a girl of eight or nine years in a garden; Peter had broken her neck with his teeth because he had once been refused alms when he asked for them there. After this crime was committed, he immediately prayed for alms there in honor of God. <margin>8</margin> Moreover, he confessed here <margin>9</margin> that he had slit the throat of a nanny goat near the field of Master Peter Bongre; specifically, he had bitten her and cut her throat with a knife.

### The confession explained in detail, and refuted. Chapter XII.

Now, according to the weakness of our strength, let us attempt the trial of tearing apart this confession which has been so widely celebrated until now.

<margin>An erroneous confession.</margin> The hinge of the matter turns on this: whether that entire confession is true. I hope, however, with the support of divine aid, to show clearly that in its main points it opposes the manifest truth. Therefore, it exists not only as erroneous, but as utterly false. I freely admit that images known only through dreams, or presented deceptively to the eyes <note>The author uses the term "prestigiosè," referring to "prestige" or "juggling," a common early modern term for demonic illusions that trick the senses.</note>, are being proposed as the things themselves; thus, it should have no place in a sane council, but ought rather to be hissed off the stage as the fable of a lethargic or cataleptic person.

# Book Six

What of the remaining outrages and homicides which they have confessed? It has now come to be agreed that these were merely devised under that transformation and wolfish mask <note>original: "larua lupina"</note>, and could not have happened in any other way. But these are surely pure delusions, and more than trifles—indeed, they are insanity. It is truly a cause for grief that the eyes of prudent men have hitherto been covered by such thick darkness that they allowed even a moment of faith to be extorted from them by these mockeries. But such was the stain and blindness of the previous century especially, in which that old deceiver <note>A reference to the Devil</note> toyed with men according to his whim in a manner far too crude, ridiculous, and harmful. Would that by the immense mercy of God, that sweetest voice, *Ephphata* <note>Aramaic for "Be opened"; see Mark 7:34</note>, might still ring out in the soul of anyone bound by this fascination. 
<margin>Mark 7</margin>
Just as that word, powerfully brought forth from the mouth of Christ, opened the ears of the deaf man to be turned toward the truth, and loosened the bond of his tongue so that he might henceforth preach the truth: so also may a ray of divine light shine forth from this grace. Thus, once the darkness so powerlessly spread by the devil has been scattered and put to flight by heavenly light, one may finally arrive directly at the sight and knowledge of the clearest truth, without the hindrance of illusions. But lest anyone charge me with evading objections, I shall examine the remaining fabrication of this fable in a few words.

<margin>4</margin>
The ointment with which those about to take on the form of a wolf were anointed was, without doubt, a sleep-inducing substance <note>original: "linimentum somniferum"</note>. I described such a substance in Book Two, chapter thirty-four. It gained its power when smeared upon the naked parts of the body and was drawn into action by the natural heat. Then, as they were oppressed by deep sleep, that master of a thousand arts <note>The Devil</note> would thrust upon them images of their conversion into wandering wolves—leaping upon others, strangling and devouring girls, even mating with wolves, and whatever other phantasms of that kind. From this also followed that swift speed, such as is accomplished without difficulty in imagination, thought, or sleep.

# On the punishments for infamous magic

Whether that powder had been given to them, or whether it possessed such great power, is doubtful; since it could not be proven that they had actually used it. For in that case of lycanthropy <note>The transformation of a human into a wolf; here referring to a specific trial</note>, Peter confessed that he had slaughtered no animal with his bite or knife except for a goat, nor did anyone else remember any other creature being killed. Furthermore, if the powder was of such high toxicity that even if a hand were rubbed with it at any time, it could kill an animal protected by thick, dense skin and long, matted hair by mere touch alone, how could these deluded men have been safe from such a fierce and immediate malice of the drug? They supposedly endured the rubbing of the powder on the left arm, the artery, and the hand—from where it could penetrate most closely and swiftly to the heart—without any harm.

15 To these points add, finally, that in the French confession there was heard such inconsistency and contradiction that what one man affirmed at one time, the other denied.

If individual confessions—frequently extorted by the most cruel tortures, or even, if you will, uttered voluntarily by the captives—were weighed with this kind of balance, that most deadly murderer <note>Referring to the Devil</note> would surely feel a heavier loss of his tyranny day by day. Moreover, the glory of Christ, who is the truth and the life, would greatly increase; the magistrate would likewise perform his duty more providently according to the will of God; and the heaps of wooden faggots <note>Bundles of wood used for burning at the stake</note>, by which the innocent are frequently burned, would be put to better use, and the expenses incurred in paying the executioners' wages would be spared. Now, let the thread of my discourse be led further, so that it may be understood what manner of punishment I believe should be used in correcting this class of people.

Within our own memory at Düren <note>original: "Marcoduri," the Latin name for the town of Düren in Germany</note>, when the garden vegetables had been scattered by hail, while the plants of a certain old woman’s neighboring garden remained unharmed—though that area is often the path of storms—the old woman was accused of sorcery and dragged to prison. While she was suspended from a beam, distracted by heavy weights hanging from her on both sides and already at death's door, the presiding judge, about to leave her in those torments, urged the executioner to go with him for a drink, saying that the old woman would confess other things when they returned. Then she, miserably tortured, humbly begged the judge that a confessor be summoned before he went for his cups; he departed, mocking her. But having returned later, he found her—still suspended in that manner—dead, and he grieved that she had meanwhile laid hands on herself while he was away. <margin>*The punishment of an unjust judge.*</margin> Not long after that time, this tyrant fell into such a mania that he did violence to himself, tearing his clothes and smearing his own face with excrement.

# Book Six

When a poor woman, arrested on suspicion of witchcraft <note>original: "maleficij"</note>, could not be driven to a confession of any crime by the torture chamber <note>original: "nificina," likely referring to the rack or similar engine of pain</note>, a petty priest approached her with flattering words. He urged her not to allow herself to be pulled apart by tortures any longer, but rather to confess the crime only lightly. He promised that he then wished to restore her to God, purified from her witchcraft by holy water <note>original: "aqua lustrali"</note> and, as they say, "repaired and roofed" <note>A Latin legal idiom meaning completely restored or in good repair</note>. Having been led on in this way by the priest and circumvented by flatteries, she confessed that she had perhaps committed some evils of this kind, hoping that she would escape in the manner the priest had persuaded her. <margin>A confession coaxed out by fallacy and deceit.</margin> Because of a confession of this sort, coaxed out by fallacy and deceit, a sentence was passed that she should be sacrificed to Vulcan <note>A classical allusion to being burned at the stake</note>. When she heard this, contrary to her expectation, the wretched woman forewarned those who were deaf to her: 
> "See to it how you kill me."

Near the village of Elten, located half a mile from Emmerich in the Duchy of Cleves, about forty-two years ago, a demon used to harass travelers along the royal road in a heathery place in strange and various ways—striking them, throwing them from their horses, or overturning their wagons. Nothing was ever seen of it except the likeness of a hand. <margin>Eckerken.</margin> The name "Eckerken" <note>A regional name for a puck or wood-spirit</note> was given to it. The incredulous neighbors, not rightly discerning this mockery and exercise of a demon, attributed the deed to the witchcraft of a sorceress <note>original: "Lamia"</note>. Would that others, warned by this wholesome example, would meet the beginnings of these tragedies with whatever legitimate and pious reasoning they could deliberate. Surely then, in a matter where so little can be established with certainty, they would not become entangled as if in an inextricable labyrinth, slipping from a simple error into a thousand others through a lack of caution, from which there finally seems to be no way of escaping or reaching an end. # Book Six

It seemed she was about to speak, which is why I opened her mouth, handled her hands, and carefully weighed the movement of her pulse. Behold the impudence of the accusation, by which the face of this extreme calamity is deformed!

The other part—namely, that the mother remembered a promise—he explained in this way: that because of the constant taunting of the common people regarding her reputation for witchcraft <note>original: "maleficij"; harmful magic</note>, she had declared to her sons that if she were perhaps snatched away to punishment for that reason, she would summon the author of her death to the most equitable tribunal of Christ, the just judge, so that on the thirtieth day from her death, he would present himself there to give an account of the sentence passed. If, therefore, the effect followed, it would be no obscure proof of her innocence, and the sons would understand their mother to be without fault; for God, the sole avenger of justice, hears the innocent when they pray, but turns a deaf ear to such feigned prayers. Accordingly, the Count, having been advised by me and better instructed in that kind of diabolical delusion, dismissed the poor little woman after the case had first been vigilantly discussed. ## *On those led astray by error, and the opinions of the Fathers that heretics should not be put to death.*
### *Chapter XV.*

<margin>The opinion of the Fathers regarding those led astray by error and not putting heretics to death.</margin>
Since it has now been sufficiently demonstrated that many of these people are corrupted in mind and led astray by Satan through error—so that they deserve the punishment of heretics rather than devouring flames—those who are better instructed, if they are converted, should by no means be afflicted with corporal punishment. It has pleased me to bring forward a few opinions of the highest Fathers <note>The "Fathers" refers to the early influential Christian theologians, specifically St. Augustine in this passage.</note> on this matter.

<margin>Letter 127.</margin>
Augustine to Donatus, the proconsul of Africa: "By the opportunity provided by terrible judges and laws," he says, "we desire our enemies to be corrected, not killed, lest they fall into the punishments of eternal judgment; we do not wish discipline toward them to be neglected, nor do we wish them to be subjected to the punishments they deserve. Therefore, restrain their sins in such a way that there remain those who can repent for having sinned. We ask, therefore, that when you hear the cases of the Church, even if you find it has been attacked or afflicted by any wicked injuries, you forget that you have the power of killing, and do not forget our petition. Let it not seem cheap or contemptible to you, most honorably beloved son, that we ask you not to kill those for whom we ask the Lord that they be corrected."

<margin>Letter 158.</margin>
The same to Marcellinus: "I ask you that the punishment of those men, even though they have confessed to such great crimes, be something short of the punishment of death, both for the sake of our conscience and to commend Catholic gentleness." To the same in Letter 159: "Fulfill, Christian judge, the duty of a pious father; be angry at iniquity in such a way that you remember to consult humanity. Do not exercise the lust for vengeance upon the atrocities of sinners,

Chrysostom, in his forty-seventh homily on the thirteenth chapter of Matthew: "Do you wish then that we go and gather them up?" <note>referring to the Parable of the Tares/Weeds in Matthew 13</note> But the Lord forbids it, lest perhaps while pulling up the tares <term>tares: weeds that look like wheat in early growth</term> they also root up the wheat with them. Therefore, if you wish them to be punished without harming the grain, you must wait for the appropriate opportunity of time. 

But what does it mean, "you will root up the grain along with them"? Certainly it means either that if you take up arms, he says, it is inevitable that when you slaughter heretics, you will kill many saints at the same time; or it is because many of those very tares might change and convert themselves into the condition of wheat. If, therefore, you pull them up prematurely, those stalks of grain which would have come from the transformed tares will perish. Not...

# Book Six.

That Saint Martin <note>Saint Martin of Tours (c. 316–397), a bishop known for his opposition to the execution of heretics.</note> also did not wish for heretics to be punished, Sulpicius Severus writes in his *Life of Martin*, Book 3, with these words:

> The Emperor Maximus, following the opinion of the bishops, had decreed the day before to send tribunes armed with supreme power to the Spanish provinces to seek out heretics and strip those caught of their lives and property. There was no doubt that this storm would also devastate a very great multitude of holy men. But Martin’s chief concern was that the tribunes should not be sent to Spain with the right of the sword <note>original: "iure gladiorum"; referring to the legal authority to carry out capital punishment.</note>. For he felt a pious anxiety to deliver not only the Christians, who were to be harassed under that pretext, but even the heretics themselves.

### *The opinion of Erasmus on how to deal with heretics. Chapter XVI.*

In his *Apology against certain articles* presented by certain monks in Spain, Erasmus writes the following to Alfonso Manrique <note>Alfonso Manrique de Lara (d. 1538), Archbishop of Seville and Grand Inquisitor of Spain.</note>, Archbishop of Seville, under the fourth title as distinguished by the monks, "Against the holy Inquisition of Heretics." In his *Paraphrase on Matthew 13*:

> *The servants who wish to gather the weeds before the time are those who think that false apostles and leaders of heresy should be removed from our midst by swords and death, whereas the Father of the family does not want them extinguished, but tolerated, in case they might perhaps recover their senses and be turned from weeds into wheat. But if they do not recover their senses, let them be reserved for their own Judge, to whom they will one day pay the penalty.*

Thus he wrote.

To this article, I believe I have responded abundantly in the *Calculations* regarding Beda’s <note>Noël Béda (c. 1470–1537), a conservative theologian at the Sorbonne and a fierce critic of Erasmus.</note> 32nd proposition. -># On the punishments for infamous magic<- <note>original: "De mag. infam. pœnis". The header refers to the legal classification of severe crimes.</note>

I do not in any way defend the example we see today in some people, who immediately drag scholastic opinions <note>theological arguments used in universities</note> toward imprisonment and the fire. For instance, we now see priests being burned who prefer to call the girl with whom they live a "wife" rather than a "concubine." Indeed, I am accustomed to seeking a remedy for such men, not to act as their patron, nor are these things said by me because I wish such people to go unpunished; I only marvel at how such great severity can be consistent with the gentleness of the Church.

It is not my place to approve or disapprove of the laws of worldly princes; they have their own rights, they have their own councils, and they have their own Judge to whom they must render an account. My paraphrase explains the sense of the Gospel parable <note>likely the Parable of the Tares, where weeds are left to grow until the harvest</note>. If this sense is true, if it is worthy of Christ, if it has pleased approved orthodox interpreters, and if it has been confirmed by the usage of the Church for many centuries, why is it rebuked? Or if it must be rebuked, why are those others not likewise called to judgment?

Up until the age of Augustine—that is, for more than four hundred years after the birth of Christ—we nowhere read of the orthodox imploring the protection of Caesar <note>the Emperor</note> against heretics, even though that had been done very frequently by the heretics themselves. Yet it never seemed right to the orthodox to imitate this example, until the persistent and incurable madness of the Donatists and the Circumcellions <note>radical schismatic groups in North Africa known for violence</note>, tolerated for far too long, drove them to it. For besides the schism—than which nothing would have been more destructive had it proceeded—they harassed and wounded the orthodox, blinding them by throwing lime mixed with vinegar into their eyes, killing some, and driving others to homicide through the fear of death. Nor were they gentler toward themselves than toward others, summoning death upon themselves either by the sword or, if swords were not available, by throwing themselves off precipices. Why say more? Their madness was so great that they should not have been tolerated even by pagan princes, nor by Christians, even if there had been no crime of heresy or schism.

# Book Six

Since no one was permitted to be at peace because of these men, and there was no limit or end to their madness, a discussion finally arose among the bishops regarding the petitioning of the Emperor's protection against the intolerable wickedness of the Donatists <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian group in North Africa who claimed that only those who had remained "pure" during Roman persecutions belonged to the true Church.</note>. To the more gentle-minded, among whom was the Saintly Augustine, the petitioning of secular power for an Ecclesiastical matter was not pleasing; they believed it was not becoming for bishops to use any weapons other than the word of God and prayers—and if the evil proved incurable, the <term>anathema</term> <note>A formal curse by a pope or a council of the Church, excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine.</note>, which is to say, separation from communion. This was then the Church's ultimate punishment, and just as among legal experts exile is called "civil death," so among the Apostles and their successors, the capital punishment was to have been removed from the fellowship of the Church.

To this opinion they were invited not only by the examples of Christ, the apostles, and the martyrs, but they were also driven by fear, considering that there would be a danger that if the matter were handled through terrors, they might have feigned Christians instead of heretics, to the greater ruin of the Christian flock. 

However, when the opinion of others had prevailed, and the matter had turned out well—with many corrected by this severity who had remained in that faction either against their will, or out of uncertainty, or merely led astray by error—Augustine strongly approved what he had previously disapproved. Yet, against such furious bandits and assassins (rather than mere heretics), a law was passed that was, in my judgment, too mild: it first touched no one's body, nor did it strip anyone of their resources. Instead, it merely transferred the resources of the heretical churches to the churches of the orthodox. For those who wished to convert, they could use and enjoy both what they previously held and what they found there. This was done with such gentleness that even the clerics and bishops who came to their senses were not deprived of their honors. Finally, a fine was imposed on the rest that was not particularly heavy—those who, being few, refused to repent. And so, nothing...

# On the punishments for infamous crimes

An attempt was made regarding the killing of such monstrous beasts <note>The author uses "monstrous beasts" to refer to those deemed extreme heretics</note>, so that when an earlier edict of Macedonius (unless I am mistaken), the governor, had been proposed in such ambiguous words that it seemed to threaten heretics with death unless they came to their senses, Augustine diligently warned him not to kill anyone, even though he held this right from the Imperial constitutions <note>original: "constitutionibus Caesareis"</note>. He even praised him for explaining the ambiguity of the words in a later edict. The same man [Augustine] warned, among others, the tribune Dulcicius not to inflict capital punishment on anyone. From these examples, it is clear enough how much their spirit recoiled from this cruelty of confiscations, prisons, executions, and burnings, which now pleases certain people far too much—and is their only recourse. This is especially true among those who profess the perfection of Christian piety, whose entire effort ought to be to heal rather than to destroy, and to mitigate the severity of the laws through their intercession. 

Now, however, there is a cruelty practiced by these "masters of mercy" that goes even beyond the edicts of princes. The Emperor's edict applies to those legitimately convicted—though how "legitimately" this is sometimes done is not for me to say, yet it is not unknown to many. For this class of men obeys almost no laws, neither ecclesiastical nor secular; rather, whatever they wish is considered holy. 

No heresy has ever pleased me, nor have I ever favored, do I favor, or will I ever favor a heretic, except in the hope of healing them—lest anyone suspect me of saying these things for my own sake. I have joined myself to no one who has been dragged away from the folds of the Church; instead, persisting most constantly in the fellowship of the Church myself, I have recalled several people to its society. I speak only of the cruelty of certain individuals who ought to be the most gentle, even if princes were to strike fear with the sword, or if any bishops were to exercise power for the terror of the wicked according to their authority. Now the opposite happens: the authority of monarchs and prelates is forced to put a bridle on the cruelty of those men. And so, the leadership of this business [is returned] to the highest [authorities] of the Church...

# Book Six

It is customary for matters to be delegated to the leading men <note>original: "proceribus," referring to high-ranking officials or nobles</note>, so that these others are not permitted to do whatever they please. However, what has actually been achieved by the seditious outcries of certain individuals before the people, and by their cruelty, the facts themselves speak clearly. Perhaps from a distant region they sometimes write to the Prince whatever they wish; he writes back: "If the matter stands thus, let punishment be exacted." By such a decree, their consciences are not liberated, but rather burdened. Furthermore, when a lay judge pronounces a sentence based on their report, rather than from his own investigation of the case, the entire weight of the judgment falls back upon them.

Now, compare for me the bishops—the leaders of the church—with the monks; compare the Donatist assassins <note>The Donatists were a schismatic Christian group in North Africa known for their rigorism and, in some factions, violent tactics</note> with those who perhaps have said that the orders of monks are not necessary to the church, or that in sermons it is more fitting to invoke the Spirit of Christ than the Virgin Mother, or that they doubt whether the confession of these times was instituted by Christ himself, and whether the celibacy of priests is a matter of divine law. Compare the leniency of the Imperial Constitution <note>original: "Caesareae constitutionis"</note> which was with difficulty obtained from Theodosius <note>Theodosius I, Roman Emperor (r. 379–395 AD), known for his religious legislation</note>, and compare the atrocity of the punishments with which common people <note>original: "idiotis," meaning unlearned or private citizens</note> are now treated—even those led into any kind of error—and you will plainly miss in some people the example of ecclesiastical gentleness.

But later, they say, a more severe law was passed, and not without cause. I do not condemn the cautery <note>A medical metaphor for a hot iron used to sear flesh; here referring to harsh legal measures</note>; I only grieve that the sins of Christians have deserved such a harsh remedy. I even feel sorrow at the punishments of parricides, yet I console this grief out of respect for public tranquility. I am affected in the same way toward those who, because they cannot be healed, are necessarily removed so that they do not drag more people into the plague. Whatever the perhaps necessary severity of the laws may do, it is certainly the duty of priests and monks to strive for healing people rather than extinguishing them. I have never disapproved of the constitutions of Princes, although it is also necessary for them to deflect the rigor of the laws toward the leniency of Christian moderation, as far as it is permitted.

# On the punishments of infamous magicians
<note>original: "De mag. infam. pænis" - likely referring to the legal penalties for those accused of heresy or "magical" infamy</note>

For there ought to be a great difference between a pagan prince and a Christian one; again, there is a very great difference between a secular prince and an ecclesiastical one. Finally, there is no small difference between a prelate endowed with public authority and a monk or a theologian, whose duty it is to teach with all gentleness. How is it that in the past, when no schools of theology had been established, the battle against heretics was fought successfully by the word of God alone; yet now, when the world is full of famous Academies, the matter is handled only with articles of law and bundles of firewood <note>a reference to the "faggots" used for burning heretics at the stake</note>?

What, however, can be criticized in my *Paraphrase* <note>The author refers to his "Paraphrases on the New Testament," a popular explanatory translation of the Gospels</note>, except that it did not mention the Constitution of monarchs devised in later years? That was not permitted, because in that work I make the Evangelist <note>the Gospel writer</note> the speaker, who did not know that constitution. Or should I have introduced him speaking in this way: "Until eight hundred years have passed, Christ wishes no heretic to be killed, but after that time another law shall arise, so that they may be burned"? 

Surely they imagine foolishly that these words are spoken by me for these present times, when they are spoken by the Evangelist for the ancient times of the church. Nor does Christ in that passage deal with the sword of princes, since for so many centuries after Christ’s passion the church lived under pagan princes; rather, he speaks of the Apostolic zeal for drawing all people to salvation with gentleness, following the example of the Chief Shepherd, who had come not to destroy souls, but to save them. 

Thus it is that this interpretation of mine does not obstruct the constitution of princes. For my work teaches evangelical gentleness; it does not take away from the prince the <term>right of the sword</term> <note>ius gladii: the legal authority of a state to punish by death</note>. It prescribes what was fitting for that ancient time, not what the wickedness of men would demand at the end of the ages. Some laws of princes are issued more for the sake of terror than for actual execution. And just as it is the duty of a secular judge to draw the sword at times, so that by the death of one he may save many; so, whenever error, or chance, or youth...

# Book Six.

If the crime is acknowledged, and there is hope for correction, one ought to remember Christian mercy. Furthermore, it must be examined whether monarchs have the right to impose the death penalty for any offense whatsoever. Then it must also be seen whether princes intended for a person to be handed over to the flames for any error that might appear heretical <note>The author questions the broad application of capital punishment for religious "errors" that may not meet the strict definition of heresy.</note>. For if the error is certain, there is no need for theologians here, since it is merely a matter of recognizing the fact; if it is doubtful, it is not for just any theologian, but primarily for the Roman See <note>original: "Romanæ sedis"; referring to the authority of the Pope in Rome.</note> to judge concerning doubtful Articles of Faith.

It is much harsher to hand a man over to the flames for articles that are not only doubtful and controversial, but even trivial. But it is by far the harshest to do so for titles which they themselves invent from time to time at their own whim—such as "this is against the Scholastic doctors" <note>Theologians who followed the medieval tradition of the "Schools," such as Thomas Aquinas.</note>, "this is suspicious," "this is scandalous," "this is against laudable custom," "this sounds bad as it stands," "this is said impertinently," and countless others of this kind. Thus, there is nothing that does not lie open to some slander if a malevolent mind approaches it. And meanwhile, they debate whether the Church can establish a new Article of Faith, while these men, whenever it is convenient, give birth to them during the very trial itself, and sometimes even after the sentence has been published.

The matter is conducted through reporters, deputies, and monk-judges, neither sincerely nor according to the legitimate form of law. The three priors pronounce the verdict in prison, with two monks as witnesses, and the pyre is prepared. The prince—whose law is used as a pretext—is ignorant of these things, as the law is made to serve the private hatred of certain individuals even though it was issued for the public good. Since it is well known that these things happen, princes had to be warned; yet this warning ought neither to support true and incurable heretics, nor to burden sincere inquisitors <term>Inquisitors: officials appointed by the Church to find and suppress heresy</term>. The eighth constitution, which is found in the *Codex* <note>The *Codex Justinianus*, a collection of Roman laws.</note>, Book One, under the title "On Heretical Manichaeans and Samaritans," orders only the books and papers to be burned; the teachers are only to be punished by death...

# On the punishments for infamous sorcery <note>original: "De mag. infam. pœnis"</note>

It is stated that disciples are to be punished with a fine of ten pounds of gold; moreover, those who not only listen to them but also, in contempt of the laws of the princes, keep their books in their possession—thereby showing manifest favor toward heresy—are ordered to be deported into exile. Nor does this constitution strike just any heretics, but specifically the Manichaeans, Apollinarists, and Samaritans, who taught manifest blasphemy. Of this sort are almost all the laws that precede under the same title, which command that the inquisition <note>The judicial investigation into heresy</note> be extended even to the penalty of death; however, they specify certain heresies. Similarly, in the same book, under the title "On the Supreme Trinity, etc.," it specifies the Arians. But these men despoiled the Son of God, and much more the Holy Spirit, of the truth of their divine nature. Just as the Apollinarists denied he was a true man, stripping away from him the better portion of a human being, namely the human soul; the Donatists were furious robbers, not merely most pestilential schismatics. 

The issue here was not whether this confession was instituted by Christ, or whether a pure human constitution binds one to a crime, or whether the Creed was published piece by piece by the Apostles, or whether the Apostles were fluent in the Greek language; rather, it concerned the majesty of Christ and the very summit of Christianity. Now, through the constitutions of the Popes, which are found in the *Decretals* <note>The main collection of Canon Law</note> Book 5, under the title "On Heretics," and in the *Sixth Book* under the same number and title, those convicted and persisting in error, or those relapsed into a heresy previously abjured, are merely ordered to be handed over to the secular court: although here the commentators <note>original: "Glossematographi," referring to the authors of the "Glossa Ordinaria" or legal commentaries</note> have added of their own accord, "Or let them be burned." 

When a fine was decreed against the Pelagians or Jovinians by the edicts of the Emperors, it was one thing. Now, a man is dragged to the fire who doubts whether the Roman Pontiff has jurisdiction over Purgatory. And formerly, in a synod of bishops, heretics were summoned to give an account of their doctrine: once convicted, they were given a free choice, whether they preferred to pronounce an anathema <note>A formal curse or rejection</note> upon their own dogma, or...

# Concerning the Punishments of Infamous Magic

From the heart, however, if **apostates** <note>Those who have totally abandoned their religious faith</note> refuse to turn back, like unrepentant **heretics**, they shall be handed over to the secular court. But if they wish to return, they are received just as repentant heretics are, according to the chapter *Ad abolendam*, paragraph *Poenitenti*, in the sixth book on heretics. This agrees with Raymond <note>Likely St. Raymond of Penyafort, a prominent canon lawyer</note> in the title on apostasy, chapter *Revertentes*, where he says: That those returning from the treachery of apostasy, since they were heretics, are to be received as those returning from heresy; and here one term is taken for the other. This is also found in the second part of the Decrees, Cause 26, Question 5, *Episcopi*.

From the aforementioned authorities, it is gathered that **soothsayers**, **diviners**, **enchanters**, and **sorcerers**, and other followers of this kind, are to be eliminated from the Church; and unless they recover their senses, they are to be perpetually excommunicated. But as for what was stated in the last Council of Aquitaine—that those things done by enchanters are said to happen not in the body, but in the spirit—**Augustine** in his book *The City of God* <note>original: "De Civitate Dei"</note> seems to assert the same, saying: "Those things which are done by the illusions of magi are proven to be not real, but phantasmal." Therefore, there shall be no place here for a criminal action.

If their own **confession** is urged here again: I dare to respond along with Lord Giovanni Francesco Ponzinibio of Piacenza, in the tenth volume of his Treatises, *On Witches* <note>original: "de Lamijs"</note>: Since such persons are deluded, as has been said, it must therefore be said that their confession is also erroneous and not to be admitted. See the laws *Error* and *Cum post* in the Code on ignorance of law and fact. Note also the law *De aetate*, final paragraph, in the Digests on interrogatory actions. For a confession ought to contain what is true and possible; as noted by the gloss of Baldus and others on the first law of the Code on confessions, and the gloss on the final chapter of confessions in the sixth book, and the law *Inde Neratius*, final paragraph. 

But these things <note>the claims made in witch confessions</note> reject both law and nature. Therefore, it does not follow that: "These women confess so, therefore it is so." For a confession stands far apart from the act (or the possibility of the act), and whatever is against nature fails in its own principles; therefore, it is naturally impossible. Furthermore, in criminal matters, one does not regularly stand—

# Book Six

<margin>In criminal cases, one must not rely solely on a confession.</margin>
...one should not rely solely on the confession of the accused, as argued by Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a renowned professor of civil law</note> and Angelus <note>Angelus de Ubaldis, a famous 14th-century legal scholar</note> in their commentary on the first law of the Code regarding confessions; I shall discuss this further in the second note below. Nor is this contradicted by what Baldus says in the law beginning "If anyone, I will not say, seizes" <note>original: "si quis non dicam rapere"</note>: because his statement applies to heresy insofar as it is completed solely in the mind and thought. In such a case, he is correct: because the thought of the mind, which God alone knows, cannot be proven otherwise than by confession; therefore, the confession alone stands. However, the confession we are dealing with in our case involves an external act—one that is legally and naturally impossible, and even highly improbable. Therefore, it can be said that although their confession may be accepted regarding what they *believe* for the purpose of punishment (since such belief depends on the mind and will), it should not be accepted as proof that the events actually occurred as they claim. So much for his argument. Nor should the Cornelia Law on assassins and poisoners <note>original: "lex Cornelia de siccarijs & ueneficis"; a Roman law established by Sulla to prosecute murderers and poisoners</note> be thrust upon me here; it will find its proper place shortly when we discuss the punishments for poisoners.

### Chapter XVIII.

<margin>Book 8 of the *Parerga Iuris*, chapter 22.</margin>
Lord Andrea Alciatus <note>A famous Italian jurist and founder of the legal humanism school</note> likewise relates that an inquisitor of "heretical depravity" (as they call it) conducted an investigation in the sub-Alpine valleys against heretical women—whom the ancients called <term>Lamiae</term> <note>mythological man-eating monsters, used here for witches</note> and we call <term>Striges</term> <note>screech-owls or hags; a common term for witches in the Renaissance</note>. Many of these women seemed to be in need of a dose of hellebore <note>A plant used in antiquity to treat madness; Alciatus implies they were mentally ill rather than evil</note> rather than a purging by fire. This continued until the peasants took up arms to stop that violence and brought the matter to the judgment of the bishop. And later he writes: And although some of the husbands, men of great faith, asserted that at the very time when the women claimed to have been at the games and dances under the Tellina tree...

# On the punishments for infamous sorcery

...were said to have been present, they maintained that they knew from their own experience that their wives had instead been in bed with them. Nevertheless, the reply was given that it was not the wives, but rather an evil spirit <note>original: "cacodæmon"</note> who, having assumed the form of the wife, had deceived the husband. But I replied: Why do you not instead presume that the evil spirit was with his fellow demons, while the woman was truly with her husband? Why do you devise a real body for a fictional game, and a phantom body for a real bed? Why is there a need here to multiply miracles to such an extent, acting not so much as a Theologian but as a teller of tall tales <note>original: "τερατόλογον" (teratologon) - a speaker of marvels or monsters</note>, and choosing the harsher side when it comes to punishments?

It was established from those legal records that once, during that mock-play, when the name of **JESUS** was called out by a certain poor woman, that entire display—all the female dancers with their lovers—suddenly vanished. How could that happen if they were real bodies and not phantoms and "Gardens of Tantalus" <note>A classical proverb referring to something that appears real but vanishes when touched</note>? This was also the opinion of Apollonius of Tyana in the fourth book of Philostratus, and of Gaius Cassius in Plutarch’s *Life of Brutus*.

For even physicians attribute the greatest effects to a corrupted mind and imaginary delusions; hence we have those suffering from nightmares <note>term: "Ephialtici" - from the Greek for nightmare, often associated with a feeling of being pressed down</note>, the "inspired," the superstitious, those possessed by incubi, those raging with love, the visionary, and those suffering from wolf-sickness <note>term: "Lycaones" - lycanthropy</note> or dog-sickness <note>term: "Cynanthropi" - a delusion of being a dog</note>, who are nevertheless cured with medicines. It appears that these are the things which Pliny and other ancients call the "mockery of the Fauns," which they believed could be corrected by the peony herb. Thus, it is very likely that most of these women could also be cured, were it not for the fact that they are all poor and mere females who lack the means for such treatment.

I would certainly grant more weight in this question to Pontifical law <note>Canon Law</note> and the common interpretation of our own doctors than to those theologians, especially in a matter decided by the synod in the Council of Ancyra <note>original: "Anquirenſ." - referring to the Canon Episcopi often associated with this council</note>, Chapter 1, where it says that such phantoms are imposed upon minds by an evil spirit. And again:

> The unfaithful person, it says, believes these things happen not in the mind, but in the body; for who is there who is not led outside of himself in dreams and nightly visions?

# Book Six

The body cannot be transformed by any art of demons, but rather the "phantasticum" <note>The 'phantasticum' refers to the imaginative faculty of the mind, which theologians argued was the only thing demons could actually manipulate.</note> is affected. This faculty varies through innumerable kinds of things while one is thinking or dreaming; and although it is not a physical body, it takes on the form of bodies when the physical senses are asleep or suppressed. Paulus Grillandus <note>An influential 16th-century Italian judge and writer on witchcraft trials.</note> in his *Treatise on Sorcery*, volume 10, relates: A certain husband from a town in the Sabine territory <note>original: "agri Sabinensis", an area in central Italy.</note> had a wife who was a sorceress, or a "striga" <note>term: striga (a screech-owl or witch). Furthermore, as rumors grew and men worthy of trust accused the wife of this disgrace to her husband—claiming she was familiar with other women known for this crime, with whom she was seen to mingle in foul wickednesses and hold nocturnal assemblies—the husband decided to watch and catch her in such acts. He began to keep watch diligently and attentively for many nights. He spent about twelve nights without sleep, attending studiously to whether she wandered out at night to the "play of demons" <note>original: "dæmonum lusum", often referring to the Witches' Sabbath.</note> or some other sorcery, and whether she remained with him in bed the whole night once she had climbed in. He never discovered any deception, but always felt her with his hands in the bed. However, when after a few days she was cast into prison along with certain others accused of the same crime and subjected to questioning, she finally confessed that she had been present at such a "play" together with the other imprisoned women guilty of this disgrace, on such a day (the eleventh of the month, etc.), at such a night, at such an hour, etc. The others confessed the same. But the husband, in defense of his spouse, asserted under a most solemn oath that on that designated night, and especially at that hour, she had been lying in bed with him.

### The Punishment with which the People of Bologna are Accustomed to Visit Witches. Chapter XIX.

In Bologna <note>Latin: Bononia</note>, they are accustomed to lead out male and female sorcerers whose condemned incantations have been less harmful to the human race or to the lives of beasts (those of the female sex are called *the witches* <note>original: "le strige"</note> in the Italian vernacular). They are led from the old palace naked to the navel, placed upon a donkey with their bodies turned backward, so that with their hands bound they hold the tail of the donkey, which was led at a slow pace by the officer's assistant. Upon the head was placed a paper miter <note>a tall, pointed hat used to shame the prisoner</note>, on which were depicted terrifying evil demons <note>original: "cacodæmones"</note> who stirred the fires of hell with their tongs. Meanwhile, as they are led around in this solemn procession, they are severely beaten on the chest and back with rods by the accompanying officer <note>term: lictor (a Roman-style judicial attendant)</note>. When, however, they have arrived from the public square at the cemetery of the Dominican church—the noble burial place of the German nation—they were taken down from the donkey and led by the executioner into a certain upper chamber, whose balcony, secured with iron bars and those spaced far apart, looked toward the cemetery. This place is said to be designated for the punishment of heretics by the monks of that monastery, the inquisitors of heretical depravity. From here, with their heads covered by a helmet and placed in a chair that was moved on four wheels, they were pushed out three times onto the projecting balcony, where they remained for a quarter of an hour. Meanwhile, they were pelted with stones by the crowd watching from outside, laughing and shouting; yet almost in vain, because of the intervening iron bars. Finally, released from their bonds and punished according to the quality of their crime, they were sent away into exile.

## Chapter XX.

It is commonly said that women, in the same type of offense, sin less and should be punished less than men, provided all other factors are equal: namely, on account of the weakness of their spirit, mind, and intellect. <note>The author cites several points of Roman Civil Law here, specifically the Digest (D.) and the Code (C.), which were the foundations of legal education in the Renaissance.</note> See the law on the penalty for sacrilege, at the beginning of the Digest *on the Julian law regarding embezzlement*; and the law *if adultery*, sections on debauchery, brothers, and incest, in the Digest *on the Julian law regarding adultery*; and the chapter *as is worthy*, at the beginning of the Extra *on homicide*; and the chapter *they are indignant*, case 32, question 6, where it is written: "Men ought to be punished all the more severely, insofar as it pertains more to them to both excel in virtue and to guide women by their example." Regarding this sentiment, in the writings of Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a Danish historian</note> in the 6th book of the *Danish History*, Eric—a man of great prudence—contended that women's errors should more often be forgiven, and punishment should not be inflicted unless correction had failed to remedy the fault. And there is that saying of Aeneas in Virgil, in the 2nd book of the *Aeneid*:

---
> There is no memorable renown
> In the punishment of a woman.

Pliny, in the 8th book of his *Natural History*, writes that the lion, when he is fierce, rages against men more than against women: as if nature itself had taught him that women are to be treated more mildly than men. Aristotle, in the 2nd and 9th sections of his *Problems*, chapter 11, asks: "Why is it more unjust to kill a woman [than a man]?"

# Book Six

He led a solitary life, being an intimate associate of Michael Psellus <note>A prominent 11th-century Byzantine monk, philosopher, and politician known for his writings on demonology.</note>; and he taught that demons possess genitals and are fertile with seed. He claimed that these lustful beings, out of a desire for procreation, pour their seed into the small cavities of those most hideous beasts (for so he calls the Lamiæ <note>In folklore, these were often depicted as female man-eating monsters or witches; here the author uses the term to describe those supposedly consorting with demons.</note>) and raise offspring. However, these offspring are unlike our own, resembling dwarfs or apes. How could Marcus <note>Likely referring to Marcus of Byzantium, a figure discussed in Psellus's dialogues.</note> have known these things, unless, while he was intimately enjoying the company of demons, they deluded his eyes in the form he described, and by their illusions cast a shadow in place of a reality? Or perhaps they corrupted his imagination, as they do with the Lamiæ, through such suggestions.

Furthermore, as a philosopher, he ought to have considered that every seed generates its own likeness. Why, then, would dwarfs be born from the seed of demons, who are spirits? What is their similarity? In what do they agree? Is it in size, or in substance? Do demons likewise resemble apes in their procreating—they who know how to counterfeit any form, even that of angels of light? If you wish to grant them the power of procreation, they would beget evil geniuses or spirits; for one must establish an analogy of things here. 

Immortal nature would also be added to this; by which reasoning, they would have grown from the beginning of creation into such a numerous progeny up to this present age, that it would be no wonder if nothing but these ghosts were constantly before our eyes, and no man anywhere would be safe from these infinite myriads. Whoever wishes to overturn this opinion should bring forward reasons by which I might be compelled to believe these trifles—or rather, these most transparent lies. I truly marvel that a learned man allows himself to be mocked and his senses to be clouded in this matter. 

In addition, he adds another reason for punishment that is far too frivolous: that the number of these Furies <note>original: "Erynnarum," referring to the Eumenides or Furies of Greek mythology, used here to describe the supposed witches or demons.</note> would grow into such an immense sea that no one could live safe from their incantations unless they were burned. On the contrary, one lives nowhere more securely from their harm than where this "sacrifice" <note>A sarcastic reference to the execution of accused witches.</note> has no place, and where they are not committed to the fire—namely, where the trickery of the devil...

### The Punishments of Poisoners. Chapter XXIII.

<margin>Punishments of poisoners.</margin>
The Cornelian Law <term>Lex Cornelia: a Roman law established by Sulla (c. 81 BC) concerning assassins and poisoners</term> should not be twisted to apply to anything other than poisoners. For whatever women have brought diseases, death, or loss upon anyone by the power of some poison, they deserve the name and punishment of Poisoners <note>original: "Veneficarum"</note>; and for these, the laws either increase or moderate the punishment according to the nature of the crime. Just as if any women strive to extort love from suitors or others by a philter or love potion, and in the meantime either drive them mad or torture them with diseases, yet do not deprive them of life: it is just that the magnitude of the harm and the intent of the will should prescribe the severity or moderation of the punishment. I wish this to be said once and for all concerning any inflicted loss of property.

<margin>The Cornelian Law. Digest, book 48, title 8.</margin>

# Book Six

**By** a Decree of the Senate <note>original: "Senatusconsulto"; a formal resolution of the Roman Senate</note>, a woman was ordered to be exiled who—not indeed with evil intent, but as a bad example—administered a medicine for conception, from which the woman who had conceived died. By another Decree of the Senate, it was established that pigment-sellers <note>original: "pigmentarij"; these were often druggists or apothecaries who sold dyes and chemicals</note> who rashly provide hemlock, salamander, aconite, pine-caterpillars, mandrake, Spanish fly, or anything for the sake of a "purification" <note>original: "lustramenti causa"; likely referring to superstitious or ritual cleansing</note>, are held under the penalty of that same law. Here the edict of Moses also has its place: <margin>Exodus 22</margin> <margin>The punishment of sorceresses established by Moses.</margin> "You shall not allow sorcerers to survive," or otherwise "to live." <note>original Greek: "φαρμακοὺς οὐκ ἐπιβιώσετε"</note> Thus the seventy translators <note>The Septuagint, the Greek version of the Old Testament</note> explained the intent of the law: "You shall not suffer sorcerers to live": or, if you prefer, "sorceresses" (in the feminine gender) as the Hebrew interpreters maintain. Certainly, none other are to be understood by this than those whom Moses and that age knew: for those "witches" commonly so-called by us, and described by me, were not even known in the times of Christ, much less those of Moses. Truly, of those enchanters whom Scripture mentions, all are infamous mages <note>original: "magi"; practitioners of ritual magic</note>.

And especially the Italian Circe, who was even enrolled among the gods? Indeed, among other writers, you will find many more: namely Mycale, Erichtho, Dipsas, Eriphia, Guthrun, that Gyge who was the servant of Parysatis (the mother of Cyrus), a certain Martina mentioned by Cornelius Tacitus in the second book of his *Annals*, and Locusta <note>A notorious professional poisoner in the Roman Empire, active during the reigns of Claudius and Nero.</note> in the same author, near the end of the twelfth book, and almost infinite others. There is an old proverb concerning the sorceries of women: <term>Thettalē gynē</term> <note>original: "Θετταλὴ γυνὴ"</note>, that is, a "Thessalian woman," mentioned by Suidas, which we use to refer to female poisoners; because that nation, and especially its women, are noted above all others by this name. Quintilian, in the fifth book of his *Oratorical Institutions*, under the title "On Arguments," says: *I would more easily believe a man committed robbery, and a woman committed poisoning.*

It is said that in Persia, poisoners were punished by having their heads dashed against a large stone, and then having their skulls crushed by another stone brought down upon them. However, as to what ought to be decided here regarding those who prepare poisons for the destruction of humans or livestock—whether they be male or female—I have judged that it should be left to the equity and judgment of a wise Magistrate. This is so that he, whose authority Holy Scripture testifies is ordained by God, may not complain that anything has been prejudiced against him outside the limits of my profession. Nevertheless, I wished to subjoin, as a finishing touch <note>original: "colophonis loco"</note> from Aulus Gellius, a rare sentence of the incomparably wise Athenian Areopagites <note>Judges of the high court of Athens.</note>, pronounced with certainly mature counsel against a female poisoner, as an example of deliberate and discerning judgment. These are his words:

<margin>Book 13, chapter 7. Valerius Publicola.</margin>
A woman of Smyrna was brought before Gnaeus Dolabella, while he was holding the province of Asia with proconsular power. This woman had killed her husband and her son at the same time by secretly administering poison. She confessed to having done it, but she claimed she had a reason for the deed: because that same husband and son had killed another son of the woman, born of a previous husband—a most excellent and innocent youth—

# Book Six.

...they had killed him, having caught him in an ambush. There was no dispute that the deed had been done. Dolabella <note>Publius Cornelius Dolabella, a Roman proconsul in Asia around 44 BCE</note> referred the matter to his council. No one on the council dared to pass judgment in such a double-edged case; for on one hand, a confessed poisoning, by which a husband and son were slain, did not seem a matter to be left unpunished. On the other hand, a worthy penalty had merely been exacted against wicked men. Dolabella referred the matter to the Areopagites <note>The high court of Athens, famous for its wisdom and antiquity</note> at Athens, as to judges of greater weight and experience. The Areopagites, having heard the case, ordered the accuser of the woman and the accused woman herself to appear before them in one hundred years. Thus, the woman's poisoning was not acquitted, which the laws did not allow; nor was the guilty woman condemned and punished, as she was deemed worthy of pardon. This history was written by Valerius Maximus in Book 8, Chapter 23.

### Recapitulation regarding Witches. Chapter XXIV.

<margin>Witches cannot do what they are believed to do.</margin>
Now at last, I believe it has been sufficiently proven that there are no causes—neither in natural reason nor in fact—for all those things which are commonly ascribed to witches <note>original: "Lamijs," referring to the Lamiae of myth, here used for witches</note>. For if they effect anything of that sort, they must certainly be able to do so; for an act presupposes a power. If, however, we wish to conclude that they have the power, it must first be defined in what manner and by what reason they are able. But they can perform these things neither by themselves, nor through incantations, nor through a demon, nor can demons perform them through the women.

<margin>They cannot do it by themselves.</margin>
We have demonstrated by a triple reason that they cannot do it by themselves. For those things which are required for every action—whether it be simple or done for a certain end—namely, the faculty of the agent, the suitability of the sufferer and the subject, and a convenient and possible application; they plainly lack all three of these. For as far as they are concerned, they are mortals; 
<margin>The faculty of the agent.</margin>
since their entire faculty depends on the analogy and harmony of the body and the soul, the soul can do nothing except understand and will, while with the body they can only do as much as the limits of earthly senses allow. Therefore...

# On the Punishments of Infamous Sorcerers

Neither do they reach the higher realms by their own power, nor can they perform anything at all that does not correspond to the senses. For as we have said, to accomplish anything, or to produce an effect upon something, the virtue and power of the <term>efficient cause</term> <note>The primary agent that produces an effect; a concept from Aristotelian philosophy.</note> is absolutely necessary, in the same way as a *relationship between things* <note>original: "πρός τι" (pros ti). A Greek philosophical term for "relation" or "relative."</note>. 

<margin>
The unsuitability of the subject.
</margin>

Furthermore, as far as it pertains to that upon which they are believed to act, for this very reason it is impossible for them to shake the earth, dissolve clouds, provoke hail, stir up winds, bring on rains, summon lightning, or draw forth thunder. For no act can be ours, or that of any other agent, unless it is performed upon a suitable and well-disposed "patient" <note>In logic, the "patient" is the object that receives the action of the "agent."</note>. However, neither the reason of the universe nor the condition of the elements is such that humans can act upon them, or act in the manner that witches are believed to do, as we have explained more extensively in the preceding books. Therefore, they will achieve these things much less through incantations. 

Nor indeed can there be more virtue in the "caused thing," as we say, than what proceeds from the influence and benefit of its own cause. The causes of incantations and songs are the witches and those who use them—just as they are the causes of all words—and what the effect of these may be, Aristotle most subtly teaches in the second book of *On the Soul*. We have already shown that witches have no force, no faculty for increasing these things. Therefore, incantations are not the cause of such effects, nor is the power of witches supported by that rule: *Whatever is the cause of the cause, is also the cause of that which is called the effect.*

And so, by this very fact, the whole business would not only be hindered, but could not even be begun. For an unskillful and inconvenient medium prevents the extremes from being joined or from agreeing in any action. Unless perhaps when...
