# Book Six

<margin>Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonic text often cited to discuss the soul of the world and celestial harmony.</note></margin>
...let us establish with the Platonists that this world is a kind of living creature that even possesses senses, having both ears and eyes; and with Pythagoras, that it is delighted and moved by songs <note>original: "cantibus"; referring to the 'Music of the Spheres'.</note>.

But we shall also demonstrate that these women do not perform these feats through the devil. For even if I were to concede that they could either compel the devil with their incantations, or that the devil does these things of his own accord when invoked by them: nevertheless, they can neither force him to act, nor can they effect through him that which is not within his power. For although he himself can do all the things we have mentioned, and many other things which to us are sometimes miracles and sometimes only appear to be so: yet he cannot provide those things which either he or a human might wish for; nor at the very moment when he might desire it, or when his clients might hope for and command it. Rather, he can only do those things which the Supreme God wills, and only then when it has pleased Him. Therefore, if ever they should obtain what they desire after their incantations, it is because it proceeds not from the whim or command of the demon or those women, but from the will of God who commands or permits it—which is not only beyond the power, but even beyond the knowledge of any spirit or man. Thus, such events must be considered accidental to both men and demons. For this reason, they are no more the cause of these things than they are of all things which are not done by us, but happen to us by chance, even if we wished for them. Finally, the power of the diabolic nature does not provide us with that objection: that it is the same whether the <term>Lamiae</term> <note>A classical term for witches or night-monsters, used here to describe those accused of witchcraft.</note> perform the acts attributed to them by themselves or through the devil;

<margin>Law: *is damnum*, Digest on the Rules of Law; Law 1, paragraph *deiecisse*, Digest on Force and Armed Force; Law: *nihil interest*, Digest on the Cornelian Law regarding Assassins. <note>These are citations from the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the body of Roman Law, arguing that in legal terms, it usually makes no difference if one acts personally or through an agent.</note></margin>
nor does it matter whether they produce the effect or provide the cause immediately.

The last point is what might be said: that the demon works through these old women whatever we have spoken of above, so that the wretched <term>Lamiae</term> are "instrumental causes." As if, truly, the "artisan of a thousand deceits" <note>original: "mille artifex"; a common epithet for the devil.</note> had need of their labor! But even if this were not the case, who does not see that toothless old women are utterly inept instruments for stirring up the heavens, the air, the clouds, and the winds? Not...

# On the Impotence of Witches

<margin>Law 1, Section "Furthermore," Digest on Acquiring Possession</margin>
<margin>Law "Uranius," Digest on Sureties</margin>
<margin>Law "Of Witnesses," Codex on Witnesses; Baldus <note>Baldus de Ubaldis (1327–1400), a highly influential jurist</note>, column 7</margin>
Therefore, should we believe those wicked spirits to be of such great foolishness and sluggishness that they would approach these women? Or that nature has fallen so low that it could be moved by them? For in order to perform any action, a suitability and fitness of the instrument is required. Even if these witches <note>original: "Lamiæ," a term for predatory female demons or witches</note> were necessary and fit instruments for the demons to carry out those things which Almighty God permits them to do, why would the wretched women deserve punishment for it? For first, we would see them *suffering* this action <note>i.e., being used as passive tools</note>; therefore, they are by no means *doing* it. These two things—acting and being acted upon—do not occur at the same time. Furthermore, it is certain that actions are not judged based on the instrumental cause, nor does the purpose of what is done depend upon the tool. This is supported by the argument in Law "He who [gave] to me as a gift," Digest on Donations. In the case of evil deeds <term>maleficia: harmful magic or crimes</term>, only the intended purpose is punished, according to Law "The Divine," Digest on the Cornelian Law concerning Assassins. And having explained these reasons quite extensively and established them with the strongest arguments through the nature of things—the best witness of truth—we have declared it impossible for witches to truly be capable of any of those things which are claimed. This is the primary argument: that they also perform nothing of this sort.

<margin>Experience teaches that witches do not do that which is imputed to them.</margin>
<margin>Gloss on the Authentica regarding the selection of ministers, at the beginning.</margin>
<margin>Law "To compel," Section "We create," Digest on the Rights of Patrons; with "When [the cause] ceases," and on Appeals.</margin>
The second argument was sought from fact, which is the best foundation of truth; for truth is the knowledge of a certain thing obtained chiefly through sight. By experience itself, we discover that these effects are most falsely attributed to witches. For not only do those calamities, of which they are said to be the causes, endure—and indeed return—after the women have already been removed and reduced to ashes; but such calamities are also sometimes just as frequent and violent in places where neither the power nor the name of witches is known. An effect, however, ought not to be ascribed to a cause if, when that cause is removed, the same thing happens nonetheless. This follows Law "On conditions," [section] "The ward," at the beginning, Digest on Conditions and Demonstrations; and by the argument of the second-to-last Law, Digest on the causes for which adults [are restored]. For when the cause ceases, the effect necessarily ceases as well. Since, therefore, we hold from the facts that witches effect these things neither through themselves nor through another, but that another <note>likely referring to God or natural providence</note> acts without them,

For those—that is, either God <term>directly</term> <note>original Greek: ἀμέσως (amesos); meaning without any intervening cause</note>, or the devil by the permission of the highest and almighty God—it is certainly not fair that others should be burdened by the act of another, or that there should be punishment where <margin>Law "The father's crime," Digest on Punishments.</margin> there is no guilt. For this <margin>Nothing is punished unless it is possible.</margin> reason, judges do not attend to what someone is said to have wanted, or what it is proven they were capable of; rather, they look at those things which a person is demonstrated to have committed and done, and which, by the nature of things, fall within both the power and the will of man. This is so true that even if someone, whether voluntarily or otherwise, were to confess to a crime which they either simply could not commit, or for certain reasons does not naturally appear to have committed, they nevertheless cannot be punished for it. For we have taught above that a confession must contain both the truth and the possible. Also in the year 1563, my sons saw in Padua a boy snatching apples in the market from an unwilling woman; having been struck lightly on the back with a rod, he immediately fell down dead. Nevertheless, it was not likely that he died from that, for it seemed most difficult to the doctors to believe. In law, the judgment regarding impossible things and extremely difficult things is almost the same. Law "At Julian's," paragraph "It is established," Digest on Legacies 1. This also pertains to the defense of <term>witches</term> <note>original: lamiæ; often used to refer to sorceresses or female demons in a legal-theological context</note>...

# Book Six

<margin>Whether the laws concerning sorcerers are applicable.</margin>
It is claimed that by magic arts, men can disturb the elements, undermine the lives of the innocent, and summon the spirits of the dead. In the law titled *Of Such Persons* <note>Latin: "l. eorum"; referring to a specific section of the Codex Justinianus</note>, it is said that sorcerers can both remove and avert diseases, rains, hail, and winds; and that those who use incantations for a good purpose should not be punished, but only those who use them for an evil end. This is the opinion of Bartolus and Salycetum <note>Bartolus de Saxoferrato and Nicolaus de Salyceto, influential medieval legal commentators</note> in their summaries. But since it has now been proven by reason, experience, and authority that none of these things are truly performed by human beings, the reasoning of the law having been corrected, the law itself seems to me to be corrected. This is noted in the standard gloss on the first law, under the word "providence" in the Digest <note>The Digest (Pandects) was a major part of Roman Law</note> regarding legal guardianship, and in the law "By what reason," in the section on "letters," under the word "direct" regarding the acquisition of ownership of things. Furthermore, in Book Three, Chapter 16, we have brought forward no slight reasons to show that witches <term>Lamiæ: a term for witches or female demons, often used in this period to describe those accused of the "Sabbat"</term> cannot stir up storms and the air.

<margin>Exodus 9.</margin>
<margin>The law "If in good faith" in the Digest regarding damage caused by a slave.</margin>
We touched upon experience above, and we can have no more certain proof than from Book Four, which we composed almost entirely of examples of those who, while suffering from either demonic possession or natural diseases and defects, were nevertheless believed to be afflicted by the witchcraft of witches. But this also is most clear: that those things which they seem able to induce and summon, they can by no power remove or drive away. This we noted in the case of Pharaoh’s magicians, who could neither drive away the frogs nor the gnats, nor could they protect themselves; indeed, being afflicted with boils, they exposed the vanity of their arts. For just as he is seen to act who does not prevent a thing when he is able <note>Latin: "l. adigere"; a legal principle that failing to stop an act one can prevent is equivalent to doing it</note>, so he does not act who, though he wishes to, is unable. They could not do it because of the Spirit of God. If it had been within their own power to drive them away, we would not deny they had the ability. It is the same thing to say someone "is able" as to say "it is within his power to do it."

There remains the Authority, the greatest of which we have from the Council of Ancyra <note>An early church council (314 AD) whose "Canon Episcopi" was a primary text used to argue that witchcraft was a delusion</note>, and no less from the Holy Fathers and their canons. See the glosses and Doctors of the law on these points; they all expressly testify that he is a heretic who...

# On the Impotence of Witches

Whoever believes that things of this sort can be performed by mages and sorcerers <note>original: "magos ac sortilegos"</note> [is in error]. See the Decree of Gratian, Case 26, Question 4, chapter "Therefore" and chapter "Accused," section "Clearly," and the section on heretics in the Sixth Book of Decretals; for such a belief attributes to a creature that which belongs to the one and only God. See also the Decree of Gratian, Case 26, Question 2, chapter "He who without the Savior," as well as the commentaries of Giovanni d'Andrea on the title regarding Sorcery, and Panormitanus <note>Nicola de' Tudeschi (1386–1445), a famous canon lawyer</note>, Andreas Sicculus in Counsel 55, and Oldradus in Counsel 210.

Since these things are so, the words of those secular laws are not to be twisted as if the Christian Emperor either believed himself, or wished others to believe, that such miracles or calamities are produced and perfected by men through evil or magical arts. Rather, they are to be understood as being taken and written according to the opinion of the common people <note>original: "opinione uulgi"</note> and according to the common form of speaking, which lawmakers for the most part observe and retain. This is best evidenced by the law "No one" <note>referring to the Code of Justinian, Book 9, Title 18, Law 3</note> and other laws. Indeed, we ought to reconcile laws with other laws by every means possible. 

However, if we look to authority, who can doubt that in this matter the highest faith and reverence must be granted to Divine Law? For in defining cases, especially those which pertain to the soul—as our present case does—the sayings of the Church Fathers and the Canons are to be preferred over secular laws, as Panormitanus notes. Nor do the laws themselves disdain to imitate the sacred Canons.

---

They argue that the will to commit a crime <note>original: "voluntatem sceleris"</note> should be punished with the same severity as the outcome itself.

See the law "Whoever" at the beginning of the Digest on the Julian Law of Majesty, and the law "If anyone does not fight" in the Code regarding bishops and clerics. They are sufficiently tortured by their own madness <note>original: "furore"</note> and punished by their own calamity. <note>Citing the Digest of Justinian: Law 'divus', Title 'on the office of the prefect'; Law 'poena', section 'sane', Title 'on the Pompeian law regarding parricide'.</note> Therefore, just as fate excuses them, so too does misfortune excuse our women. # Book Six.

error. <note>original: "C. de iur. & fact. ign." refers to the Code of Justinian regarding ignorance of law and fact</note> And for this reason, the first objection falls away. Although I do not deny that it is a more serious matter to offend against the Divine Majesty, it must also be understood that men fall into this crime more easily and more quickly. For that eternal, infinite, and spiritual majesty and will is incomprehensible and far removed from our senses. Therefore, we who are as sharp-sighted as lynxes in earthly affairs, immediately become as blind as moles in spiritual matters and those which pertain to God. It is no different than those who, while they think themselves endowed with the highest visual acuity when they look most keenly at things on earth perceivable by the senses, find that if they wish to look at the sun, all that sharpness becomes utter darkness in the face of such great brilliance.

There are, therefore, two reasons why the lapse of men in spiritual matters is easier: first, because of the nature of divine things, which is superior to all human thought; and second, because of both the blindness of our understanding and the depravity of our will. Therefore, if anyone offends or errs in this area, the punishment ought to be milder and the pardon more just—and this is all the more true if a woman, and even more so if a decrepit little old woman, should fall.

# Book Six

...to commit damnable idolatry. This is an Error.

**Twelfth**, the belief that holy words, certain devout prayers, fasts, ritual washings, and bodily abstinence practiced by children and others—as well as the celebration of Masses and other naturally good works—when performed for the sake of practicing these arts <note>referring to the "forbidden arts" of magic and divination</note>, excuse these acts from evil rather than further condemning them. This is an Error. For through such things, sacred objects—and indeed God Himself in the Eucharist <term>Eucharist: the consecrated bread and wine used in the Mass</term>—are attempted to be sacrificed to demons. The demon procures this either because he wishes to be honored in this way as "like the Most High," or to hide his frauds, or to more easily ensnare the simple-minded and destroy them more damnably.

**Thirteenth**, the belief that the holy Prophets and other saints obtained their prophecies, performed miracles, or cast out demons through such arts. This is an Error and a blasphemy.

**Fourteenth**, the belief that God, either directly by Himself or through good angels, revealed such sorceries <term>maleficia: harmful magic or "evil-doing" through supernatural means</term> to holy men. This is an Error and a blasphemy.

**Fifteenth**, the belief that it is possible through such arts to coerce a human's free will toward the will or desire of another. This is an Error; and to attempt to do this is impious and nefarious.

**Sixteenth**, the belief that the aforementioned arts are good and from God, and that it is permitted to observe them because things sometimes or often happen just as those using them seek or predict, or because some good occasionally comes from them. This is an Error.

**Seventeenth**, the belief that through such arts demons are truly forced and compelled, rather than merely pretending to be compelled in order to seduce mankind. This is an Error.

**Eighteenth**, the belief that through such arts and impious rites—through sorceries, incantations <term>carminationes: ritual chants or songs used in magic</term>, and the invocation of demons, through certain insults <note>original: "insultationes," likely referring to ritualized taunting of spirits to command them</note> and other evil deeds—no effect is ever produced by the ministry of demons...

# On the Impotence of Witches

...whether it follows. This is an **Error**. For God sometimes permits such things to happen, as was evident in the case of Pharaoh’s magicians <note>original: "magis Pharaonis"; a reference to the Book of Exodus where the Egyptian sorcerers mimicked Moses' miracles</note> and many other times elsewhere; either because those using or consulting these arts, on account of their bad faith and other nefarious sins, are given over to a "reprobate mind" <note>A biblical phrase meaning a mind abandoned by God to its own corruption</note> and thus deserve to be so deceived.

**The Nineteenth Error:** That good angels are enclosed in stones, or that they consecrate images or garments, or do other things contained in those arts. This is an **Error and blasphemy**.

**The Twentieth Error:** That the blood of a hoopoe <note>A bird often associated with magical rituals in medieval grimoires</note> or a kid or any other animal, or "virgin parchment" <note>Parchment made from the skin of a stillborn or newborn animal, considered "pure" for magical use</note> or the hide of a lion and similar things, have the efficacy to compel or repel demons through the ministry of such arts. This is an **Error**.

**The Twenty-first Error:** That images made of bronze, lead, gold, white or red wax, or other material—when baptized, exorcised, and consecrated (or rather, desecrated) according to the aforementioned arts and on certain days—possess the marvelous powers described in the books of such arts. This is an **Error in faith, in natural philosophy, and in true astronomy**.

**The Twenty-second Error:** That to use such things and to place faith in them is not idolatry and infidelity. This is an **Error**.

**The Twenty-third Error:** That some demons are good, others benign; some all-knowing, and others neither saved nor damned. This is an **Error**.

**The Twenty-fourth Error:** That the fumigations <note>The burning of incense or herbs to summon spirits</note> performed in such operations are converted into spirits, or that such things are owed to them. This is an **Error**.

**The Twenty-fifth Error:** That one demon is the King of the East (and especially by his own merit), another of the West, another of the North, and another of the South. This is an **Error**.

**The Twenty-sixth Error:** That the "moving intelligence of heaven" <note>The medieval philosophical concept that celestial bodies are moved by spiritual intellects</note> flows into the rational soul just as the celestial body flows into the human body. This is an **Error**.

### Epilogue of the Work.

<margin>Epilogue</margin>
I have no doubt, fair Reader, that there will be many with whom I shall find little favor, who will return me spite for whatever work I have performed. Most of these, as is the way with unjust judges, will find fault with what they do not understand. Others, wishing to defend by any reasoning an opinion rooted in the minds of men by a long series of years and solidified, as it were, by customary law, will want to champion it by any means. Nor will there be lacking those who, becoming insolent as usual with the itch of a "Theonine tooth" <note>original: "dentis Theonini"; a classical idiom referring to a malicious or biting critic, named after a Roman wit known for his sharp tongue</note>, will greedily seek an occasion for biting. # 676

...of Mantua, the greatest and most famous philosopher of his time. If his work *On the Causes of Natural Effects, or On Incantations*, which is full of abstruse philosophy, is consulted and more carefully examined so that I might oppose and destroy it, I would be at risk—unless, firmly established upon the unconquered foundations of Christian philosophy, I held the mere plausibility of his speech in contempt. <margin>Colossians 2</margin> I follow the counsel of Saint Paul, that "chosen vessel," who studiously warned that we must see to it that no one plunders us through philosophy and empty deception, according to human tradition and the elements of the world, and not according to Christ. For in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead in bodily form. Regarding Pomponazzi <note>Pietro Pomponazzi (1462–1525) was a controversial Italian philosopher who sought to explain "miraculous" phenomena through natural causes rather than demons, which often put him at odds with Church doctrine.</note>, I wish to hope that through the singular mercy of God he repented before his final breath and did not remain an <term>atheist<note>original Greek: ἄθεον ("atheon"); one without God.</note></term>. Indeed, I have heard more than once from that distinguished ornament of medicine, Master Helidæus of Forlì, who was once his student, that such was the case.

However, many of the more morose theologians will cry out that an injury is being done to them by a physician who examines certain passages of Holy Scripture and leaps over the boundaries of his own calling. They will bark quite bitingly: <note>original: "Ne sutor ultra crepidam"; a Latin proverb meaning "Let the shoemaker not judge above the shoe," used to tell someone to stay in their lane.</note> *Let the shoemaker not go beyond his last.* To these men, I wish to give no other answer than that Saint Luke the Evangelist was a physician of Antioch, and that I am among the number of those whose study is directed toward this goal: <margin>Royal priesthood. 1 Pet. 2. Isaiah 61.</margin> that if in any way, through the immense mercy of God and the ineffable grace of Christ, they might finally reach that **royal priesthood** mentioned by the Apostle Peter and the prophet Isaiah.

As for the fact that I have accused certain impure men of the ecclesiastical college of the crime of witchcraft <note>original: "maleficij"; refers to harmful magic or sorcery.</note>, if they take offense at this, I could not have done otherwise given the nature of my argument. I could even have been more pointed by expressing their names, had I not been taught modesty by Theology. I have instead decided to forewarn these subverters of the Christian faith and disturbers of our disgraced commonwealth, so that they might yet desist.

### Book Six.

677

V 3

My dispute is with those accused of magical crimes, not with pious men, whom I honor and cherish above all else, more than anyone. If they complain that they have been unfairly misrepresented, I do not refuse to step out into the public theater with them and defend their cause.

To some of the more learned men of our profession, or even to the more refined, if I have not given sufficient satisfaction (which I freely admit, for I am well aware of how short my resources are), I seem to have provided at least some occasion—commensurate with the poverty of my talent (which I acknowledge is great)—for them to weigh the matter more exactly, search more deeply, and describe it with a more learned method, a more coherent order, clearer speech, more fitting words, and stronger arguments for the truth. If I am warned of any slip or proven wrong by them, I will owe them much gratitude, as I would to anyone else who follows me with the same zeal; I will never be ashamed to retract my errors. I am not so much a <note>Suffenus was a character in the poems of Catullus known for being a bad poet who was nevertheless delighted with his own work.</note> **Suffenus** to myself, nor am I so affected by the lust of <term>self-love<note>original Greek: φιλαυτίας ("philautias"); excessive self-love or conceit.</note></term>. It is something to advance to a certain point, even if one is not permitted to go further.

Regarding the fact that I dissent from common opinion and the fictions of poets concerning the authority of the **Laws of the Twelve Tables** <note>The earliest code of Roman law (c. 450 BCE). Table VIII contained laws against "charming away" a neighbor's crops.</note> about those who **charmed away the harvests**, if the legal experts take this badly, they return bad grace for a benefit. This is because I wished to offer some opportunity for the truth to be sought by others in this type of argument, and for a criminal sentence to be drawn out and pronounced in due order—not according to the decrees of a blind age in the Christian religion, but from the mysteries of truth itself. Indeed, if it was my intention to prejudice anyone in their legitimate vocation, I do not refuse the mark of a reckless man, as I would deserve.

However, if there are biting and envious minds not satisfied with this defense of mine, who tear me apart with insults, convict me of ignorance, or unfairly accuse me of a crime...

# On the Powerlessness of Witches

### 678

...and should they be pleased to draw a petulant pen against me, I trust that the Almighty God will strengthen me with such endurance that I shall overcome whatever teeth and insults my adversaries may bite with, simply by bearing them.

Furthermore, these impious and sacrilegious mages find their machinations against me to be utterly useless. I am not moved even a hair’s breadth by their tricks or their "terrors," even if these monstrous evildoers strive to transform me with their dire curses or diabolic exorcisms, or if they attempt to drive me into the <term>air<note>original Greek: ἀέρας ("aeras"); Weyer refers here to the "transportation" of people through the sky, a common myth in witchcraft trials.</note></term>, or (if they prefer) into the sewers by their loathsome arts. I utterly despise those lost men who would use the **Delphic oracles** of "divine" matters to prophesy nothing but misfortune for me—associating me with the punishment established by the tyrant **Pisistratus** for the man caught defecating in the Temple of Pythian Apollo <note>Weyer uses a crude historical anecdote to mock the gravity and "sanctity" of his accusers' claims.</note>. The gloomy necromancer shall try in vain to terrify me with spirits of the night, the shades of the dead, or ghostly apparitions. Nor do I summon the sprinkling of lustral water or the fire of torches near graves against the shadows of <term>Goetic<note>from "Goetia," a term for low magic or sorcery involving the invocation of spirits, often viewed as more "demonic" than high "theurgy."</note></term> spirits; they shall by no means weary me with their specters. If a wicked exorcist provokes me with the barbarism of hellish voices or the mockery of his murmurs, I do not care. I do not care a straw—indeed, I laugh—at the "ligatures" <note>Spells or "knotted" charms believed to bind a person's will or physical health.</note> of the enchanters, by which they are believed to be able to summon prodigious diseases, or to impede natural sexual intercourse, or even to take away and restore the male organs at their own whim. If crazed hags are able to do anything against me by a malignant curse or the impulse of a corrupted will, I both permit them and dismiss them. In short, as **Horace** says:

> Dreams, magical terrors, miracles, hags,
> Nightly spirits, and Thessalian <note>Thessaly, a region in Greece, was legendary in antiquity for being the home of powerful witches.</note> portents, I receive
> with laughter. —

I fear only one art of the "poison-witches" <note>original: "ueneficarum"; Weyer distinguishes between "imaginary" witchcraft and the "real" crime of poisoning.</note>, who are able to inflict many harms truly and not just fantastically—whether through poisons that are drunk, or applied externally, or struck into the victim through the drawing in of vapors. Of these...

# Book Six

### 679

I have not at all undertaken to defend this cause here, but I leave it to be discussed and decided by the just judgment and censorship of the magistrate.

However, having extricated myself somewhat from the labyrinth of **demonic delusions** and **incantations**, I shall make an end of speaking about these monstrous mockeries. They were certainly devised to obscure the glory of God and the truth of both sacred and <term>physical<note>Weyer refers here to "natural philosophy," what we would today call the natural sciences or the laws of nature.</note></term> doctrine, and to hide and clothe the wicked arts of the devil, which are <term>abominations<note>original Greek: βδελύγματα ("bdelygmata"); a term used in the Bible for things that are ritually or morally detestable to God.</note></term> to the Lord God. Let us turn away from these, flee them, and curse them, no matter what skillful or artistic appearance they are presented under.

Let us also resist their allurements and the opportunities offered to us, which at first glance seem to flatter and please. Nor should we merely make our bodies into the involuntary slaves and dwellings of **Satan**; instead, we must block every entrance to his attacks—even though he is the <term>most cunning<note>original Greek: τῷ πανουργοτάτῳ ("tō panourgotatō"); literally "the one capable of all villainy," a common epithet for the Devil's deceptive nature.</note></term>—through true faith and holiness of life. We must constantly implore help from the Son of God with burning prayers, and fortify ourselves vigilantly with the living word of God and the help of the Holy Spirit, as if we were diligently stationed on guard duty. In this way, even if that sworn enemy more boldly insults and attacks us while we are hedged in on all sides by this fortification (as if by a most firm rampart), he still may not break through or capture these strong barriers.

<margin>Job 1, 2</margin>
<margin>Psalm 2</margin>
<margin>1 Samuel 28</margin>
<margin>Acts 19</margin>
Whatever afflictions are imposed upon us, let us bravely endure them with an even mind alongside **Job**. Let us by no means rage against God alongside the Gentiles, nor seek out forbidden help as **Saul** did. Nor should we, as curious men like the **Ephesians**, or as wanton ones, anxiously investigate what it neither concerns us to know, nor is permitted, or is less than helpful. Let us not inquire of those from whom God has severely forbidden us to seek answers. Instead, let us insist upon and cling to those paths which the truth of the Gospel points out, turning away from the furious delusions of the devil and his slippery crossroads. We must do this lest, just as **Jannes and Mambres** <note>Also known as Jannes and Jambres; according to tradition and 2 Timothy 3:8, these were the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses.</note> resisted the truth, we too—by kicking back against God’s command—should be found among those on the left hand...

# LETTERS

### 681

Certainly, I have not so much read that book as I have devoured it completely, with I know not what profit and with the greatest pleasure of the mind. I see indeed that it is of such a quality that it will undoubtedly transmit your name to posterity with immortal glory. Oh, happy **Cleves** <note>original: "Cliuiam"; the Duchy of Cleves, where Weyer served as physician to the Duke.</note>, which possesses such heroes of literature; happier still, which nourishes them with ample stipends and increases their fortunes as they most deserve, as is fitting; and happiest of all, over which a Prince presides who is not only learned, pious, and talented, but also favors learning, true piety, and noble and fortunately-born geniuses wonderfully and, as they say, **with both thumbs** <note>original: "utroque pollice"; a Roman idiom meaning to give one's full and enthusiastic approval, derived from the gesture of spectators at gladiatorial games.</note>. ...dead frogs, lizards (which he had collected from the fields for this purpose), and slugs fell into the pit. He eventually ensured that the whole tragicomedy vanished into smoke; indeed, it was a narrow escape for the trickster, who, along with his trifles, was nearly pelted with rotten eggs by the boys and with distaffs <note>A "colus" or distaff was a tool used in spinning wool; being attacked with one was a sign of public humiliation, particularly by women.</note> by the women. But enough and more than enough about these things. Commend me to your truly most noble Prince <note>Referring to Weyer's patron, William V, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg.</note>, and may you forever fare well in our sole Savior. Written in great haste, on the third day before the Kalends of July <note>June 29th</note>, in the year 1563.

->The greatest lover of your name,<-
->A. H. H. A. E.<-

# OF LEARNED MEN

...two **friars** of the same order in this city, openly in the name of a thousand demons, stirred up a diabolical tragedy, the most terrible of all, the history of which I believe you have received. A classical reference to the god of fire, meaning the women were executed by burning at the stake.</note>. 

But even this severity did not bring the cure that was expected. The present disaster among the virgins of the same convent of Kentrop <note>original: "Kenterpen." Furthermore, your book <note>Referring to Weyer’s famous work "De praestigiis daemonum" (On the Illusions of Demons).</note> expresses in a wonderful way the nature, character, skill, care, zeal, and rage of Satan, with which that "craftsman of a thousand arts" <note>original: "mille artifex." A traditional epithet for the Devil emphasizing his many ways of deceiving humans.</note>, deceitful and powerful, rages against the unbelieving; he mocks their vision with various tricks, just as their sins deserve.

For all our possessed ones <term>energumeni: individuals believed to be inhabited or tormented by evil spirits</term>, fifteen in number, have now been freed by the grace of Christ—not by exorcisms or external ceremonies of the elements <note>Gall refers here to the use of physical objects like holy water, salt, or incense in traditional Catholic exorcism rites, which he, as a Protestant preacher, rejects in favor of prayer.</note>, but by the power of faith in the Holy Spirit, through faithful instruction in the Word of God, and through constant prayer and fasting, which we used diligently as the best means of true conversion to God. 

To this was added the most manifest experience of the vanity of incantations, which you also urge in your book with very weighty arguments and, in my judgment, the most certain demonstrations, however much they may seem to disagree with the common opinion of the ancients. When, by the grace of God, she had understood the vanity of diabolical deceptions and looked upon them with open eyes, she easily left behind the smoke of lies and was converted to the light of truth. I will say in one word that I have learned enough from experience that a good part of incantations are mere dreams <note>original: "insomnia." In this medical and theological context, it refers to illusions or hallucinations experienced while the mind is in a dream-like or altered state.</note>. Anyone who has at least looked more deeply into the doctrine of dreams will recognize this more clearly. It is proven from **Aristotle**, **Hippocrates**, **Galen**, and other philosophers—indeed, it is established by daily experience—that dreaming is natural in both man and beasts, and that visions mostly dwell within the <term>imagination: the faculty of the mind that forms mental images of things not present to the senses (Latin: phantasia)</term>. This is experienced above all others by the blind, the sleeping, the melancholic, the <term>frenetic: those suffering from "phrenitis," an acute fever or mental disturbance believed to affect the brain</term>, and others who are impaired in their common sense and mind. 

But if we look into the **Sacred Scriptures** regarding dreams, we will find that dreams have also very often been sent supernaturally <note>original: "praeter naturam" — literally "beyond nature."</note>, and this either through a good spirit or an evil one, sometimes obscurely, sometimes more clearly. And sometimes in these dreams, such manifest visions, images, and specters are presented that even a holy man would swear...

# DOCTORS
<note>original: "DOCTORVM." Likely a section header indicating the opinions of learned men or teachers of the church.</note>

...that all things were acted out so visibly, bodily, and in truth. <note>Gall is likely concluding a point about how true divine miracles or appearances are physically real, unlike demonic illusions.</note> Pharaoh, and his cupbearer, and his baker—as well as Nebuchadnezzar the king of the Babylonians—received forms of future things proposed by God more obscurely and outside the natural order, with Joseph and Daniel acting as their interpreters. However, Jeremiah saw more evident forms and appearances, to whom a boiling pot was shown turned toward the North, along with many other things. Likewise, Ezekiel, and the impious Belshazzar, the successor of Nebuchadnezzar, while he perceived the joints of a writing hand upon the wall. 

I omit the dreams and visions of the saints in the New Testament: of Joseph the husband of the Virgin Mary, of Peter, Paul, and John, of the wife of Pilate, and of others. Furthermore, the <term>evil spirit</term> <note>original: "cacodæmon." From the Greek for "bad spirit."</note> imitates God like an ape among his own slaves; this is abundantly testified not only by the daily examples of our **Witches** <note>original: "Lamiarum." A term used for child-snatching demons in antiquity, but in the 16th century, it specifically meant "witches."</note>, but also by the monuments of the ancient heathens. Did not Satan once deliver his oracles in those places where men stayed overnight to obtain dreams and visions? Such were the places of Amphiaraus, Amphilochus, Trophonius, and Aesculapius. Indeed, in those places, the malignant spirit showed medicines and remedies to the sleepers by which the sick might be helped, and at the same time, he gave answers concerning other business. 

And for the purpose of obtaining dreams and visions of this kind, certain choices of food, and sleeping apart, and specific pure and chaste days were commanded to those seeking answers. The **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras.</note> abstained from beans, for the reason that they produce turbulent dreams. These things and similar ones, my Lord Weyer, whoever considers and understands them exactly, will very easily judge the vanity of the witches’ arts and will approve of your judgment. For Satan remains always like himself; and those illusions and maddenings which he once worked among the infidels, he still practices even now: namely, selling perpetual smoke and the most vain shadows—you might rightly call them dreams—in place of the truth. You have, briefly, my Lord Weyer, my opinion.

### THE JUDGMENT OF LORD BALDWIN RONSSE, 
->*physician, most celebrated for his learning and the practice of his art.*<-

Our friend <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568) was a famous printer in Basel who published the works of many great thinkers, including Weyer.</note> Oporinus, a man born to assist scholarly studies, sent to me at the recent <term>Frankfurt Fair</term> <note>The Frankfurt Book Fair was the primary international market for books and intellectual exchange in the 16th century.</note> a fragment of your work (for I suspect you had not yet placed the final finishing touches upon it) regarding *The Deceptions of Demons*. For although twenty years ago Jacob Savage, a physician of Antwerp, shared a book on the same subject with me while I was still a young man—which he had decided to commit to the printing press had not an unexpected death seized the man—that book did not, however, seem to be of the sort that could uproot an opinion already deeply planted. For even if he declared certain things to be ravings by using certain physical demonstrations, he nevertheless conceded many points which you refute most sharply and with the greatest reason. Nor did he (to speak with the good grace of a man who was otherwise very learned) rely so heavily upon the testimony of Holy Scripture...

## THE JUDGMENT OF LORD JOHANNES EWICH, PHYSICIAN,
### *both most learned and excellent.*

I can hardly explain in words, Weyer, how much pleasure I have derived from your books on *The Deceptions of Demons*, <note>original: "ὦ ἀγαθῶν πατρὸς ἰατρῶν ὦ ἡδονὴ πολυϰοτάτη" — "O most sweet delight of a good father of physicians!" A poetic Greek greeting acknowledging Weyer's skill and perhaps his medical lineage.</note> **O sweet delight of a good father of physicians**. For I see in them a singular prudence, solid judgment, an abundance of necessary facts, a wonderful order, and an incredible diligence. Finally, I see a piety of soul (let all suspicion of flattery be absent) and a purity of the Christian religion, as well as an unbroken courage in defending it everywhere against all the insults of impious men and the frauds of demons. Furthermore, I have found in those books more than enough of what I have often thought to myself, and even what I have uniquely desired and expected. That which I sought is chiefly this: what should be thought concerning the <term>witches</term> <note>original: "Lamiae." This term refers to the legendary child-eating demons of antiquity, used here to describe women accused of witchcraft.</note> (as they call them) of our time; what their vain incantations can [actually] effect; and finally, whether their punishment should be extended even unto death. These three things I wish were as correctly understood and believed by everyone today as they are mostly...

L E T T E R S.

...and rashly believed by both the unlearned and the learned alike. Indeed, I am almost ashamed of our current age, because it has been numbed by such a great lethargy <note>original: "veterno" — literally a "sleepy sickness" or senile sluggishness; here used to describe an intellectual or spiritual stupor.</note> that it has not more diligently investigated matters so useful and necessary, nor brought them into the light sooner. For almost all, both **Physicians** as well as **Legal Experts** and **Theologians** (whose greatest interest it should have been to know these things <term>perfectly</term> <note>original: "ad unguem" — literally "to the fingernail," a Roman idiom referring to a sculptor checking the smoothness of a joint with their nail; meaning to know something with absolute precision.</note>) being content with the custom of their ancestors, have lent too ready an ear to fables. They have pronounced judgment concerning the life and death of many too rashly, if not to say unjustly.

But when I consider that the same thing is observed today—and was before our time—regarding those who were judged **heretics** (namely, because they disagreed with the Roman church in the interpretation of certain articles of doctrine or the use of ceremonies, without any sedition), whose minds were nevertheless devoted to God and whose lives were blameless, even by the testimony of their adversaries: it seems less surprising that in this cause of **Witches** <note>original: "Lamiarum." In this period, "lamiae" referred to sorceresses or witches believed to harm children or cause illness.</note>, which has always been full of darkness and the mockeries of **demons**, they are blind, and in their blindness they often strike the innocent.

Indeed, from the time when, with the maturity of age along with some degree of education and experience, I began to look upon human affairs, I have always been accustomed to greatly deplore the ignorance of men. For that seemed to me to be the cause of all the evil that rages so multifariously in our lives. And although, while being myself still very ignorant, I have by the grace of God recognized and wept over this, I was nonetheless hindered by the common blindness in the present matter; I could not yet lift my eyes higher and look upon the truth itself.

Therefore, since I knew well the smallness of my own intellect, I had decided neither to deny nor to assert anything. But now, confirmed by your judgment, I seem to see the light, and I sufficiently understand both where I must go and where I must stop. And I give thanks to the immortal God that by your work He has revealed those things to us which [are necessary] to be known not only by the learned and those with the title of doctor, but even by all men, and most especially by **Christians**...

# OF DOCTORS

...are necessary. Therefore, I shall hereafter place no trust in those who think they must cling so tightly to every current custom that they refuse to hear, investigate, or accept a modestly proposed opinion from other men, however pious and learned they may be. Such people differ greatly from the counsel of that famous prince <note>A reference to a character from Homeric epic, likely Nestor, who valued wisdom from any source.</note> who, when necessity demanded it, said: <unclear>“Whoever speaks blameless counsel, whether he be young or old, it would be better for me.”</unclear> <note>original Greek: ὃς δ' αὖτ' ἀμάμονα μῆτιν ἐνίσπει, ἢ νιὸς εἰ παλαιὸς, ἐμοὶ δέ κε κερδίοιν εἴη.</note> For since, as I have said, the origin and fountain of every evil arises from ignorance—and this ignorance stems first from sin, and sin further derives its beginning from the devil (who is truly the father of darkness, falsehood, and confusion)—then wisdom and knowledge must deservedly be seen as the cause of all good. Indeed, it is these that give birth to and preserve light, truth, and order in our whole life and in all our actions.

Away then with all stubbornness and ill-temper! Let there be a free faculty for hearing, as well as for speaking and writing—provided, however, that the labor of both looks toward the remarkable benefit of the **Commonwealth** <note>original: "utriusque Reip." — literally "of both Republics," referring to both the Church and the State.</note> and serves excellently to propagate the kingdom of Christ our Savior, while undermining the tyranny of the devil and the Antichrist.

Farewell, most illustrious Weyer, our age's very own Hercules against monstrous opinions. Farewell, I say; and continue to be what you have so fortunately and gloriously begun: <unclear>“A great joy to your father and to her who bore you, and to all the people; a grief to your enemies, and a sorrow to the evil demons themselves.”</unclear> <note>original Greek: πατρί τε τῷ μέγα χάρμα τελῇί τε, πάνti τε δήμῳ, δυσμενέσιν μὲν πῆμα, κακοῖς δ' ἄχα δαίμοσι αὐτοῖς.</note>

At Duisburg, in the year 1563, on the very Calends of June <note>June 1st.</note>.

# LETTERS

...are snatched to the flame, there was a conversation between us: your excellence truly and seriously judged that great prudence must be used in judging this wrongdoing <note>original: "maleficio"; here referring specifically to the crime of witchcraft or harmful magic.</note>, lest we rashly and lightly determine anything in inflicting punishments. This is especially true since the civil laws command us to be more inclined toward leniency, so that even in more serious punishments we maintain a regard for kindness <note>Borcholt cites specific Roman laws here: *l. respiciendum* and *l. absentem* from the section *de poenis* (on punishments) in the Digest of Justinian.</note>. Indeed, it is clear from this how many things in this business of wrongdoing are now handled confusedly and turbulently, based solely on sinister, fanatical, and pestilential suspicion. Specifically, that laudable distinction between profane or infamous mages, **Lamiæ** <note>original: "Lamias"; a term for female witches or sorceresses often portrayed in folklore as baby-stealing demons.</note>, and **poisoners**—who harm beasts and humans with poison, whether it is drunk, smeared, or placed where it might infect the ground, and are therefore deservedly struck by the sword under the **Cornelian Law** <note>The *Lex Cornelia de sicariis et veneficis*, an ancient Roman law against assassins and poisoners.</note>—has become blurred. Up to now, these cases have been handled and decided with great confusion.

However, so that this difference—from which punishment is assigned according to the quality of the crime—might become better known to your excellence, I promised I would send you the book by the most illustrious man, Doctor **Johann Weyer**. Written some years ago, his work *On the Deceptions of Demons, Incantations, and Poisonings* <note>original: "de Praestigijs daemonum, incantationibus ac ueneficijs"; Weyer’s landmark 1563 book arguing against the persecution of witches.</note> is written so ingeniously, acutely, and learnedly that it is held in the highest possible regard <note>original: "numinis loco"; literally "in the place of a deity," a hyperbolic expression for something of ultimate authority.</note> by all the most learned men in Burgundy and the whole of the Low Countries.

Indeed, whenever I remember the most excellent legal consultant of this age, **Jacques Cujas** <note>A famous French legal humanist known for applying historical methods to Roman law.</note>—who was formerly my teacher at Bourges in France, and whom I must respect in every way (and I remember him often)—I am compelled to confess along with him that I have read no book with greater pleasure. He and I agree that our legal **Glossators** <note>Medieval scholars who wrote explanatory notes (glosses) on Roman law; Borcholt suggests they were too literal or superstitious compared to Weyer.</note>, if compared without bias to this writer, have left us nothing but trifles and fables whenever they undertook to handle this business. Since I am well aware that your excellence possesses the finest judgment, I ask that however much time...

# DOCTORAL LETTERS

...that you might steal some time from public business to spend on reading this present book. And write back to me when you have the opportunity your opinion of this book, which is of great weight to me. If indeed, after reading through this entire book, you find anything rightly and justly said regarding the proposed question about **witches** or **sorceresses** <note>original: "sagis uel lamijs"</note> not being so indiscriminately and cruelly burned—a matter now handled with such great contention in the Republic—then embrace that, and as much as you can, defend innocent blood. And would that all Princes bore such a mind in this bloody business as the most Illustrious Prince, most learned in experience and letters, **William**, Duke of Jülich, Cleves, and Berg: whose opinion on **Witches**, worthy of a princely man, is annexed in the Preface of the book <note>Duke William V (the Rich) was Johann Weyer's patron and shared his skeptical, more humane view toward witch trials.</note>. I also do not fear, since you are (as Cicero says of Cato) a **great glutton for books** <note>original: "librorum helluo maximus"; a playful academic compliment for a voracious reader.</note>, that any boredom will come to you in reading; for the book is so stuffed with histories and pleasant stories that I would dare to affirm hardly any more pleasant book exists. Farewell. Given at the castle of Sturwolt, the 7th day of August, the year [15]64.

->THE END<-

### From the Satire of the excellent Scottish poet GEORGE BUCHANAN,
### which he titled "The Franciscans."
<note>George Buchanan (1506–1582) was a famous Scottish humanist whose poem *Franciscanus* was a biting satire against the Franciscan order, accusing them of hypocrisy and corruption.</note>

> *Although our sect is built especially upon these columns,*
> *Nevertheless not a few, nor small [tasks] remain:*
> *But they are nearly already well-known, and need neither our art*
> *Nor our voice: but each person hands them to themselves, and learns*
> *Them by use; such as how to arrange marriage chambers,*
> *Or how to dissolve poorly joined marriage-torches* <note>original: "taedas"; torches were used in Roman wedding processions, here signifying the marriage contract itself.</note> *by making excuses,*
> *Or where concord has been broken because a lover was caught...*

...to win pardon for a wife from a harsh husband.
Once, for our fathers, there was a most fertile harvest
In inventing nocturnal ghosts <note>original: "lemures"</note> and wandering spirits <note>original: "Manes"</note>,
Restraining them with holy water and magical whispers.
Now it is all cold: for the sharp-nosed youth <note>original: "nasuta iuuentus"; a metaphor for sophisticated or skeptical young men of the new generation.</note>
Laughs at the overly-credulous hearts of their dull grandfathers;
Nor do they believe anything unless you prove it with the testimony of Scripture,
Even though the Sorbonne <term>Sorbonne: The prestigious faculty of theology at the University of Paris, often viewed by humanists as a bastion of old-fashioned, rigid orthodoxy.</term>, sworn with great seals,
Affirms these fictions. But in better years,
This engine used to break the closed doors of the bedchamber,
It changed the tablets of a will; and the husband
Would travel abroad to Rome or Jerusalem, while boredom
Seized the adulterer in a bed now permitted to him.
But when a wealthy ghost, forgetting his own interest,
Had bequeathed only a few Masses for his funeral,
And preferred upon departing to leave his goods to his own children
Rather than to "grease our cabbages" <note>An idiomatic way of saying "to enrich our kitchen" or "fill our coffers."</note>,
Our Elders were not accustomed to let such an outrage pass unpunished.
This resentment gave weapons to the noble brothers
By the waters of the Loire <note>original: "Ligeris"</note>, where Orleans <note>original: "Aurelia"</note>,
Rich in fields and rich in wine <note>original: "Iacchi"; Iacchus is a name for the god of wine.</note>,
Shows her beautiful towers from afar.
And if their cautious piety had not been somewhat lacking while preparing the fraud,
And had they not been caught among so many watchful Arguses <note>Argus Panoptes was a hundred-eyed giant in Greek myth; here it refers to vigilant investigators who saw through the monks' trickery.</note>,
It would have brought honor and dignity to our sect.
Indeed, we often cause ourselves many evils, such as when
One order arms itself to the detriment of another:
Bern <note>original: "Berna"</note> had already fashioned a "new Francis" <note>Referring to St. Francis of Assisi, founder of the order.</note> for itself,
And already the clear stigmata <term>Stigmata: Bodily marks, scars, or sensations of pain in locations corresponding to the crucifixion wounds of Jesus Christ.</term>
Of the feet and the pierced hands were visible;
Had not a neighbor’s envy, grieving at their increasing profit,
Exposed the manufactured mockery with great laughter,
And with no light loss. Greater is the wisdom
Of that Italian shore, which, silently concealing the lies
Of Catherine of Siena's wounds, weighs them for profit,
And by these arts draws "barbarian gold" <note>Likely a reference to the wealth brought to Italy by foreign pilgrims and devotees.</note> to itself.

*But however, I would not wish miracles to be rashly invented in this age,*
*Except among mountain-dwellers and thick-headed*
*Shepherds: nor is it safe now to despise even the bakers <note>original: "piftores" (pistores). In this context, Buchanan is listing "common" or "simple" professions easily fooled by superstition.</note>;*
*When wisdom even migrates into the lonely woods,*
*Who would have thought that the stiff Scots, under the peak of a frozen sky,*
*Had either a mind, or ears, or eyes?*
*And yet that clever Langius, a hunter of old women,*
*When the foul place favored the error, and the blind night was kind,*
*Could not hide the mockeries of his "pious fraud." <note>original: "piæ ludibria fraudis"; a term for a deception carried out with supposedly good or religious intentions.</note>*
*The field was widely uncultivated; no flowers of the garden*
*Smile there, no harvest in the fields, no leaves on the trees,*
*Scarcely is the sterile sand clothed with dry tamarisks:*
*And rare are the tracks of cattle in those lonely lands;*
*The neighbors call it the wilderness. There, beneath the rocky*
*Caves, Vulcanian seeds <note>original: "Vulcania semina"; a poetic way of describing volcanic or geothermal activity, referencing Vulcan, the god of fire.</note> cover the black crags:*
*Fires conceived everywhere in sulfurous veins*
*Roll a smoke-filled cloud, and with pitchy vapor*
*The ground always gasps; and the raging flame, shut in*
*Blind caverns, while struggling to penetrate into the air,*
*Splits vents <note>original: "spiracula"; openings or blowholes in the earth.</note> everywhere across the fields, and opens the earth with a huge gap.*
*A foul odor, a dismal appearance, and the face of the place:*
*There, Langius [claimed] that souls were often tortured; there*
*He often heard them complain, and draw out long voices into weeping—*
*Or rather, he wanted it to be believed he heard them frequently—*
*And he spoke of frolicking evil spirits <term>Cacodaemons: From the Greek "kakodaimon," meaning an evil spirit or demon, as opposed to a "good" spirit.</term>, and along the sands*
*How they drew the long trails of their tails in winding paths.*
*Often too (whenever he approached the caves while fasting),*
*He seemed to himself to breathe in the stench of an infernal kitchen.*
*When he had already soaked the dull ears of the common folk with these rumors,*
*He prepares an Exorcism: a huge circle*
*Is drawn, and within this, smaller ones in a shorter space:*
*In the middle stood a stake, and next to it a basin...*

[The vessel was] full of water, but to which the priest had added ash and salt with much muttering and heavy, panting breaths. <note>Traditional rituals for exorcism or the blessing of salt and water often involved specific prayers and physical gestures like breathing upon the elements.</note> Once the scene was prepared with this equipment, Father Langius himself, looking venerable in his sacred robes, sprinkles everything around with the spray from his bristly scepter <term>aspergillum|a liturgical brush or perforated metal orb used for sprinkling holy water</term>. Churning out convoluted, tongue-twisting words in a headlong rush, he adjures the heavens, the lands, and the waves, along with the trembling Acherontian <note>original: "Acherontia"; referring to Acheron, a river in the underworld, used here to mean the realm of the dead.</note> kingdoms in their deepest caverns.

And now night had arrived, a witness to the secret rite; already the people from neighboring fields had gathered—mothers and men, boys and unwed girls. They were eager to see what would come of such great promises, had he not—fearing eyes and ears might witness his secret—ordered the "profane" <note>In a religious context, "profani" refers to the uninitiated or those not ritually pure enough to witness a mystery.</note> to keep their distance with a booming voice. He also excluded anyone who had not that day clearly whispered all their crimes into his ear, to be kept silent. <note>This refers to the requirement of auricular confession before participating in the rite, which Buchanan suggests is a tool for control.</note>

He claimed this was lest the trembling spirits flee the company of laypeople, or lest a hungry Evil Spirit <term>Cacodæmon|from the Greek 'kakodaimon,' a malevolent spirit or demon</term>, gaping for prey, should seize and tear the limbs of the wicked with its claws. The Peasant <term>Rusticus|a common term for a simple countryman or farmer</term> himself is led to a stake like a sacrificial victim. Though he knew it was all a sham, he was as stunned with terror as if he were emerging from the Stygian <note>original: "Stygia"; relating to the Styx, the river of the underworld.</note> depths to see Cerberus <note>The three-headed hound of Hades.</note> devouring naked ghosts.

Perhaps it was a fear rooted in his mind since childhood—those "old wives' tales" that bring such dread to weeping children—or perhaps it was the location, dark with smoke and a blinding mist, which looked terrifyingly like a kitchen in Hell. Everything else was performed in secret after the common folk had been sent away. Yet groans could still be heard, along with voices threatening demons and mingled prayers; sometimes answers were heard though no one had asked a question. Langius would now lift his gaze to the heavens, now fix it upon the ground, now beat his breast, and sprinkle the "temple" <note>Here referring to the makeshift ritual space in the wilderness.</note> with holy water,

Buchanan highlights the psychological manipulation used by the clergy, blending folk superstition with religious performance.</summary>

Until the bird that heralds the light [the rooster] warned the ghosts to withdraw and hide themselves away once more in their old nests. Then, having left the church, Langius began to recount things both speakable and unspeakable: the punishments of the shades, the swift power of the purifying flame <note>A reference to the fires of Purgatory.</note>, how many pots the executioner-demons <term>Cacodæmones|from the Greek 'kakodaimon', meaning an evil spirit or malevolent demon</term> brought forth, how many souls they skewered on spits, how many shades they plunged into frozen waves, and by how many Masses the punishment of each soul might be lightened—just as if he had lived his life as a citizen of the Stygian underworld <note>original: "Stygio... Auerno"; referring to the River Styx and Lake Avernus, classical literary terms for the realm of the dead.</note>.

He detailed everything in due order, and the man did not lack a gullible crowd; the revived glory of the embers of Purgatory grew ever greater, much to the indignation of Luther <note>Martin Luther (1483–1546), the primary figure of the Protestant Reformation, who attacked the sale of indulgences and the doctrine of Purgatory.</note>. And it would have continued to grow, had not that misshapen rustic companion—alas, the betrayer of the Exorcism!—revealed all the lies of that "silent" rite, whether seized by fear, bribed by a price, or overcome by wine.

From that moment, the hope of profit began to ebb and slip away, while the glory of the all-too-vibrant truth began to rise. Therefore, I warn you: henceforth be sparing in your invention of dreams, nighttime ghosts, and miracles—unless, perhaps, they are said to take place among the distant Spaniards <note>original: "Iberos"</note>, the Americans, the Ethiopians, or under the burning equator, where the Nile hides its source in unknown sands; from where no witness will come to refute your claims.

Your clever ingenuity might perhaps evade external enemies, but no amount of caution can guard against a plague born within one's own guts, clinging to the very veins of men. If the provident power of God had not looked upon our ancestors in times past, the "Rope-bearing Order" <term>Funiger ordo|A satirical name for the Franciscans, derived from the knotted rope cord (funiculus) they wore as a belt.</term> would long ago have perished miserably, betrayed by its own followers. If any of the brothers, persuaded by a demon, should dare to reveal to the common people our hidden mysteries, our secret frauds, the arcana of the nighttime rites, the embezzled funds <note>original: "negatum depositum"; literally a "denied deposit," referring to property or money held in trust that the friars kept for themselves despite their vow of poverty.</note>, or the girls murdered after unspeakable lusts...

It concludes with a dark list of the crimes the friars fear will be revealed by whistleblowers, including financial fraud and murder.</summary>
